events.title: Nine Korean startups vie for a spot in Disrupt 2027’s Startup Battlefield 200 competition
events.summary: TechCrunch’s yearly Startup Battlefield 200 competition sees hundreds of companies from across the world trying every year to get a chance to pitch in front of VCs and the international tech community at the Disrupt conference. This week, nine early-stage South Korean startups pitched at DETO 2026 , a technology conference in Seoul, to earn a spot in next year’s Startup Battlefield 200. The startups work across the deep tech sector, including healthcare, fintech, energy, semiconductors, and AI. All nine startups are looking to enter the U.S. market as part of the broader international expansion plans. Voinosis, which develops AI to detect changes in brain health through voice analysis, won the competition. The other eight startups are listed below in alphabetical order. Voinosis is developing an AI tool that analyzes speech patterns such as pitch, pauses, rhythm and response times to detect changes linked to brain health. Each voice check takes less than five minutes. The company says its technology has been tested in Greek, Japanese and English, and its product doesn’t require separate training for each language. In a clinical study involving 146 participants, the startup claims its tech achieved 88% accuracy in screening for potential cognitive issues. Voinosis targets hospitals, senior living facilities, insurers and individual consumers. It also plans to link voice checks with cognitive training, assessments, and treatment provided by healthcare professionals. The startup was founded by Grace Shin, who spent more than 25 years as an otologic surgeon. The startup is currently raising a Series A round and has already secured a South Korean pharmaceutical company as a strategic investor. Awesome Lab, based in Seoul, makes ThermoFlux, a heating system that uses water electrolysis and ionization to generate heat. The system can manage heat production for buildings, water supply, and industrial processes. The company says its technology can reduce energy consumption and carbon emissions. For its international expansion, Awesome Lab is taking a different approach in each market. In the U.S., it plans to supply core OEM modules, and work with boiler, water heater and HVAC companies on product development. Crosshub helps travelers and international visitors verify their identities and set up payment methods abroad. Its platform, IDBlock, combines identity verification and payment services using Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) and zero-knowledge proof. The company says its platform helps users prove their identity across borders without sharing unnecessary personal information. Crosshub is also integrating this technology with payment systems to improve access to financial services for travelers. DeepFusion AI has developed a 4D radar-based imaging system with additional sensors for autonomous mobility, robotaxi, maritime surveillance, and defense applications. The system combines RF sensors with radar and lidar to detect objects, movement, or distance without a direct line of sight. All sensors are supposedly packed into a single, customizable unit. EFLOW develops special motors that can produce more torque, or rotational force, while taking up less space for use in robots, drones, satellites, and other mobility applications. The startup also develops actuators that control how robotic joints move. Otition Medical makes two medical devices: one specializes in measuring body temperature, while another can capture ear canal images and analyze the eardrum. The company says its AI was trained on about 55,000 images of eardrums, and the device has received medical certification in South Korea. Riibotics says it can deploy robots into warehouses within a day. Riibotics wants to reduce deployment costs for warehouses by streamlining setup, which includes infrastructure setup, warehouse mapping, system integration through custom middleware, task programming, and safety checks. Ternell, a semiconductor startup based in Ulsan, is developing a new type of memory to help AI chips use less power. Unlike conventional two-state memory, Ternell’s T-SRAM system adds a third state for more efficient data storage. Founded in 2019 by KyungRok Kim, a former Samsung Electronics engineer, Ternell reports that tests with 28-nanometer chips showed a 33% to 102% increase in memory capacity per area, and a 55% to 71% reduction in energy needed to access data, compared with conventional SRAM. Testbank is a Korean edtech startup developing Solve, an app that converts printed study materials, such as workbooks and test-prep books, into interactive digital versions. The startup uses AI to identify question and answer spaces in publishers’ PDF files while preserving the original layout. events.title: I paid my friend's 12-year-old to play with my little ones while I did housework. For months, it was a lifeline.
events.summary: Solo parenting was tough: My husband couldn't step back from work, and we couldn't afford a babysitter. So I hired my friend's son as a mother's helper of sorts. Cara Howlett During the pandemic, I was home alone with my young kids all of the time. It was challenging. So, I made an arrangement with my friend and her 12-year-old son: I'd pay him to entertain my kids. The kids loved their new friend, he made money, and I was able to get things done while they played. Parenting through a pandemic was not part of my plan. In mid-March 2020, our province shut down all schools, and life as we knew it. My 5-year-old son had just started a new preschool , but now he'd be spending all his time at home with his 2-year-old sister and me. Between all of the restrictions, we spent most days trapped inside our townhouse. I was no stranger to solo parenting , but pre-pandemic I had my methods to keep sane — attend a local Moms & Tots group, visit the playground, see our friends for playdates, attend evening book club, use a drop-off program designed for moms to spend time together without kids, and bring the kids to storytime at the library. I was busy and social, and we were active in our community. These connections made motherhood feel slightly easier. But in the blink of an eye, all of the threads of connection had been severed. Every day I was by myself with the kids. Just get through today," I would tell myself. "Just one day at a time." I managed, I struggled, and it was one of the most difficult seasons of my life. By summer, I was desperate for a solution. I turned to my friend and her 12-year-old son for help My kids benefited from having another kid to entertain them while I got chores done. Cara Howlett My husband is the primary earner in our home, and his fledgling business did not allow him to be home more often to help. Hiring a babysitter was also out of the question as we could not afford it. So to get the help I needed, I had to think outside the box. My friend homeschooled her kids pre-pandemic, and her eldest was 12. Since he was not required to do online school with his classmates all day like the public schoolers in our town, he had some free time. I asked his mom if he might be willing to come and play with my kids for a few hours a couple of times a week. She agreed, and he was keen. She would drop him off at our house, and he would play trains with my son, read books to my daughter, and entertain the kids with whatever they wanted to do for the afternoon. It was great. While they played, I kept an eye and an ear on their activities. I was still responsible for everything parenting-related — changing diapers, dealing with tantrums, breaking up sharing-related arguments between the kids, and feeding them — but my friend's son was in charge of the fun. And while he was at our home, I was able to clean the bathrooms, vacuum the carpets, get some administrative work done, and have a few minutes to myself. Although this wasn't a complete break from the kids, it was a helpful reprieve, and I could catch my breath. Whenever I dropped him back off at his house, I'd hand him about $15, or about $5 an hour, too. The arrangement felt like a win-win for all of us It was nice for my kids to have time without me. Cara Howlett My kids loved having their "big-kid friend" come over, and they'd often ask when he'd be hanging out with them next. In the end, this arrangement worked for everyone. We were a one-income family, even before the pandemic, and a 12-year-old with extra money in his pocket was one happy pre-teen. The kids had a break from Mom, and Mom had a chance to get things done. Plus, I'm sure my friend appreciated seeing her son develop a sense of responsibility and being able to spend some time outside his house. The arrangement ended after about 10 months, as life slowly went back to normal and I regained my footing. However, I still think it's a great arrangement for stay-at-home parents on a budget who have young children. I would do it again in a heartbeat. And as my son approaches his pre-teen years, I wonder if he might be a mother's helper one day, creating a village for another family. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is still very much a car guy
events.summary: A TikToker said he met Sam Altman during a California car meet. @2023coyote50 on TikTok, Jeff Chiu/AP A TikToker and his buddies stopped at a gas station during a chill car meetup. Then, "a bunch of cars I've never seen" joined, he told Business Insider. Moments later, Sam Altman was walking around the vehicles. Sam Altman : Silicon Valley leader, Elon Musk rival , and bona fide gearhead . On Sunday, a TikToker posted a video showing a large block of sports and exotic cars — from Ford Mustangs and an Acura NSX to a Pagani Utopia and a Koenigsegg Regera — parked on the side of a winding road. And a few feet away from a silver Lexus LFA stood the OpenAI CEO. The gathering was unplanned, the TikToker, Miguel Godinez, told Business Insider. He and eight friends had taken their sports cars for a drive through the canyon near Lake Berryessa, just Northeast of Napa, California, when they pulled over at a gas station. Then, he said, "a bunch of cars I've never seen" joined. "We talked for a minute, and he was super nice and chill," Godinez, whose channel posts mainly sports car content, said about Altman. "I felt like he was a normal person driving his car just like us, with the same hobbies." Altman and OpenAI didn't respond to a request for comment. (They also didn't tell us which car Altman thought was the coolest). This isn't the first time we've seen Altman with the Regera, which can cost up to $4.6 million. In April 2024, an onlooker took a video of the exotic car driving through city streets in Napa, California. Months later, when he zoomed in on the driver's seat, he spotted Altman behind the wheel . Godinez said he wasn't sure which exotic vehicle Altman was driving. However, the Regera was the same color as the one spotted in 2024, and the exotic car company only made 80 units for the entire world. Or maybe Altman was driving the Utopia, which also only has about 260 siblings in the world. Either way, it's safe to say Altman was driving something pretty fun. And, based on the way he gawked at the Lexus LFA, the TikToks serve as proof that even Silicon Valley's elite can still get a little starstruck at a cool set of wheels. events.summary: The latest warnings come amid rising concerns ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠in Europe about hybrid warfare threats. ⁠More than 1,800 ⁠schools in Italy were sent emails containing bomb threats on Thursday, the government said, a day after some 6,300 schools received similar alerts . Many schools closed immediately after receiving the latest warnings, causing widespread disruption as parents rushed to collect their children. list 1 of 3 Pro-Russian hackers leak Italian foreign minister’s data on dark web list 2 of 3 Who is behind Europe’s suspected hybrid attacks? list 3 of 3 If hackers can take over a supermarket fridge, what else is at risk? Like Wednesday’s emails, the messages were reportedly signed by “Mikhail Andropov”, who presented himself as the “leader of the Vilayat of ⁠⁠⁠⁠Misoginistan”, according to Italy’s Ansa news agency. events.title: Lutnick should ban Chinese memory maker CXMT from U.S., Sen. Cotton says
events.summary: Sen. Tom Cotton is urging the Commerce Department to add Chinese memory maker CXMT to its "Entity List," which would sharply restrict its access to U.S. technology. Cotton, in a letter obtained first by CNBC, warned Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick against allowing the company to grow its global footprint. The company is challenging memory heavyweights Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix — and pushing into HBM, the high-bandwidth memory used in AI chips. Sen. Tom Cotton , R-Ark., is urging the Trump administration to take a harsher stance toward Chinese memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies . "CXMT, one of Communist China's national memory chip champions, poses a growing risk to our economic prosperity and military superiority," Cotton wrote in a letter sent Thursday to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. "The U.S. must take action to prevent CXMT from gaining a stronger foothold in the global market." CXMT is the world's fourth-largest producer of DRAM – or dynamic random access memory – which powers many basic functions of computers and smartphones. Cotton, in a letter first obtained by CNBC, is asking Lutnick to push CXMT onto the department's Bureau of Industry and Security Entity List, which would significantly restrict U.S. firms' ability to do business with the company. "It basically means that U.S. companies are not allowed to do business with that entity-listed company, and that entity-listed company does not get access to U.S. technology," said Kyle Chan, a Brookings Institution fellow who studies China's technology development. DRAM is a "commodity," MS Hwang , research director at Counterpoint, told CNBC, meaning it is made to a global standard and is generally interchangeable from one manufacturer to another. However, with the right production technology, it can also form the building blocks of HBM, or high-bandwidth memory. HBM is an extremely high-demand product that powers AI chips made by Nvidia , Google and Amazon Web Services, which are central to the growth of artificial intelligence giants including Anthropic and OpenAI. It's made by just three main companies: Samsung , SK Hynix and Micron . Those same three companies control the lion's share of the DRAM market, but CXMT has made inroads. The company's share of the DRAM market jumped from 4% to 10% by revenue in a year, from the second quarter of 2025 to the same quarter of 2026, according to Counterpoint using the most recent reporting available. And in July, the company went public and its stock price soared, making it the most valuable company listed in China at the time . While the company's HBM capabilities are nascent, according to Counterpoint, Reuters reported that the company was to begin production of the chips, even though yields are low at just 20% to 30%. That means that the majority of the chips it produces are faulty. CXMT is already on the Pentagon's "1260H" list , which identifies several dozen Chinese companies with ties to Beijing's military. But Chan says that list doesn't come with stringent restrictions for U.S. businesses. "It's not a list that has that much teeth to it, in terms of restrictions to U.S. companies working with Chinese firms on that list," Chan said. The Wall Street Journal reported Aug. 9 that Apple was considering using CXMT's memory in iPhones and Macs in light of the global shortage driven by the AI buildout. Being on the Entity List could change that. "From the U.S. government standpoint, their concern is that working with CXMT would – even as a customer, just buying their products – would help to improve their ability to ramp up memory chip production, and also maybe help China get further down the road towards HBM," Chan said. "It's part of the broader effort to stymie or slow down China's own chip development." Cotton alluded to CXMT's efforts to break into the HBM market in his letter. "[CXMT's] decision to move forward in less than ideal conditions highlights both Communist China's desperation for chips and manufacturing struggles without advanced equipment and knowledge," he wrote. "More can be done to ensure that CXMT is cut off from the financial and technological resources that aid its supply chain and undercut American growth."

events.title: I live rent-free in NYC by pet-sitting full time. I've slept in a car and dealt with cancellations, but it's worth it.
events.summary: The author lives rent-free in NYC by pet sitting. Courtesy of the author I moved to New York to pursue comedy but struggled to afford a comfortable place to live. I discovered pet sitting and started staying in apartments for free in exchange for caring for pets. Now I live rent-free with my boyfriend while pursuing comedy, though the lifestyle has challenges. I moved to New York with a dream, one suitcase, and not that much money. I had just visited a friend there, but something felt different this time. I felt like I belonged. Like the streets were whispering to me, it's time. While I was there, I met up with another friend who had just moved from Dallas . He told me there was an extra room available at the place he had found. I thought, if it's meant to be, it will align. I went back to Texas and decided to take the chance. I wanted to challenge myself, take my comedy to another level, and fine-tune my craft. So I sold my expensive camera, made and sold friendship bracelets, and, with help from my comedian friends, saved enough for a deposit and a couple of months' rent. I made the jump. I was full of excitement and hope for this new chapter , until I actually started living in my new room and realized I had no peace. I looked into pet sitting My room was basically in the kitchen, between the bathroom and living room. My landlord lived with us and worked from the living room, so there was almost always noise around me. On weekends, just when I thought I'd finally get some peace and quiet, I'd hear my other roommate fighting through the wall. The author moved to New York for a comedy career. Courtesy of the author At first, I kept telling myself  it's OK; this is normal in New York. But I was getting more and more stressed, and I didn't have enough money to get another place. Moving back to Texas wasn't a choice because it was gonna look like I'd scammed everyone! "Hi guys, I'm back!! Thank you for funding my two-week New York vacation!" Then I remembered my comedian friend Kirstie had told me about a pet-sitting app and how she was doing it full time in Austin. At first, I didn't even think about doing it full time. I just wanted a getaway. A break. I started pet sitting full time I found a weeklong sit for a beautiful goldendoodle on the Upper West Side . It was honestly the best first sit I could have had. The dog was so sweet and loving, and the apartment was quiet and comfortable. The first couple of days, I just slept a lot. I hadn't realized how exhausted I was. Once I finally felt rested, I started browsing the website and saw how many other sites were available. Then it hit me: Why not just do this full time? It wasn't paid, but it gave me peace, a comfortable place to stay, and cute furry company . The author says cancellations can be stressful. Courtesy of the author So I did it. I moved out of my room, left the furniture for my landlord, and he was kind enough to give me my deposit back. I started booking sits one after another, and for a while everything felt perfect. I had so much more peace and energy to do comedy and be creative again. Cancellations can be stressful Then I had a last-minute cancellation and suddenly had nowhere to stay for three days. On my birthday, it hit me: I am homeless in New York. One of my old roommates helped me out and let me crash in his car. That was when I realized there was another side to this lifestyle. I had to start thinking about cancellations and gap days between sits. I hated asking friends if I could stay with them and always worried about being an inconvenience, so I bought flight passes that let me fly back home cheaply whenever I had a gap longer than a couple of days. That became my backup plan. A couple of months into pet sitting, I met my boyfriend, who is also a comedian. Since he had roommates, he started spending a lot of time with me at the sits. I didn't want him to be a secret, so I added him to my account, and eventually we started doing the sits together full time. My boyfriend and I live rent-free My first winter in New York didn't feel as cold because of him. From one sit to another, everything would change, but he was there by my side. He was the reason the sits started to feel like home. Eventually, he gave up his place and fully joined me in this rent-free lifestyle. The author's boyfriend joined her in pet-sitting. Courtesy of the author It definitely hasn't always been easy. We cared for a dog who almost died after having a bad reaction to a new medication, and my pet-parent instincts kicked in as we helped nurse him back to health. We also had an owner who was supposed to be gone for a week but kept extending the trip until it became almost a month. When we couldn't keep extending the sit, we ended up getting our only one-star review. We've also stayed in homes with anxious owners and multiple cameras, which can make it hard to ever fully relax. Living this way definitely comes with trade-offs. You're constantly moving, finding new gyms, grocery stores, and delis, and trying to build routines around completely different pets and schedules. And because pet sitting is an exchange of services, not a paid job, you still have to find another way to make money while giving the pets the time and attention they need. For someone with a flexible schedule or who works remotely, I think pet sitting can be an amazing way to live for a while. For me, it gave me something I really needed in New York: enough peace, flexibility, and freedom to keep choosing comedy. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
events.summary: Alan Milburn will publish his review next week Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to under a radical overhaul of the welfare system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review. As reported in the Times, , external Alan Milburn's year-long report, to be published on Tuesday, is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits. Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 16 to 24 year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet". He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants. His report is expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of universal credit or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales. Disabled people in Scotland can claim the devolved Adult Disability Payment. Instead, under Milburn's plan, under-25s would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit. Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions. Some claimants would receive less under the plans - although the exact amounts will not be clear until early next year, when the government publishes legislation to implement the changes. People can claim Pip to help them with the additional cost of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions. It is available to those both in and out of work. Of the four million people claiming Pip in England and Wales, around 430,000 are aged between 16 and 24. In his interim report, , external Milburn said survey data found that 19% of young people claiming disability or health benefits were in work. Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers. Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate. Milburn told the Times: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system. "But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances. "I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around." Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets , data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year. Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare changes last year under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer. Meg Hillier, who helped spearhead a backbench rebellion against Starmer's reforms, suggested she and her colleagues were broadly supportive this time around. "What happened last year was a cut was being proposed and none of us could explain to people what would happen to them," the Labour MP told the BBC. "Milburn has done some very good work on this so I'm giving him a fair wind," she added. But Bell Ribeiro-Addy, one of the Labour backbenchers who revolted last year, said she was "not sure" she could vote to cut the benefit entitlement of existing claimants. "I don't think you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them get into work," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. Tom Ashforth, a 19-year-old student at Sheffield Hallam University, receives both components of Pip at the higher rate. He said the financial support helps him manage additional expenses linked to his visual impairment, including prescriptions, mobility aids and accessible learning resources. "If I were to lose it, I would struggle to afford essential things," he said. Student Tom said he relies on the money he gets from Pip to support him through his time at university He said he believes decisions over disability benefits should be made on a case-by-case basis, rather than according to age. "You cannot assume that everyone under the age of 25 is in the same position," he said. In his Times interview, Milburn acknowledged that changing the rules for existing claimants would be "difficult politically" but stressed it was necessary. Disability groups have welcomed extra employment support, but expressed concern that disabled young people could lose out.

events.title: UAE billionaires optimistic about foreign investment despite eight months of war
events.summary: UAE officials and billionaires had a unified message to foreign investors today: After eight months of conflict, the country has emerged as an even more attractive destination for global capital. They can be forgiven for talking up their own book, but foreign investors seem bullish too. At the Bloomberg Invest Dubai conference on Thursday, Blackstone executives said the firm had deployed more capital in the region over the past year than ever before, and opened a DIFC office for its growing private wealth business. Meanwhile, PIMCO highlighted opportunities to finance infrastructure projects. UAE Investment Minister Mohamed Hassan Alsuwaidi said the country plans to draw more foreign capital into energy, industry, infrastructure, AI, and logistics. He also pointed to shortages of offices and warehouses as opportunities. Real estate has gone through multiple boom-and-bust cycles over the past two decades, but when viewed over the long term, the trend line has clearly been up. Mohamed Alabbar, founder of Emaar Properties — which built the world’s tallest skyscraper — was characteristically upbeat. The developer recently unveiled a $3.3 billion business district at Dubai Creek Harbour, with 300,000 square meters of commercial space. And while the war has taken a toll on its hotel business, Emaar’s hospitality unit was able to boost profits last quarter by cutting costs. Alabbar acknowledged rising construction costs, but dismissed concerns that the property market was set for a sharp decline. Though the eight-month Iran conflict was a test, “I would say that if there was a bubble, it would have burst.” — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Fallout from Nvidia CEO’s likely ouster could slow Gulf AI buildout
events.summary: The fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s likely ouster will reach the Gulf, where ambitious AI buildouts depend on advanced US chips. Fear over China’s access to American technology through intermediaries has forced local AI champions like PIF-owned HUMAIN and Abu Dhabi-backed G42 to fight hard for chip access. Huang’s affair with a woman US intelligence officials allege is a Chinese spy will no doubt sharpen that scrutiny. Lawmakers are already pushing for new curbs on chip diversion, a move that could threaten the speed of development here. A friend-of-the-Gulf in Washington is also under pressure as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who greenlit the supply of tens of thousands of advanced GPUs to Saudi Arabia and the UAE, faces allegations that he stalled action against the Singapore firm tied up in the Huang scandal; Commerce denies the account. Still, the region’s relationship with the world’s largest chipmaker has long been one of customer and vendor: Great fortunes are tied to Nvidia, but the loss of the company’s leader shouldn’t undermine its ability to produce silicon. The question for the Gulf is, as it’s always been, about access. Dubai real estate tycoon Hussain Sajwani — who is building data centers around the world and expects his early investments in Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX will yield a “few billion dollars of profit” — said at the Bloomberg Invest conference in Dubai that “Nvidia is the most important company today in the world. It is by far. It has a genius CEO … I think if he’s forced to depart, it will be a big loss for the whole. This guy has done a great job.” — Kelsey Warner

events.title: Saudi oil production rebounds to near prewar levels
events.summary: Saudi oil production rebounded in October, driving up overall output by OPEC members to near prewar levels for the first time and helping keep down crude prices even as Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz have picked up. OPEC production rose by 1.97 million barrels a day, the majority of which was accounted for by higher Saudi output, according to the latest data from the cartel. Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said last week that the company aimed to “maximize production” in the fourth quarter, with the expectation that demand will be bolstered by efforts to replenish global oil inventories drained during the initial months of the Iran war. US military escorts, ship-to-ship transfers, and pipelines to ports away from the Strait of Hormuz have all helped restore output, although Saudi Arabia has stepped up shipments through its eastern ports as Houthi militias in Yemen threaten the Bab el-Mandeb strait. Iraq and UAE output also hit fresh highs for the year. Boosting oil flows is essential for Gulf states as they look to restore public finances bruised by the war and higher spending on new trade routes and defense. In contrast, Iranian production was almost half of prewar levels, according to OPEC. — Matthew Martin

events.title: As credit card balances hit a record high, medical bills can become 'shadow debt,' expert says
events.summary: CNBC Global Financial Wellness Advisory Board Medical bills can move onto credit cards and other forms of borrowing, making their medical origin harder to see in broader debt totals. Collectively, Americans held a record $1.29 trillion in credit card debt in Q3 2026, according to the New York Fed. Review medical bills for errors and ask providers about financial assistance before moving a balance onto a credit card or financing plan. Total household debt rose $334 billion in the third quarter, to $19.1 trillion, according to new data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York . That total doesn't include medical debt — at least, not directly. An estimated $220 billion in medical debt exists, according to an analysis of 2021 federal survey data by KFF, a national nonprofit healthcare research group. But medical expenses can become hard-to-track "shadow" debt if consumers pay them with a credit card or other forms of borrowing , said Jim Triggs, the CEO of Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling organization. "Technically, as soon as that consumer pays that debt off with another mechanism, now it becomes credit card debt, or housing debt, or whatever mechanism you used to pay it off," Triggs said. He said 20% of MMI's debt and budget counseling clients in 2025 cited a medical hardship as the reason they went into debt. Separately, about 17% of households surveyed in 2024 reported still owing money on a loan or credit card used to pay a medical bill, according to a 2025 study by researchers at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Here's a look at more stories on how to manage, grow and protect your money for the years ahead. Living abroad doesn't end U.S. tax obligations. What young expats need to know Inheriting a home can leave siblings with financial headaches — how to avoid mistakes Is the K-shaped economy ending? Finance pros weigh in SEC proposes investor exam to expand private-market access — how it could work You can't 'borrow your way out of debt,' expert says, but more people are trying Americans' credit card debt rose to a record $1.29 trillion in the third quarter, the New York Fed found, while home equity lines of credit saw their biggest quarterly jump since 2005, to $481 billion. Those increases come amid broader affordability pressures for consumers, including pricier everyday expenses amid persistent inflation . It is "kind of hard to parse" how much of Americans' debt load comes from medical expenses, said Julie Margetta Morgan, president of The Century Foundation, a New York-based progressive nonprofit think tank. "There's a big piece of medical debt that is about people being on high-deductible health plans , so they have insurance, but they're still getting these big medical bills that they can't pay," Margetta Morgan said. Nationwide, among households with medical debt, the median amount in collections is $1,492, according to the Urban Institute . The nonprofit research organization's report drew the data from more than 10 million anonymized credit bureau records from August 2026. Jessica Colon has used credit cards to pay medical debt. She and her husband were both self-employed at the time with a high-deductible health insurance plan. Colon, now 50, says the debt started with an unexpected $16,000 hospital bill for her son's care in the mid-2010s. "Because I could barely keep up with that payment, I kept charging on my credit card all my monthly payments, and that's where it all compounded," Colon said. "I was just drowning." The credit card debt grew to more than $45,000 before she turned to a nonprofit credit counselor, who negotiated lower rates and put together a five-year plan to pay it off. "It's embarrassing, honestly, how much money was interest, and then of course you're building the interest on the interest," Colon said. She zeroed out that debt in early 2024. Before taking on debt, experts advise reviewing medical bills and billing codes for errors, including duplicate charges. Consumers should also ask medical providers if they offer assistance before signing up for a medical credit card, experts say. Many nonprofit hospitals are required by law to have a written financial assistance plan. "A lot of nonprofit hospitals are not actually offering this plan to people, and in many cases, they're offering them a medical credit card before they offer that financial assistance," said Margetta Morgan, a former associate director of research, monitoring and regulations at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Colon said she wishes she had tried to negotiate the medical bills before putting the balance on a high-interest credit card. "You don't want to confront the place that's helping your child. So I didn't realize that I could do that," she said. — CNBC's Sharon Epperson contributed reporting.

events.title: Jensen Huang on Nvidia succession weeks before scandal hit: 'Just as I can be fired, the next CEO has to be hired'
events.summary: Jensen Huang said he didn't "hope" the CEO job on his daughter and instead said the position must be earned. Joel Saget / AFP via Getty Images Jensen Huang said last month the next Nvidia CEO must earn, not inherit, the job. Huang said he hopes Nvidia's next chief executive is already working somewhere at the company. He said the next CEO must be hired, just as Nvidia's board could fire him at any time. Weeks before Jensen Huang's extramarital affair scandal rocked Nvidia, the CEO made comments about his succession that now seem eerily prescient. "Just as I can be fired, the next CEO has to be hired," Huang told Bloomberg's "The Circuit" in a video released on Thursday and recorded on October 14. Huang, who has led Nvidia for 33 years, was asked during the interview whether his daughter, Madison Huang — a senior director of product marketing for physical AI at Nvidia — was in line to take over. "First of all, I don't hope the job on her," Huang said. "And the reason for that is because if that's their aspiration, Spencer or Madison's, they have to go earn it." Spencer is Huang's son, who works as Nvidia's director of robotics product. Huang's newly released comments come following a week of tumult for Nvidia. The CEO admitted on Sunday to being "unfaithful" to his wife while the company's board said it was investigating whether he was targeted by a foreign-intelligence effort. The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Huang had a second affair with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reported directly to him, citing five unnamed former employees. On Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia's board was preparing to remove Huang , sending the company's shares down as much as 8% in after-hours trading. Nvidia did not immediately respond to Business Insider's request for comment. Nvidia's succession crisis The reports have raised a question that has long shadowed the world's most valuable chip company: Who, if anyone, is ready to replace Huang ? Nvidia has not publicly named a successor. Its famously flat structure, in which Huang has as many as 60 direct reports, has made it difficult to identify a clear No. 2. Analysts and former employees have pointed to CFO Colette Kress, who could serve as an interim leader, and Ian Buck, the longtime executive who leads Nvidia's data-center and accelerated-computing business, as potential contenders. Huang said last month that he hoped the next CEO would come from inside Nvidia — even if he said at the time he had no intention of leaving soon. "I'm really hoping that the next CEO of the company's already at the company," he told Bloomberg . "But 20 years from now, I hope I stay healthy and I hope I continue to earn my keep." Huang said it was his job to ensure Nvidia develops its own next CEO. "We should create the conditions by which the company continues to thrive," Huang said, "and that the next leader of the company is already at Nvidia." The CEO said running Nvidia carries responsibilities that should not be taken lightly. "I'm responsible for an entire industry," Huang said. "The pressure of being the CEO is high, and it's supposed to be high." Read the original article on Business Insider

Energy prices are soaring, and there are big questions about how countries will tackle the climate crisis. Expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance, and whether negotiators can agree on meaningful action. events.title: Unions helped Democrats win big in 2026. Now they want action
events.summary: Unions spent millions of dollars and mobilized thousands of members to get out the vote for Democrats in the midterm election. The CNBC Voter Poll showed a 22-point Democratic margin among union households in 2026, reversing a recent decline. Labor leaders say they expect newly elected Democrats to act on affordability and workers rights if they want to keep their support in the future. When Brody Rutledge wasn't working 60-hour weeks or raising his four children this year, he was busy helping secure political victories for Democrats . The 25-year-old was part of a group of Ohio union members who planned social-media blitzes in support of Amy Acton 's campaign for governor and Sherrod Brown 's effort to reclaim a Senate seat. On his lunch hour, during break times and after his kids went to sleep, the electrician helped create posts and videos to help raise the profiles of the two candidates among blue-collar voters. The posts attracted more than 15,000 views. Rutledge's efforts paid off: Acton and Brown won their respective races, part of the blue wave that swept Democrats to power in Washington and in state houses across America — including in many states, like Ohio, that had been considered Republican-leaning, or reliably Republican. "People are realizing that there needs to be a change," Rutledge told CNBC. "We are extremely excited with the results." Rutledge was a part of what organized labor considered one of its biggest political efforts yet. Unions spent millions of dollars and mobilized thousands of members to get out the vote for Democrats in the midterm election . Now, they expect newly elected politicians to deliver. Democrats, they say, need to get a handle on inflation, enact worker protections and deliver union jobs. The AFL-CIO launched a seven-figure paid media campaign for the election and said its members since Labor Day had engaged with nearly 15 million voters. By the AFL-CIO's count, more than 600 members of unions themselves were elected in the midterm, including dozens heading to Washington and hundreds who are bound for statehouses. The CNBC Voter Poll shows midterm voters who were union members or lived in a union household went for Democrats over Republicans by a margin of 22 percentage points, the highest of the last four election cycles. That's more than double the margin for the rest of the electorate: When looking at voters in non-union households, the gap shrunk to 10 percentage points. "We are very proud of the impact that the labor movement made on this election," said Liz Shuler, president of the AFL-CIO , a federation of unions that represents almost 15 million workers. "It was our biggest and boldest effort ever." In some cases, unions got involved before party nominees had been decided. In Michigan, the United Auto Workers organized behind Democrat Abdul El-Sayed ahead of what became a contentious primary race for U.S. Senate that he eventually won against Haley Stevens . The union believes that about one out of every 10 early voters in the August primary were UAW members. "It was incredibly impactful," Connor Farrell, a progressive fundraiser who worked with El-Sayed, said of the UAW's endorsement. "I'm not sure we would have won without them." El-Sayed and Jocelyn Benson — the Democratic nominee for Michigan governor, who also had early backing from the UAW — cruised to victory in last week's general election. It was a sharp reversal for the Wolverine state, which backed President Donald Trump in 2016 and 2024. The UAW held a rally on the eve of Election Day headlined by El-Sayed and Benson, along with other Democrats running for statewide office. The Detroit-based union said its volunteers knocked on more than 100,000 doors and made half a million phone calls for the election. The CNBC Voter Poll showed union households made up about 22% of the electorate in Michigan in the 2026 midterm, above the 16% mean nationwide. Union households in Michigan broke for El-Sayed and Benson by higher-than-average margins of 25 and 27 points, respectively. "There's a direct correlation between a ballot box and a bread box," said UAW President Shawn Fain, who described the union's 2026 political efforts as the largest in his lifetime. "What we bargain for today can be taken away in the legislative halls tomorrow." In Nevada, another swing state, members of AFL-CIO unions canvassed for a list of candidates including Aaron Ford , the Democrat who unseated Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. Down ballot, the AFL-CIO endorsed candidates in state assembly, mayoral and city council races. Vladimir Ortega, a member of the National Association of Letter Carriers living in North Las Vegas, said displeasure with how Republicans had managed the economy led him to volunteer to canvas with the AFL-CIO for the first time. The 34-year-old met Ford and other candidates at political events, and he plans to volunteer for candidates backed by AFL-CIO again in 2028.

events.title: ‘A dark day for Nvidia’: Here’s what analysts are saying as markets brace for news on Huang's fate
events.summary: Global markets are awaiting news on Jensen Huang's future as CEO of Nvidia. The company's board convened Wednesday evening after reports emerged of Huang engaging in a second extramarital affair, this time with an employee. One analyst said Huang is "toast," while another described the developments as "a dark day for Nvidia." Nvidia investors were on tenterhooks amid reports that the chip giant's board had convened to discuss CEO Jensen Huang 's future with the company. In total, six analysts had downgraded the stock between Wednesday night and Thursday morning. The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Huang had engaged in a second extramarital affair with an employee. The CEO was already under scrutiny after Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence believes is a Chinese spy. Nvidia is yet to make a public statement about Huang's future with the company. However, CNBC confirmed late on Wednesday that the board was meeting to decide whether to oust him after more than 30 years at Nvidia's helm. Analysts then raced to downgrade the stock following the latest events, including longtime Nvidia bull Ben Reitzes of Melius Research. The company's stock is down 7% so far this week, after tumbling 4.3% on Monday and 5.5% on Tuesday as Huang dominated headlines around the world. Shares rebounded 2.9% on Wednesday, but were last seen roughly 5.4% lower in premarket trading on Thursday. Here's what analysts and investors are saying about the company and the stock. Reitzes changed his rating for Nvidia to hold from buy. His price target is now $185 — down from $315 — is 6% above the level at which shares last closed. "We thought we had experience, but nothing prepares you for what has happened at Nvidia over the last few weeks - and especially since Saturday. The only situation remotely close to this we can recall was HP in 2010. Waiting to see what that Board would do (and who they would hire) that time didn't work out. It was really cheap, too, at ~9x EPS right after its initial swoon. Nvidia is a much stronger, more important company, but its market moves far faster, and this story touches geopolitical flashpoints. In this unique crisis, we have decided (reluctantly) to step aside on Nvidia (now a Hold) after recommending it since we launched our AI platform coverage universe in July 2023," he said. Analyst Mark Lipacis downgraded Nvidia to in line from outperform. He also lowered his price target on shares to $186 from $465, implying 7% upside from Wednesday's close. "The Wall Street Journal reported Nvidia's Board was 'preparing to oust' its CEO after he had two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. The NY Times reported that Nvidia's Board hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead an investigation into the matter. While Nvidia's Board said that it 'has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,' we believe that the investigation will take time and we expect NVDA's P/E multiple will continue to compress consistent with our 'Late-Innings of the Semi Cycle' thesis, especially since Nvidia has no obvious succession plan or number 2 operational executive," he said. William Blair's Sebastien Naji downgraded Nvidia to market perform from outperform. "After a head-spinning week of news and allegations around CEO Jensen Huang, Nvidia's board is reportedly preparing to remove him, according to the Wall Street Journal. The full story will take time to emerge and may require several investigations, including the board's own independent probe and a requested U.S. House briefing. What is already clear is that Huang's likely departure and heightened scrutiny of the company will be a significant overhang on NVDA shares in the near term. Meanwhile, the potential for a slower AI buildout and more intense competition from other chipmakers will only add to execution risk...governance and regulatory pressure, the potential for more serious fallout, and a sudden change in management are likely to muddle both execution and sentiment. As a result, we are downgrading NVDA to Market Perform and will wait for the dust to settle before reassessing," he said. Analyst Rick Schafer downgraded the AI stock to perform from outperform. "We are downgrading shares of NVDA and removing our price target following reports (WSJ, NYT) of founding CEO Jensen Huang's imminent departure amidst allegations of a 2nd extramarital affair. Credible media reports circulated Wednesday evening that NVDA's board is preparing to part ways with Huang following a widely reported relationship with an alleged Chinese spy compounded by new allegations of a relationship with an NVDA executive. events.title: The cracks in venture are beginning to show, just as Anthropic gets ready to IPO
events.summary: On the eve of a historic IPO for Silicon Valley’s investor community, the fragilities of venture are as clear as they’ve ever been to me.  I’ve been thinking about this irony for days: Anthropic is set to go public as soon as next week (everything I’m hearing says “Jensen Huang’s affair be damned, all systems go”), and while this is primed to be a banner moment for VC, venture seems to be structurally over its skis. Consider recent data from PitchBook: Hitting a $5 billion valuation takes 80% less time, but 74% more capital, according to the company’s latest U.S. Valuations report.  “Higher valuations raise the bar to achieve profitable exits, and AI is expensive to run,” said Emily Zheng, PitchBook senior research analyst, via email. “Cracks are beginning to show in venture, including large amounts of AI-related debt and a likely slowdown in data center expansion given the recent election.” The reality is this: Valuations are soaring higher and more readily, but exits are still tough. Zheng is clear that the IPO window—unless a company is in a very select group like SpaceX or Anthropic—remains shut.  “The IPO window has not reopened,” she said via email. “Most listings this year have been in health care, with the high-growth tech names LPs need for distributions largely absent. Removing mega IPOs from 2026’s totals reveals that exit value remains at the same constrained level that has defined every year since the pandemic.” M&A remains a viable option, but in many deals, Zheng said, “valuation compression remains the dominant theme, as Q3 revealed with Bending Spoons’ acquisitions of Airtable and Miro at significant discounts.” (Airtable, for example, was acquired for $1.28 billion in cash, a vertiginous drop from its 2021 $11.7 billion peak valuation.) Rising rates and broader economic uncertainty are primed to render these pressures worse.  Historical data also suggests the current venture vintage could be in trouble, according to PitchBook’s recent U.S. VC Fundraising and Returns data: Past funds haven’t necessarily performed well during periods characterized by high interest rates (new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh already hiked rates once in 2026, and another hike’s on the table for December). There’s no way to prove causality, but the stressors of high rates, high valuations, and sluggish exits definitionally create pressure.  “The current market is a strange mix of high prices, low liquidity, and a relatively uncertain outlook,” said Zheng via email. “ The outlook for current vintages will likely not look as great as their current markups.” And as the day of Anthropic’s seemingly imminent IPO approaches, it’s worth remembering that post-IPO performance has been dicey for the few major IPOs we’ve seen: CoreWeave and Circle, up about 52% and 116% respectively since their listing days, are the exception. Figma’s down about 42% in its life as a public company, while Cerebras is down roughly 45%. Nevertheless, what happens next with Anthropic will be the harbinger of where venture and startups go from here.  “Strong performance would validate AI’s enormous private valuations, spurring dealmaking and exit activity as real distributions are injected back into LP portfolios,” said Zheng via email. “Weak performance would bring into question whether AI companies are wildly overvalued.” That is, of course, the multi-trillion-dollar question. See you tomorrow, Allie Garfinkle X: @agarfinks Email: alexandra.garfinkle@fortune.com Submit a deal for the Term Sheet newsletter here . Joey Abrams curated the deals section of today’s newsletter . events.title: AI helped UK defy expectations – but will economy’s resilience fizzle out?
events.summary: Despite John Healey’s defiance, the economy faces threats from a tech slowdown and energy bills this winter AI helps UK economy grow at fastest pace for more than two years The forecasters were clear when John Healey became chancellor in July: Britain’s resilience to the war in the Middle East would not last. The global economic headwinds were too strong, inflation was beginning to rise and growth would slow to a trickle. Four months into the job, the economy is continuing to defy expectations after growing by 0.7% in the third quarter – the fastest expansion in two and a half years. It puts the UK on course to be the second-fastest growing G7 economy this year. On his first day in Downing Street the memo from the Treasury showed the most optimistic City analyst expected 0.3% quarterly growth. Most had pencilled in a figure close to zero. Some were warning that the UK could edge towards a recession. Despite the gloomy outlook households have continued to spend and business investment has powered ahead, driven by the rollout of AI. Underneath the bonnet, growth is being spearheaded by IT and professional services – together contributing about half of the rise in activity. As the central sectors in the AI boom, that is hardly surprising – with analysts at ING suggesting the strength in IT was “very clearly a datacentre story” thanks to the UK’s status as a leading destination in Europe for investment. Overall, Deutsche Bank estimates that AI-related spending has added about 0.3% to 0.4% to GDP growth this year. It is clear to see why Healey is keen to build on the groundwork laid by his immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, to harness AI amid government efforts to court global business investment. Meanwhile, household consumption is up by 1.6% so far this year – helped by spending over the warm summer months even as consumers faced a living standards squeeze because the Iran war fuelled a surge in petrol and diesel prices. However, the fear is that the UK’s initial resilience to the global economic storm emanating from the Middle East will soon fizzle out. Both of Britain’s recent growth engines face a tougher period ahead. After the US midterm elections and revelations at the chipmaker Nvidia , the outlook for the AI investment boom is less certain. Financial markets have been rocked in recent weeks amid fears that a bubble in AI stocks could be about to burst . A slowdown in technology investment could hit the UK. Still, the hope is that swelling demand for AI will not evaporate overnight. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning For households, however, a tough winter lies ahead. Energy bills are poised to increase by about a quarter in January, with the average annual household gas and electricity bill expected to climb to more than £2,000. Analysts say it is hard to see how consumer spending would not come under greater pressure in the new year. In the latest data there were some early warning signs: retail sales and consumer discretionary spending fell in September. Real wage growth is cooling and the headline inflation rate is on track to reach a fresh peak of close to 5% next year. With growth proving resilient, the Bank of England will feel emboldened to raise interest rates to combat imported inflation. City investors expect at least two more quarter-point increases to 4.5% before the end of next year. That will hit the brakes on the economy and add to the cost of living squeeze. At last month’s budget Healey struck a defiant tone by arguing that the UK could continue to defy forecasters expectations. That task, however, is becoming increasingly tough.

events.title: Nebius falls 10% as company expects increased 2026 capex spend, issues weak outlook
events.summary: Nebius' earnings report comes after fellow neoclouds IREN and CoreWeave showed better-than-expected results in the past week. The companies' stocks have bounced back this week after a brutal past month that reflected concerns about a slowdown in the AI buildout. Nvidia, which invests across the neocloud space, is creating added volatility due to the crisis surrounding CEO Jensen Huang. Nebius shares sank 10% on Thursday as one of the biggest publicly traded neoclouds reported third-quarter revenue that beat analysts' estimates, but issued disappointing guidance. Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus: Loss per share: Loss of 13 cents per share Revenue: $980.8 million vs. $907.5 million It was not immediately clear if the loss per share was comparable to the 69 cents expected by analysts. Revenue jumped 571% in the quarter, according to a statement. The company reported a net loss of $37.5 million, a loss of 13 cents per share, compared with $119.6 million, a loss of 50 cents per share, a year earlier. In a letter to shareholders , CEO Arkady Volozh said the company expects fiscal year 2026 revenue at the low end of the company's $3 billion to 3.4 billion range. FactSet expected full-year revenue of $3.35 billion. Nebius also shared an initial outlook for 2027, expecting revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion, "reflecting a conservative approach to the pace of our build-out." FactSet expected 2027 revenue of $12.09 billion. The company expects FY2026 capital expenditures of $27 billion, higher than its previous capex guidance of $20 billion to $25 billion and the FactSet expectation of $23.85 billion. Nebius' expected FY2027 capex of $40 billion to $45 billion came in much higher than the FactSet expectation of $28.77 billion. Nebius' results come after fellow neoclouds CoreWeave and IREN reported better-than-expected financials in their earnings announcements over the past week. That's provided a boost to the companies' stocks, which had suffered steep selloffs in recent weeks on concern about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence buildout. The neocloud companies posted a robust rally on Wednesday, with Coreweave booming nearly 25%, Nebius climbing 15%, Applied Digital rising more than 7% and IREN adding nearly 6%. Each of the stocks fell Thursday premarket after the Nebius Q3 report. Last week, CoreWeave's bond yields spiked past the 16% mark. In its earnings report on Tuesday, CoreWeave told analysts it expects to keep parent-level debt financing under $5 billion through 2027. The political backdrop has created further volatility as Nebius races rivals to open up new data centers. Last week U.S. voters supported dozens of ballot initiatives to restrict the development of such facilities, while Democrats won sweeping victories in both houses of Congress. Then there's the Nvidia problem. Following stinging revelations about CEO Jensen Huang's affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, the Wall Street Journal reported late Wednesday that Nvidia's board was planning to push out the company's co-founder. Nvidia, which has developed the neocloud market by investing in the companies and backstopping some of their projects, held about $329 million in Nebius shares at the end of June, according to a filing . During the quarter, Nebius said it raised $5.75 billion in debt financing. Executives will discuss the results with analysts and issue guidance on a conference call starting at 8 a.m. ET. events.title: Hackers exploiting ScreenConnect plugin flaw to spread malware across hundreds of PCs
events.summary: Hackers have used a dodgy third-party ScreenConnect extension to push malware onto at least 288 machines across 48 organizations, prompting ConnectWise to disable a handful of plugins in hundreds of customer environments. Security outfit Huntress first raised the alarm in a Reddit post on Wednesday, warning of an active campaign targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances. At the time, its security operations center was tracking six compromised managed service providers (MSPs) and more than 286 affected endpoints, with the numbers still climbing. ConnectWise acquired popular remote supporttool ScreenConnect in February, 2015. Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT service providers. All 288 endpoints were hit within 90 minutes, with roughly a third compromised in the first ten minutes. Huntress suspects more MSPs may have been compromised, as the attackers appeared to be numbering their victims sequentially, with the numbers suggesting earlier attacks that it hadn't detected. The attackers deployed a 16-file malware toolkit dubbed SCKit, which installs a separate ScreenConnect client to maintain remote access even if the legitimate connection is shut down. It also contains code designed to spread the infection to IT technicians and potentially other customers under their control. Huntress has since traced the activity to a possible authentication weakness in RMM+, a third-party extension that lets other management tools issue commands through ScreenConnect without technicians using its console. Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of the extension contain a flaw that means installations without a configured access key will accept a blank one. Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands without defeating MFA. Huntress said the findings matched what its investigators saw during the attacks, with commands reaching machines across several ScreenConnect installations despite no corresponding login activity. The researchers also confirmed that the attacks affected ScreenConnect versions 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, meaning administrators running the latest releases weren't necessarily safe. ConnectWise has acknowledged that third-party extensions may have been involved but has stopped short of confirming how the attackers initially gained access. In a security advisory , the company said it was investigating unauthorized access to certain partner environments and had identified approximately 400 installations containing at least one extension from the RMM+ family. It has disabled five extensions, including RMM+, RMM Plus, and Labtech Plus, wherever it can do so remotely, and urged customers running their own ScreenConnect servers to follow suit. ConnectWise stressed that the 400 environments were identified because they had the extensions installed, not because they were necessarily compromised. The company said: "At this time, we have found no evidence of a compromise of ConnectWise infrastructure or a vulnerability in ScreenConnect itself." There's another nasty trick buried in SCKit. According to Huntress, the malware is designed to turn an infected computer into a trap for the technician sent to investigate it. If the technician connects through ScreenConnect, the toolkit attempts to transfer malware back to their workstation, steal authentication cookies, and use their access to infect other machines. That could give attackers a route from one compromised customer into others managed by the same IT provider. However, Huntress says it has yet to see that part of the attack succeed. "We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far," the researchers wrote. Huntress also suspects that some of the malware's C# code was generated using an LLM, pointing to unusually detailed comments explaining what the code is supposed to do. Apparently, even malware authors appreciate a little help with their homework. Both Huntress and ConnectWise are urging administrators not to investigate suspected infections by remotely connecting through ScreenConnect, since doing so could put the technician's own machine at risk. Administrators are being advised to use other security tools to investigate affected machines, look for rogue ScreenConnect clients, and check what commands have been run. Any malware left behind will also need to be removed before the machines are brought back online. Huntress warned on Reddit that some machines were becoming reinfected within minutes of being taken out of isolation because the malware had not been properly removed. Simply disabling the vulnerable extensions won't necessarily undo the damage, either. As ConnectWise warns, "Disabling extensions and resetting credentials alone may not remove unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already established on endpoints." And with the attackers already able to install their own remote access software, kicking them out could prove considerably harder than closing the door they came through. ®

events.title: Thanks to American oligarchy, Jensen Huang’s midlife crisis is a problem for all of us | Moira Donegan
events.summary: Thanks to American oligarchy, Jensen Huang’s midlife crisis is a problem for all of us At a time when individual men wield massive power, the ramifications of the Nvidia CEO’s affair could be enormous O ne of the reasons you want to distribute power and responsibility in powerful organizations and high-stakes enterprises is so that the narcissism or myopia of one man do not come to carry outsized consequences. When power is spread out across multiple people, it matters less if one of those people is prone to flattery, or in the midst of a midlife crisis, or perhaps just a bit stupid; the limits on his power become limits on the fallout of his character flaws. A broad distribution of authority also has the virtue of making any one man disposable, replaceable: if he turns out to have poor judgement or counterproductive preoccupations, he can be dispensed with, and his role can be filled anew with someone better suited to its responsibilities. But if one man becomes synonymous with a company – or a country – then untold numbers of other people live and die by that man’s decisions. And when his decisions are bad – petty, selfish, shortsighted, small-minded or dumb – then it is other people who will pay the price. And the price is often quite steep. Because we live in an era of massive inequality, tightly consolidated corporate leadership, and rule by a billionaire class with large egos and deficient dignity, the US economy is now experiencing one of the latter scenarios, in the form of Jensen Huang , a Silicon Valley billionaire who this week confessed to having an extramarital affair. This would be tacky and embarrassing for Huang on its own. But because Huang is the CEO of Nvidia , one of the country’s largest companies and the manufacturer of advanced chip technology that is powering the US’s AI boom, his petty midlife crisis – the kind of small-minded narcissism that can usually be dispensed with in the form of a red sportscar, or indeed with one of the cheesy leather jackets that Huang is prone to wearing – is now a problem for the US economy, and potentially for national security. Because Huang’s mistress was not just any of the interchangeable young women that such men usually go for. This one happened to be a suspected Chinese spy. It’s unclear how much the woman, Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang – no relation – learned from her relationship with the tech billionaire, or how the information she may have gathered could undermine US economic and military interests. Alice Huang worked in television in China before becoming an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company and one of the largest purchasers of Nvidia’s advanced chips. Megaspeed was under investigation by the US commerce department on suspicion of smuggling the advanced chips to China, which is banned from importing them by US law. (Megaspeed said it had offered to cooperate with the US government’s investigation but those offers went unanswered.) According to the New York Times, the investigation was abruptly halted last year after the general counsel for Nvidia, Jensen Huang’s company, intervened. Among other things, Jensen Huang is known for his close relationship with Donald Trump. On Sunday, Huang issued a statement admitting to an affair, and his company announced that it would be launching an investigation into the incident. “The Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” which is perhaps a bit too hopeful. But the statement itself is a reflection of the depth of Huang’s control over the country. If you or I had endangered corporate secrets and state security in a flight of reckless, narcissistic frivolity, the way Huang may have done, then our employers would not be announcing the investigation while we kept our jobs. Nvidia’s stocks were down when the markets opened on Monday. They may well go down further still. And yet the scandal is fitting for our current era of Silicon Valley, in which loyalty to Donald Trump has gone from a strategic move by major tech companies to ensure favorable contract and regulatory terms to much more full-throated embrace of the ideology and style of the far right. Following the lead of its major male executives, the tech industry has become reckless and irresponsible, proud of itself for accelerating technologies it plainly claims to be unable to control, demanding investments in datacenters and government contracts from taxpayers whom it smugly brags about putting out of jobs, and flooding our aesthetic and informational worlds with low-grade slop that is frequently factually inaccurate, often dangerous for vulnerable users, and uncanny in its unpleasantness, bearing a creepy and inhuman sheen in its images and language.

events.title: Which business moats will still matter in the age of AI?
events.summary: For many investors, a company’s economic moat is one of the most important things to understand. A strong moat can protect market share, support pricing power and help a business earn attractive returns for years, even as competitors try to take those profits away. The best moats usually come from something genuinely hard to replicate: a unique product, valuable intellectual property, scarce assets, scale or some other lasting competitive advantage. But not every moat is built that way. Some businesses may be protected, at least in part, by the fact that their customers are human. People are busy. We forget things. We don’t always read the fine print. We put off switching banks or insurance companies because it sounds like a hassle. We keep paying for subscriptions we barely use. And when shopping for something becomes too complicated, we often settle for good enough. I think of these as behavioral moats . And the rise of personal AI agents could put some of them at risk. We got an early look at that concern in September, when Meta’s Muse AI agent caught investors’ attention. Shares of companies that could be vulnerable to declining consumer inertia sold off. Charles Schwab fell more than 6%, insurer Allstate dropped 5.5%, Planet Fitness fell as much as 11%, and travel companies including Expedia and Booking Holdings also came under pressure. ( Bloomberg ) The reaction may prove overdone. Agentic AI is still young, and there are major questions around security, trust and how much authority consumers will actually hand over to software. But the underlying question is worth considering now: Would a company’s advantage still exist if every customer had a tireless personal assistant constantly looking for a better deal? When switching is the moat Financial services may be one of the clearest examples. Consumers routinely leave money in accounts paying less interest than they could earn elsewhere. That isn’t necessarily because they believe their bank offers the best deal. Moving accounts can mean comparing alternatives, filling out forms, changing direct deposits and reconnecting automatic payments. Most people have other things to do. An AI agent does not. In theory, it could regularly compare savings rates, credit card rewards or brokerage products and tell its owner when there is a better alternative. Eventually, agents could handle more of the switching process themselves. That possibility has already gotten the attention of financial companies. Schwab CEO Rick Wurster recently said the company is blocking unauthorized outside AI agents attempting to access customer accounts or move money. Schwab is instead building controlled ways for outside AI systems to connect to its platform, while limiting what they can do. Other major banks are taking similar precautions. ( Bloomberg ) There are legitimate security reasons for that. Giving software free access to your life savings is very different from asking it to order paper towels. Still, the situation illustrates the broader issue. Friction can protect a business, whether that friction exists for good reasons or not. As agents become better at safely handling tedious financial tasks, some of that protection could weaken. When figuring out the price is the moat Sometimes consumers don’t stick with a company because switching is hard. They stick because comparing the alternatives is hard. Insurance is a good example. Comparing two policies means looking beyond the headline premium to deductibles, coverage limits, exclusions and other details. Telecom plans can involve different data limits, bundles, promotional prices and fees. A person may eventually decide the potential savings aren’t worth the effort. Software doesn’t get frustrated after the sixth page of fine print. This is another area where businesses are already preparing for change. Kin Insurance recently said it would welcome AI shopping agents rather than block them and has since built tools designed to make it easier for agents to obtain home insurance quotes. Insurance marketplace Insurify has also launched an AI Agent Gateway that allows agents to gather and compare real-time quotes while preserving details such as deductibles, limits and disclosures. ( Kin / PR Newswire ) That may offer a preview of how companies adapt. If AI makes comparison easier, businesses can try to fight the change—or make themselves easier for agents to shop. In some industries, being the company that gives an agent the clearest information and easiest path to a transaction could eventually become an advantage of its own. When forgetting to cancel is the moat Subscriptions may be the easiest behavioral moat to understand. Many of us have looked at a credit card statement and found something we forgot we were still paying for. Sometimes it is a streaming service. Sometimes it is an app. Sometimes it is the gym membership that seemed like a great idea in January. There is good evidence that this matters to businesses. A 2025 study published in the American Economic Review looked at subscription companies and found cancellations rose sharply when replacement credit cards forced customers to make an active renewal decision. The researchers estimated that cancellation friction roughly doubled seller revenues on average, holding the starting subscriber base constant. ( American Economic Review ) An AI agent could make that kind of inattention much less common. It could regularly scan recurring charges, compare them with usage and ask whether you still want to keep paying. That concern helped send Planet Fitness shares sharply lower following the launch of Muse, as investors considered what easier cancellation might mean for businesses that rely on recurring memberships. ( StreetInsider ) Netflix is a more interesting case. There may be some customers who keep Netflix because canceling is one more thing they haven’t gotten around to doing. Agentic AI could put pressure on that part of the business. But Netflix also has something much harder for an agent to eliminate: content people actually want to watch. If a consumer wants a show that is only available on Netflix, an AI agent cannot shop around and recreate it somewhere else. That is the difference between a behavioral moat and a real one. When settling for good enough is the moat Even when prices are relatively clear and switching is easy, comparison takes time. Most people do not check every travel site each morning to see whether another hotel has dropped its price. We don’t constantly search every retailer to make sure something we bought last week is still the best deal. At some point, we stop looking and buy. AI agents could keep looking. Travel companies are already building around this idea. Priceline’s Penny can compare destinations, prices and availability and move from a broad travel request toward an actual booking within one conversation.
