events.title: FIFA Under-17 World Cup to kick off in Qatar despite US withdrawal
events.summary: FIFA says its ‘security assessments’ for the 48-team tournament remain unchanged after US Soccer pulled out. FIFA says the Under-17 World Cup in Qatar will kick off as scheduled on November 19, despite the United States’ decision to withdraw its team from the tournament. US Soccer withdrew its national team citing safety concerns, but the sport’s global governing body, which is hosting the tournament in Qatar, confirmed on Thursday that its plans remain unchanged. “The safety and security of all participants and fans remain paramount. As with all FIFA tournaments and events, we are in close contact with the relevant authorities and ‌‌‌‌are looking forward to the tournament kickoff in Qatar,” FIFA told Al Jazeera in a statement hours after the USA’s announcement. “In recent months, Qatar has successfully hosted several international events,” it added. Qatar hosted two major international tournaments in the past two weeks. MotoGP’s Qatar Grand Prix was successfully held on 8 and the FIP Padel World Cup 2026 concluded on the same day. With a week until the Under-17 World Cup kicks off, FIFA confirmed that its security assessments “remain unchanged” and that no new ⁠⁠⁠⁠developments affecting the security situation around the tournament have occurred. “FIFA understands that US Soccer’s decision was made in light of the existing US ⁠⁠⁠⁠Level 3 travel advisory,” it said. In a letter sent to players, the US Soccer Federation ⁠⁠⁠⁠said it was cancelling the team’s pre-tournament camp and its participation in the event “in light of current circumstances”, according to the Reuters news agency. The US State Department updated its advisory for Qatar last month, urging Americans to reconsider travel because of the risk of armed conflict. The update referred to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian ‌‌‌‌airports and critical infrastructure. “The well-being of our players and staff will always be our top priority,” the US federation’s letter said. The 48-team Under-17 tournament runs from November 19 to December 13. USA had been due ⁠⁠⁠⁠to open against Montenegro on November 21 before ⁠⁠⁠⁠facing Chile and Algeria in Group J.

events.title: Canada won’t let Russian players enter for ice hockey junior championship
events.summary: Russian, Belarusian athletes and officials will be prevented from entering Canada regardless of their visa status. Canada says it will prevent Russian athletes and officials from entering the country for ice hockey’s World Junior Championship in Alberta, effectively barring their participation weeks before the tournament begins. Canada’s Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden said on Wednesday that Ottawa opposes Russian and Belarusian participation in international sport “as long as Russia continues its war of aggression against Ukraine with Belarus’s complicity”. list 1 of 3 Nordic nations refuse to face Russia in ice hockey World Championship list 2 of 3 World chess body suspends Russia over activities in occupied-Ukraine list 3 of 3 International Olympic Committee recommends ending Belarus restrictions The minister for immigration, refugees and citizenship “will take measures to individually assess and prevent Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials from entering Canada to compete, regardless of whether they already hold valid visas”, Van Koeverden said. Hockey Canada has previously said it supports the government’s position. Late last month, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ordered the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) to admit Russian teams to five upcoming championships, beginning with the World Junior Championship. The IIHF, which has barred Russia from most international competitions since Moscow’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, said it disagreed with the CAS decision. The hockey federation’s statement followed announcements from Norway, Denmark, Sweden and the Czech Republic that ⁠⁠their national teams will refuse to play against Russia at next year’s men’s World Championships in Germany. Latvia and Finland have also said their teams will not play Russia, while the Finnish city of Turku threatened to ⁠⁠drop its hosting duties for the 2028 World Junior Championship. Belarus’s team will not participate in the championship following a separate decision by the IIHF. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has previously said Ottawa would not permit Russian athletes to compete for their country on Canadian soil, a statement some perceived as keeping the door open for their participation as neutrals. Van Koeverden said Canada allowed neutral participation only by individual athletes, ruling out the option for the Russian team. “Canada’s position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues its war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual,” he said. “Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine.” The World Junior Championship runs from December 26 to January 5.

events.title: Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate election over incumbent Republican Hyde-Smith
events.summary: Democratic nominee Scott Colom won the Mississippi Senate election over Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Associated Press reported. Colom will be the first Black senator from Mississippi since the post-Civil War Reconstruction Era. Democrats will have a majority of at least 55 seats in the Senate, having flipped at least eight seats from Republicans. Alaska is the only remaining Senate election to be called. Democratic nominee Scott Colom won the Mississippi Senate election over Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith , the Associated Press reported Wednesday. Colom, a local district attorney, will be the first Black senator from Mississippi since the post-Civil War Reconstruction Era. His projected victory — which was not considered likely by national analysts before Election Day — is the latest in a series of stunning wins by Democrats this midterm cycle. Two sources close to Colom's campaign said Hyde-Smith called him late Wednesday afternoon to concede. "While this is not the outcome we worked for, or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," Hyde-Smith said in a video posted on X . "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state," Hyde-Smith said. Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling Democrats now will have a majority of at least 55 seats in the Senate, having flipped at least eight seats from Republicans. Alaska is the only remaining Senate election to be called. In that state, Democratic nominee Mary Peltola, a former House member, has a narrow lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent. "Blue Mississippi is here," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said in a post on X. "Scott Colom is the only person who could've gotten this done. I knew it from the moment I met him," Schumer wrote. In addition to the Senate, Democrats have won more than enough seats to take control of the House of Representatives when the next Congress begins in January. This is breaking news. events.summary: But experts say Washington’s shift away from Europe runs deeper than Trump and is unlikely to be reversed. During the campaign for the midterm elections in the United States, neither the Democrats nor the Republicans spoke much about issues related to Europe. US President Donald Trump’s handling of the Ukraine war, his approach to Greenland and his aggressive posture towards the European Union were not on the agenda. list 1 of 4 Ukraine’s position ‘may become stronger’ as US Democrats regain some power list 2 of 4 Trump’s White House calls Democratic plans for congressional probes ‘abuse’ list 3 of 4 US election results could be positive for Lebanon, Hezbollah chief says list 4 of 4 Who is Scott Colom, Mississippi’s first Black senator in 150 years? Yet while the Democratic Party’s victory last week could produce a Congress that is friendlier towards Europe, experts do not expect major shifts in US foreign policy in some areas. “Europeans are looking much less in horror towards the US than they have in the past two years, but they should not exaggerate the significance in terms of transatlantic relations,” said Erik Jones, director of the Robert Schuman Centre for Advanced Studies at the European University Institute. “The trend line has been moving in a consistent direction across administrations, and this midterm election does not change that trend.” For decades, the transatlantic relationship was built on the assumption that Washington needed a free, prosperous and secure Europe, while European governments relied on American security guarantees. But that consensus has gradually eroded, and it did not start with Trump. Over time, there was a loss of popular support for global engagement on both sides of the Atlantic. The pattern began under Barack Obama, whose administration started a strategic reorientation towards Asia, analysts say, because of perceived threats to US security from the region. That has become a rare area of agreement across the political divide: Republicans and Democrats alike support Europeans taking greater responsibility for their own security. The US president has accelerated that shift with his America First approach. He has repeatedly lashed out at NATO, threatened to seize Greenland and has shown greater respect for Russia than Ukraine, undermining European efforts to isolate and weaken Moscow. A Democratic-controlled Congress will have more power over federal spending, legislation and congressional oversight to challenge some of Trump’s decisions. But the president would retain considerable authority over foreign policy. “All speak in favour of better transatlantic ties, more predictable and more open to take into account European expectations from America,” said Fredrik Erixon, an economist and director of the European Centre for International Political Economy, noting that the Democrats lack a veto-proof majority. “But on issues such as Ukraine, Iran and tariffs there is still a lot of space for the president to behave in the same fashion as in past years.” With the Iran war, which has pushed up global energy prices, there is no easy way out. Trump could either cut a deal and declare victory, potentially leaving Iran with leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, or resume military action – a deeply unpopular prospect among US voters. In either scenario, European allies are left with a cost of living crisis that is driving protests across the continent. Some Democrats have discussed using the next government funding bill to block flows for the war in Iran, a proposal that is popular with antiwar lawmakers. In Ukraine, the new Democrat-dominated Congress may favour greater support for Kyiv, but that support may not be a game changer for the war-torn nation. Ukrainian officials are anxious about the two-month window before the new Congress takes office in January and fear that Trump could use the period to pursue further talks with Putin. Even so, the Democrats are likely to invest more energy in improving social services and economic conditions at home. Some experts also suggest that a politically weakened Trump may now look abroad to demonstrate strength, score wins and build his legacy. His domestic electoral setback could therefore translate into an even less predictable and less accommodating foreign policy. Last week, the US president said there would soon be a “big, beautiful agreement” on Ukraine, one that “might involve all of Europe”. The comments came ahead of trilateral talks between Ukrainian, Russian and US officials in Abu Dhabi, which have so far failed to yield any breakthrough. The prospect of a broader deal has raised questions about how much say European governments would have in negotiations that affect their security. “Trump’s moves are difficult to predict,” said Michele Valensise, president of the Institute for International Affairs and former secretary-general of Italy’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

events.title: Smaller NATO militaries can't match Russia's manpower. Autonomous weapons could help close the gap.
events.summary: Weapons with greater autonomy mean that there doesn't need to be one soldier for every weapons system, which would be a big boost for smaller militaries. Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images Autonomous weapons could help smaller NATO militaries offset Russia's manpower advantage. Defense companies say autonomy could allow fewer soldiers to operate more weapons. A Norwegian officer argues that humans won't always be needed in front-line combat roles. Autonomous weaponry capable of performing some of the roles of human soldiers could be key for smaller NATO militaries unable to match larger militaries in manpower. Maj. Sebastian Langvad, a Norwegian Army officer and lecturer at the Norwegian Military Academy, told Business Insider that advancing technology is increasingly eliminating the need for humans to perform certain combat roles, such as pulling a trigger. These developments could be particularly meaningful for smaller nations with limited manpower . Investment in remote systems that can take over some soldiers' roles is key because "we can compete with Russia when it comes to technology and funding, but we cannot compete when it comes to putting soldiers in the field," Langvad said. "We have more to gain from breaking that link between volume of combat power and the amount of people," he said. Norway, a NATO member, has a population of fewer than 6 million, compared with Russia's more than 143 million. Norway also faces higher personnel costs. "Each individual soldier just by wage levels is so much more expensive for us than it is for Russia, relatively speaking," Langvad said. He said technology cannot yet completely replace human soldiers on the front lines and likely won't be able to for years. "The human still has an unsurpassed combination of flexible modes of mobility, decentralized intelligent decision-making, and often being readily available." But as technology and weaponry become more powerful, militaries should accept that "there is no intrinsic value to the human on the front line," he said, adding that every feature of a human soldier that has made them ubiquitous throughout history "can logically be replaced by a combination of different technologies if used correctly," even if that technology is not yet fully realized. He distinguished conventional combat from missions such as peacekeeping and state-building, where the presence of human soldiers can itself be important. The growing autonomy in weapons systems means it's time to reevaluate the intrinsic value of humans in frontline positions, Maj. Sebastian Langvad said. ANATOLII STEPANOV/AFP via Getty Images Langvad said he believes that weaponry with enough autonomy to take over all of the roles of a human in a foxhole is "quite close to existing" and that its limit could soon be an ethical one imposed by militaries, rather than a technological hurdle. A boost for smaller militaries Smaller NATO militaries have acknowledged the advantages of greater autonomy. Estonia's 2026 Defense AI Strategy, issued by its defense ministry, says AI and autonomous systems can create "asymmetric and cost-effective advantages, despite the size discrepancy vis-à-vis the adversary." Some industry figures have expressed similar ideas. Agris Kipurs, CEO of Latvian drone maker Origin Robotics, previously told Business Insider that smaller nations need weaponry that allows fewer operators to do more tasks, "and pretty much the only answer to that is autonomy." Eliot Pence, the founder of Canadian defense firm Dominion Dynamics, which makes autonomy, communications, and command-and-control systems, told Business Insider that "Canada has a real need for autonomy," in part because it has one of the lowest per-capita soldier ratios among NATO members. "The ability to extend command and control across this vastness is not just sort of a nice-to-have; it's a need to have," he said. German defense technology company ARX Robotics has systems in Ukraine and with Western militaries, and the UK has ordered an initial batch of its GEREON robots. David Roberts, CEO of ARX Robotics UK, told Business Insider that having one soldier controlling a single system won't work "for a smaller force like the British Army trying to control the number of systems required for its length of front line and expected concept of operations." "As a result, autonomy will be required to cope," he said. For NATO militaries, the value of autonomous systems extends beyond simply addressing manpower shortages, Langvad said. Countries have the resources to send systems in place of human soldiers, preventing the unnecessary sacrifice of human lives at war. Taking over some front-line roles Ukraine's fight against Russia's invasion has accelerated the use of remotely operated weapons and driven advancements in autonomy. Drones perform reconnaissance and strikes, even medical evacuations, while ground robots carry supplies, evacuate the wounded, and operate weapons. Remote weapons have become central to the fighting, with Ukrainian officials attributing the vast majority of Russia's front-line casualties to drones. They have likewise been used to harm Ukrainian troops as Russia also invests heavily in uncrewed systems. The degree of autonomy in those weapons varies. Some are simply remote-controlled, while others can identify and track targets. But as autonomy grows, Ukraine says human troops still make the final decision to fire. Langvad said that Ukraine has "supercharged" an existing trend toward more remotely controlled weaponry. He described Ukraine's approach as the right "core military logic," but said each country needs to adapt its lessons to its own military. Norway, like many other allies, is moving towards having more remotely operated and uncrewed combat systems, though nowhere near the scale of Ukraine. Its defense ministry published its Drone Strategy for the Defence Sector last December. It said uncrewed systems let high-risk operations "be carried out without endangering personnel" and "can supplement and replace large, personnel-intensive, and costly platforms, achieving similar military effects at a lower cost." events.title: Metro Bank up for sale, with billionaire investor in line for £420m windfall
events.summary: Metro Bank is putting itself up for sale three years after its near-collapse, in a move that could hand a £420m windfall to its Colombian billionaire investor, Jaime Gilinski Bacal. Metro Bank made the rare decision to publicly announce it was open to bids on Thursday, paving the way for a wider pool of suitors. The announcement pushed the share price up by 7% by mid-morning, valuing the bank at about £1.3bn. If successful, the sale would allow Gilinski Bacal a chance to sell out of the bank he helped save from near-failure in late 2023. The 68-year-old banking tycoon, who took a seat on Metro’s board after securing a 53% stake three years ago, has already seen a sixfold increase in the value of his shares, which he bought for just 30p each as part of a wider rescue deal. That means that at Thursday’s 190p share price, his British Virgin Island-based vehicle Spaldy Investments, could cash out with a £427m windfall. It would mark the latest turnaround success for the billionaire, who made his fortune snapping up assets of struggling lenders on the cheap, before overhauling their operations and selling them on for a big profit. Gilinski Bacal is one of the wealthiest people in Latin America, worth about $16.9bn (£12.7bn), according to Forbes. Metro Bank has been focused on a turnaround plan – which has involved lending more heavily to businesses and people with more erratic incomes – since it was forced into the £925m rescue deal in 2023. Metro was the first high street bank to open in the UK in more than 100 years when it was launched by another billionaire, the US businessman Vernon Hill, in 2010. It attracted a wave of customers, and offered dog-friendly branches with seven-day openings. However, it struggled after a major accounting blunder in 2019 that prompted investors to dump their shares and fearful customers to pull their cash. It led to the resignation of top executives, as well as the then chair, Hill, who was well-known for having his yorkshire terrier Sir Duffy (and later Sir Duffy II) in tow. Metro’s shares took another dive in 2023. That year, it emerged that the bank would need more cash from investors, having failed to convince regulators that it could be trusted to assess its own risks. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The lender finally secured a rescue, which was brokered in part by UK regulators at the Bank of England, in 2023. It has since embarked on the turnaround plan, which has increased its profits but came at a cost for staff and customers. Metro’s chief executive, Daniel Frumkin, slashed more than 1,000 jobs in spring 2024 and decided to close branches on Sundays. The bank said on Thursday that a sale was just one of the options on the table and that it would still be able to go it alone if no suitable bidder came through. Metro’s board “unanimously believes that evaluating potential interest in the company” through a potential sale “will maximise the value creation opportunities available to shareholders and deliver benefits for all stakeholders”, the bank said.

events.title: Emaar’s mall footfall down 10 per cent due to Iran war, says Alabbar
events.summary: Footfall and retail sales at Emaar’s malls have fallen by about 10 per cent and hotel occupancy has dropped sharply as the Iran war weighs on tourism and consumer spending in Dubai, Emaar founder Mohamed Alabbar said on Thursday. “In our mall business, we are 10 per cent less in traffic. We were growing 10 per cent per year for the last five years,” Mr Alabbar told the Bloomberg Invest event in Dubai. He did not specify which malls were affected or over what period. He also said retail was down about 10 per cent after growing by a similar percentage annually in recent years. The hospitality business was affected too, with occupancy levels falling to about 65 per cent from 80 per cent, he added. The war, which started in late February with attacks by the US and Israel on Iran, has affected sectors in the UAE including property, tourism and aviation. The countries have yet to reach an agreement to end the war, now in its ninth month. However, US President Donald Trump has hinted that he is not planning to resume the bombing campaign as he faces calls to wind down the conflict after his party's defeat in last week's midterm elections. Mr Alabbar said the company was not slowing down its development activity, with construction continuing and projects being delivered ahead of time. “Development contractors are moving on time … material coming in … cost increasing about 5 per cent, which is OK,” he said. However, the company is “holding back” on tendering a big tower until the regional situation cools down. He did not provide further details on the new project. In June, Emaar Properties announced an “extraordinary” Dh200 billion ($55 billion) megaproject in Dubai , set to house nearly 150,000 people. The master plan, spread across more than 4.5 million square metres, is to feature residential towers, villas and mansions, Grade-A commercial offices, shops, luxury hospitality and other amenities. “It will all depend on what happens between Donald Trump and the Iranian leadership. That's really the key to everything, and [if] that happens in one month, I think the market will take 12 months, and then [it] will be in good shape,” Mr Alabbar said. He is also betting big on India, which he said “will be a major [market] for us” in the next five years as part of the company's global expansion plans. Emaar already has a presence in the country with projects in Gurugram, Mohali and other cities. The company will continue to grow in the Middle East, including the UAE, Egypt and Syria. Mr Alabbar’s developer Eagle Hills is working on two major projects in Syria, including a residential and tourism development, as part of a framework agreement the company signed with the Syrian government in October. Data centres and Anthropic investment Damac Properties founder and chairman Hussain Sajwani also spoke during the Bloomberg Invest event, outlining global expansion plans of the company. Damac is looking to expand in the UK and Australia with new data centre projects, after announcing $20 billion of investment in US data centres last year. The company is present in 14 countries and “we are in serious negotiations in the UK for a big parcel of land. We are in serious negotiation in Australia for a big parcel of land”, Mr Sajwani said. The company hopes to reach 10 gigawatts of capacity by the end of next year. “Our focus is on large data centres, which are 100MW and above. We go into where the large populations are, so the US, the EU and Asia.” The company also has investments in AI firm Anthropic and is making a lot of money from them, he said. “What I have made in 30 years [since starting his business], I made in Anthropic in less than two years. At [an] $18 billion valuation, it is going public at $1.4 trillion.” Last week, Anthropic reported revenue of nearly $17 billion in the period ending September 30, as investors brace for its potentially record-breaking IPO . The maker of Claude , a family of large language models and an AI chatbot, reported $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ending on September 30. “Between only three companies, OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic, we're making [a] few billion dollars a month.” Mr Sajwani also spoke about Nvidia and its chief executive Jensen Huang, who is embroiled in controversy over alleged extramarital affairs. “If he is forced to depart, it will be [a] big loss for the world, not for America, for the world. This guy has done a great job.”

events.title: Nvidia board prepares to oust CEO, name interim chief
events.summary: The Scoop Some members of Nvidia’s board favor appointing Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO at the beleaguered chipmaker if CEO and founder Jensen Huang is ousted, according to people familiar with the matter. The board met on Wednesday evening, though it has not yet announced its decision. Nvidia’s board has debated whether, as part of its potential replacement of Huang, to introduce a chief operating officer to serve alongside the interim chief executive, some of the people said. Semafor earlier confirmed that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang as soon as Wednesday, after media reports detailed that he had a second extramarital affair. The Nvidia board briefed the White House on its planned meeting, according to a senior administration official. Nvidia has tapped an outside search firm to find the company’s next CEO, Bloomberg reported. One person being considered for the top job is Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who was among the executives considered for Intel CEO in 2019, according to another person familiar with the matter. Whirlwind Saga Nvidia’s stock fell more than 8% in after-hours trading, hitting a 52-week low. Spokespeople for the company didn’t immediately provide a comment. Huang’s firing would cap a whirlwind saga that’s seen the global frontman for the AI boom admit to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The $4 trillion company’s long-tenured board announced a Wachtell Lipton-led probe into whether Huang may have divulged corporate secrets or endangered US national security. In addition to providing many of the most advanced chips for hyperscalers, Nvidia has entered into billions of dollars worth of financing deals underwriting the AI buildout. Democrats Move In Sens. Chris Coons, D-Del., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., sent a letter to members of President Donald Trump’s Cabinet on Wednesday asking them to preserve documents related to Nvidia’s chip exports to China or entities that could divert such chips to the country. They also asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller to preserve documents and communications concerning Huang and the suspected Chinese operative he had an affair with, as well as the correspondence between Huang and Trump. “This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote in the letter . “Reports suggest that officials within the government — including at the White House, State Department, and Commerce Department — were aware of concerns about NVIDIA, its relationship with Megaspeed, and the suspected Chinese intelligence operation, yet did not move to block the continued flow of advanced AI chips.”

events.title: ‘Greater Israel’: How Christian Zionism infiltrated US policy
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Israel, the US, Christian Zionism and the search for Armageddon. 'Greater Israel': How Christian Zionism became policy | Al Jazeera Originals A sermon becomes a map. A map becomes policy. And policy becomes land taken, homes emptied and borders redrawn. ‘Greater Israel’: How Christian Zionism Became Policy – a 22-minute Al Jazeera Originals documentary directed by Awad Joumaa – traces how a centuries-old biblical idea travelled from English fringe pulpits to the heart of US politics, and from prophecy into the machinery of modern power. Blending archival footage and AI-assisted visuals, the film explores a question that no longer belongs only to theologians or historians: what happens when a religious vision of territory is backed by votes, money, military infrastructure and state policy? In a megachurch in San Antonio, Texas, Pastor John Hagee reads the map aloud. God, he says, promised the Jewish people “one-half of modern-day Egypt, all of Israel, all of Lebanon, all of Syria, all of Jordan, all of Kuwait, and three-fourths of Saudi Arabia”. This is not a negotiation, he tells his congregation. “God’s not saying, ‘Let’s make a deal’. He’s saying, ‘This is the deal.'” Hagee is not a fringe preacher. He is the founder of Christians United for Israel, or CUFI, which claims more than 10 million members and has become one of the most powerful pro-Israel organisations in the United States. The film explores a world in which scripture is read as geography, geography becomes entitlement, and entitlement is carried to Washington, DC, through lobbying, elections and policy. The voting bloc behind the prophecy Christian Zionism is often described as a belief system. In the United States, it is also a political force. White evangelical Protestants account for roughly 13 percent of the US adult population, about 35 million people, and most identify as Republican. Their views on Israel are unusually firm. A 2018 LifeWay Research survey for Chosen People Ministries found that 80 percent of evangelicals believed the creation of Israel in 1948 was a fulfilment of biblical prophecy that would bring about Christ’s return. Roughly two-thirds said the modern state of Israel was an outgrowth of the biblical covenant. That belief translates into votes. Pew Research Center’s analysis of the 2024 election found that 82 percent of white evangelical voters backed Donald Trump in the recent midterms, the highest support of any religious group. It also shapes attitudes towards war. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs found in 2024 that 64 percent of white evangelicals said Israel’s actions in Gaza were justified, roughly double the share of Americans overall, while 60 percent opposed cutting US military aid to Israel. “The bedrock of support for the State of Israel is there because American evangelicals think it will bring Jesus back quicker,” former evangelical insider Frank Schaeffer says in Al Jazeera‘s 2024 documentary Praying for Armageddon . “And without the Republican bedrock evangelical voter, no Republican anywhere in America, for any office, gets elected. We don’t want peace, we being evangelicals. We want Armageddon.” The theology is preached from pulpits. The machinery runs through donations, lobbying and tax-exempt advocacy. The International Fellowship of Christians and Jews says it has raised more than $3.6bn since 1983, with 92 percent of its donors identifying as Christian. Mother Jones, the US publication, has traced how Christian Zionist networks have channelled money into Israeli causes, including organisations linked to settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. CUFI’s political arm is smaller in dollar terms but influential in access. OpenSecrets records $679,410 in federal lobbying spending by CUFI Action Fund in 2025. God’s not saying, 'Let’s make a deal.' He’s saying, 'This is the deal' by Pastor John Hagee, founder, Christians United for Israel The Congressional Research Service, in its 2024 overview of US aid to Israel, notes that both AIPAC and CUFI “express unequivocal support for US security assistance to Israel”. Inside Washington, the influence is structural. Ralph Drollinger’s Capitol Ministries – which advocates a “ Biblical case for defending Israel ” – runs weekly Bible studies attended by members of Congress. During the first Trump administration, it convened a cabinet-level Bible study. The theology is not only in churches; it is in the room where power gathers. The Christian Zionist map of Israel itself comes from scripture. In Genesis 15, a part of the Torah and Old Testament, God promises Abraham’s descendants land “from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates”. For Christian Zionists and some Israeli ultranationalists, that passage is not a metaphor. It is a title deed.

events.title: Nvidia stock slides after report board is preparing to oust Jensen Huang after second affair
events.summary: Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia. Joel Saget / AFP via Getty Images Nvidia stock drops 8% after two major reports dropped about CEO Jensen Huang. The WSJ reported the board was preparing to oust him days after announcing an investigation. The NYT reported Huang had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Nvidia's stock fell sharply in out-of-hours trading after new reports dropped concerning CEO Jensen Huang late on Wednesday. The Wall Street Journal reported the Nvidia board was preparing to remove Huang. Days earlier, the board said it was investigating whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort after the CEO acknowledged having an extramarital affair. The New York Times also reported new allegations on Wednesday, saying Huang had a second extramarital affair with an executive at Nvidia who reports to him, citing five unnamed sources who worked at the company. The Times said the executive was Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare. Nvidia declined to provide a statement to The New York Times. On Thursday morning, Nvidia's stock remained significantly lower in premarket trading and looked set to drop as much as 8% at the open. That would represent a fall of around $340 billion from the company's closing market value on Wednesday. Other stocks with direct ties to Nvidia also seemed to move in response to Wednesday's news. CoreWeave, a cloud computing company that uses Nvidia chips and counts Nvidia as an investor, jumped 25% during Wednesday's trading but was set to drop 5% on Thursday morning. Micron, which supplies memory used alongside Nvidia's chips, was down nearly 3% in premarket trade, while Supermicro, which builds servers, was down nearly 5%. TSMC, which manufactures the chips Nvidia designs, was down over 2.5%. After Wednesday afternoon's reports on Huang, Bernstein, a global equity research and brokerage firm, downgraded Nvidia's stock and slashed its price target in half to $200. "We admit to struggling mightily with this call, and can sympathize with the case to buy the dip," researchers at the firm wrote in their report. "But our gut tells us that we probably haven't yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here; we've had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines." On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair in a memo to employees and said he was cooperating with the board's investigation. He did not name his affair partner. The New York Times had previously reported that US intelligence officials believed Alice Huang, a tech executive who had grown close to the CEO, was recruited to gather information for Beijing. Days before disclosing his affair, Huang told Bloomberg his interactions with Alice Huang were related to their business dealings and "all completely normal and not unusual." A photo shows NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang with a woman confirmed by a Reuters source to be Alice Huang in Taipei, Taiwan released on June 7, 2024. Obtained by Reuters/via REUTERS Alice Huang , a Chinese national who is not related to the Nvidia CEO, has worked as an executive at Megaspeed, a cloud computing company in Singapore that was also an Nvidia customer. Nvidia's board hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, an elite Wall Street law firm, to carry out the investigation, with partner Joon H. Kim , a former US attorney, tapped to lead it. Lawmakers last week also sent a letter to Huang requesting he testify about his relationship with Alice Huang, citing "significant national security concerns." Nvidia succession plans Nvidia's CEO has become nearly synonymous with the company he cofounded, but the question of succession at one of the world's most valuable companies has gotten major attention this week. Nvidia has not publicly shared a succession plan . On Sunday, the board told Business Insider that "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." Analysts and former employees said there were several potential successors, including vice president Ian Buck and chief financial officer Colette Kress. Huang's two adult children, Madison and Spencer , also work at Nvidia. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Lori Huang, not Jensen, is president of the Huangs’ $9 billion foundation—and co-trustee of the trusts holding most of their Nvidia stake
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s future at Nvidia hangs in the balance as the board is reportedly preparing to oust the CEO , people familiar with the matter told The Wall Street Journal. The move follows two extramarital affairs by Huang, one of them with a suspected Chinese spy and another one reportedly with Kimberly Powell , the company’s vice president of health care, according to The New York Times . Huang admitted in a company memo made public on Nov. 8 to extramarital actions: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Lori has not commented publicly on the memo.  Huang’s position has raised questions about Nvidia’s future, including who would take the reins in his absence, given that he’s the face of the $4 trillion chipmaking giant. But in the family’s philanthropy, his wife, Lori Huang, holds the top title. Lori is president of the Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation , which reported about $9.2 billion in assets at the end of 2024, according to its most recent tax filing reviewed by Fortune. Jensen is listed as the foundation’s secretary and CFO, and Lori has held the president title on every filing available dating back to 2014. Her role also extends to most of the Huangs’ Nvidia shares. As of March 23, Lori and Jensen were co-trustees of three family trusts holding nearly 669 million Nvidia shares, according to Nvidia’s latest proxy statement reviewed by Fortune . That’s most of the 870.6 million shares (worth roughly $151 billion as of late Nov. 11) the proxy reports as beneficially owned by Jensen, a figure that also includes the foundation’s stock. The proxy also says that as board members of the foundation since 2007, the couple may be deemed to share voting and investment power over its 58.7 million Nvidia shares, though neither has a financial interest in them. Nvidia’s board said Nov. 8 it was investigating reports Jensen had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, but said it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” The independent directors later hired former acting U.S. Attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to run the probe. China’s foreign ministry has called the spying allegations groundless . Lori Huang’s role in the foundation Lori, born Lori Mills, met Jensen when the two were paired as lab partners in an electrical fundamentals class at Oregon State University, where she graduated in 1985. He was 17 and she was 19. They married in 1985, and a few years later she left the workforce to raise their two children. Both children, Madison and Spencer, now work at Nvidia. Its net assets climbed from about $819 million at the end of 2020 to more than $9.1 billion at the end of 2024, and about $8.6 billion of its holdings that year were in stocks, according to its tax filings. In 2024 alone, it gained about $5 billion in paper gains. Nvidia’s proxy shows the foundation held 58.7 million Nvidia shares as of March. In June and September 2024, Jensen and Lori, as co-trustees of their living trust, gave the foundation a combined 1.3 million Nvidia shares, according to Jensen’s Form 4 filings and the foundation’s tax return. The foundation valued those gifts at about $160 million. In September, the trust also gave 688,000 shares to an unnamed donor-advised fund. The foundation reported paying no salaries in 2024. Its only listed officers, Lori and Jensen, each report working one hour a week, unpaid, and its paid outside help consisted of an investment manager and an accounting firm. In 2024, the foundation paid out about $126.3 million in grants. More than $82 million went to Schwab Charitable Fund , which sponsors donor-advised funds, and the filing notes the foundation gave to a donor-advised fund over which it or an insider had advisory privileges. Its 2025 return, which would show whether it met that requirement, hasn’t been made public. Some public announcements from 2025 show the foundation matched $22.5 million in donations to the California College of the Arts, and in November, the Huangs announced a multi-year commitment of $5 million a year to San Francisco Opera. This year, the foundation bought about $108.3 million worth of computing capacity from CoreWeave to donate to universities and nonprofit research institutes, a filing Reuters reviewed shows. events.title: The latest FreeBSD report is here, and the AI debate is ongoing
events.summary: The FreeBSD project's status team has published FreeBSD's third status report of 2026, showing plenty of ambitious work underway and a community still undecided on how to treat code from AI coding assistants. The FreeBSD Status Report Third Quarter 2026 is a substantial document, with 51 entries from five teams covering 16 projects, plus six other sections with more detailed reports. There are updates on the progress of the Sylve project, which is an attempt to bring a smooth polished GUI for managing FreeBSD virtualization hosts – something akin to Proxmox for FreeBSD. We mentioned this when we looked at the new Daemonarchy project last month. Another covers the new AppJail effort – a containerized app distribution system for FreeBSD, including for GUI apps, which aims for something broadly comparable to Snap, Flatpak and AppImage on Linux. In other words, interesting and quite radical stuff is happening in the FreeBSD space. What this particular LLM-skeptical vulture was most interested to see, though, was an update on the internal discussion about how to handle code generated by AI coding assistants in the project. We first reported on this vexed subject back in September 2025 and no final answer has yet been published. NetBSD banned AI-generated code in 2024 and although the bot-boosters say this will doom it to irrelevance, as we reported last month, the project is thriving . Also back in October, we looked at OpenBSD 8.0 , whose launch materials are full of mockery for AI users. Under the FreeBSD Core Team section , there is a subsection headed "FreeBSD Developer AI survey." The survey was created by Baptiste Daroussin, and received 140 responses. Although the percentages show that there is some resistance to AI, there are hints here as to why it’s taking so long. Some project committers are against it, yet many more are proponents. Since there are only seven bullet points, we thought we would quote them in full: Policy: 88 percent want the Project to adopt a policy, either a formal, written policy (49 percent ) or light guidance and best practices (39 percent ). Six percent said that AI should be explicitly discouraged, and three percent that the existing contribution rules are sufficient. AI-assisted code: 35 percent said it must be disclosed, 25 percent that it must be reviewed more strictly than human code, 22 percent that it should be treated like any other contribution, and 16 percent that it should be rejected outright. Safeguards: mandatory human review (78 percent ) and mandatory disclosure (69 percent ) were requested most often, followed by provenance or licensing documentation (47 percent ) and mandatory testing (39 percent ). Disclosure: 84 percent want AI use disclosed, either always (48 percent ) or when its involvement is significant (36 percent ). 79 percent want AI-assisted commits marked in the commit log, and 56 percent prefer a tag that names the tool. Concerns: the main concerns about quality are correctness and subtle bugs (39 percent , licensing and provenance (26 percent ), and maintainability (21 percent ). 75 percent are somewhat or very concerned about copyright and licensing. Principles: accountability, meaning that a human remains responsible (91 percent ), and transparency (78 percent ) were selected most often, and preserving code quality was the top-ranked goal for a policy. Other uses: 65 percent would allow AI-generated documentation with human review. 54 percent would allow AI tools on Project infrastructure, most of them with restrictions, and 29 percent would not. Only six percent for explicit discouragement, 16 percent for outright rejection, and 35 percent against LLM-generated documentation. This plus the usual sort of calls for responsible use and disclosure, concerns about copyright issues, and so on. The Reg is strongly reminded of the Debian developer poll we reported on in August . This had no fewer than four slightly different AI-refusal options out of eight, and despite the Condorcet voting method it uses, the result was giving permission to use bots . With such relatively weak opposition, we suspect that FreeBSD will go the same way as Debian: tell developers to be careful, but allow bot usage, resulting in LLM-extruded code being committed into the project. ®

events.title: Former Sen. Roy Blunt: Trump’s latest China crackdown puts American lives on the line
events.summary: During my 12 years in the U.S. Senate, I fought to ensure the United States dominated the global biotech industry. I did so not only because that leadership helps save American lives and drive economic growth, but also because it’s critical for our national security. When American companies are second to none, we can respond quickly to public health emergencies without depending on foreign adversaries. I’ll always be proud that, in my role as chairman of the subcommittee overseeing the National Institutes of Health, I worked with colleagues in both parties to secure a nearly 50% increase in agency funding and accelerate research progress. That investment paid off during the Covid-19 pandemic, when President Trump’s Operation Warp Speed built on NIH initiatives to help end the pandemic and save countless American lives. That’s why I’m worried about a well-intended, but counterproductive, new proposal from the Treasury Department that would restrict U.S. companies’ biotech investments in China. It’s meant to enhance our national security by preventing American resources from building up China’s already growing biotech capabilities. Yet as written, the proposal is so broad that it could hurt American biotech companies far more than it hurts Chinese ones. By hampering U.S. companies’ ability to develop breakthrough medicines as efficiently and quickly as possible, the proposal risks harming American patients and undermining our national security. American drugmakers have often used acquisitions, joint ventures, and other partnerships to bring promising discoveries made abroad into our own research and development pipeline. As Chinese firms develop an increasing share of the world’s innovative drug candidates , these partnerships have only grown in their strategic importance. These arrangements give American patients greater opportunities to participate in clinical trials and potentially gain access to lifesaving treatments. They also give American companies greater influence over how and where new medicines are developed and manufactured, helping secure reliable supplies. Far from making America dependent on China, these partnerships keep American firms at the top of the global leaderboard, and ensure that China relies on the United States for medicines. In 2025, the United States recorded a $3.7 billion trade surplus with China in pharmaceuticals. In late October, the Treasury Department proposed expanding the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security (COINS) Act, which limits U.S. investments in strategically sensitive Chinese industries, to cover the biotech sector writ large. That would broadly prevent U.S. companies from investing in, acquiring, or partnering with Chinese biotech firms. Those broad restrictions are more likely to weaken the United States than China. If U.S. firms are functionally banned from partnering with Chinese biotechs, those Chinese firms won’t simply abandon their promising discoveries. Instead, they’ll seek to partner with American companies’ global rivals—or focus on building out their own research, manufacturing, and commercialization capabilities to replace the need for American partners. Over time, America could lose influence over the development and supply of the next generation of innovative medicines. Patients could face longer waits for promising treatments and fewer opportunities to participate in clinical trials. Our country could also become more reliant on foreign companies for access to future innovative drugs—a potentially serious national security vulnerability. Treasury officials would be wise to narrow their proposal to focus on biotech deals that pose clear security threats—such as agreements involving technologies that could be used to produce biological weapons—without blocking ordinary research partnerships. Treasury must also clearly define which arrangements are prohibited. Although the proposal is designed to allow standard licensing agreements, its broad language suggests that partnerships with common licensing terms could potentially be treated as prohibited joint ventures. That uncertainty could force companies to walk away from useful partnerships. At the same time, policymakers should devote more attention to strengthening America’s own scientific capabilities. That means sustaining federal investment in scientific research, strengthening our intellectual property system, safeguarding our research institutions from foreign interference, and expanding domestic research and manufacturing capacity. President Trump and his administration are right to be wary of China’s ambitions. But America can’t preserve its biotech lead by cutting itself off from promising advances made overseas. By targeting genuine security threats while preserving beneficial research partnerships, we can strengthen America’s national security and ensure that American patients continue to benefit from the world’s most promising medical discoveries. events.title: UAE has come out of the war 'exceptionally well', investment minister says
events.summary: The UAE has come out of the war “exceptionally well” and the continued economic momentum despite uncertainty is driving the government to open new sectors for foreign investment, a senior official has said. “I think we have to show investors the positive side of this, which is there is opportunity in every crisis, and [we are looking into] how do we present those opportunities to investors, how do we open up sectors that previously weren't open to investors, especially around infrastructure projects,” Mohamed Alsuwaidi, Minister of Investment, told Bloomberg Invest on Thursday. The UAE is investing heavily in infrastructure with new pipelines and ports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. It is also looking to expand port capacity on its eastern coast, including at Fujairah, projects that are expected to cost billions of dollars. The scale of the financing needs was underlined by First Abu Dhabi Bank's plan to raise as much as Dh15 billion ($4 billion) in the country’s largest rights issue, which will help support the country’s infrastructure expansion and diversification beyond oil. “I don't see a slowdown in what we're doing. We see more opportunities for investors, bigger projects coming to life,” Mr Alsuwaidi said. “AI is booming, logistics is booming, air freight is becoming a bigger business. Multiple sectors are opening up, and we need to help our investors see that and follow those trends.” The UAE continues to grow despite the impact of the Iran war. The country was attacked with hundreds of missiles and drones after the conflict broke out in late February, with damage to civilian infrastructure and energy sites. The UAE's real gross domestic product grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion in the first half of the year, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the war's impact . Foreign direct investment into the UAE rose by about 6 per cent last year to a record $48.24 billion, the ninth highest total in the world, according to UN Conference on Trade and Development data. The Emirates was also the top recipient of FDI in the Middle East, ahead of Saudi Arabia, which ranked 13th, Unctad said in its World Investment Conference 2026 report released in July. There is no dearth of capital or talent in the country and the government is moving towards new capital models to fund the massive infrastructure needs, Mr Alsuwaidi said. “I don't see a challenge in the UAE on the funding front. I see opportunity to attract third-party capital in ways we haven't in the past,” he said. “More and more projects around energy, around industries, around infrastructure in general, are being open to the public through either public-private participation, but also through partnerships with governments or local governments, but also privatisation of certain government assets.” There's also a high demand in the housing market because people are interested in coming to the UAE, and “we can't keep up with the demand, so we keep building”. Some parts of the property market, particularly offices and warehouses, were facing shortages, he added.

events.title: Fertiglobe boosts UAE exports to 95% of production but logistics costs hit profit
events.summary: Fertiglobe, the world’s largest seaborne exporter of urea and ammonia, said it has restored UAE exports to 95 per cent of production in the third quarter, despite continuing disruption at the Strait of Hormuz . That is up from 56 per cent in the second quarter, it said in a statement on Thursday to the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, where its shares trade. Reaching that figure involved extensive efforts by Fertiglobe's production and supply-chain teams as well as working with majority shareholders XRG and Adnoc, and even the government, Ahmed El Hoshy, chief executive of Fertiglobe, told The National , without disclosing the specifics on how it was achieved. The company, however, said UAE exports were supported by active inventory, logistics management and a “focused commercial approach”. The effective closure of Hormuz, through which about one third of global seaborne fertiliser passed before the Iran war began on February 28, has significantly affected the supply chain. While Fertiglobe has been transporting the stocks it had stored during the peak of the war, “we still have inventory left over, so I'd even like to export more than we've produced”, Mr El Hoshy said. However, higher freight and logistical costs have affected earnings. Net profit attributable to the owners of the company for the third quarter dropped by 90 per cent to $22.7 million. Revenue for the period, however, rose by 19 per cent to $904.5 million, driven by higher ammonia prices and sales volumes. Along with the higher logistics costs, “sometimes the logistics to get product out also made it a little bit challenging to know the timing of exports”, Mr El Hoshy said. The company also carried out a turnaround at its EBIC plant in Egypt, and during that process had to use inventories to continue selling products. “When you use inventory to sell in Q3 instead of actual production, you end up getting charged with the fixed cost for the product … [and] you end up paying a larger amount,” he said. And while ammonia prices were higher, the lower cost of urea also brought down margins, he added. Urea, the most commonly used chemical for fertiliser, recorded a significant price increase to about $720 a tonne in mid-April from about $465 a tonne on the eve of the war, according to Trading Economics. Prices have now cooled to about $430 a tonne. Fertiglobe is the largest producer of nitrogen fertilisers in the region, with a production capacity about of 6.6 million tonnes of urea and ammonia through subsidiaries in the UAE, Egypt and Algeria. Last year, it also established Fertiglobe Australia to operate assets it acquired from Chinese-based company Wengfu. Gas price impact While Fertiglobe uses long-term contracts for gas that are not linked to European gas prices, the benchmark acts as a bellwether for the industry, Mr El Hoshy said. High European gas prices have caused about 35 per cent of European ammonia capacity to remain offline, he said. Dutch front-month futures, which tracks European gas prices, was at about €90 ($100) per megawatt-hour on Thursday, more than double annually. “There's 19 million tonnes of ammonia capacity that sits in Europe today,” Mr El Hoshy said. “Their cash cost today to produce ammonia is $1,000 a tonne, and the price that is in Europe today is $750 a tonne. So there's some mismatch. Either their cost needs to come down, or the price of ammonia needs to go up to justify them restarting their plant.” Given the current situation and how low the inventories are, “we continue to be relatively constructive on the outlook for the market for ammonia and urea because the Europeans are now operating at a rate where they're not able to make money unless the price of ammonia goes up”, he said. Robots cleaning up Fertiglobe, which has implemented its initial $55 million cost optimisation target, has launched FIT3, a new programme aimed at achieving a further $30 million of annual non-gas cost savings by the end of 2028. “Together with maintenance capex normalising from 2027, this will strengthen our competitiveness and cash generation through the cycle,” the company said. The turnaround programme in Egypt and the UAE is expected to deliver strong results, Mr El Hoshy said. At the EBIC plant, production has increased by more than 20 per cent on a run rate basis. Outside of regular maintenance, the programme in Egypt used artificial intelligence to go through data from every single interruption the plant has had since it started in 2009 and it came up with a list of things needed to be done. “We discovered things and took care of it. We also used robotics for the first time to clean areas in the plant that humans couldn't get to, never been touched in 17 years, and that has allowed us to remove dust and debris,” Mr El Hoshy said. “Since we started up in September for our plant in Egypt, we have achieved rates not achieved ever in these plants, so record daily production.” Outlook The company is preparing for different scenarios and aiming to see how it can reduce costs when faced with issues such as higher temporary logistics costs. “What we've done internally is looked at … how we procure things, how we do things logistically, how we load product, where it's basically across all functional groups, [we are looking for] ways that we can reduce costs using simplified processes,” he said. Looking ahead, if the war continues, “I still think that we're in a very tough position having the Strait of Hormuz compromised for exports of sulphur, which is a which is a very important input for fertiliser, urea, ammonia and natural gas”, Mr El Hoshy added. The products must get to global markets because it's in a “very vulnerable position”. Any impact will be felt mainly in low to medium-income countries in terms of not being able to secure the adequate fertilisers they need to increase the crop yields to feed their populations, he said.

events.title: Burberry returns to profit as sales soar, from £85 socks to £9,000 coats
events.summary: CEO says ‘democratic approach’ has helped brand outperform tough market, with big rises in China and US Burberry has returned to profit as its back-to-basics strategy drove strong sales of the British brand’s coats, jackets and handbags over the summer. Joshua Schulman, the chief executive, said the luxury brand had outperformed a “challenging luxury market” to achieve sales growth of 6%, helped by strong online and wholesale sales particularly in China and the US. “Our strategy is working,” he said. Burberry said it made a pre-tax profit of £19m in the six months to 26 September after a loss of £48m a year before, as sales rose to £1.1bn. Sales rose 15% in China and 14% in the Americas but fell 1% in the Europe and Middle East region, partly due to the Iran war. Schulman said Burberry’s focus on a “pyramid of pricing” ranging from more “affordable” scarves, starting from £195, and cotton-cashmere socks from £85, to its top-tier bags and coats, which can cost more than £9,000 for a leather version, had helped it achieve growth despite a tough market. Wealthy shoppers around the world are travelling less and being more cautious about spending, hitting luxury brand sales globally. Sales of lightweight jackets and “tropical” gaberdine raincoats as well as its Cotswold range of leather bags and accessories featuring the brand’s famous check had proved popular. Schulman said: “Luxury customers around the world are experiencing some fatigue with exorbitant pricing and in this context our strategy of having great value for money is resonating strongly with Chinese customers.” “Burberry has always had a somewhat more democratic approach than some of our European peers and has a universal appeal,” he added. Schulman said the brand had spent the last two years of its Burberry Forward strategy returning to its historical position at the “sweet spot in the luxury market”. He said investment in locally relevant marketing, such as special product for China’s Valentine’s Day celebrations this spring and for the upcoming lunar new year, were also helping drive sales. “It is no secret global tourism is down but the local customer has been spending in their respective regions,” Schulman said. “This is a trend we have been seeing all year long.” While people were spending less as tourists which was hitting sales in discount outlets, Schulman said local spending was holding up in the brand’s flagship city centre stores including in London. He said that while “nobody has a crystal ball” about whether customers would begin spending more freely, history suggested “this is a very cyclical business”.

events.title: Bracing for Nvidia's impact
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's apparent from grace is a shock to a company at the core of the U.S. markets and the AI ecosystem that he did much to create. Why it matters: CEO scandals happen at companies. Their stocks fall. But there is no other company quite like Nvidia. Its size, financial resources and strategic position in the AI boom have made both the chipmaker and Huang, personally, pillars of the industry that has come to drive both the stock market and the economy. Catch up quick: Following revelations this week that Huang had admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman believed by the U.S. government to be a Chinese intelligence asset, the New York Times reported Wednesday evening that Huang also had a romantic relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him. The Wall Street Journal and other outlets are reporting that the company's board of directors was preparing to oust Huang. Nvidia shares plunged in the after-hours trading session. Context: The uncertainty surrounding Huang's position comes as the AI trade is going through one of the crises of investor confidence that have periodically hammered AI shares in recent years. The concern this time centers on the ability of the AI build-out to continue, as rising interest rates and a saturated market curtail the sale of bonds to pay for data centers. Chip makers like Nvidia have been particularly hard hit by this recent AI slump. Its shares were down roughly 30% from their recent high through Wednesday's close, vaporizing nearly $1.59 trillion in shareholder wealth. There have been market drawdowns around AI before, says Eric Sheridan, a research analyst at Goldman Sachs, in a big new report on the investment cycle. "The stakes are undoubtedly higher now as we're further along in the cycle and the dollars being spent have grown considerably, which may be adding to investor skittishness." Stunning stat: Since the end of last week, the company lost over $600 billion in market value through Wednesday's after market session. Zoom out: Those losses will touch a lot of portfolios. With a market capitalization of roughly $4.18 trillion — through Wednesday's close — Nvidia is the world's second-largest publicly traded company, behind Apple, giving it significant sway in market capitalization-weighted indexes, such as the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq 100. Yes, but: If anything, a focus on Nvidia's massive size obscures how important the company is. It dominates the market for the graphics processing units, or GPUs, that are the costliest input into AI data centers — about 75% of a data center's total cost, per Goldman. It also finances and backstops significant chunks of AI computing power. That means Nvidia is bankrolling a small army of AI firms: AI coding companies, data center operators, neoclouds. For example: Nvidia has put more than $2 billion into CoreWeave, the troubled neocloud that's seen its borrowing costs soar in recent weeks. It has equity stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI. Follow the money: Such was Nvidia's — and Huang's — stature in the tech world that in recent years, the mere mention of a company by the Nvidia CEO could create big market winners and losers . In June, for example, positive comments from Huang about Marvell Technology sent the company's stock soaring nearly 33% in a single day. State of play: Now, it's Nvidia shares that might need words of encouragement. On Wednesday the stock received a downgrade to "market perform" from "outperform" from Bernstein Research. "We admit to struggling mightily with this call, and can sympathize with the case to buy the dip," Bernstein's analysts wrote. "But our gut tells us that we probably haven't yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here; we've had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines." Morgan Stanley also removed the company from its list of "top picks" earlier in the day, after the stock had declined more than 25% since it was named top pick last month. What's next: Whatever comes next for Nvidia, the company is likely to be in an extended period of strategic paralysis. "Decisions about acquisitions or investments or product roadmaps, those are the kinds of things that will now have to be paused, if — again — if this happens, all these things are going to have to pause," Gil Luria, an analyst covering Nvidia for the brokerage firm D.A. Davidson, tells Axios. "So it just slows the company down when it can't make the most important, biggest decisions." The big picture: Huang has presided over one of the most remarkable explosions of wealth creation in market history. From the closing price on its first day of trading, Nvidia's total compound return with dividend reinvestment is 462,906%, according to FactSet. He has been at the helm of the company since he co-founded it in 1993. The bottom line: But depending on how the situation plays out, shareholders may be about to find out what an Nvidia without its charismatic leader looks like.

events.title: UK appoints climate security envoy as Thunberg criticizes COP31 leaders
events.summary: The United Kingdom has appointed a special envoy to address climate change security threats ANTALYA, Turkey -- The United Kingdom on Thursday announced the appointment of a special envoy to tackle security threats from climate change while small island leaders called for urgent action, describing planet heating as a life-or-death issue for their people at the climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya. Alix Sebastien Pillay, the vice president of Seychelles, a 115-island archipelago in the Indian Ocean, said his country's very survival is at stake. “It is time to move past the talking,” Pillay said. “For Seychelles, climate action is not simply an environmental priority.” Pillay was speaking on the second day of the leaders' summit at the U.N. climate talks, where government leaders addressed the state of a warming world and what they plan to do about it. While the entire globe is threatened by souped-up storms, hotter heat waves, worsening droughts and floods, island nations are among the hardest hit by climate change as they also have to deal with rising seas swallowing up their land. Pillay said Seychelles is experiencing millions of dollars of damage as a result of storms and floods, despite contributing little to increased global warming. He said a U.N. fund created for compensating for climate-related loss and damage needs to be urgently strengthened. “Climate recovery must not come at the expense of our development or push vulnerable nations further into unsustainable debt.” Speaking at the talks, Dalton Tagelagi, prime minister of the small Pacific Island of Niue, said the El Niño conditions which have driven up global temperatures are a warning of what might happen if planet heating is not controlled. “Sea temperatures in the central Pacific are more than three degrees above normal. It is a warning of what is coming if we do not cut emissions now," Tagelagi said. The comment came as a report said the world has failed to slow global warming trends in the past five years because plans weren’t realized and efforts that would have helped were canceled out. “Aggregated climate action has now essentially stalled for five consecutive years with positive and negative actions canceling each other out,” the independent Climate Action Tracker said in its report. The first five years after the 2015 Paris Agreement, the world did so much that it trimmed an entire degree Celsius (1.8 degrees Fahrenheit) from warming projections, but nothing has changed since, the report said. Climate change is caused mainly by the release of greenhouse gases, which happens when fuels like gas, oil and coal are burned. Confronting climate change means finding ways to drastically cut the amount of emissions put into the atmosphere each year. Countries establish plans to reduce emissions, called nationally determined contributions. The speed of reductions and ways to achieve them are different by country. Because collective efforts of countries haven't significantly reduced global emissions, the world is now “headed toward an irrecoverable overshoot of 1.5 degrees Celsius” (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures, which is the warming threshold the world adopted during the Paris Agreement, according to the report. The report said if the nations of the world fulfill all their climate promises — which is a big if — the globe will end the century 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than preindustrial times. On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the appointment of a special representative to deal with security risks from the climate crisis, one of the first such appointments anywhere in the world. “Climate is a national security issue,” Burnham said at the summit. “The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is upon us all now devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere." He said Britain would place climate resilience high on the agenda when it assumes the G20 presidency next year. Climate activists said, however, that Burnham’s policies do not fully align with the sense of urgency he expressed in his speech. “Burnham needs to start bridging the widening chasm between words and deeds on climate action,” said Ami McCarthy of Greenpeace UK in a statement. “The future we feared has become the present we are living. Climate change knows no borders. No nation can face it alone. Solidarity must mean real action,” said Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

events.title: England vs Croatia: UEFA Nations League – preview, team news, predictions
events.summary: Who: England vs Croatia What: UEFA Nations League, Group A3 Where: Wembley Stadium, London, United Kingdom When: Thursday, November 12 , at 8:45pm (19:45 GMT). How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:45 GMT ahead of our live text commentary stream Harry Kane will lead with a spring in his step and a newly acquired Ballon d’Or trophy on his arm as England host Croatia in a Nations League clash, with a spot in the quarterfinals up for grabs. The England captain will be man of the hour on Thursday after a prolific few weeks that saw him win the coveted individual honour and he will present the trophy in front of home fans ahead of the match at Wembley Stadium. Kane, 33, will also become England’s most-capped men’s player, making his 126th appearance. This surpasses the record set in 1990 by former goalkeeper Peter Shilton, who will be in attendance to mark the occasion. The Bayern Munich forward is also England’s record scorer with 91 goals. “Definitely up there with the biggest [achievements of my career],” England captain Kane told reporters at former club Tottenham Hotspur’s training ground on Wednesday after being given a standing ovation when he entered the room. “It showcases consistency at the highest level and to reach the number of caps I have is a testament to the things I spoke about in my [Ballon d’Or] speech behind the scenes, the dedication, and for sure it is one of the biggest milestones of my career.” Tuchel said Kane was the “perfect captain and a leader by example” and described his playing style as unique, adding that he is getting smarter with age. Manager Tuchel also said he has no intention of leaving the England job before the 2028 European Championship regardless of any offers from major clubs. England eye Nations League quarters England only need a draw to make it to the quarterfinals having won three and lost one of their four games so far. They sit second with nine points behind leaders Spain with 12 points, and both teams should make it to the last eight. Croatia are seeking redemption after a 7-0 thrashing from England in their previous encounter last month, followed by a narrower 2-1 defeat to Spain. The 2018 World Cup runners-up are third in the group, and manager Slaven Bilic emphasised the importance of finishing third to maintain their Nations League A status. Czechia, meanwhile, have only won once and cannot reach the quarterfinals. England will travel to Madrid to face world champions Spain on Sunday while Croatia take on Czechia in a home fixture. Bellingham brothers could feature together A major talking point for England’s squad selection was the exclusion of midfielder Cole Palmer. But a more captivating storyline is that of Jobe Bellingham finally playing alongside older brother and England star Jude. The younger Bellingham received his maiden senior call-up after impressing at Borussia Dortmund and England’s under-21 side, which he captains. Jude had previously said it would be the highlight of his career, while Jobe said it would be an emotional milestone. “I can’t ignore it, but obviously with Jude being here too, it’s a great, great feeling for the family,” Jobe said. If he features against Croatia, they will be the 22nd set of brothers to play for England and the first since Gary and Phil Neville in 2007. What happened in the last England vs Croatia game? England ran riot in Rijeka last month to obliterate Croatia 7-0 thanks to a brace each from Kane and Bukayo Saka, while Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers were also on target. Tuchel’s men took just eight minutes to go ahead with an incisive raid that exposed the talent gap between the sides. “It was the highest level from everyone and from first to last minute as well,” Tuchel said, summing up his side’s dominance. Tuchel: “For us, it’s important not to chase the same result … we want to win the match to have a chance to win in Spain, and that’s where our focus is. We expect a reaction from Croatia and we expect to overcome this mental challenge for us to start from scratch.” Bilic: “I told the players that the way we played against Spain last month is our standard. That is how we want to play, with togetherness, aggression and everything else. Tomorrow we have a chance to show that what happened in Rijeka was just a collective bad day.” The Opta supercomputer heavily favours England, with a win probability of 67.2 percent. Croatia were assigned a mere 14.8 percent chance, while a draw was estimated at an 18 percent likelihood. October 3, 2026: Croatia 0-7 England (Nations League) June 17, 2026: England 4-2 Croatia (FIFA World Cup) June 13, 2021: England 1-0 Croatia (European Championship) November 18, 2018: England 2-1 Croatia (Nations League) October 12, 2018: Croatia 0-0 England (Nations League) England will be without defenders Ezri Konsa and Djed Spence — both expected to recover for Sunday’s clash against Spain — and Tuchel is looking at James Hill for cover.
