events.summary: Uzma and Noreen released from a Lahore jail but Aleema Khan still detained nearly two months after their arrest. ⁠Uzma Khan and ⁠Noreen Niazi Khan, sisters ⁠of Pakistan’s jailed ‌former Prime Minister Imran Khan, have been ⁠released from ⁠prison, their lawyer and Khan’s political party said. “Dr Uzma Khan and Ms Noreen Niazi have been released. They have arrived home safely,” lawyer Mudassar Umer said in a post on X on Thursday. list 1 of 3 Could US midterms reshape Pakistan’s relationship with Washington? list 2 of 3 Pakistan top court orders Imran Khan’s hospital transfer amid access battle list 3 of 3 Ex-Pakistan PM Imran Khan left with 15% vision in right eye, court told The sisters were released from Kot Lakhpat maximum-security prison in Lahore, nearly two months after they were arrested. A third sister, Aleema Khan, who was detained the same day as Uzma and Noreen, remains in jail, Imran Khan party’s the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) said. “Aleema Khan remains behind bars. The release of two sisters does not end the injustice or erase the suffering inflicted on Imran Khan’s family,” PTI leader and close Khan confidant Zulfiqar Bukhari told Al Jazeera. “The demand is clear: No selective relief, no intimidation, and no further persecution.” Uzma Khan’s son, Wali Khan, called for an explanation as to why his mother had been detained for ⁠53 days and then released, saying the decisions were ⁠not based in law. “Their jailing was arbitrary, and so is their release,” he said in a post on X. The sisters were arrested and placed under 30-day detention orders a week before a planned PTI protest march on September 27 to demand their brother’s release. Imran Khan, 74, has been jailed since August 2023 following a series of convictions his party calls politically motivated. All but one have since been suspended or overturned on appeal. Concerns over his health, in particular the condition of his right eye , which has required months of specialist treatment, have driven the PTI campaign to demand his release. His sisters’ release comes a day after Khan was taken to hospital in Islamabad, where ⁠he was given medical treatment. Pakistan’s government said it detained the sisters because they could have been a threat to ‌law and order ahead of the planned march on Islamabad, which ultimately did not go ahead. The federal government suspended the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provincial government, led by Khan’s party, that had been organising the demonstration.

There might be a culprit… Microsoft has admitted that a change has caused linked server queries to fail to close connections. Linked servers via OLE DB providers have been around for years and are a useful way of, for example, using additional data sources in queries. Once a provider is added, SQL Server can open a connection to grab data, and close it again when the query is complete. Or, at least, that's the theory. The problem is that after the October 13 (KB5126646) update, connections created by SQL Server linked server queries might remain open. According to Microsoft, "As additional queries are performed, connections to external databases can accumulate instead of closing as expected. "This can slow or degrade server performance after prolonged run time." You think? Administrators will likely have already noted a suspicious number of open connections to external databases on affected systems. Microsoft said the issue affects SQL Server linked server queries that use OLE DB providers to connect to external databases. It gave PostgreSQL and Oracle as examples of connections known to be affected. And the fix? "If idle connections can be identified, it is possible to manually close them to temporarily relieve server load. "It is also possible to temporarily restore system stability by restarting the SQL service." The Windows behemoth went on to state the obvious: "However, these steps can also interrupt active queries or transactions, and the problem can resurface again after sufficient operation time." Bouncing a SQL Server to deal with connection leakage is less than ideal, although it would at least be a good failover test and, let's face it, having to restart Microsoft services regularly is something many administrators will be all too familiar with. There is a mitigation available, although only through Microsoft support for business. Otherwise, an out-of-band update should be along within the next few days to deal with the problem. According to Microsoft, the technical glitch affects every version of Windows except Windows 11 26H2, stretching back to Windows 10 1809 and LTSC 2019, and Windows Server from 2025 back to 2012. Microsoft, or rather the unfortunate souls responsible for administering their server products, has not had the best time of late. events.title: Nvidia may lose Jensen Huang. The repercussions reach far beyond chips.
events.summary: Alex Kraus/Bloomberg via Getty Images This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Jensen Huang's days appear to be numbered. That's the sentiment following a report of another affair, this time with one of his direct reports. Kimberly Powell , Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, had an extramarital relationship with Huang, according to a New York Times report on Wednesday that cited five company sources. It's the second report of Huang cheating on his wife of over 40 years, Lori . The first was Alice Huang , who has been an executive for Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. The Times reported last month that US intelligence officials believed she was passing information to Beijing. Now, The Wall Street Journal reports that Nvidia's board, which was already planning an investigation into Huang, is preparing to remove him . We've compiled what top business and tech executives are saying about the news . It's a shocking turn of events considering how a Huang ouster was considered a long shot just a few days ago. Early this week, prediction markets had the odds of him leaving before the end of 2026 below 20%. Now, the bet is less on if he'll go and more on when he'll go . When I met with Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, on Wednesday morning, he put the chances of Huang getting completely removed from Nvidia at 5-10%. "You have to handicap stuff that's really hard to handicap, right?" Mulberry told me. "But he is such a big part of whatever happens next with Nvidia, just like Elon is with Tesla and SpaceX, that it could be incredibly disruptive." But exactly how disruptive? And to whom? Let's get into it: Nvidia: Tech bull Dan Ives previously said Huang's departure would shave 30% off Nvidia's stock price . The issue isn't just Huang's massive profile in the AI ecosystem. There's also no clear successor waiting in the wings . That could force the board to look outside its own ranks. Huang: The leather-jacket-toting executive's image has certainly taken a hit. But three decades spent building Nvidia into the king of the AI trade has built him enough goodwill with some. Elon Musk said it would be "an honor" to hire Huang if he gets pushed out. China: In a race, sometimes it's less about speeding up and more about the leader stumbling. That's the current situation in AI. Chaos at Nvidia, a key asset for the US, is a chance for China to close the gap . The AI trade: AI-related volatility has been the name of the game in the market for a while. But removing arguably the highest-profile executive from his seat creates a different type of turbulence. Or does it? The broader market was up on Monday after initial reports of Huang's affair and spy scandal. Was that because investors thought Huang would survive, or a sign that the wider market's resilience is greater than that of one larger-than-life CEO? Anthropic's IPO: Entering the public market isn't something you want to do when the water is choppy. One of the world's largest companies unexpectedly replacing its CEO won't keep things smooth. Bonus points if the aforementioned company is also participating in the $26 billion private placement you're running alongside your IPO. Tech relationships: Huang potentially getting caught in a honeypot could have everyone else in the tech industry second-guessing their romantic partners . (Don't worry, I'm sure it's your personality and not your access to GPUs that she's into.) Grand Theft Auto 6: Who would have guessed that before the game's long-awaited release we'd potentially get one final submission to its long-running meme: We got a new Nvidia CEO before GTA 6. events.title: Cisco’s people chief: ‘We can’t transform our workforce without fundamentally rethinking how we lead’
events.summary: Cisco is preparing its 85,000 employees to learn new skills, experiment with AI, and rethink how they work. That takes more than teaching people how to use the technology. It takes time to learn, freedom to experiment, and leaders who are willing to change alongside them. Cisco has invested in AI tools, role-specific training, coaching, mentoring, and new career development opportunities.  That focus on its people has helped earn it the No. 2 spot on the 2026 Fortune World’s Best Workplaces™ list. Cisco is also seeing record business performance. It closed its 2026 fiscal year with record revenue and a record quarter, including record revenue per employee. “Our focus is building learning agility: the ability to learn, unlearn, experiment, and apply new capabilities as work evolves,” says Francine Katsoudas, Cisco’s executive vice president and chief people, policy & purpose officer. “We want our people to be able to influence what changes, rather than simply react to it.” Human skills matter more as AI does more Katsoudas says human judgment is one of the most important capabilities employees will need, “and the critical thinking, curiosity, and creativity that make it possible.” “As AI takes on more work, we need people to challenge assumptions and make thoughtful decisions,” she says. Research from the AI Workforce Consortium found growing demand for human capabilities, including ethical reasoning and systems thinking, in cybersecurity-related jobs. At Cisco, employees are developing human skills alongside technical ones through coaching, mentoring, and opportunities to experiment with AI. That requires something employees rarely have enough of: time. If learning matters, make time for it Cisco’s Time to Grow initiative gives every employee four dedicated hours each month to learn. “We’ve all experienced how easily learning can fall to the bottom of the priority list when business demands take over, but the skills our people will need tomorrow require investment today,” Katsoudas says. Leaders have to make time for learning, too. “When leaders openly invest in their own development, they help establish a culture where personal growth is expected and supported at every level.” At Cisco, some executives are taking that a step further: They’re learning from employees. When employees teach executives Cisco’s AI Mentorship Program, or CAMP, pairs employee AI “super users” with senior leaders. Employees are the mentors; executives are the mentees. “Understanding AI at a strategic level is very different from seeing how people actually use it in their work,” Katsoudas says. Executives aren’t just learning about AI. Every participant in the first cohort said CAMP created space for candid conversations, shared learning, and experimentation. “Our first CAMP cohort reinforced that AI fluency is less about mastering technology and more about building trust.” That trust matters when employees are being asked to try new things. Give employees room to experiment “We can’t ask people to innovate if they’re afraid to take risks or try something that might not work,” Katsoudas says. Eighty-nine percent of Cisco employees say management recognizes honest mistakes as part of doing business, compared with 38% at a typical global technology company. That makes Cisco employees 134% more likely to report that experience. And 87% of Cisco employees are learning AI through experimentation, Katsoudas says. For Katsoudas, what happens when an experiment doesn’t work is just as important. “When things go wrong, do we create opportunities to learn and improve together? If we want to innovate faster, we have to accept that some experiments won’t work and learn from them.” Eighty-eight percent of Cisco employees say people who try new and better ways of doing things are celebrated, compared with 65% at a typical global technology company. The same percentage say people quickly adapt to change, compared with 68%. Connecting people and performance For Cisco, getting more from AI starts with leadership. “The biggest lesson is that we can’t transform our workforce without fundamentally rethinking how we lead,” Katsoudas says. How leaders use AI matters, too. Cisco employees are twice as likely to use AI when their direct leader does. But role modeling is only part of the job. Employees also need to understand where the company is going and the role they have in getting there. “In periods of significant change, people need clarity about where they’re headed, confidence that they have a meaningful role in getting us there, and trust in the decisions being made,” Katsoudas says. Cisco also had its strongest year for employee productivity in 30 years, Katsoudas says. Nine in 10 Cisco employees say people are willing to put in extra effort, compared with about two-thirds at a typical global technology company, according to Great Place To Work data. Katsoudas says Cisco is seeing higher productivity and engagement among employees who consistently use AI. “That’s encouraging because we’re seeing benefits that extend beyond efficiency,” she says. Cisco also wants employees to spend more time on customers, relationships, and solving complex problems. For Katsoudas, the companies that ultimately get AI right will be as intentional about investing in people as they are in technology. “AI is changing what technology can do, but we need to be equally ambitious about what people can become.” Roula Amire is the senior content director at Great Place To Work . events.title: Current price of oil as of November 12, 2026
events.summary: By 6:30 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil had reached $94.58 per barrel, measured using the Brent benchmark. That’s $1.14 less than it cost yesterday morning and about $31.50 above its price a year earlier. Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $95.72 -1.19% Price of oil 1 month ago $106.68 -11.34% Price of oil 1 year ago $63.01 +50.10% Will oil prices go up? Oil prices are inherently unpredictable. While many variables come into play, the basic push and pull of supply and demand is what ultimately matters. In times of heightened concern about recession, war, or other major disruptions, oil can swing suddenly. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices Each gallon you pay for at the pump bundles together several costs. Crude oil is one piece, but you also pay for refineries, wholesalers, government taxes, and the price markup set by gas stations. Because crude oil usually accounts for more than half of the price per gallon, it tends to move the needle the most. Sharp increases in oil almost always show up quickly at the pump. Declines in the price of oil, on the other hand, often translate into slower, more delayed drops in gas prices—the “rockets and feathers” effect. The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve When an emergency arises, the U.S. has a reserve of crude oil called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its chief function is to secure energy during disasters like sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also help take the edge off brutal price spikes when supply gets hit. It’s not a solution for the long haul. It’s more of an immediate safety net to support consumers and keep crucial sectors of the economy running (think key industries, emergency services, public transportation, and the like). How oil and natural gas prices are linked Oil and natural gas are two of the main fuels that keep the world running. A big change in oil prices can end up affecting natural gas. As an example, if oil prices increase, some industries may sub natural gas for certain areas of their operations wherever possible. This can increase demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil The oil market typically tracks two benchmarks: Brent crude oil (the main global oil benchmark) West Texas Intermediate (WTI) (the main benchmark of North America) Between the two, Brent offers a clearer view of global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. It’s also often the preferred gauge for tracking historical oil trends. In fact, the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. Looking at the Brent benchmark over multiple decades, you’ll find oil has been anything but stable. It’s seen sharp rises due to factors like wars and supply cuts, along with steep declines tied to global recessions and oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s saw the first major oil shock when the Middle East slashed exports and placed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices fell in the mid-1980s for reasons including lower demand and the entry of more non-OPEC oil producers. Prices jumped again in 2008 with increased global demand, but then plunged alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand collapsed like never before—bringing prices below $20 per barrel. Bottom line, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. It’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more. Energy coverage from  Fortune Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage: Anthropic inks $3.4 billion deal for gas-powered data centers Lumen CFO expects up to $1.5 billion from legacy copper amid pivot to AI connectivity Venture Global plans to become the world’s largest gas exporter in a year Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. events.title: Xi Jinping says Taiwan’s ‘complete reunification’ with China will happen
events.summary: Chinese president says the tide of history ‘cannot be stopped’ as Taiwan rejects ‘one country, two systems’. Chinese President Xi Jinping has said the tide of history cannot be stopped, while urging peaceful “reunification” with Taiwan. Resolving the Taiwan question is an “unwavering historical mission” of China’s Communist Party, Xi said in a speech at Beijing’s Great Hall of the People on Thursday. list 1 of 3 China sanctions Paraguay, Belize ministers over Taiwan ties list 2 of 3 ‘Hybrid warfare’: Taiwan drives away 16 Chinese ships list 3 of 3 War, tariffs and China: What the US midterms mean for the Asia-Pacific “The tide of history ⁠⁠cannot be stopped,” Xi added. “The complete reunification of the motherland must be realised, and it will certainly be realised.” China views democratically governed Taiwan as ⁠⁠its own territory, despite Taipei’s strong rejection of that claim, and has repeatedly offered a “one country, two systems” model of autonomy not supported by any major Taiwanese political party. Xi’s comments came in a speech on the 160th birthday of revolutionary hero Sun Yat-sen, who helped lead a 1911 ‌‌revolt that ended centuries of rule by emperors and empresses and ushered in the Republic of China. Taiwan’s government dismissed the remarks. Its Mainland Affairs Council said neither the government nor Taiwan’s people could accept “one country, two systems”, which would ultimately mean submitting to the Communist Party’s rule. “As for the wording on Taiwan unification, it isn’t much different from the past,” council spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh told reporters. Xi said China adheres to “peaceful reunification and the policy of ‘one country, two systems'” and is willing to talk to Taiwan while upholding the “one China principle”, or Beijing’s position that both sides of the Taiwan Strait are one country. All Chinese, including those in Taiwan, should join hands to jointly oppose Taiwan independence “separatist” forces and strive for peaceful development of cross-Strait ties, Xi added. Although Xi did not mention the use of force, which China has never renounced for Taiwan, China’s military operates around the island on a daily basis and is extending its reach further into the Pacific. Taiwan’s defence ministry said it had detected 29 Chinese military aircraft, including J-16 fighter jets and drones, carrying out a “joint combat ⁠⁠readiness patrol” around Taiwan in conjunction with Chinese warships, starting on Thursday. Xi’s speech comes a ⁠⁠week ahead of the APEC summit in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, where he is due to again meet US President Donald Trump, and also a little more than two weeks before important local elections in Taiwan. The Chinese president made a state visit to Washington in September, during which he told Trump to show “prudence” over Taiwan and urged the US to oppose the island’s independence. Washington had already paused a $14bn weapons purchase by Taiwan in May, with Trump calling it a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China, which raised fears that Taiwan’s security could be traded away.

events.title: Nvidia board weighs Jensen Huang’s future: Can it remove its founder?
events.summary: CEO of chip maker is under scrutiny after reports of affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Jensen Huang may be ousted as the CEO of Nvidia after the tech giant lost more than $600bn in market value this week, following reports that he had extramarital affairs with two women, including a businesswoman accused of spying for China. Nvidia’s board of directors met late on Wednesday to decide whether to remove Huang, who cofounded the $4.2 trillion company, which supplies most of the chips used for advanced artificial intelligence (AI). list 1 of 3 Trump says FBI probing Nvidia CEO Huang’s affair with alleged spy list 2 of 3 Nvidia spy scandal fuels debate over chip exports to China list 3 of 3 Xi Jinping says Taiwan ‘reunification’ with China must happen Huang, 63, admitted on Sunday in a memo to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife, following the reports of a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom United States officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence, a claim China has denied. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Huang had another extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reports to him. The newspaper cited five people who worked at the company. Nvidia’s shares fell more than 8 percent in after-hours trading on Wednesday after The Wall Street Journal reported that the board was preparing to oust Huang. Under Nvidia’s bylaws, Huang can be removed “with or without cause” by a majority vote of directors. The board has 11 members, and all but Huang are considered independent. Huang owns about 3.6 percent of the company, according to LSEG data, and has no majority voting control. That sets Nvidia apart from other tech giants. Huang does not have majority voting control, unlike executives at other companies in the sector, such as Meta and SpaceX. Nvidia also has no board chair, which Steve Okun, a Singapore-based geopolitical analyst, called “pretty astounding”. “But what this certainly shows is the utter lack of appropriate governance at Nvidia,” Okun told Al Jazeera. “This should never have been allowed to happen.” On Sunday, the board launched an independent investigation into whether Huang had been “the target of a foreign intelligence effort”, while saying it had “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team”. Bloomberg reported that the board had been working with an outside firm to identify possible replacements. Huang has never named a successor, but the Reuters news agency reported that analysts see two likely internal candidates: Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress and engineer Ian Buck. Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at the technology research group Omdia, described Buck as “a highly regarded industry veteran”, but said: “This remains a speculation until the final decision”. What would his departure mean for Nvidia? Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it ever since, turning a maker of graphics chips for video games into the world’s leading supplier of processors that power AI. Nvidia controls an estimated 80 to 90 percent of the market for the chips used to run advanced AI, and is the world’s second-most valuable company after Apple. “Jensen is no doubt the de facto leader of Nvidia,” Su told Al Jazeera, pointing to his “willingness to make early bets, identify major technological shifts, and steer the company in the right direction”. Su said the impact on short-term continuity would be minimal, but a new leader could change the company’s long-term direction, “as a different CEO may have a different view of the future”. Investors are bracing for that outcome. “The market is starting to price Nvidia without its founder as the likely outcome, not a tail risk,” Armina Rosenberg, cofounder of Minotaur Capital, which holds Nvidia shares, told Reuters. For Okun, the question is whether Huang is bigger than Nvidia, or whether the company has become so unique in what it makes that it no longer needs him. “That’s the question everybody’s going to try and figure out from a business perspective,” he said. The alleged spy link “spices up the story quite a bit”, Okun said, adding that even without it, Nvidia faced “an extraordinarily damaging question”: Why Megaspeed received so many of its chips, and where they went. Megaspeed bought about $4.8bn worth of equipment from Nvidia, according to The New York Times. US authorities have been investigating the company since 2024 over suspicions that it helped China obtain advanced Nvidia chips in breach of export controls, an allegation Megaspeed denies. But Carsten Holz, an expert on the Chinese economy at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, told Al Jazeera that the likelihood that Huang “could pass on significant technical information to another person, whether a spy or not, would seem extremely low”.

events.title: Who is Scott Colom, Mississippi’s first Black senator in 150 years?
events.summary: Mississippi is home to a large Black American population but no Black person has held a Senate seat since the 1800s. United States prosecutor and Democrat Scott Colom has made history in Mississippi by becoming the deeply conservative state’s first Black senator in more than 150 years and ushering in the first Democratic victory there in more than four decades. Senator-elect Colom’s narrow victory against Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith was declared late on Wednesday, more than a week after the US midterms, which many have called a “blue tsunami” as Democrats firmly seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives. list 1 of 4 Democrat Scott Colom wins closely watched US Senate race in Mississippi list 2 of 4 What’s delaying the US Senate election results in Mississippi and Alaska? list 3 of 4 John Thune re-elected as US Senate Republican leader after midterm losses list 4 of 4 Zohran Mamdani’s influence grows as Democrats eye 2028 strategies It has been 43 years since Democrats last won a Senate seat in the state, in 1982. But Colom’s win is significant beyond party politics and marks a turning point for Mississippi’s African American community too: he’ll be the first Black American senator since 1874. What was the Mississippi Senate result? It was a narrow victory. Colom beat Hyde-Smith, the incumbent and an ally of President Donald Trump, by fewer than 5,000 votes after 99 percent of ballots had been counted late on Wednesday. Hyde-Smith had been ahead in polling for Mississippi, where Trump won by 23 points in 2024. Colom’s win puts Democratic Senate control at 55-44. Another tight race in Alaska is still being counted, although Democrat Mary Peltola is also leading there by a slim margin. Only 14 Black senators have ever been elected or appointed in the US. Colom will be one of seven new Black senators. On Wednesday, after the results were called, Colom told supporters at his victory party in Jackson that he had come close to giving up. “There were times when I was tired, and I felt like I couldn’t keep going, but I kept the faith,” the politician said, speaking at the historically Black Tougaloo College. “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.” Colom continued to thank his supporters in a series of messages on X on Thursday. “This victory belongs to all of us, and I am honored to be your new senator-elect,” he posted. Colom, 43, is a lawyer who has served as a Mississippi prosecutor since 2016 until this year. He is married to Nadia Colom and has two children. His identical twin brother, Andrew, played a major role in his campaign. The politician was born in Columbus and comes from a family of lawyers. Despite having one of the largest populations of Black Americans in the country, there has not been a statewide elected Black official in more than 140 years in Mississippi. In interviews, Colom has said he decided to run to “look out for the people”, especially on the issue of affordability. He accused incumbent Hyde-Smith of neglecting the state and “selling out” Mississippians. In 2015, Colom became the first Black American to be elected as district attorney for the 16th Judicial District, which includes the white-majority counties of Clay, Lowndes, Noxubee and Oktibbeha. One of his most notable cases was Eddie Lee Howard, a Black American man who had spent 26 years on death row for murder but was released in 2021 as a result of a lack of evidence. After a judge dismissed the murder charge against him, Colom confirmed that prosecutors were dropping it. In 2022, Colom was nominated as a US district judge by ex-President Joe Biden, but his nomination was blocked by Hyde-Smith, who claimed he was supporting transgender athletes and that he received funding from left-wing billionaire George Soros. How did Colom win over Republican voters? Many have credited Colom’s endearing personality, his respectful rhetoric, and especially his simple but effective campaign advertisements that supporters say are both funny and thought-provoking. He naturally appealed to Black voters, but also managed to reach the white majority. In one advertisement, Colom played on his opponent’s weaknesses. In February, a TV reporter had asked Hyde-Smith, a rancher, how Republicans were attempting to address rising beef prices amid the US-Israel war on Iran. Hyde-Smith suggested that Mississippians find alternatives. “You know, you have so many proteins to choose from,” she said. The response drew outrage. Colom’s advertisement called on people not to pick another protein, but to “pick another senator instead”. Colom’s wife, Nadia, featured prominently in the campaign. In one advertisement, just as Colom tells a reporter he does not have a nickname, Nadia appears and calls him “Sweet Thang”. Colom’s final campaign video struck a more melancholy tone.

events.title: European tech buyers add digital sovereignty to cyber shopping list
events.summary: European tech buyers are increasingly choosing cybersecurity vendors from their own continent in a bid to reduce their reliance on American technology. Digital sovereignty isn't only prompting enterprise customers to question their clouds of choice, it is also reshaping other parts of the industry too, and the shift is marked. According to sales figures compiled by Context, distributor sales in EMEA of cybersecurity products from EU-headquartered vendors jumped 35 percent in the two years to calendar Q3 2026. Total cybersecurity sales grew up 10 percent over the same period, and sales by US-run companies went up just 8 percent. That growth is from a relatively small base, though EU vendors gained nearly three percentage points to reach 15 percent of tracked sales by value. There is still a long way to go as US-headquartered vendors accounted for 62 percent. The trend coincides with a loss of trust in the Trump administration among customers outside of America, after it cosied up to autocratic rulers while criticizing and punishing allies with tariffs and more. Context stopped short of assigning blame. It said organizations are reviewing their reliance on third-party tech in light of EU compliance regimes: the NIS2 Directive and Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA). NIS2, transposed into national law in October 2024 , requires organizations in the bloc to raise their common level of security in the face of digital threats and risks to critical infrastructure. DORA, introduced in January last year, is designed to strengthen cyber security in the financial sector. "Digital sovereignty is becoming a buying decision. As customers and resellers get clearer about what it means in practice, they're asking who holds the encryption keys, who can access sensitive logs and where that data is stored," said Context veep of research Joe Turner. "We're seeing a measurable shift in the EMEA channel. EU vendors gained nearly three points of sales share in two years. An organization can keep its existing identity platform and still choose a European supplier to manage its security logs. That's the kind of decision that gives European vendors an opening." The stats indicate that EU-HQd vendors comprised 92 percent of tracked sales in security awareness training, 82 percent in vulnerability management, and 52 percent for SIEM and log management. US-headquartered companies held into 74 percent of identity and access management sales and 54 percent of cloud security sales. The Reg has asked Context for UK-specific figures to see whether British customers are also voting with their wallets for European alternatives. That certainly isn’t the case for tech purchases in the British public sector, despite Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s professed desire to buy British. Data released yesterday by the Institute for Public Policy Research showed just £1 in every £6 spent by government with the biggest technology suppliers goes to Brit businesses. Still, Burnham only came to power in July so there is time yet for him to put his money where his mouth is. Sovereign AI is another area of concern for enterprise customers. Analyst Omdia said last month that despite the marketing adjective meaning "local assets," almost a third AI providers disclose no proof of sovereignty, and some "expect enterprise to pay for audits to verify their claims." Omdia also found that 80 percent of contracts say network resilience is "out of providers control or responsibility," and "US-headquartered AI providers offer better service transparency and contract terms than a majority of local sovereign AI providers, with providers in India a notable exception." Sovereign services in Omdia's classification include data residency, operational autonomy, jurisdictional sovereignty, and technological autonomy. "Local hosting is not sovereignty. Serious providers must demonstrate their credibility through transparent operations, fair contracts and proof of competence. That includes the network, because data in transit must be sovereign too," said Camille Mendler, research director for telco B2B at Omdia. Someone should tell Microsoft and Anthropic . ®

events.title: Scout Motors has 212,000 vehicle reservations as $2 billion South Carolina plant nears completion
events.summary: Scout Motors has roughly 212,000 reservations for its Terra pickup and Traveler SUV, CEO Scott Keogh told CNBC. Construction of Scout's more than $2 billion South Carolina Production Center is in its final phase. Keogh said roughly 87% of reservations are for extended-range models and about 75% are for the Traveler SUV. BLYTHEWOOD, S.C. — Electric vehicle startup Scout Motors has notched roughly 212,000 reservations for its upcoming EVs as the company nears completion of its new $2 billion plant in South Carolina, CEO Scott Keogh told CNBC. The reservations are for the Volkswagen -backed company's Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV, which are expected to start full production next year before deliveries begin to customers in 2028. Reservations do not necessarily translate to sales, as the U.S. automotive industry has learned during the past decade, especially with highly anticipated all-electric trucks such as the Ford F-150 Lightning, Tesla Cybertruck and others that garnered strong interest that didn't lead to meaningful numbers of purchases. Keogh said he expects Scout could roughly double those reservations by the time customer production begins, but he said the more important thing is to convert early interest into actual sales as production nears. "It's been a consistent drumbeat," Keogh said during an interview at Scout's plant site outside Columbia, South Carolina. "I think we could easily be up over 400,000 with reservations without doing too much effort. The big thing for us is how much of the initial production can we 100% presell." Keogh said achieving an order book of 12-to-18 months "would be great" and something he thinks the company can do before production. Scout on Thursday said construction is "in its final phase." Scout's vehicles will be offered as all-electric versions as well as electric hybrid variants, known as extended-range electric vehicles , or EREVs, that include an engine as a backup generator for the electric motors and batteries. Scout, a former American vehicle brand from 1961 to 1980, was expected to exclusively offer EVs in a bid for the German automaker to expand its presence in the U.S. However, slower-than-expected adoption of EVs and higher costs led the company to decide to offer EREVs as well. Keogh said the EREVs and SUV are dominating reservations thus far, with roughly 87% choosing EREV models and 75% being SUVs. Given the interest signaled by reservations, Keogh said the company is expected to launch with the EREVs first, followed by the EVs. He also said the company plans to launch with mid-level models first, a deviation from many companies that begin with their highest-priced models. "The No.1 thing for me is I want to go get the best volume as soon as possible," Keogh said. "In my mind, it's how quick can you get to 100,000 units? It's at 100,000 units where you can start to punch through." His comments come months after Rivian Automotive received criticism online for launching its R2 SUV with its highest-priced models first, despite that being a common practice across the automotive industry. Keogh said Scout's South Carolina plant is about 85% complete, but supporting infrastructure and a $300 million supplier park continue to be installed. Reservations for Scout's vehicles initially opened in October 2024, when it revealed the Traveler and Terra , which feature sleek, yet rugged, exterior appearances that pay some homage to the brand's historic models.

events.title: What playing cricket for the U.S. taught me about the hardest decisions CEOs face
events.summary: Long before I became a CEO, I played international cricket for the United States. The lesson I draw on most in business is this: Before deciding how aggressively to play, you have to read the pitch. In cricket, the pitch is the strip of ground at the center of the field. Its condition can change the game. On one surface, 200 runs might be an excellent score. On another, 400 may be achievable. You have to judge the surface, the opposition, and your team. Misread it, and you can execute exceptionally well and still lose. You might reach the target you set, only to discover you aimed far too low. CEOs face a similar risk. We spend enormous energy asking whether teams are performing and plans are being executed. Those questions matter, but they come after a harder one: Have we correctly understood what is possible? A CEO’s highest-leverage contribution is setting the right ambition. That requires three judgments. 1. Identify the few decisions that actually change the game CEOs don’t create value by making the most decisions. If an organization works properly, people make thousands of decisions about products, customers and operations every day. The CEO’s disproportionate value often comes from a few choices that determine where all that execution is directed. I faced one within my first few months at Bluebeam. There was pressure to move more aggressively from 2D into 3D. Newer technologies were attracting attention, and it was reasonable to ask whether our established approach would remain relevant. I had to decide without anything close to perfect information. I had customer conversations, research, and pattern recognition from other industries, where technologies sometimes remain valuable long after people predict their replacement. I came to believe 2D was not a declining market we needed to escape. It was a growing market where Bluebeam already had a significant advantage. We made two deliberate choices: stay focused on 2D rather than aggressively pursue 3D, and resist becoming a broader platform company. That simplified our strategy and freed resources to invest in what we did well. We chose where our innovation could matter most. The results reinforced our conviction. When we made that decision in September 2023, Bluebeam had more than 3 million users worldwide. By the fourth quarter of 2025, that number had reached 4 million. Bluebeam also experienced approximately 45% new-user growth from 2024 to 2026. No single decision explains a company’s growth, and user counts alone don’t show what caused it. But the results strengthened my belief that focusing on a proven strength could be more valuable than chasing an adjacent opportunity simply because it was attracting attention. I knew the decision carried real risk. Had I misread the market, we might have directed the organization away from its future. But that is exactly where CEOs have to add value: choosing among plausible paths when information is incomplete and waiting for certainty has a cost of its own. Organizations naturally gravitate toward visible problems: a struggling product, a weak geography, a missed target. The most visible problem, though, is not always the largest opportunity. Sometimes the best allocation of leadership attention is to contain a weakness and put disproportionate resources behind a strength. 2. Decide what the conditions actually support When I joined Bluebeam , I had to determine not simply whether the company was performing well, but what it could become. Those are different questions. I looked at the market, product, team, and broader environment and believed the company had more potential than we were asking of it. The cricket analogy I used internally was simple: We were playing as though we were on a 200-run pitch. I believed it was a 400-run pitch. So we raised the ambition. Importantly, much of the same team began performing against a higher bar. That experience reinforced a mistake leaders can make: confusing limited ambition with limited capability. Leaders’ instinct is often to change the people, rewrite the strategy, or reorganize. Sometimes that is necessary. But a company can hit its plan and still underperform its opportunity. “Think bigger” is not a strategy. Ambition must be grounded in what the market, product, and organization can support. Sometimes the right diagnosis requires lowering expectations. Other times, the greater failure is asking too little of a capable team. 3. Know what would prove your diagnosis wrong Experience makes those calls possible. Over time, leaders build a library of patterns from markets that turned, products that succeeded, and strategies that failed. But experience can also become a trap. You begin seeing the same pattern everywhere. I try to treat pattern recognition as a hypothesis, not a verdict. The question is not only why I believe I am right, but what evidence would change my mind. When we made the 2D decision, I knew which signals to watch. If customer conversations shifted decisively toward other needs, or sales and revenue failed to respond, we would need to reconsider our judgment. But once a strategy has been funded, presented to a board and communicated to employees, reversing course becomes psychologically expensive. Leaders can end up defending the plan rather than testing its assumptions. The answer is not to react to every new data point. Constantly changing direction makes sustained execution impossible. It is to distinguish noise from evidence, and conviction from stubbornness. Execution starts with diagnosis Cricket taught me that before deciding how aggressively to play, you must understand the game in front of you. Business leadership is much the same. Before concluding a team is underperforming, ask whether the objective is right. Before fixing the most obvious weakness, ask whether a bigger opportunity deserves your attention. And before celebrating that the company hit its plan, ask whether the plan captured the opportunity in the first place. Sometimes the most consequential thing a CEO can do is see the same company and the same market everyone else sees — and recognize that they are playing a 200-run game on a 400-run pitch. events.title: Ukraine warns of fresh Starshield disruptions as U.S. envoys arrive in Moscow for talks with Putin
events.summary: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday that fresh restrictions on Starshield operations over Ukraine had been imposed. He said Ukraine is trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side. Similar speed limitations were imposed last month at speeds above 160 kilometers per hour. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was investigating what he described as fresh restrictions on SpaceX's Starshield service over the country, after similar speed limitations were temporarily imposed last month. "Our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now – along the entire front line and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," he wrote on X early Thursday. Starshield is SpaceX's satellite network for government and national-security use, built on Starlink technology. CNBC has reached out to SpaceX and the White House for comment. "The Ukrainian military have already investigated the circumstances, and these are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions," he said, adding that they are trying to establish the circumstances with the U.S. Zelenskyy said the restrictions imposed an effective speed limit on terminals moving at speeds above 161 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour), disconnecting anything that was moving faster and making it harder for Ukraine to intercept Russian jet-powered drones. "There have already been strikes that got through because our interception systems cannot reach sufficient speeds and are unable to intercept in time." On Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by cutting connectivity speeds and thereby disrupting military operations. On October 24, Zelenskyy confirmed that systems had returned to their previous operating speeds. According to The Wall Street Journal, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk ordered those restrictions, rendering some Ukrainian strike and interceptor drones virtually unusable. The newspaper later reported that U.S. President Donald Trump had asked Musk to reverse the move. Trump has denied that the White House ordered Starlink restrictions in Ukraine. Musk initially appeared to pin responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government, writing on X that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government." He later claimed Ukraine had violated Starlink's terms of service, prompting the company to restrict its access to the high-speed satellite technology, something that Ukrainian officials have strongly contested . Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense tech advisor to Zelenskyy, said at the time that Ukraine cannot use commercial Starlink for medium- or long-range drone strikes because the service does not operate over Russian territory and had imposed drone speed limits of 70–90 kilometers per hour for months. On Thursday, Beskrestnov confirmed that "the speed of Starlink operation during movement was again limited." "We did not rejoice for long," he said, adding that "any terms can be changed and discussed, instead of leaving our country without sky protection." The comments came as U.S.-brokered peace talks wrapped up in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday and U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow for further talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin . Witkoff and Kushner were met by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev as they arrived at Vnukovo Airport on Thursday morning, according to Russian state news agency Tass. The pair were expected to discuss a lasting resolution to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which has now raged for more than four-and-a-half years. Later on Thursday, Witkoff and Kushner are poised to meet with Zelenskyy on the sidelines of a political summit held in Ireland. Trilateral talks in the United Arab Emirates between Ukrainian, Russian and American negotiators ended earlier this week without a major diplomatic breakthrough on a ceasefire or territorial settlement.

events.title: What smart people in business and tech are saying about the Nvidia board potentially ousting Jensen Huang
events.summary: Jensen Huang's potential ouster as Nvidia CEO has got people in tech talking. Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty Images Nvidia stock fell 8% following a Wall Street Journal report that the company's board plans to oust CEO Jensen Huang. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang had a second extramarital affair, this time with an Nvidia employee. This is what smart people in business and tech are saying about Huang's potential exit from Nvidia . Speculation over what Nvidia's future could look like without its high-profile chief executive ramped up on Wednesday. The chipmaker's stock fell 8% in after-hours trading Wednesday after The Wall Street Journal reported that its board was preparing to remove CEO Jensen Huang . The New York Times also reported Wednesday that Huang had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him, citing five people who worked at the company. The report came days after Huang said in a memo to employees that he had an extramarital affair , and after Nvidia's board launched an investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The New York Times previously reported US officials believed Huang had grown close to a tech executive, Alice Huang , who had been recruited to gather information for the Chinese government. As the chip giant's succession plans remain unknown, here is what smart people in business and tech are saying about Huang's potential exit from Nvidia . Ross Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management Ross Gerber has been bearish on Tesla. Emma McIntyre/Getty Images Ross Gerber said Huang's departure would be a disappointment for Nvidia shareholders but said the company could move forward without him. "Looks like Jensen is done. What a disappointment. Sad day for Nvidia shareholders and looks like another tough day for the stock. Never would have guessed he'd go down this way," Gerber wrote in one of several posts on X on Wednesday. "Jensen will be replaced and Nvidia is still Nvidia. That's business. He must go and Nvidia needs to focus on selling chips!" Gerber added. Eric Wallerstein, chief macro strategist at Clocktower Group Eric Wallerstein wrote on X on Wednesday that Huang's likely ousting could shake investor confidence in the broader AI trade , given Nvidia's role in financing the industry. "Jensen has helped foster a complex web of circular financing relationships, and ultimately backstopped the AI trade, with Nvidia's balance sheet," Wallerstein said. "Removing that Put, or even placing uncertainty on its availability, will cause investors to increase the risk premium on AI-related assets," Wallerstein added. Ed Zitron, CEO of EZ Primary Research Carlos Rodrigues/Sportsfile for Web Summit via Getty Images Ed Zitron said in a post on X that he questions what else Nvidia might be withholding from investors, pointing to the company's past regulatory troubles. "Oh so NVIDIA knew about this affair already, huh? What else is this company not telling us?" Zitron wrote on Wednesday. Zitron also cited two previous SEC cases involving Nvidia, one in 2002 over accounting practices and one in 2022 over disclosures related to cryptocurrency mining and gaming revenue. Jason Calacanis, co-host and executive producer of the All-In Podcast Jason Calacanis said that the ban was "smart" because of the risk of terrorism. Bloomberg/Getty Images Jason Calacanis said the company shouldn't be so quick to remove Huang. "A much better solution for NVIDIA's board, shareholders, customers and employees (and America) would be to (a) finish their investigation and (b) make @JensenHuang the chairman if it comes to that," Calacanis wrote on X on Wednesday. "China doesn't need NVIDIA's chips. America needs NVIDIA to win. Act accordingly," Calacanis added, alongside a screenshot of his new Nvidia share purchases. Keith Urbahn, president of Javelin Keith Urbahn, president of Javelin, a literary and creative agency that has repped prominent figures like James Comey and Tucker Carlson, said Wednesday in an X post that the situation was "a generational case study in how not to manage a crisis." He outlined several lessons to take away from the ordeal, including: "Never let a CEO's personal crisis take precedence over the interests of the company and its shareholders." "The board must speak with its own voice. It cannot outsource its institutional credibility to the CEO," he added. Byrne Hobart, venture capitalist and founder of The Diff Byrne Hobart, general partner at Anomaly Fund and founder of The Diff, a finance and tech newsletter, suggested ousting Huang could lead to new competition for Nvidia. "On one hand, boards have to do what they have to do. On the other hand, he's a guy who's worth $150bn, knows everyone in hardware, named his company after the Latin word for "spite," and he lives in a state where you can't enforce noncompetes," he wrote in a post on X. Anthony Pompliano, crypto investor and entrepreneur Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images for Anthony Pompliano Anthony Pompliano, a crypto investor and entrepreneur, wrote on X: "Jensen's yet-to-be-launched Nvidia competitor is going to do numbers in the seed round." Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management Peter Foley/Bloomberg via Getty Images Gene Munster, a tech analyst and managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, said in an X post that Nvidia will go on, with or without its famous CEO. "Remember: AI infrastructure customers will act in their best interest," he said. "That means they'll keep buying just as many $NVDA chips with or without Jensen." He also said he guesses the stock will open on Thursday at $150, or about 20% lower than the close at the end of last week, but that he expects it to "quickly rally back." Jim Cramer, host of CNBC's Mad Money Jim Cramer said Apple's new filing was "gloves off." John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images Jim Cramer, who has interviewed Huang on several occasions, questioned how investors should value Nvidia if Huang were suddenly gone. "As I said this morning, there is a bench. As Mike from Coreweave said, there is a company," Cramer said on X on Wednesday. "What is it worth when a key man is just erased?" "Let me think about how sickening this is and then i will come back to you," Cramer added. "I want to throw up." Vinod Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures Vinod Khosla said he agreed that Huang had shown grace in his handling of the affair. Olivia Vanni/Getty Images The founder of venture capital firm Khosla Ventures backed calls to treat the matter seriously while praising Huang's record. Khosla wrote, "Agree with Ron!" on X in a response to VC Ron Conway's post. Conway said the situation should be taken seriously, but urged people to remember Huang's "determination and vision," which he said laid the foundation for much of today's technology industry. He added that Huang's statements had shown "grace." Dan Niles, founder and portfolio manager

events.title: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
events.summary: Computer programming and consultancy services in particular contributed to overall growth (generic photo) Published 12 November 2026, 07:05 GMT ﻿The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September. Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the previous three months, official figures , external show. The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer, despite the impact of higher energy prices from the Iran war. Strong growth in the services sector - the largest part of the economy, which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and computer programming as well as hotels and restaurants - helped boost the numbers. Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by cloud computing and AI-linked spending. The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year. Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East. But he says households may still not feel better off, and that prices might soon start to rise more quickly than wages. However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news". "Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future," he said. Chancellor John Healey told the BBC the figures showed a "remarkable resilience" in the face of global conflicts, and hopes they "bring back confidence in Britain". Asked about how government decisions could be the reason for growth when AI investment has been a main driver, Healey said ministers can always "help or hinder" business confidence and investments. Although investors have recently been concerned about slower artificial intelligence development in the US and the long term viability of AI firms' business models, businesses have continued to invest in the technologies. Sarah Coles, from investment platform AJ Bell, said that since the start of the year, "it's the less visible back-office work that has delivered, with administrative and supportive services seeing strong growth" noting that these are the areas benefitting from the increasing use of AI. The latest figures put the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France. However, Jake Finney, senior economist at consultancy PwC, cautioned that growth was likely to slow over the coming months "unless energy markets stabilise". A sharp rise in energy bills is forecast for January, which is likely to hit consumer spending and confidence, he said. High energy costs have been stoked by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and Russia's invasion of Ukraine. US and Israeli attacks led to Iran blocking the Strait of Hormuz - a vital shipping route for the world's oil and gas. Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine have been attacking each other's oil refineries, leading to a squeeze on global refining capacity, hitting diesel and petrol prices. What's happening to the UK economy and how does it affect you? Published 4 hours ago Entrepreneur Richard Benc says the UK watch market and exports have been surprisingly resilient Richard Benc, founder of mechanical watch company Studio Underdog, says sales are better than he expected. "We've seen more resilience than we had forecast for and expected. We are still projecting growth this year," he says. The business exports about 80% of its watches. "We've seen a surprising amount of resilience, particularly from our US customers," he adds, although some UK customers are now taking longer to buy watches. events.title: Billions lost and markets roiled by one man’s indiscretion. Isn’t it now clear that these tech bros are too powerful? | Aditya Chakrabortty
events.summary: Billions lost and markets roiled by one man’s indiscretion. Isn’t it now clear that these tech bros are too powerful? Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair must be the costliest fling in human history – and a preview of what awaits when the tech bubble bursts O ne thing we all know about the tech billionaires is they are super-smart. We know this largely because they never stop telling us. The “ cognitive elite ”, to use their favoured phrase, are entitled to shape our future without our say-so. When Elon Musk goes hiring, he wants “super-high-IQ small-government revolutionaries”. Long before they got private jets, what fuelled these boys was faith in their own brainpower. As a teenager, Jensen Huang wooed his future wife, Lori, thus: “If you do homework with me every Sunday, I promise you you’ll get straight As.” Lord Byron: I believe it’s your move. Which raises the question: if you’re that clever, why act so dumb? At last week’s midterms, it was Musk who backed Team Trump to the tune of $446m. With unhedged bets like that, why wouldn’t you want him gambling with your livelihood? This week, it is 63-year-old Huang and his affair with a much younger woman, who the US government strongly suspects is a Chinese spy. That scandal wiped more than $400bn off the value of his company in just two days, making it the costliest fling in human history. But who knows? Perhaps she loved the centibillionaire for his mind. Forget Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: no one is more central to the future of technology than Huang. He runs Nvidia, which makes the chips powering AI. Previous generations of chips have been compared to kitchen knives: however sharp, they only chop one vegetable at a time. But the graphics-processing units made by Huang’s business are more like food blenders – they can blitz an entire veg patch. That’s what makes Nvidia the foundational infrastructure company of AI and one of the most valuable businesses in the world. And it uses its power: in some of the biggest funny-money deals over the past year in AI, Nvidia has been the money printer . It also stumped up at least $20m for Donald Trump’s new ballroom . Smart! Not only is Huang one of Trump’s favourite businessmen, he’s warmly welcomed by leaders around the world – including Andy Burnham, who last month in London sank a whisky with him . Even as he falls from grace, Huang’s supporters have brought out the superlatives : “torchbearer”, “irreplaceable”, “incredible human”. Huang is boss of the most strategically important business in the fastest-growing, biggest-spending industry in the world’s No 1 capitalist economy. He is part of a tiny coterie of people, who may well feel they sit above the norms and laws that govern the rest of us. That’s certainly the way he has been treated so far by Trump, who was personally warned aboard Air Force One that Huang’s love interest is believed to be a spy for Beijing. Not only is China an ever-greater threat to US AI dominance, it has been banned by Washington from getting Nvidia’s top-of-the-range chips. And the US president takes no discernible action. Some people are in a huge tizz about the spy part of this story, notably the Tory MP Tom Tugendhat, who, after Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine , demanded that every Russian in Britain be rounded up and expelled. The force is not strong in that one. Personally, I can’t get too excited about the threat to the Trumpian model of AI. Neither, it seems, can Washington: it’s been more than a year since Nvidia was revealed to be selling some of its best stuff to a “ dilapidated storefront ” outside Kuala Lumpur, which sounded awfully like a pit stop on the way to China. Again, no action. The message ordinary Americans can take from this is that a company so vital to America’s AI-military complex is too big to subject to ordinary laws. In the everyday world, a CEO who gets into both a sex scandal and a national-security imbroglio wouldn’t stay CEO for more than a minute. At Nvidia, the board has moved with incredible sloth. It declared on Sunday that it “has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised” – before any independent investigation. It finally met on Wednesday evening after further revelations of a separate extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive. Huang’s fate now reportedly hangs in the balance, but the company board, it may surprise you to know, includes several of his longstanding business associates . You’ll also be gobsmacked to learn that several members of his family are serving in senior positions at Nvidia. One of the protections for Huang, like Musk and Zuckerberg and Altman, is that there appears to be no succession plan in place should any of those men fall under a self-driving automobile. A suggestion doing the rounds is that the father may now be replaced by one of his children. The Vatican has a more codified succession process for the pope, even if it includes white smoke and Ralph Fiennes .

events.title: Catching rogue agents and preventing cyberattacks—quantum computing is about to have its ‘ChatGPT moment’
events.summary: A boardroom’s job is to see around corners. Ten years ago, large language models were the approaching challenge, a fledgling technology with a wide range of plausible applications. Today it is quantum computing. Quantum will change the way we consider computing power. At present, classical computing encodes everything using “bits”. Bits only have two states, 0 or 1. Quantum uses quantum bits, or qubits, which are more adventurous. They can be 0 or 1 or a mixture of both, called “superposition.” This flexibility allows them to perform many more tasks than classical computing at a speed high enough to revolutionize how we work.  This has advantages as well as risks. Most of life is more complicated than a series of ones and zeros. Understanding the delicacy of a human protein and its relationship to disease, how the climate works or the interaction of sub-atomic particles in fluids requires significant amounts of computing power. In the battle to keep business and personal data safe from bad actors, the more powerful the technical smarts at our fingertips, the better. Financial services firms already have quant capabilities to help them trade and would like more.  But qubits can be erratic and prone to error. Small fluctuations in temperature and atmospheric pressure can cause malfunctions. Expensive isolation chambers are the norm. We might all like to drive a supercar, but sometimes a basic family runaround—classic computing—is more reliable.  Many companies are working hard to make quantum computing the next ubiquitous technology. IBM, Google, and Microsoft have significant quantum divisions . Pure play operators such as D-Wave Quantum, Rigetti Computing, and IonQ are seeing valuations in the multiple billions of dollars. Europe is getting in on the scene. In June, Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) executed the biggest C-series raise for a quantum computing company in Europe at £260 million ($345 million). The next stage is commercial applications with a clear return on investment.  “Some of the earliest use cases of quantum are the ability to conduct vulnerability analysis on your network, and also to be able to detect threats,” OQC’s CEO Gerald Mullally told me. “And that’s really where the possibility of strengthening our cyber security defenses through the earliest use of quantum compute becomes possible.”  “Quantum can have a profound impact on being able to identify the anomalous behavior of rogue agents.” oxford quantum circuits CEO Gerald Mullally The good guys need to get there first. A scenario where quantum computing becomes so powerful it can eat through all classical computer encryption defenses is not outside the realms of possibility. By then—and it could be as little as five years away—every company and individual will need powerful quant on their side.  “The first area where we generate advantage is anomaly detection—the ability to be able to spot something different in a pattern of data,” Mullally said. “Fraud detection and anti-money laundering are two of the very first use cases in financial services.  “Classical compute can really struggle to identify patterns or the relationships between data. Quantum moves that data to a higher dimensional plane, like a sphere, rather than two points. If it’s a sphere, you can then see more easily that there’s a relationship between data that you wouldn’t be able to spot if it was classical compute.”  When it comes to encryption, quantum will give businesses an “offensive capability” sufficient to head off the threat. Fortunately, quantum computing’s capabilities are becoming stronger by the day. Average quant algorithms can regularly execute a thousand steps before being overwhelmed by errors. Soon that number will grow to a million steps.  “We will hit millions of steps before an error takes over in the years 2028 to 2031,” Mullally said. “That’s the point where we move past the capabilities of classical compute in those narrow areas like anomaly detection. That will be our version of the ChatGPT moment, and that will be the point where the confidence will grow. We’re going to hit billions, and we’re going to hit trillions of quantum operations, and we’ll start to then have this real commercial advantage for a corporate.” Many executives are tired of tech bros bearing gifts and have spent considerable amounts of money experimenting with artificial intelligence. Bottom lines have remained resolutely flat. Quantum is different, a mechanism for problem solving which comes closer to understanding the complexities of the world. OQC already has applications helping data centers operate more efficiently. As AI goes rogue with greater regularity, executives will be glad of a new, well-armed hunter to defeat the errant agent.  “I think quantum can have a profound impact on being able to identify the anomalous behavior of certain agents, and that’s the rogue agent type,” Mullally said. Nervous CEOs won’t be the only ones heaving a sigh of relief. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters UK staff get their say while a separate union-busting dispute heads towards its conclusion White House nixes NASA unions amid budget uncertainty September 1, 2025 BT won't budge over pay hike for manager grade employees June 9, 2025 More layoffs at Microsoft as axe falls in Washington June 3, 2025 Apple settles unfair labor charges brought by fired engineering manager April 10, 2025 Amazon accused of using algorithms to push warehouse workers to breaking point March 18, 2025 More than 1,600 Rockstar Games employees in the UK will begin voting on union recognition on Thursday, with the ballot kicking off just a week before the long-awaited launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. The ballot, which opens on November 12 and runs until November 26, will determine whether Rockstar formally recognizes the Rockstar Game Workers Union, part of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB). Nearly all UK employees below director level are eligible to vote. If successful, the union would become the largest recognized union in the UK games industry, giving workers a collective voice. The proposed recognition agreement follows four months of negotiations between Rockstar management and employees. It would allow workers to negotiate over pay, overtime, pensions, bonuses, leave and other employment conditions, while securing consultation rights over HR policies and AI. The vote comes at a particularly busy time for Rockstar, with GTA VI finally due to arrive on November 19, more than 13 years after its predecessor. The game is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment launches in history, although the people responsible for making it have rather more immediate concerns than sales records. "I am incredibly proud of the work we've put into making this game. I'm also proud of the union we've built here. For me, those two things are connected," said Nestor Uriate, an animation programmer and Rockstar Game Workers Union representative. "We care deeply about the games we make, and we want to make sure we can continue doing that work in an environment where we're respected, have a meaningful say over our conditions and can feel secure about our futures." The vote follows a year of bad blood between Rockstar and the IWGB. The union accused the GTA developer of union busting after it fired 31 members in October 2025, claiming they had been singled out for taking part in a private Discord group. Rockstar denied the allegations, insisting the workers were dismissed for gross misconduct rather than their union activities. The dispute subsequently reached an employment tribunal, where Rockstar unsuccessfully attempted to have blacklisting allegations struck from the case . Closing submissions are expected on November 17 and 18, meaning the legal proceedings will reach their final stages just as GTA VI prepares to hit shelves. Despite the ongoing dispute, Rockstar's head of publishing, Jennifer Kolbe, recently indicated that management would respect the outcome of the recognition vote, telling Bloomberg : "We go where the team goes. So if they want a union, they will have a union." The union campaign has also attracted support from elsewhere in the games industry, including SAG-AFTRA and the Communications Workers of America (CWA), which represents workers at Blizzard. Alex Marshall, president of the IWGB, said the vote was an opportunity for Rockstar employees to take greater control over their working conditions. "What happens at Rockstar matters beyond the studio. Workers across the games industry are watching, and this ballot is an opportunity to show what can be achieved when people come together, organize and build the collective power to shape their own working lives." For Rockstar, November was already shaping up to be a big month. By the time GTA VI has been in players' hands for a week, the company should also know whether its UK workforce has voted to secure a formal seat at the negotiating table.
