events.title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?
events.summary: It is built of wood, resembles an Ikea and its power is totally renewable. Plus, it was built with the local community in mind. Is this facility in Falun the best datacentre in the world? ‘I t was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden , which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms. One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. Huge panels of cross-laminated timber arrived at the site pre-cut, and were assembled by crane according to instructions, like flatpack furniture. Aesthetically, this section of the datacentre is more like an Ikea before the fit-out, a cavernous, echoey, immaculately clean hangar. The wood is not EcoDataCenter’s only claim to sustainability; it is more than just cosmetic, says Wernvik, the company’s chief external relations and sustainability officer. “Compared with a traditional datacentre built with steel and concrete, we lower the embodied carbon of the full structure by three times.” With a complex the size of a football pitch, that is a lot of wood, but, says Wernvik, “the amount of timber one of our datacentres uses takes the Swedish forest about 10 to 15 minutes to grow back”. Datacentres have become a dirty word and a political issue in much of the world – especially the US, where opposition to them was said to be a factor in the recent midterm elections – but here in Sweden, not so much. There is a familiar litany of reasons why datacentres are bad: they are being built without the consent or knowledge of local people; they consume vast amounts of land, electricity and water, with knock-on effects for communities and the environment; they provide no jobs and enrich rapacious tech companies. What’s remarkable is how little any of those arguments apply in Sweden, especially here in Falun, a former copper-mining town a few hours north of Stockholm. If your abiding image of a datacentre is something like xAI’s Colossus facility in Tennessee , built at lightning speed with little public notice, partly powered by banks of unpermitted, methane gas-burning temporary generators, releasing huge amounts of CO 2 and harmful pollutants into the atmosphere and the community, then EcoDataCenter is practically the polar opposite. “I’m biased, but we believe that we build datacentres in a somewhat different way,” says Wernvik. For starters, the company’s electricity supply is 100% renewable: 75% from hydroelectric power and 25% from wind. Sweden’s power mix as a whole is virtually carbon-free – just 1% of it comes from fossil fuels (in the EU as a whole, the figure is 29% , in the US it is 55%). In rural areas like Falun, there is sometimes too much electricity being generated by nearby hydroelectric, solar and wind, so power-hungry datacentres are actually helpful in balancing the grid. Conditions for datacentres are pretty good in Sweden as a whole. The cold northern climate means less cooling is required; the energy is not only green, it is cheap and reliable; there is plenty of water and space; and the country is relatively politically stable and well-regulated – as Wernvik puts it, “it’s very hard to develop something in Sweden where there’s not a consensus”. Energy is still a concern at EcoDataCenter, considering this place has a capacity of 80MW (the equivalent of about 60,000 homes). There are two key measures of datacentre performance. One is carbon usage effectiveness (CUE): the carbon emissions for each kWh of energy consumed. The average for US datacentres is 414gCO2/kWh, the European Union’s is 263gCO2/kWh, EcoDataCenter’s is 1.17gCO2/kWh. Another key measure is power usage effectiveness (PUE); how efficiently the datacentre uses the power going into it. The EU average is 1.36 (where a score of 1 would be 100% efficiency), EcoDataCenter’s is 1.15. The company is bringing down both its CUE and PUE year by year, according to EcoDataCenter’s sustainability report . The primary use for energy is powering the graphics processing units – the expensive chips that do the computing, mostly made by the US company Nvidia. (Wernvik reminds me that although 70% of their computing power goes towards AI, almost everything online is run through datacentres somewhere, from banking transactions to streaming TV.) The supply must be constant – even a small drop in current for a few milliseconds could be consequential – so there are numerous backup generators on site, but even these are fuelled by hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), a biofuel made from waste vegetable oil and animal fat, so also fossil fuel-free. The other main energy use is cooling; removing the vast amounts of heat the chips generate. This is where controversies have arisen in the US over extracting from the local water supply, but it is less of an issue here, says Wernvik.

events.title: New business-class seats, Air India plans among key takeaways from SIA’s first-half results briefing
events.summary: Higher jet fuel prices meant that SIA’s net profit for the first half was 43.9% lower despite a strong second quarter, but it was cushioned by a lower share of losses from its stake in Air India. SIA may adjust its new business-class seats after mixed feedback. The airline will review the design to “further enhance” customer travel, while the $2 billion cabin overhaul stays on track. SIA posted $5.6 billion in revenue and $209.7 million net profit for Q2. First-half net profit still fell 43.9% to $134 million, hit by higher jet fuel costs from the Middle East conflict. Air India is chasing profit under new leadership and new growth plans. SIA also said its AI push is widening, with use cases up 67% and work with OpenAI and Meta’s Muse. SINGAPORE – A week after receiving mixed feedback on its newly unveiled business-class seats , Singapore Airlines chief executive Goh Choon Phong said the airline would explore the possibility of making adjustments where it deemed fit. Without elaborating on the extent of any possible changes, Goh said at SIA’s results briefing on Nov 12 that the group acknowledges the feedback it had received and would review it so that it could “further enhance” the travel experience for its customers. SIA also elaborated on the growth strategy for loss-making Air India, in which it holds a 25.1% stake , noting that the airline is aiming to achieve profitability under new leadership and with growth opportunities emerging in the market. The company posted $5.6 billion in revenue , 14.3% higher year on year, for the second quarter ended Sept 30. Net profit also quadrupled to $209.7 million. Despite the strong quarter, the airline’s net profit for the first half of its financial year still fell 43.9% to $134 million, as rising jet fuel prices driven by the Middle East conflict took a toll on its performance. Jet fuel prices were lower in the first quarter than the second quarter, said group chief financial officer JoAnn Tan. The surge, however, still led to a 90.3% increase in fuel costs before hedging for the first half of the financial year. Here are the key takeaways from SIA’s results briefing for the first half of its 2027 financial year: Possible changes to the business-class seat SIA’s long-haul business-class seats, revealed on Nov 7 alongside refreshed products across all its other cabin classes, has sparked substantial debate. Central to the discussion were the seat’s shape and grey palette, which drew comparisons to a dental chair, and the bright yellow stripe across the backrest, which critics said strayed too far from the colours traditionally associated with the airline. The business-class cabin was designed by BMW Group’s Designworks, one of three design studios hired by SIA to design its fleetwide overhaul for $2 billion in total. Due to launch in the second half of 2027, the seats will be introduced progressively on 41 Airbus A350-900 long-haul and ultra-long-range aircraft as they are retrofitted, as well as on SIA’s upcoming Boeing 777-9 planes. Deliveries of the Boeing aircraft have already been delayed by five years, and the model is still awaiting certification. SIA has defended the seat’s design following the public outcry and now says it will consider adjustments in response to feedback. A petition on Change.org is calling for the airline to remove the yellow accents. Asked by The Straits Times whether engaging a single agency for the entire redesign could have produced a more unified look and reduced costs, Goh said the airline’s decision was based on the different requirements of each cabin class. “What we’ve done is to choose the most appropriate agency for the needs of that specific business class,” he said. An SIA spokesperson added that the airline has historically hired multiple agencies for its cabin overhauls. This includes the 2017 refresh for its Airbus A380 aircraft, where one design studio was involved in its Suites design and another for the business-class and premium economy seats. Design studios must comply with both US Federal Aviation Administration and European Union Aviation Safety Agency regulations before they are invited to bid. The spokesperson added that the $2 billion investment was not a huge sum when compared with SIA’s financials. Air India pursuing new growth opportunities A lower share of losses from Air India helped support SIA’s earnings for the second quarter. SIA, which owns a 25.1% stake in Air India, recorded a $361.7 million share of the carrier’s losses, down from $429.5 million a year earlier. Tan said this was mainly due to a reversal of provisions that SIA had made in previous years, and not because Air India had performed better. In its next stage of growth, Air India will pursue opportunities within and outside of India, Goh said, adding that the airline has already taken steps to improve revenue generation and cost management under a new CEO.

events.title: Reddit's traffic is down 13%, thanks to Google's AI Overviews
events.summary: Reddit's traffic is down, thanks to AI Overviews. Reddit; BI Reddit's traffic is down 13% year over year, according to Similarweb. CEO Steve Huffman recently said that Google's AI Overviews have eaten into Reddit's search traffic. Back in 2024, search traffic was a boon for Reddit. Times have changed! New data sheds further light on Reddit's search traffic woes. Reddit's traffic dipped 13% in global visits from October 2025 to October 2026, according to analytics firm Similarweb. The decline traffic sent to Reddit from Google search has driven Reddit to go (mostly) logged-in-only . However, Reddit reported in a recent letter to shareholders that the number of weekly active uniques were up 16% year over year in October. That's a slightly different measurement than Similarweb's estimate. A spokesperson for Reddit told Business Insider that Reddit's reporting is based on daily and weekly active uniques rather than total visits. Reddit's traffic is down 13%, according to Similarweb. Similarweb Reddit's traffic has been hurt by the way people are increasingly going to chatbots for answers, and especially the way that Google increasingly shows people AI Overviews instead of a list of links. In Reddit's recent Q3 earnings , CEO Steve Huffman said that Google AI Overviews "are not traffic drivers" and have led to a drop in search traffic to the site. In a letter to investors, he said that Google search traffic was "down meaningfully" and that if the trend continued it could lead to a low double-digit drop in unique visits. Reddit's shift to a logged-in experience is because that's where its most lucrative, non-logged-in web traffic (the kind that took a dip). Huffman said: "Search referral trends do not determine our relevancy, and they do not define our future. Logged-in and app DAUq are our most valuable users, and they are our primary focus." It wasn't always this way — in 2024, Reddit made a deal with Google to license itself for AI training at a time when Reddit's search traffic was surging thanks to Google. Reddit's traffic shot up 39% from May 2023 to May 2024, according to Similarweb. But as AI Overviews have become more and more frequent and useful, Reddit's traffic has dipped. Once the logged-in-only experience starts, web traffic will likely dip even more, since some people will get shut out from the site. But Reddit seems to be leaning into where it has the most value for people. Just this week, the company announced it would be launching Reddit Reviews , which will organize user recommendations for products. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: China says US ‘fabricating’ Nvidia spy claims to justify tech ‘blockade’
events.summary: Nvidia CEO is under investigation for an affair with a woman whom US intelligence believes to be a Chinese spy. China has urged ⁠⁠⁠⁠the ⁠⁠⁠⁠United States to stop “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade”, amid national security concerns that emerged over an affair involving Nvidia’s CEO. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning made the comments at a press briefing on Thursday when asked about allegations that the woman with whom Nvidia’s Jensen Huang had a relationship was a Chinese spy. list 1 of 3 Nvidia spy scandal fuels debate over chip exports to China list 2 of 3 Chinese university buys Nvidia AI H200 chips despite US ban, records show list 3 of 3 Why China’s $1 trillion trade surplus isn’t all good news for its economy Mao said that China’s scientific and ⁠⁠⁠⁠technological progress was ⁠⁠⁠⁠driven by independent innovation and open cooperation, adding that Beijing was willing ⁠⁠⁠⁠to work with the US to implement a consensus reached ‌‌‌‌by their two heads of state. US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to ease tariffs and lift restrictions on tech to de-escalate tensions following tit-for-tat tariffs in a trade deal in Busan , South Korea. The remarks come ahead of a meeting next week between Trump and Xi at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen, southern China. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and turned it into the world’s leading supplier of the chips that power artificial intelligence (AI), has admitted to having an extramarital affair. The woman was reported to be Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who US officials believe worked for Chinese intelligence. Megaspeed on Thursday said it takes compliance obligations under US export control laws “extremely seriously” and that it “is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government”. Nvidia’s 63-year-old boss has spent years lobbying against curbs on sales of advanced chips to China. Last year Trump cleared Nvidia’s H200 chips for export to China despite objections from Republicans and Democrats who fear Chinese dominance in AI technology. China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has denied the claims, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”. Huang’s position at the top of the $4.2 trillion company hangs in the balance after Nvidia launched an investigation into him on Sunday. It is unclear whether the tech giant has a succession plan.

events.title: Arada and Alya target $1.63bn property pipeline across UAE and Saudi Arabia
events.summary: UAE developer Arada has teamed up with Alya Developments to explore co-investment opportunities in premium property in the Emirates and Saudi Arabia, following the former's entry into the kingdom. Arada's newly established investment management platform, Arada Capital, and Alya signed a preliminary agreement to explore premium developments in the Emirates and Saudi Arabia under a potential Dh6 billion ($1.63 billion) pipeline, they said in a joint statement on Thursday. The companies will initially pursue two projects in the UAE, with Abu Dhabi's Yas Island and Downtown Dubai earmarked as potential areas, they said in a joint statement on Thursday. It did not provide plans for Saudi Arabia. Arada Capital, the investment management platform of Arada Group, was announced in July and is aiming for $5 billion in assets under management within four years. Arada Group is jointly owned by Saudi businessman Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed’s KBW Investments and Sharjah-based Basma Group. Alya is backed by Canada's Brookfield , which manages about $1 trillion in assets, and Abu Dhabi-based Lunate , a global investment firm with more than $125 billion in assets. The move follows last month's launch of Arada's Dh14 billion residential project in Riyadh, as the developer expands into the kingdom. Arada's group chief executive has separately outlined plans to build 100,000 homes across Saudi Arabia over the next three to five years. Arada also has operations in Australia, Syria and the UK. “This partnership represents an important milestone in Arada Capital's ambition as a fund manager … we see significant potential to bring forward premium residential projects distinguished by their quality, thoughtful design and disciplined delivery,” said Moustafa Fahour, chief executive and managing director of Arada Capital. “Our shared ambition is to create homes of enduring quality and value, for the people who live in them and those who invest in them,” added Otto Dreyer, chief executive of Alya. Property developers are continuing to launch projects in the UAE despite concerns about the slowing of the market as the Iran war continues. This week, Dubai’s Nakheel unveiled the new Palm Springs master development next to Palm Jebel Ali, while Abu Dhabi’s Aldar Properties last month said it plans to launch a major development of villas and townhouses in Dubai by the end of this year as part of the company’s expansion across the UAE. In September, Arada and Aldar teamed up to build new housing projects on Yas Island and at Seih Sdeirah in Abu Dhabi, representing a combined value of about Dh15 billion. Arada also unveiled plans for a $7 billion “UAE-style” development in Damascus. Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, has boosted its real estate sector as it continues its economic diversification strategy. In January, the kingdom began implementing an updated property ownership law for non-Saudis, allowing foreign individuals and companies to acquire real estate subject to regulatory and geographical restrictions. The authorities expect the changes to attract international developers, stimulate investment and support economic diversification. “The UAE and Saudi Arabia continue to present compelling long-term opportunities and our focus is on bringing together the right partners, capital and expertise to deliver sustainable value for investors and communities alike,” Mr Fahour said. Second Australia approval secured Separately on Thursday, Arada said it has received approval for its Dh1.6 billion Wattle Green residential community in Castle Hill, New South Wales, Australia. The 14,000-square-metre project is planned to feature 445 residences across three buildings. The approval is Arada's second major planning consent in Australia within a little over a month, after securing a similar decision for the 33-storey London Place residential project in Campsie, south-west of Sydney, early last month. “We are pushing ahead with our pipeline of projects at a time when we know delivery in this market demands real conviction,” Arada group chief executive Ahmed Alkhoshaibi said.

events.title: Long John Silver’s White Sands outlet to shutter on Nov 18
events.summary: The upcoming closure of the Long John Silver’s White Sands outlet marks the latest of several in 2026 for the fast-food chain known for battered seafood. Long John Silver’s White Sands outlet in Pasir Ris will close on Nov 18, with its last day of trading on Nov 17. The chain has not given a reason. The closure adds to several Long John Silver’s shut-downs in 2026, including Woodlands and Jurong Point. Its Singapore outlets have fallen from 17 in July 2025 to 10 now. Some diners were upset about losing another halal option, while others said there are still other food choices nearby. The outlets are run by Zensho Food Singapore, a unit of Japan’s Zensho Holdings Group. SINGAPORE – Fast-food chain Long John Silver’s will be closing its restaurant at White Sands shopping mall in Pasir Ris on Nov 18. According to a notice pasted outside the outlet, its last day of operations is Nov 17. A homemaker, who wanted to be known only as Afifah, said she often takes her children to the White Sands outlet for meals after school. “I’m sad that there will be one fewer halal meal option after this place closes. My children like the food here,” said the 40-year-old, who was having lunch there . Another diner, human resources executive Benjamin Lee, who works in the area, said he sometimes patronises the White Sands outlet during his lunch hour. “I don’t feel much about the outlet closing as there are always other lunch options around,” said the 38-year-old. “But it seems like a lot of food and beverage outlets have been closing in 2026, so that’s a pity.” The impending outlet closure marks the latest of several in 2026 for the fast-food chain known for its golden battered seafood. Its Woodlands outlet was permanently shuttered on Oct 31. Long John Silver’s Singapore website now lists 10 outlets, including White Sands. This is down from the 17 outlets reported by the media in July 2025. Its Jurong Point outlet shut on Oct 19, and checks show that at least four other locations closed earlier in 2026. Based on social media posts as well as media reports, those affected outlets were in Suntec City, Admiralty, Commonwealth and Tampines. Long John Silver’s traces its roots in Singapore back to the 1980s, as part of the wave of US fast-food chains that entered the local market. Today, its outlets here are all managed by Zensho Food Singapore, a subsidiary of Japanese conglomerate Zensho Holdings Group, which is listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. The parent group manages a global portfolio of popular F&B brands, including Japan’s leading beef bowl restaurant chain Sukiya and Ichikokudo Hokkaido Ramen, which both have a presence in Singapore . The Straits Times has contacted Zensho Food Singapore for more information. Rosalind Ang is a business journalist who has been with The Straits Times since 2021. She covers e-commerce and stories on retail businesses.

events.title: AWS's AI and tech chief says exceptional software engineers focus on one key thing
events.summary: Matt Wood is the chief AI and technology officer at AWS. Business Insider Matt Wood, AWS chief AI and technology officer, said exceptional engineers fall in love with problems. Wood said that AI has enabled developers to explore multiple solutions at once. He said those who focus more on problems than solutions are much more responsive and faster-moving. AI has reshaped the role of software engineers by automating code. However, some say that the job was never just about writing code. It was about solving problems. Matt Wood, AWS's chief AI and technology officer, said that nowadays, the most exceptional engineers are those who fall in love with a problem, rather than a solution. "You want them to have less love for their specific solution and more love for the specific problem," Wood told Business Insider. He leads technology in Amazon's division that provides cloud and AI services to millions of organizations. This is part of a series of stories from Business Insider's conversation with Matt Wood, chief AI and technology officer at AWS. To be alerted when the next piece publishes, follow reporter Ana Altchek here. The AI and tech chief added that these engineers aren't just using AI to write code but also to understand a problem more deeply and pursue multiple paths to solve it. Wood said that developing software used to be more expensive, and it paid for teams to align on building a single solution. Now, AI lets developers go deeper on the problem and explore multiple ways to solve it at the same time. His comments come amid a greater shift in expectations for software engineers at the tech giant. Last month, Amazon released a memo sharing new guidelines for software engineers, leaning into what it calls the "era of the Renaissance Developer." The company revised its guidelines for the role to focus more on long-term impact on customers and the business, rather than on maximizing AI usage. Engineers once spent days waiting for code reviews, manual testing, and design revisions. Now that AI can generate code, humans are freed up to focus on more complex reviews. Wood said that engineers who can avoid becoming too attached to a single solution are much more responsive and tend to move faster, he said. "They're much happier and have a lot more momentum in their career," Wood said. As AI changes the work of software engineers, many technical leaders have weighed in on the qualities that define the top developers. Many have said that taste and judgment are the most important traits as engineers shift into managing agents and making more decisions. AWS principal engineer David Yanacek recently shared another take: The strongest developers are "paranoid and lazy," he said. That makes them eager to automate repetitive work, but cautious enough to set guardrails so agents can operate safely without constant oversight. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: From Emmett Till to Robert Johnson, the Delta powered Scott Colom's historic Senate bid
events.summary: Scott Colom 's path to a historic U.S. Senate upset ran through the Mississippi Delta — where Emmett Till was abducted, Fannie Lou Hamer fought for the ballot and the blues became an American art form. Why it matters: Nearly 150 years after Reconstruction, Mississippi sent a Black American to the U.S. Senate for the first time since 1881. The votes pushing Colom toward that milestone came from communities where Black residents spent generations fighting for the ballot. Driving the news: The Associated Press projected the race for Colom on Wednesday, handing Democrats a historic upset over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. By the numbers: An Axios analysis of AP county returns found Colom ahead in 16 of the 18 counties in the Mississippi Delta National Heritage Area . Colom collected roughly 100,000 votes to Hyde-Smith's 62,000 — a 38,000-vote advantage. In 2020, Democrat Mike Espy carried 15 of those counties by about 25,000 votes, according to Mississippi's certified county returns . Colom's share of the two-party vote climbed from about 56% to 62%. Statewide, Colom led Hyde-Smith by about 4,700 votes out of more than 962,000 counted when the AP called the race Wednesday — a margin of roughly half a percentage point. What they're saying: "Mississippi voters made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out," NAACP president Derrick Johnson said in a statement. Johnson said Mississippi voters showed up despite efforts to remove voters from the rolls . Zoom in: Colom's electoral map traces some of the most painful and defining chapters of Black American history. Coahoma County: Home to Clarksdale and the famed crossroads associated with the legend that bluesman Robert Johnson sold his soul to the devil. Colom led with about 4,700 votes to 1,300. Leflore and Tallahatchie counties: Emmett Till was abducted near Money in Leflore County in 1955. His body was recovered from the Tallahatchie River in Tallahatchie County, where an all-white jury acquitted his killers. Colom led by about 4,200 votes in Leflore and 1,300 in Tallahatchie, according to AP returns . Sunflower County: Fannie Lou Hamer, who lived in Ruleville, challenged Mississippi's racist voting restrictions. As late as the spring of 1965, only 155 Black residents had registered to vote in the county, according to the Mississippi Department of Archives and History . Colom led with about 5,300 votes to 1,700. Washington County: Robert F. Kennedy visited Greenville during his 1967 tour of Delta poverty . 29.4% of Washington County is still in poverty per the Census Bureau's 2020–2024 estimate . Colom led with about 8,700 votes to 2,400. Zoom out: Colom didn't suddenly turn the Delta blue. Espy won most of it in 2020. But Colom widened the Democratic margin. In DeSoto County, which falls within the heritage area but outside the Delta's historic heartland, Colom led by about 3,300 votes. Hyde-Smith won there by roughly 12,100 in 2020. Colom also swept the Golden Triangle counties of Lowndes, Oktibbeha and Clay, his home region in northeastern Mississippi. He won all three by double-digit margins and improved on Espy's 2020 performance. Between the lines: The historical symbolism stretches beyond the Delta. Colom led with about 12,100 votes to 9,700 in Forrest County, named for Confederate Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest, the Ku Klux Klan's first grand wizard. Hyde-Smith faced criticism during her 2018 race against Espy after saying she would sit in the front row if invited to a public hanging . She later apologized to those offended. The bottom line: The region where Black Mississippians fought some of America's fiercest battles for voting rights helped elect the state's first Black U.S. senator in 145 years — and raised a new question. Can political representation finally bring economic change to the Delta?

events.title: Saudi Arabia sets October 2027 date for next iteration of flagship FII investment summit
events.summary: Saudi Arabia's annual international investment and economic conference, the Future Investment Initiative, has been postponed to 2027 after it was stopped this year because of attacks on the kingdom by the Houthi rebels in Yemen The 10th iteration of the flagship investment conference will take place from October 25 to 28 next year in Riyadh, the Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute confirmed. It was set to be held in October, but Houthi strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport disrupted air travel and raised security concerns among international executives and investors. The rescheduled summit, held under the patronage of King Salman, will take place under the theme The Power of Legacy, marking a decade of global investment dialogue and partnerships, the institute said on Thursday. “We are deeply grateful for the continued support of the kingdom’s leadership,” said Princess Maha Al Saud, chief executive of the FII Institute. “The decision to move this landmark edition to October 2027 reflects our commitment to ensuring the highest level of international participation, visibility and impact.” Launched in 2017, FII has become a key platform for Saudi Arabia to attract international investment and advance its economic diversification agenda under Vision 2030. The annual gathering has attracted senior policymakers, global investors and business leaders, with previous events focusing on investment opportunities and economic growth . At last year's summit, the kingdom called for greater private sector investment in its major development projects, while its sovereign wealth fund has since outlined plans to increase its domestic investment allocation . The postponement also affected a major gathering for the kingdom's technology sector, which continues to pursue large-scale artificial intelligence investments . Ahead of FII10, the institute will host its FII Priority Miami summit from March 31 to April 2, 2027, followed by an Asia summit, with dates and location yet to be announced.

events.title: Manchester United sack Michael Carrick as manager
events.summary: Carrick exits after United drop to 18th in Premier League table; he led them to three wins across all competitions. Manchester United have sacked manager Michael Carrick, the Premier League club confirmed in a statement, amid a torrid time for the global football giants, who find themselves in the league’s relegation zone. Carrick’s departure, which had been imminent after United made their worst start to the English top flight in 40 years, was announced on Thursday by the club, which said it would “appoint a permanent successor as quickly as possible”. “Manchester United can confirm that Michael Carrick has departed his role as men’s first-team head coach”, the Old Trafford club said in a statement. “After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions.” United, 13-time Premier League champions, have been heavily linked with US Men’s National Team coach Mauricio Pochettino . Pochettino – whose release from the contract extension he signed as USA head coach has reportedly been arranged – would become the eighth permanent man in charge at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s departure in May 2013 after more than 26 years in the job. United’s statement termed Carrick a club legend. “Just as he [Carrick] did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club,” the statement added. “His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.” The 45-year-old’s last game as United’s head coach ended in a dramatic late draw against Aston Villa at Old Trafford, where the furious home fans voiced their anger towards the club’s ownership. United needed a stoppage-time equaliser to eke out a point against 10th-placed Villa, but it was not enough to lift them out of the Premier League’s relegation zone. The Red Devils briefly dropped to the bottom of the table before results elsewhere in the league took them back to 18th place with eight points from their 10 games this season. Carrick, who was handed the United job on an interim basis in January , knew his managerial position was under threat following a series of disappointing results in recent weeks. United have endured four losses and five draws, with their solitary win coming against Ipswich Town in late August. They were also knocked out of the English League Cup in the third round, and have made an unconvincing start in their Champions League campaign, with two wins and as many losses. Overall, United have won only three times in 15 games across all competitions this season. Carrick’s sacking marks the end of a rollercoaster reign at the club. The former United midfielder, who also captained the club in his final season as a player, took over from the sacked Ruben Amorim last term, when the team were seventh, but lifted them to a third-place finish and secured Champions League qualification at the end of the 2025-26 season. The players looked like a better, more exciting version of themselves under Carrick when he first took over, but fans’ optimism vanished when the revival did not continue into the current campaign. United’s defeat to newly-promoted Hull City in their opening match of the league season marked an embarrassing start for the former champions. What followed was further humiliation on and off the field, with a dressing room rift damaging Carrick’s image, and the club’s hierarchy losing faith in one of their own. British media have linked several high-profile managers to the job. Newcastle United boss Eddie Howe and ex-Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann were among the frontrunners, but USA men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino has seemingly overtaken both as favourite. Pochettino, who previously took charge of Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea in the English top flight, has been widely favoured by US and British media. Former Chelsea coach Antonio Conte is also in the running. A managerial change is expected during this international break, with a new face likely to lead United on their trip to Anfield to face longtime rivals, Liverpool, on November 22.

events.title: UK drone maker founded by Ukrainians hits £4.5bn value after raising £500m
events.summary: Britain’s national wealth fund invests £113m in UForce, whose equipment has been used heavily in war with Russia A London-based naval drone maker founded by Ukrainians has reached a £4.5bn valuation after it raised more than £500m from investors including the UK government. UForce, which makes military drones for land, air and sea, received £113m from the UK’s national wealth fund. The investment makes UForce one of the UK’s fastest-growing unicorns – or startups with a valuation of more than $1bn. Its drones have been used extensively in the war in Ukraine . The UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, met the UForce chief executive, Oleg Rogynskyy, on Thursday onboard the British aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales during a defence conference in Oslo, Norway. The UK’s Ministry of Defence noted UForce’s maritime capabilities in particular, amid concerns over the increasing threat from Russia in the north Atlantic and North Sea. Russian naval vessels and its “shadow fleet” have been accused of sabotage and spying operations on cables and pipelines , while the UK is planning a fleet of sea-borne drones in the northern seas to track Russia’s nuclear submarine fleet . Streeting on Thursday piloted a UForce MV7 uncrewed vessel located more than 1,500 miles away in the Atlantic Ocean near Portugal. Rogynskyy grew up in Dnipro, an industrial city in eastern Ukraine, before founding People.ai, a Silicon Valley tech unicorn focused on data on sales and operations performance for businesses. Rogynskyy said UForce wanted to “make aggression unaffordable”. The investment would allow UForce to scale up production for Ukraine as well as for its allies, he added. “The war in Ukraine has shown that in an increasingly volatile world, effective defence requires systems that can keep improving as threats change,” he said. “Governments and the technology ecosystem need to come together to develop cost-effective, interoperable, and autonomous platforms that are ready to fight now, and can evolve to meet future needs.” The other lead investor was Valor Equity Partners, a private equity investor founded by Antonio Gracias, a former director of Tesla who is also on the board of Elon Musk’s rocket launch company, SpaceX. One of Valor’s partners is Christopher Cavoli, a retired US general who was Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe until last year. Cavoli will join UForce’s board. The Ministry of Defence said UForce would invest in a British supply chain as part of the deal, with hulls, engines, electronics and fit-out sourced in the UK. The MoD said more than 70% of the content of each UK-built boat would come from British suppliers. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Streeting said: “Ukraine is rewriting the rules of warfare. In just a few years the UK has gone from training Ukraine to being trained by Ukraine, as they prove that who can innovate fastest is a key measure of modern military power. “Bringing battle-tested expertise to the UK will create high-skilled jobs, spur innovation and strengthen our war-fighting readiness, enhancing our ability to deter our adversaries.” The former Conservative UK defence secretary Ben Wallace is also on UForce’s board.

events.title: Democrats debate taking a page from Trump's economic playbook
events.summary: President Trump is turning the federal government into an investor in dozens of private companies, and some Democrats are considering following his lead as their party emerges emboldened from the midterm elections. Why it matters: Democrats are gaining new power to scrutinize Trump's corporate investments, even as his approach gains traction within their own party. They're looking at investments and aid for clean energy and other priorities, like support for energy infrastructure. State of play: The Trump administration's investments in energy, critical minerals and other industries are already drawing calls for congressional investigations . "The Trump administration has widened the aperture for industrial policy," Jennifer Granholm, who served as President Biden's Energy Secretary, said at a gathering of energy and climate experts Axios attended in Berkeley, Calif., last month. "You're not going to have state ownership of enterprises," Granholm told Axios in an interview afterward. "But maybe you do take a little bit of an ownership slice" for national security or global competitiveness reasons, she said. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) has also expressed openness to federal ownership stakes, while raising concerns about the Trump administration's lack of transparency and accountability, he told Semafor . Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) has argued that the U.S. needs to consider a more aggressive industrial policy to compete with countries like China, while warning against direct government ownership. "We are long overdue for having a conversation about, 'should the United States even have an industrial policy?'" Casten said at a recent University of Chicago event . "For a long time, we viewed industrial policy as something that socialists do." Casten said he would support the U.S. ensuring domestic manufacturing of certain parts of supply chains, like electronic control systems that operate energy infrastructure, and even pursuing "smart tariff policy" to have competitive markets. The big picture: The Biden administration spent billions subsidizing clean energy and semiconductor manufacturing. Trump has taken government intervention a step further by acquiring ownership stakes in companies ranging from Intel to critical mineral producers. It's been a striking reversal for a president who has repeatedly criticized Democrats for government overreach. How it works: The Trump administration has announced more than $30 billion in investments across nearly 50 deals involving government ownership and related financial arrangements, according to a Council on Foreign Relations tracker . The investments span semiconductors, critical minerals and energy — strategically important industries where high costs and long development timelines can make private financing difficult. Flashback: Washington has taken ownership stakes in private companies before, including during the 2008 financial crisis. But those investments were intended as temporary measures to rescue struggling businesses, unlike Trump's national security-focused investments. What they're saying: "Equity from the U.S. government can act as patient capital that helps derisk an investment with a long time horizon or technological risk that would otherwise not attract sufficient private investment," said Jonathan Hillman, a Council on Foreign Relations fellow behind the tracker. Hillman said the deals announced since January 2025 have also mobilized $28.5 billion in private capital. Yes, but: Some politicians and energy leaders warn that direct government ownership could open the door to political favoritism and market distortions. "Government is not a venture capital fund. It's not a private equity fund. It's not well suited to pick winners and losers in the marketplace," said Tim Pawlenty, former Republican governor of Minnesota who now leads the Solar Energy Industries Association, at the same University of Chicago event. "If it starts to go down the slippery slope of 'it's just the flavor of the day company because we like it' or they're well connected or whatever, then you got problems." Threat level: "Buying stakes in public companies is so, so, so dangerous," Casten said. "I have no idea how a future president unwinds our stake in Intel without totally tanking Intel stock," he added, referring to the administration's roughly 10% stake in the semiconductor giant. To avoid such concerns, Hillman suggests creating a federal chief investment officer to oversee investments and eventual sales. The other side: The White House defended the investments as a way to rebuild American manufacturing and secure critical supply chains, emphasizing that companies participate voluntarily, spokesman Matthew Middleton said. What we're watching: Democrats could spend the next two years scrutinizing Trump's investments — while debating whether a future Democratic administration should make similar deals of its own.

events.title: Democrats unite against Big Health Care
events.summary: Newly elected Democrats from ruby red states are leading a charge to take on corporate health care and some business practices that they say drive up health care costs. Why it matters: Democrats may not be anywhere close to agreement on Medicare for All, but they're relatively united around confronting Big Health Care after campaigning hard on the populist theme. Driving the news: While expanding Medicare, reversing GOP Medicaid cuts and reviving enhanced Obamacare subsidies are getting most of the attention, there's a subtle shift in rhetoric and policy positions toward blaming big health companies for the affordability crisis. It reflects the reality that a substantial expansion of the federal government's role in health care isn't in the cards while President Trump is in office, but populist themes could unite the rank-and-file and even draw in some Republicans. Even candidates who didn't constantly rail about drugmakers or insurers have adopted policy ideas that, until recently, were confined to left-leaning think tanks. Case in point: Incoming Texas Sen. James Talarico ran on breaking up big health care companies and "stop[ping] hospitals and insurance companies from overcharging patients." (He also supports allowing Americans under 65 to join Medicare.) South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews ran on limiting insurer profits per enrollee, expanding the number of drugs subject to Medicare drug price negotiations and banning private equity-owned hospitals. Incoming Kansas Sen. Adam Hamilton supports expanding Medicare drug price negotiations and extending the negotiated prices to private health plans, as well as addressing Medicare Advantage overpayments from the federal government. Other targets include medical debt, pharmacy benefit manager practices and caps on out-of-pocket drug costs. Many of these ideas already have buy-in from more-senior progressives. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) has sponsored the Break Up Big Medicine Act, which is co-sponsored by Republican Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, which would prohibit common ownership of health plans and providers. Incoming Michigan Sen. Abdul El-Sayed, an avid Medicare for All supporter, ran on support of the Warren-Hawley bill, as well as expanding Medicare drug price negotiations. The House's health care working group , made up of both progressives and moderates, pitched capping "excessive" hospital prices and enacting site-neutral payments. The big picture: Voters have made clear that they want lower health care costs. So while a broad overhaul of the health system may not immediately be on the table, Democrats are looking for ways to deliver. Powerful health industry groups are poised to push back, arguing that the populist policies would threaten patient care and access in some communities. But the ideas under discussion could gain favor with some Republicans. What they're saying: When asked at an Axios event on Tuesday whether Congress should address ownership ties between insurers, PBMs and pharmacies, Rep. Morgan Griffith — the top Republican on the House Energy and Commerce's Health Subcommittee — said, "I've only heard the case for breaking them up." "There's just something in your gut that bothers you when your pharmacy, your PBM and your insurance company are all owned by the same people," he added. What we're watching: Forcing drugmakers to lower prescription drug prices could be a particularly compelling target, given Trump's demonstrated interest in the topic. He has previously called on Congress to codify the "most-favored-nation" deals he made with pharmaceutical manufacturers that require the companies, in some cases, to offer Americans prices on a par with what's paid abroad. The Senate Finance Committee's top Democrat, Ron Wyden of Oregon, told reporters this week that he's open to a deal codifying those agreements in exchange for an expansion of the number of drugs Medicare can negotiate on, according to InsideHealthPolicy . The bottom line: It was only four years ago that Democrats struggled to find enough votes for the modest drug price negotiations that exist today, marking the first successful legislative attempt to directly lower health care costs in any sector by either party. Now, they're more willing to push for change and confront big industry players.

events.title: Scoop: AOC shakes up team again as 2028 decision looms
events.summary: New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is shaking up her team for the second time in the past few months as she prepares to make the biggest decision of her political life. Why it matters: The overhaul comes as the democratic socialist leader is debating whether to run for president in 2028 — or Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's seat, which is up the same year. Zoom in: Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with her longtime digital fundraising firm, Middle Seat, according to three people familiar with the decision. At the same time, sources said, she's brought on Aisle 518 Strategies — the company led by Democratic strategist Tim Tagaris, who oversaw Bernie Sanders' record-breaking online fundraising strategy in his two presidential campaigns. Middle Seat has been key to Ocasio-Cortez's operation. Over the past two years, she has paid the firm more than $6 million — about a quarter of her operation's disbursements during that period. AOC is close with Sanders, and if she decides to run for president, progressives say, she would be able to quickly staff up with his former advisers. But Ocasio-Cortez's latest move doesn't necessarily signal that she's leaning toward a presidential run or a Senate bid. Tagaris' firm has helped power the small-dollar fundraising operation for California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who's widely expected to run for the White House. It also has worked with other Democrats who are potential contenders for president — Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Vice President Kamala Harris, according to the company's website . Middle Seat, the firm AOC is leaving, has Sanders roots as well: It was founded by alumni of the Vermont senator's 2016 campaign. Flashback: Ocasio-Cortez's reorganizing follows several changes she made to her staff this year, as Axios previously reported . They included parting ways with her longtime campaign manager and creative director, as well as bringing aboard a few former aides. The Washington Sun reported this week that AOC had hired Freeland Ellis, a Sanders alum, as a communications aide. What they're saying: A spokesperson for Ocasio-Cortez declined to comment. Tagaris declined to comment, and Middle Seat partner Kenneth Pennington did not respond to a request for comment.

events.title: How the midterms swing each party's economic feelings
events.summary: Note: Figures compare average daily sentiment readings over the seven days before each election with the five days after. Election Day is excluded; Data: Morning Consult; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios There was an unusually sharp partisan mood shift in the wake of the midterms, according to sentiment data from Morning Consult that was shared exclusively with Axios. Why it matters: While big partisan swings in consumer sentiment are typical after a presidential election, they have been much smaller in midterm races. The latest numbers show just how tightly Americans' views on the economy are now intertwined with politics. By the numbers: Democratic consumer sentiment rose 6.5 points in the five days after the election compared with the week before, while Republicans' mood fell 6.4 points. How it works: Morning Consult's index considers survey responses from approximately 5,000 U.S. adults. They're asked five questions, including on people's personal finances and financial outlook, as well as their views on overall business conditions. Zoom in: The biggest shifts in sentiment were in respondents' feelings about the future. Republicans' outlook across all five metrics fell after the election. Their confidence in business conditions over the next five years plummeted 12 percentage points. Democrats, meanwhile, had a jump of 9 percentage points in confidence about business conditions (although they remain negative about it) and an even bigger increase — 12 percentage points — in optimism that their own finances would improve over the next year. Of note: Both sides were more negative about their own finances compared with a year ago. Zoom out: Overall sentiment, which includes Independents, barely moved — ticking up less than one point, per Morning Consult. The opposing partisan shifts appear to have canceled each other out. Reality check: It's early days, and sentiment could shift quickly. Between the lines: Consumer sentiment was once a telling measure of how people would actually spend their money: Good vibes meant more spending. Lately, it's looked more like a political measure. "Sentiment matters because it's vibes," says Eli Yokley, a U.S. politics analyst at Morning Consult.

events.title: Alex Karp Said He’s a ‘Progressive.’ OK! Here’s Some Other Stuff He’s Said Recently
events.summary: When Palantir chief executive Alex Karp sat down with Politico this week, he reportedly used the word “progressive” eight times to describe both his political philosophy and his company . “I’ve been a Democrat my whole life,” Karp told Politico, which noted that he called the Democratic Party “ totally irresponsible ” in the distant time of October 2025. “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.” This isn’t the first time Karp has called himself a progressive. In 2018, The New York Times reported that Karp described himself as such. In the same article, he claimed to have voted for Hillary Clinton. Karp has also donated money to Democratic candidates. In 2023, for instance, he donated $360,000 to a joint fundraising committee for Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. The next year, he donated $1 million to MAGA, Inc. Palantir has a share of supporters from the Democratic party. However, it’s not necessarily clear how the products of Palantir—a company that built the technology that underpins much of the Trump administration's brutal arrest and deportation campaign, sold tools to the US military that can use generative AI to help plan and execute drone strikes, and partnered with the Israeli military to assist in its devastating war on the Gaza strip, among other things—could reasonably be seen as progressive. It’s instructive, then, to look at what else Karp has said in recent weeks, and how it lines up with his idea of what’s “progressive.” In his most recent quarterly letter to Palantir shareholders, Karp actually doubled down on his basic premise. In it, he argued that Palantir employees are “the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement.” “We are all, in no uncertain terms, living through what John Lewis Gaddis, the professor of naval and military history at Yale, presciently described decades ago as the long peace ,” Karp wrote, despite the fact that the US and Iran are currently engaged in direct warfare. During Palantir’s corresponding earnings call on November 2, Karp was asked to clarify the statements in his letter. “Our products are built to avoid war, meaning the adversary knows that they will have such pain inflicted upon them that in fact it's not worth going to war,” Karp said. He did not, however, address the relevant possibility that the US is the party that initiates war. “I grew up as a lefty,” Karp continued. “I don't actually like war. I want to avoid war. I don't support wars.” But he said, “Sometimes they are necessary, and when they are necessary, America and its allies need the very, very, very best tools.” Karp went on to say that Palantir has both a “moral imperative” and a “mission reason” for having the “somewhat crazy aspiration” of dominating its market. That mission, Karp said, is supporting the war fighter. Conveniently, it’s also very profitable. “We are delighted that we can support the war fighter even more because we're making so much money,” Karp said. Karp’s recent comments in Politico could also be seen through the lens of convenience. Democrats will have a majority in both chambers of Congress next year, and since about half of Palantir’s revenue comes from government work, it’s pragmatic to sow goodwill. Palantir has seen continued success, after all, across Democratic and Republican administrations. However, Karp doesn’t care about cultivating favor with everybody. He pointedly excludes anyone who has criticized Palantir in what he calls “ridiculously stupid and malicious, incredibly hard to understand attacks.” (Karp didn’t name examples, although many critiques of Palantir have come from the American left.) “What motivates me is helping to make sure we are fighting for you,” Karp said, addressing Palantir investors, “and quite frankly, making sure that the people that made fun of you and made fun of us are suffering.” In your inbox: Inside WIRED’s newsroom with Katie Drummond They war-gamed dimming the sun —it went worse than you think The Big Interview: Nathan Fielder tells us everything Live tracker: Elon Musk’s America PAC is spending big on the midterms Introducing the app: More ways to make the most of WIRED © 2026 Condé Nast. events.title: AI data centers need more raw materials. One investor is betting on recyclers.
events.summary: Tazia Smith, CEO of Closed Loop Capital Management, spoke with Business Insider's Dan DeFrancesco on Wednesday. Business Insider As hyperscalers race to build data centers, opportunities for recycling are opening up. Tazia Smith, the CEO of Closed Loop Capital Management, works with companies that do this. Smith spoke to Business Insider's Dan DeFrancesco on Wednesday. Massive data centers , it turns out, are pretty resource-intensive. And the AI sector's demand for raw materials like aluminum and copper is only increasing, Tazia Smith, the CEO of Closed Loop Capital Management, told Business Insider on Wednesday. "That integration and demand for certain resources, as you alluded to, feels pretty structural going forward," she said during Business Insider's Tech Insider video event. "Not a cyclical blip, but a more permanent systemic transition." Smith's company funds businesses that reuse raw materials in their supply chains. She told Business Insider's Dan DeFrancesco that as AI hyperscalers race to construct data centers across the country, opportunities to recycle at scale are multiplying. Components inside data centers, for instance, need to be repaired or replaced relatively frequently. Smith said she works with companies that recycle these expensive components, rather than dumping them in a landfill. "The large players that are focused on AI are also focused on resilient supply chains and material security," she said. Data centers (or, as OpenAI now wants you to call them, " compute campuses ") received a severe drubbing in last week's midterm elections, as voters shot down ballot measures supporting their expansion. The often gargantuan server farms handle millions of chatbot queries daily, and companies like Microsoft and Meta consider them instrumental to their ambitions to dominate the rapidly expanding AI industry. A principal critique of data centers has been what some describe as their deleterious environmental impact. Smith said she works with a company that specializes in plugging water leaks inside of data centers to minimize environmental harm. Another company Smith works with, Moog, repairs valuable computing components like semiconductor chips, so data center builders don't have to buy replacements every 5 years. "That equals value," she said. "That equals cost savings and opportunity to have wider margins." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Murders plunge 15% in America's biggest cities
events.summary: Data: Major Cities Chiefs Association (MCCA) ; Note: Tulsa Police changed crime-reporting systems, which may affect year-over-year comparisons.; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios Homicides fell 15.2% across major U.S. police jurisdictions through the first nine months of 2026, extending a retreat from pandemic-era violence that began under President Biden and continues under President Trump . The big picture: A new Major Cities Chiefs Association report found declines in all four major violent-crime categories among 66 reporting U.S. large law enforcement agencies from January through September, compared with the same period last year. Homicides dropped 15.2%. Robberies fell 9.1%. Rapes declined 3.5%. Aggravated assaults decreased 3.4%. State of play: Combined, the four categories fell 4.9% — or 13,822 fewer reported offenses. Fifty-one of the 66 agencies reported overall declines. Homicides dropped in 49 jurisdictions, increased in 15 and remained unchanged in two. Zoom in: Some of the nation's largest cities recorded striking homicide declines. Memphis: Homicides plunged 36.5%, from 156 to 99. San Antonio was down 36.5%, Indianapolis down 33.6%, Philadelphia down 21.2%, Aurora, Colorado down 65.2% and Newark, New Jersey down 59.1%. The other side: New York City was a major outlier and reported more violent crime in all four categories, including 24.5% more homicides and 14.2% more robberies. Its combined violent crime total was up 5.1%. San Diego reported 45.2% more homicides and Las Vegas recorded a 23.4% jump. Washington, D.C., saw homicides fall 29.9%, but robberies surged 41.1%, pushing its combined violent-crime total up 9.7%. The caveat: The figures remain preliminary. Houston reported no data because of a records-system transition, and Tulsa recently transitioned to a new crime reporting system, the report notes.

events.title: HPE's CEO went from working in a call center to the C-suite. Here's his advice for getting noticed at work.
events.summary: Antonio Neri, CEO of Hewlett Packard Enterprise, has some timeless advice if you're trying to get noticed at work. Angel Garcia/Bloomberg via Getty Images HPE CEO Antonio Neri said if you want to get noticed at work, start by consistently doing what you promise. Neri said ambitious employees should share their career goals with their manager. He also recommends seeking out stretch projects to help grow your network. The recipe for opening doors at work starts with first doing what seems the most obvious: Do what you say you will. Antonio Neri, the CEO of Hewlett Packard Enterprise, told Business Insider that delivering on the promises you've made is where opportunity begins at work. Neri knows a thing or two about getting on your boss's radar and climbing the corporate ladder. He started working at the company at a call center in Amsterdam during the mid-1990s when the firm was known as Hewlett-Packard. He rose through the ranks and eventually took the helm of HPE in 2018. Neri said in addition to delivering on the work you were hired to do, make sure you are communicating your career goals to your manager about where you want to see yourself in three to five years. "Hold the manager accountable, but most importantly, hold yourself accountable, too, because it's a two-way street," Neri said. He said if you are looking to climb the ladder at work, you should ask for developmental opportunities that will help build your network amongst colleagues and other leaders in the organization. This will help keep you on their radar, and possibly considered for new opportunities when they open up. Neri added that once opportunities present themselves, you should be intentional about the ones you take on. "Don't overdo it, but also don't be quiet behind the scenes," he said. "Speak when it's necessary and then listen most of the time." "But again, it starts by delivering what you say you're going to do," Neri said. Neri's advice echos that of Walmart chief people officer Donna Morris who told Business Insider in October that one of the two traits she looks for in people to promote are those who are excelling at the job they were hired for. She said that employees who get promoted quickly "are focused as much, if not more, on just being exceptional at what they're doing today." She said the second thing that employees who move up quickly do is demonstrate that they can take more on. "Be the type of person that takes on over and above what's being expected of you. Be the person that asks, or provides, volunteerism for new ideas or new initiatives," she said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Orbit Global Menu: A working global menu addon for GNOME
events.summary: A new extension brings a working global menu bar to the GNOME desktop, even for some apps that don’t have menu bars at all. Orbit Global Menu is a new GNOME extension that gives the GNOME desktop a feature it was intentionally designed without, and one that some users miss very badly – this vulture being one of them. It adds a working global menu bar to the GNOME top panel. We suspect this is something that will cause strongly contrasting opinions among many GNOME users: some will by puzzled why anyone would bother, while others may think "at last!" and rush to try it. There have been other attempts to do this before, and the Reg FOSS desk has tried several of them, but we never found one that worked with the majority of applications. Our fondness for this UI feature was visible in the two-part series we wrote in September on how to customize Xfce and then in part two how to get the global menu working with more apps. The problem is getting worse over time, as in recent versions (since GNOME 40 and Gtk4), the GNOME human-interface guidelines encourage smartphone-style hamburger menus, replacing the traditional horizontal menu bar. It is tricky to add global menu bar support to apps that lack a menu bar, but Orbit's developer "Unmade" found a rather labor-intensive solution. The menu bar applet contains maps of keyboard controls for 292 different apps, so it can show a menu all on its own and then send those apps simulated keystrokes to operate it. It's not the programs' full menu trees, just a subset of them, but it works. It's also not the most elegant solution, but it is a solution and it works. We tried it on Ubuntu 26.10 and every app in the full install worked to at least some extent. If you are willing and able to build and install a small additional connector, it lets the global-menu applet talk to lots more applications. The GNOME shell is unusual among open source desktop environments, to an extent that we have criticized before. GNOME Shell was designed with a distinctive look and feel of its own, unlike almost all other desktops. It has a minimalist, stripped-down layout that doesn't look or work quite like anything else, and it's intentionally not very customizable. To change how GNOME works means writing new Javascript code, then packaging it as an extension that users can install from the GNOME Extensions website. This requires both a browser extension and a "native host messaging" connector to be installed into the underlying OS – or a purpose-written app. By default, the desktop comes with neither. The end result is that GNOME lends a visual identity to the Linux desktop, one that is clear and distinct from either Windows or macOS. (Back in 2013, this vulture argued that when Microsoft threatened to sue multiple Linux vendors over infringing Windows UI patents, some 20 years ago, this UI fragmentation was just what the company wanted .) GNOME 2 was the Linux world's default desktop. GNOME Shell was controversial in its early days, and lost pole position, but it has since won it back. Today, GNOME is the default desktop on all the major distros: Ubuntu, Fedora and Red Hat Enterprise Linux and the RHELatives, as well as Debian and SUSE, all default to GNOME. GNOME does away with a lot of features that are significant functional parts of other graphical desktops. For instance, it has no desktop icons, no system tray or defined place for status indicators, and neither GNOME nor GNOME-compliant applications have menu bars, either inside windows (Microsoft style) or in the top panel (Apple macOS style). This is disorienting and confusing for those used to controlling software mainly using their menus – but now, that's mainly older hands. This design suits those who grew up on smartphones and tablets, or who feel more comfortable with their stripped-back keyboardless UI than a full desktop WIMP, which can be overwhelming to newbies and non-techies. If you've followed the evolution of graphical desktops for some 40 years, as this gray-plumed vulture has, some trends are very apparent that aren't so clear if you came in once evolution was underway. Apple introduced the first global menu bar in the Lisa, and improved on that in the Macintosh. DR GEM copied it very early on , but Apple sued and DR changed the PC version of GEM to be less Mac-like. Microsoft's Windows came along after this, and moved menu bars inside windows instead. When Apple acquired NeXT in 1996 , it moved NeXTstep's patent-avoidant vertical menus back to a global bar at the top, along with the clock and some status indicators. There they remain, 30 years later. In 2007, it launched the iPhone, containing a very cut-down OS based on OS X, replacing the Finder with a cut-down version of the Dashboard layer from OS X 10.4 . The panel remained, shorn of its menus, which were too fiddly for a small screen. As The Register mentioned in 2017 , in its preliminary releases, Android started out as a keypad-driven Java phone that looked and worked very much like BlackBerry. When the iPhone appeared, Google changed course . The new Android UI resembled iOS, complete with that top panel, still without menus. GNOME 3.0 was not far behind: in 2009 the team promised a revamp of the user experience, and in 2011, launched GNOME 3.0. It too has the fixed top panel — now huge on a laptop or desktop landscape screen – and mostly empty. Now that top panel regains its original 1983 function. We're rather impressed by the Orbit global menu. It does the job, and it even works with apps that don't have menu bars. It's not perfect: for instance, over-long menus have to scroll, and may fail to do so if new submenus appear. The GitHub repository has extensive instructions, including how to build and install the optional connector module that lets more apps export their real menus to the extension. It also tells you how to instruct some apps, notably Firefox, that there is a global menu for it to use. We are saddened to note that, as is so often the case, Wayland gets in the way here. It works rather well with some other extensions, too. With a menu bar, GNOME's strangely centered clock seems out of place, but several extensions, such as F rippery Move Clock , shove it over to the right where we still feel it belongs. If you prefer a lighter-colored panel and dock, it also plays nicely with Blur my Shell . ®

events.title: Jensen Huang's looming ouster triggers an AI earthquake
events.summary: Jensen Huang's potential ouster from Nvidia has plunged the AI industry into uncharted territory — a corporate earthquake that dwarfs even the chaos unleashed by Sam Altman's temporary firing from OpenAI in 2023. Why it matters: Nvidia is the backbone of the global AI economy , with its chips, investments and financial guarantees sustaining an entire ecosystem of companies worth trillions of dollars. At the center of that vast financial flywheel is Huang, who spent 33 years making himself synonymous with Nvidia — and Nvidia synonymous with the AI revolution. "This is no ordinary CEO. This is no ordinary company. This is no ordinary sector. This is no ordinary time," economist Mohamed El-Erian wrote on X , warning of contagion across the AI industry. Zoom in: As recently as two weeks ago, the notion of Nvidia without Jensen was unthinkable. Even after his affair with a suspected Chinese spy came to light, President Trump and Nvidia's board stood behind him, Silicon Valley's elite rallied to his defense and betting markets suggested he would survive. It took revelations of a second affair — this time with an executive who reported directly to Huang — to shatter that consensus and bring his storied reign to the brink of a stunning end. Driving the news: After that second affair came to light Wednesday night, Nvidia's board reportedly met to settle Huang's fate, though there was still no decision as of early Thursday morning. The White House was read in. The market reaction has been brutal. Nvidia had already shed more than $1 trillion in market value since the initial scandal erupted, and shares plunged further in after-hours and pre-market trading overnight. One of Wall Street's most prominent voices on tech, analyst Dan Ives, said Nvidia was worth 25% less without Huang. Zoom out: Huang's rise was the stuff of Silicon Valley legend: The Taiwanese immigrant went from cleaning toilets at a Kentucky boarding school and waiting tables at Denny's to building one of the most valuable companies in history. Huang and two fellow engineers hatched the idea for Nvidia at a Denny's booth in 1993, launching a chipmaker that would revolutionize gaming, transform modern computing and ultimately power the AI revolution. Clad in his trademark black leather jacket, Huang became a global AI rock star — with a cult of personality that drew adoring crowds, calmed markets and commanded the attention of world leaders. The big picture: Huang's apparent downfall comes amid mounting anxiety over the AI industry's future, as new financial, political and regulatory risks threaten one of the largest infrastructure buildouts in history. The timing is especially fraught for Anthropic , whose historic IPO — backed by a $10 billion commitment from Nvidia — looms as a referendum on Wall Street's faith in the AI trade. Huang spent years defending the industry's soaring valuations and dismissing warnings of a speculative frenzy. Now his own scandals could help burst the bubble he insisted didn't exist. What to watch: The blast radius could extend far beyond Silicon Valley and Wall Street, threatening to engulf the Trump administration in a scandal over its handling of sensitive technology exports to China. Huang forged a close alliance with Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who loosened restrictions on chip sales even as other officials raised concerns about Chinese espionage and smuggling. Top Senate Democrats are already demanding that Lutnick and other senior officials preserve records of their dealings with Nvidia and Huang, laying the groundwork for a sweeping investigation. The bottom line: As veteran China watcher Bill Bishop wrote after Huang acknowledged his first affair: "There is rarely just one lie."
