events.title: What we know as pressure builds on embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
events.summary: Watch: Jensen Huang's future at Nvidia 'doesn't look good', the BBC's Lily Jamali explains One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures could be ousted from his role amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs with two women - one a suspected Chinese spy and the other a company executive. Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset. Now the firm is reportedly weighing whether to remove Huang after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair. Huang admitted , external earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. Nvidia's board was reportedly meeting on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company. The BBC called Nvidia representatives and board members for comment, but received no reply. Nvidia has 11 directors on its board, including Huang, and the CEO can be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors, according to Reuters news agency. Should Nvidia's board choose to oust Huang, or place him on leave, it was not immediately clear who might step into his shoes, even on an interim basis. One possibility is Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky. He has been at the company as long as Huang, and for years led its product engineering work. Huang's children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez also work at Nvidia in senior roles, but they are relatively young and inexperienced. Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress could serve as interim CEO, according to analysts. Kress would be the natural choice, Armina Rosenberg, co-founder of Minotaur Capital, which holds Nvidia shares, told Reuters news agency. A New York Times report at the weekend revealed Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who US intelligence officials believed was a spy for Beijing. Alice Huang had previously been photographed with the Nvidia chief on several occasions. Nvidia's board of directors launched an independent external investigation on Sunday following the reports. They earlier said Huang's interactions with the woman were "not unusual or unexpected". Then on Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with a Nvidia executive who reports directly to him. She did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - at an event US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. Bloomberg News reported that she was currently living in China. Her company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia said this was investigated and debunked. However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC contacted Megaspeed for comment. It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not. China has rejected the spying allegations as "entirely groundless". Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy Published 2 days ago Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Published 2 days ago Nvidia hires major New York law firm to investigate Jensen Huang affair Published 1 day ago Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire boss's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers. Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the concern is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of companies like Nvidia, working with producers such as the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Jensen Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero.

events.title: Wheelock Place renamed Landmark Orchard after $1.1 billion acquisition by Hongkong Land
events.summary: The 21-storey building, which has been in Orchard Road for more than 30 years, houses offices and shops and is directly linked to Orchard MRT station. Hongkong Land renamed Wheelock Place as Landmark Orchard after its Singapore fund bought the Orchard Road site for about US$1.1 billion (S$1.4 billion). The 21-storey building has offices and shops, links to Orchard MRT, and existing tenants will stay while the new owner plans improvements. The deal is the fund’s first Orchard Road purchase and expands its reach beyond the Central Business District, as it targets about $15 billion in assets under management. SINGAPORE – Wheelock Place has been renamed Landmark Orchard, the first time property group Hongkong Land has used the Landmark name outside Hong Kong. The new name took effect on Nov 12, three months after Hongkong Land’s Singapore Central Private Real Estate Fund bought the Orchard Road property, the developer announced that day. The fund agreed in July to pay about $1.1 billion to an entity owned by Hong Kong-listed Wharf Real Estate Investment Company. It was the fund’s first acquisition since its launch in February . The 21-storey building, which has been in Orchard Road for more than 30 years, houses offices and shops and is directly linked to Orchard MRT station. Existing office and retail tenants will continue to operate under the new name. Hongkong Land said it plans to improve the property, but did not provide further details. In Hong Kong, Landmark is at the centre of the group’s Central portfolio, which is undergoing a revamp under a more than US$1 billion (S$1.3 billion) programme. Foo Pei Teng, chief executive of the Singapore fund, said the group would bring its long-term approach to investing in its properties to Landmark Orchard. The purchase extends the fund’s reach into Orchard Road from its initial portfolio in the Central Business District. That portfolio comprised Asia Square Tower 1, Marina Bay Financial Centre Towers 1 and 2, One Raffles Quay and One Raffles Link. The fund is targeting about $15 billion in assets under management. Hongkong Land manages the fund and is its largest unit holder. Correction note: In an earlier version of the story, we said Wheelock Place was acquired for $1.4 billion. It should be $1.1 billion. Kang Wan Chern is deputy business editor at The Straits Times.

events.title: Asian stocks fragile, Nvidia plummets as board to decide CEO’s fate
events.summary: Asian stocks were mixed as Nvidia fell more than 8% after reports its board may decide on CEO Jensen Huang’s future amid affair allegations. Wall Street rose on Nov 11, with the S&P 500 up 1.3%, as renewed optimism around AI lifted US shares, helped by CoreWeave and Anthropic news. The dollar stayed near a high, and traders priced in an 87.3% chance of a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike in December; bitcoin and ether also fell. SINGAPORE – Global stocks wobbled at the start of Asian trade on Nov 12 , while Nvidia shares plunged in after-hours trading on news that its board may oust long-time chief executive Jensen Huang. Nvidia’s board is meeting late on Nov 11 to decide whether to oust Huang , a source familiar with the matter said, as the world’s dominant supplier of AI processors grapples with the fallout of allegations that he had an affair with a suspected spy for China. The New York Times has also reported that Huang had an affair with a company executive who reported to him. “It looks bad from every single angle,” said Jake Dollarhide, CEO at Longbow Asset Management in Tulsa, Oklahoma. “I believe the board won’t oust him until they have an all-star, a known entity in the tech sector, to replace him,” he said. “At the end of the day, let’s not forget that the Nvidia chip is the centrepiece of the AI story.” Regional indexes fared better after a choppy start. South Korea’s Kospi rose 0.2%, Taiwanese shares gained 0.5%, Japan’s Nikkei 225 climbed 0.5% and MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was 0.1% lower, weighed down by shares in Hong Kong. Stocks on Wall Street made gains on Nov 11 , with the S&P 500 rising 1.3% and coming close to retracing all the losses since last week’s US midterm elections. “Renewed optimism around AI drove US equities higher overnight, with positive developments around CoreWeave and Anthropic adding to enthusiasm around the sector and helping the S&P 500 and NASDAQ rally,” Westpac analysts wrote in a note. The dollar index, which measures the greenback’s strength against a basket of six currencies, was steady in Asian trade at 102.87, its highest level since April 9, 2025 in the aftermath of Trump’s Liberation Day tariff announcement. The currency rose 0.6% on Nov 11 as traders repriced the odds the Federal Reserve will lift interest rates in December . Fed funds futures are pricing an 87.3% chance of a 25-basis-point hike at the US central bank’s next two-day meeting on Dec 9, compared to a 12.7% chance of a larger 50-basis-points hike, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool. In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin slipped 0.9% to US$73,617.58 (S$94,600), while ether was 0.9% lower at US$2,049.44. REUTERS

events.title: 'If they're winning, we're winning': Suppliers on David Jones closures
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts David Jones suppliers saddened but understanding of plans to close half the store network David Jones has announced plans to close half its stores. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) David Jones's receivers are set to close 19 of its 38 stores. Suppliers say they are sad but supportive of the decision. The affected stores are expected to continue trading through the peak seasonal period. While news of David Jones's plans to close half of its stores may sadden some customers, some suppliers say a streamlined operation could boost sales by attracting more shoppers into fewer, higher-performing stores. The 188-year-old department store went into administration last week. On Wednesday, its receivers announced plans to close 19 of its 38 stores. Owner of Spice brand Lord and Lion, Eresha De Zoysa, whose products have been stocked across the David Jones network for five years, said she was concerned the closures would wipe out a significant amount of her business. "The way that we were able to access people in communities that we ordinarily would not be able to access was by David Jones," she said. "So even though, on the whole, those stores may not make commercial sense for Anchorage to keep or David Jones to keep … our brand did really well, and we were successful in those stores. "It's a sad day, but I think we just have to be a bit more clever in how we're going to access [those customers]." Eresha De Zoysa says she is grateful to be stocked in David Jones. ( Supplied ) Documents seen by the ABC show an uncertain future for suppliers that have been asked to continue supplying the store despite unpaid debts. Ms De Zoysa, a former corporate lawyer who has worked in administration and previously advised David Jones, said she had no doubt a restructured David Jones would succeed and thrive. "I do hope that the suppliers find a way to renegotiate an outcome with David Jones to continue supplying into the future because it is actually those brands that make David Jones worthwhile," she said. David Jones 'could not continue operating' McGrath Nicol has been appointed administrator for David Jones, but separately FTI Consulting has been appointed as receiver for the company's biggest lender, Hilco. An email sent to suppliers from David Jones chief executive Erica Berchtold, seen by the ABC, said the store portfolio was "no longer the right shape for the business" and the change was about "creating a network that is financially sustainable for the future." It said the last day of trade for the 19 stores marked for closure was anticipated for later in the year, with the stores expected to continue trading through the peak seasonal period. David Jones will close 19 of its 38 locations. ( ABC News: Daniel Irvine ) "The business could not continue operating as it was. We had a plan to reset the business, and we still have a plan to reset the business," the email said. Carlos Martins, owner of men's fashion brand Coast Clothing, said the store closures were the "right way forward". "Fewer stores will be better for me in the long term," he said. "Loyal customers will likely shift to online shopping, which will bring greater exposure to my brand, compared to instore where we didn't have a presence." Slow Down Studios owner Jacob Leung. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) Jacob Leung, owner of handwoven blankets business Slowdown Studio, which is not stocked in the closing stores, said although the news was sad, it was good for suppliers. "It's going to have a massive impact on all of those employees, as well as the communities of the stores that are closing down," he said. "We only want the best for David Jones because if they're winning, that means we're winning. "At the end of the day though, it's clear that the business model that David Jones currently operates in is not working, and that's why we are all in this situation." David Jones in Claremont in Perth's Western Suburbs is one of the stores continuing to trade. ( ABC News: Zahra Anwary ) Mahala Joyce, co-founder and director of distribution business Over The Fence, has organised pop-ups in David Jones flagship stores for international brands, including Bellroy and Topologie. Like other suppliers, he said he had negotiated 14-day settlement terms that came with a 5.75 per cent discount. Yet across three purchase orders over six months, he said none was paid on time, while the discount was still applied. Relevant documents have been seen by the ABC. "Essentially the way that their system is set up is it's set up that those discounts are applied at the start, prior to any payment date," he said.

events.title: HSBC explores bolstering Singapore to balance China reliance: Sources
events.summary: HSBC’s review highlights how some of the world’s largest financial groups are moving to insulate their Asian assets from mounting geopolitical risks. HSBC is exploring ways to make its Singapore business more independent to reduce reliance on China and Hong Kong. The project is called “Project Sirena”. The bank plans to combine its main Singapore banking units first. It may later move other regional operations there, creating a second Asian base alongside Hong Kong. HSBC says there are no firm decisions yet and no plan to change its Hong Kong-led structure. The move could upset regulators and Beijing, while Singapore gains as a stable wealth hub. HSBC Holdings has been exploring ways to ease its reliance on China, including Hong Kong, and give more independence to its Singapore operations as the bank seeks to diversify risk across its Asia business, according to people familiar with the matter. The London-based lender, which generated about 40% of its pre-tax profit in the first half from Hong Kong, has internally discussed several options to give its Singapore arm greater autonomy, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing a private matter. The initiative is being carried out under the name Project Sirena . HSBC’s review highlights how some of the world’s largest financial groups are moving to insulate their Asian assets from mounting geopolitical risks. Singapore, bolstered by relative political stability and its standing as a premier wealth and banking hub, has emerged as a top beneficiary as firms look beyond Greater China for operational flexibility. It comes even as chief executive officer Georges Elhedery has repeatedly voiced confidence in Hong Kong’s prospects, predicting the city would overtake Switzerland to become the world’s largest cross-border wealth hub by the end of the decade, even before it happened late in 2025. In a first step, HSBC plans to combine its major banking services in Singapore under one entity over the next few years. A possible next move would be to bring in the other regional operations under the Singapore subsidiary, with the ultimate goal of establishing a second regional base alongside Hong Kong, according to the people. In a statement, Surendra Rosha, co-CEO of Asia and the Middle East, confirmed the bank will combine its separate units in Singapore as part of a simplification drive, though he said it had no further plans after that. “All of our Asia-Pacific banking entities remain under the ownership and management of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation subsidiary head office in Hong Kong, and there is no plan to make any changes to this,” Rosha said in a statement via e-mail. The deliberations remain fluid, with no firm decisions on the path forward, the people said. Like other multinationals, HSBC is also wary of appearing to hedge its bets, given its significant exposure in Greater China and concerns about provoking regulators, the sources added. HSBC shares fell as much as 0.8% in early Hong Kong trading. Making its Singapore operations more independent would be a major step for the 161-year-old lender, which was founded in Hong Kong and moved its headquarters to London in 1993. At the same time, the bank is becoming more reliant on the Chinese territory after announcing in 2025 a US$14 billion (S$18 billion) takeover of partly owned Hang Seng Bank, while it has also exited businesses in Europe and the Americas. Any signs of hedging Hong Kong, where HSBC serves as one of three currency-issuing lenders, would face stiff local pushback. It would also risk alienating Beijing, where the bank maintains expansive China operations. HSBC’s assessment is not without precedent. In 2019, smaller rival Standard Chartered consolidated its operations into a locally incorporated subsidiary, creating dual hubs in Singapore and Hong Kong to simplify its network and trim costs. HSBC has recently faced intense scrutiny on other fronts from the Hong Kong authorities over its allocation of artificial intelligence talent to Singapore as both Asian financial hubs battle for dominance. The lender operates a hybrid structure in jurisdictions such as Singapore. In May 2016, HSBC locally incorporated its retail banking and wealth management business in Singapore under HSBC Bank (Singapore) while also operating a branch under Hong Kong. It runs locally incorporated subsidiaries in countries such as Malaysia and Indonesia, though both remain under its Hong Kong-based business. A subsidiary is more freestanding than a branch, with its own governance, capital needs and deeper local regulatory oversight. Such a structure also faces different treatment in the event of financial difficulties. The lender has, over the past couple of years, radically overhauled its business following the appointment of CEO Elhedery in September 2024.

events.title: The world's super-rich are piling into alternative investments. Here's why
events.summary: The super-rich are increasingly piling into alternative investments, diversifying portfolios once dominated by traditional assets. The shift comes as investors grapple with increasingly concentrated equity markets and geopolitical uncertainty. The world's wealthiest investors are increasingly looking beyond stocks and bonds, pouring money into hedge funds, private equity and infrastructure assets, as market volatility and fears about stubborn inflation spur diversification. From Asian billionaires to global family offices, alternative investments are becoming a bigger part of portfolios once dominated by traditional assets, said industry watchers JPMorgan Asset Management's private wealth alternative assets in Asia-Pacific surged 40% over the past 12 months, according to Dan Watkins, the firm's regional chief executive officer, underscoring the growing appetite among high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients. "So you really have this huge appetite for alternative exposure happening in that ultra-high-net-worth, high-net-worth category," Watkins said recently at a media summit in Singapore. The shift comes as investors grapple with increasingly concentrated equity markets, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns that stocks and bonds may not provide the same protection against market downturns as they once did, experts said. "We are seeing a sharp increase in planned asset allocation to alternatives among the family offices we speak to," said John Woods, chief investment officer for Asia at Lombard Odier. Alternative investments now account for 60% of single-family office portfolios, surpassing traditional assets for the first time, according to BNY Wealth . Traditional assets accounted for 41% of allocations, the report found. Wealthy investors are seeking diversification, income and access to investments outside listed markets, and concerns over elevated valuations, tight credit spreads and the growing correlation between stocks and bonds have accelerated the trend, Woods added. Hedge funds are emerging as a favored option among wealthy investors seeking protection against market swings, particularly as traditional diversification strategies face growing challenges. Olaolu Aganga, head of portfolio construction and analytics at Citi Wealth, said hedge funds have attracted the strongest recent interest among qualified clients, who are seeking returns less dependent on the direction of equity markets. Private credit is another area drawing interest, offering investors contractual income streams, while some hedge fund strategies seek to profit from differences in performance between companies rather than relying on broad market rallies, said Woods. Citi's 2026 survey of 351 family offices found that inflation was their biggest concern, followed by interest rates, financial system stability and market volatility. Wealthy families are increasingly seeking investments that can generate income and help preserve purchasing power amid persistent inflation and interest-rate uncertainty, while diversifying portfolios against market volatility, according to Aganga. The Citi survey, however, also showed public equities recorded the strongest net increase in allocations, suggesting wealthy investors are adding alternatives rather than abandoning traditional markets. "This is not a wholesale rotation away from public markets," Woods said. Infrastructure has emerged as another major beneficiary of the shift, with the artificial intelligence boom creating enormous demand for data centers, electricity networks and digital connectivity. Thomas Roland Guyot, head of private markets investment specialists for Southeast Asia at UBS Unified Global Alternatives, said investors are increasingly targeting assets that support AI, electrification and energy security. Such investments potentially offer a combination of long-term growth and relatively predictable cash flows, particularly where revenues are supported by essential demand or long-term contracts. Investor appetite is already showing up in fund flows. Net inflows into open-ended infrastructure funds rose 30% year on year in the 12 months through the first quarter of 2026, according to PitchBook data cited by UBS. Private equity remains a cornerstone of wealthy investors' alternative portfolios, although they are becoming more selective. Family offices are increasingly favoring direct investments in companies, co-investments alongside private equity managers and purchases of existing fund stakes on the secondary market, rather than relying solely on traditional pooled funds, according to Citi Wealth's Aganga. Such approaches can give investors greater control over their investments or opportunities to acquire assets at discounts, said Lombard Odier's Woods.

events.title: Who could replace Jensen Huang? A highly unscientific list of possible successors
events.summary: It’s almost inconceivable that Nvidia would fire its rock star CEO. Yet here we are, on the precipice of this happening. Over at Kalshi, Jensen Huang’s odds of surviving the week are sitting at a lowly 30% . Even though he built one of the world’s most valuable — and, many would argue, dangerously powerful — companies, the tides have completely turned against him. He has confessed to an extramarital affair, but as of Wednesday afternoon it isn’t even clear whom he meant: Alice Huang, the Chinese executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for her country, or Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reports to him and who, five sources told The New York Times in an explosive new report, was also a paramour. Even if Huang is pushed out as CEO, the board members he has made very rich are unlikely to cut him loose entirely. Barring another shoe dropping, they could keep him on as chairman, a role Nvidia doesn’t currently have. But someone still has to run the company, and there’s no apparent succession plan, which leaves us, like everyone else, to speculate while we wait to see what happens next. While Huang’s 60 direct reports undoubtedly get a closer look, consider this our own parlor game, featuring some obvious and less obvious candidates: Lisa Su . The AMD CEO runs Nvidia’s most credible rival, as well as a distant cousin of Huang. The Information floated her name this week, but why would she leave her job for his? Her company stands to benefit from every day that Nvidia spends distracted by an investigation, congressional briefings, and all the mini dramas that are sure to follow. Her best move might be to send a nice note and keep her current corner office. Eric Schmidt. He was the pick of Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management, who we talked with earlier this week. Schmidt could “parachute in tomorrow and do a very good job,” Sonnenfeld said, and perhaps he could. He ran Google from 2001 to 2011, chaired the National Security Commission on AI from 2018 to 2021, and now runs the rocket company Relativity Space. Chips, software, government, rockets — it’s an impressive range. Then again, Schmidt would bring a lot of baggage when it comes to his own extramarital dalliances . It’s hard to see him clearing the board for that reason. Lip-Bu Tan . Intel’s CEO knows chips, and right now he might welcome a very soft landing. Last month, Intel reported third-quarter revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion, then warned its fourth-quarter results would fall short of Wall Street’s forecasts. The AI boom has caused a memory-chip shortage, pushing up PC prices and cutting PC sales. That’s hurt Intel (PC chips are a big part of its business), and its stock plunged 20% in after-hours trading on the warning, having already slid more than 30% since September. A move to a company that’s eating everyone’s lunch would be a pretty amazing escape hatch. Bret Taylor. The former Salesforce co-CEO and OpenAI board chair now runs the AI startup Sierra, and his resume includes a lot of the biggest brands in Silicon Valley. He co-created Google Maps, served as Facebook’s CTO, and chaired Twitter’s board through its sale to Elon Musk. He then took over as OpenAI’s board chair after the “Blip,” Sam Altman’s firing and fast return. When companies need an unflappable, likable adult in the room, they call Taylor. He probably knows nearly every customer Nvidia has, too. Ian Buck. If the board feels strongly about having a “builder” at the helm, they could do worse than the Nvidia VP who helped develop CUDA, the chip software that has become central to Nvidia’s dominance in AI. Analysts and former employees have floated him as a possible successor, and Kalshi traders give him a middling shot . He’s no household name, but the Stanford PhD seems more viable if Huang can can keep that chairman title and push for a successor he can work with. Someone else down the hall. Andrew Bell, Nvidia’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, arrived 25 years ago as a fresh Cornell grad and has been on an upward trajectory at the company ever since. Like Buck and dozens of other executives who are presumably being scrutinized, he reports directly to Huang. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is the insider most often named, but analysts say she isn’t necessarily a natural successor as an innovator and visionary, and Bell has the chip pedigree. The wild card? Lori Huang . Nobody has floated her, but hear us out: Jensen met his wife as lab partners at Oregon State, so she has been working with him since before Nvidia existed. After graduating, she worked at Silicon Graphics as a micro chip engineer (making more money than her husband, he has said), then scaled back to raise the couple’s family, and she now co-leads the family trusts. If the board wants continuity, they could do worse than a humbler Huang who is also a brainiac.

events.title: CFTC investigates if Kalshi improperly self-certified event contracts
events.summary: Kalshi called it a minor issue in how the contracts were filed and said it is working with the CFTC to address the matter. Prediction market platforms are allowed to self-certify event contracts without the federal agency's approval, as long as they comply with the Commodity Exchange Act. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is investigating whether prediction market platform Kalshi failed to properly inform the agency of proposed event contracts, Kalshi confirmed to CNBC. Kalshi called it a minor issue in how the contracts were filed and said it is working with the CFTC to address the matter. The CFTC flagged weather-related contracts, Kalshi said. The leading prediction market platform didn't say when the agency began investigating Kalshi. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig told CNBC that the agency does not comment on investigations. Politico first reported on the probe on Tuesday, noting charges could happen soon, based on the CFTC's private notification to Kalshi. The platform declined to comment on any possible charges. Prediction market platforms are allowed to self-certify event contracts without the federal agency's prior approval, as long as they comply with the Commodity Exchange Act. The self-certification allows for faster introduction of new contracts. "The notice is about a procedural error involving the submission of a handful of contracts, many of which weren't live," said Elisabeth Diana, head of communications at Kalshi. "We are already addressing the issue." The move is the latest by the CFTC as it seeks to rein in prediction markets, which face growing scrutiny in Washington from regulators and members of Congress . In August, the CFTC ordered Kalshi to take down sports-related " mention markets " — where speculators can trade on what individuals will say in a broadcast or speech — while it looked into the event contract type. The agency is also conducting a broad probe into competitor Polymarket , which includes reviewing if the company violated a 2022 settlement with the CFTC to prohibit U.S. traders from accessing its international trading platform. Polymarket's domestic exchange operates separately from the global platform. Prediction markets are also expected to face heightened scrutiny once the Democratic Congress is sworn into office in January. Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., in a Tuesday social media post on X , called for a ban on sports prediction markets — which account for the overwhelming majority of volume on leading platforms. — CNBC's Talia Kaplan contributed to this report Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

events.title: CDL shares fall 6.7% after developer warns of significantly weaker second half
events.summary: CDL shares were trading at around $6.50 at 10am on Nov 12, down almost 8.6%. At the start of 2026, they were trading for as much as $10. CDL shares fell as much as 8% after it warned second-half 2026 results will be much weaker, hit by inflation, high rates and delayed deal completions. The company expects foreign exchange losses and possible impairment losses after revaluing its property portfolio, adding pressure on earnings. CDL still saw stronger Singapore sales, plans more launches in 2027, and aims to sell $6 billion of assets and cut net borrowings by about $3 billion by 2029. SINGAPORE – Shares of City Developments Limited (CDL) slipped 6.7% when the market closed on Nov 12, after the property developer warned that its second-half performance for 2026 would be significantly weaker than a year earlier. CDL shares closed at $6.64 on Nov 12, down 6.7%. At the start of the year, they were trading for as much as $10. In an operating update released after the market closed on Nov 11, CDL said persistent inflation and elevated interest rates had pushed back some deals it had expected to complete by the end of 2026. The year-on-year decline is likely to look more stark as the company booked a $473.1 million gain in the second half of 2025 from the sale of its stake in South Beach Consortium. The slowdown comes after the developer in September revealed a new strategy targeting $6 billion in asset disposals by 2029. CDL said foreign exchange losses are likely to also weigh on earnings. It noted specifically that the Korean won’s appreciation against the Singdollar since July has led to significant foreign exchange losses for its South Korean subsidiary on a Singdollar-denominated loan owed to it by another group entity. The developer added that it is revaluing its property portfolio, a process that could lead to impairment losses. It said its Singapore property sales picked up in the third quarter, although demand came mainly from existing projects due to the absence of new launches. CDL and its joint venture partners sold 124 units worth $322.6 million, up from 88 units worth $313.2 million a year earlier. In the first nine months of 2026, CDL and its partners sold 476 units worth $1.2 billion. Sales were largely driven by Newport Residences, a 246-unit freehold project in Anson Road that is now 83% sold. In October, CDL launched the 570-unit Lucerne Grand in Lakeside. It sold 61% of the units over the launch weekend at an average price of $2,480 per sq ft. The project was 73% sold as at the Nov 11 update. The developer plans to launch two executive condominium projects – Wynwood Grand in Woodlands and Solano Grand in Senja – in the first quarter of 2027. CDL, which is aiming to cut net borrowings by about $3 billion and bring net gearing down to 55% by 2029, noted that net gearing stood at 75% as at Sept 30, after accounting for the fair value of its investment properties. The group attributed that level mainly to spending on two government land sale sites in Tanjong Rhu Road and Peck Hay Road, which were secured in the first half of 2026.

The memorabilia's proud owner, a former Boag's worker, has no plans to sell it, and has had himself tattooed in honour of the brewery. The final Tasmanian-brewed James Boag beer has sold for $1,300, as the brewery that predates electricity in the state closes its doors. Former brewery electrician Sam Cox, who spent 14 years working at the Launceston institution, has become the proud owner of the final can and case of locally brewed Boag's Red. events.title: Outgoing Trump foe Massie forces new Epstein files showdown
events.summary: Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) secured the 218 signatures needed to force another House showdown over the Jeffrey Epstein files Wednesday, just one day after fellow Republicans blocked his attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Why it matters: Congress overwhelmingly voted last year to force the release of the Epstein files, but survivors and lawmakers say the Trump administration has still withheld records. The new bill would give them the power to sue the DOJ and help state prosecutors pursue investigations. Driving the news: Massie announced Wednesday afternoon that his discharge petition for the Epstein Files Transparency Act II had reached the required 218 signatures. Rep. John Garamendi (D-Calif.) provided the final signature Wednesday, according to the House clerk's records . Just four Republicans signed the petition: Massie, Nancy Mace of South Carolina, Ralph Norman of South Carolina and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania. The other 214 signatures came from Democrats. What he's saying: "I'm working closely with @RepJayapal, @RepTeresaLF and @RepRoKhanna to get this to the floor for a vote soon," Massie wrote on X . The White House and Speaker Mike Johnson's offices have not yet provided comment. The intrigue: President Trump helped drive Massie out of Congress by backing a primary challenger, but the Kentucky Republican is using his final weeks in office to challenge the administration on some of its most politically sensitive topics. This latest effort could force Republicans to revisit a scandal that dogged the Trump administration for more than a year, even after Congress overwhelmingly voted to require the release of Epstein's files. This time, Massie wants to give Epstein survivors, state prosecutors and lawmakers the power to sue the Justice Department over records they believe it has unlawfully withheld. Catch up quick: Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) led the original push to force the release of the Epstein files. Their first bill passed the House 427-1 in November 2025 after they secured enough signatures to bypass Speaker Mike Johnson. Trump ultimately signed it into law. The law required DOJ to release its Epstein-related investigative records by Dec. 19, 2025, with limited exceptions to protect victims, ongoing investigations and other sensitive information. The department missed that deadline but announced in January that it had released nearly 3.5 million pages. The controversy: Epstein survivors and lawmakers have accused DOJ of withholding too much information while simultaneously exposing victims through inadequate redactions. A report released Tuesday by the Republican-led House Oversight Committee faulted the Trump administration's handling of the disclosures, including failures to protect victims and excessive redactions concealing alleged co-conspirators. The committee also said its investigation found no evidence implicating Trump in Epstein's crimes. What's next: Massie's petition is expected to become eligible for a floor vote by early December, with more than enough legislative days remaining under the House's current schedule. But passage is not guaranteed, and Senate Republican leaders could still decline to consider the measure before the new Congress takes office in January.

events.title: How India is marketing its skilled workforce to Australian businesses
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Qantas the latest in list of companies to outsource jobs to India Qantas is cutting 850 local jobs with some roles to be outsourced to Accenture workers in India. ( ABC News: ABC News: Adriane Reardon ) Qantas's announcement to shift 850 local jobs to India is the latest in a wave of white-collar jobs moving offshore. Some of Australia's biggest companies are outsourcing jobs to India. India has marketed its large, mostly English-speaking workforce to businesses for decades, but the nature of the jobs has changed. From clothing to credit cards, some of Australia's largest companies are shifting hundreds of jobs overseas, and the trend is not slowing down. NAB, Westpac, Telstra, Bank of Queensland, Coles, Officeworks and Qantas are among companies that have announced plans to cut Australian jobs and move roles to Asia in recent years — most under so-called global capacity centres (GCCs). Qantas announces cuts to 850 corporate jobs Qantas announces it will slash 850 roles in the coming years, with the first changes expected to be in place by mid-2027. GCCs are subsidiaries of foreign companies that allow them to maintain full control of their business rather than contracting a third party. Bunnings announced plans for a GCC in India in 2020, but has not yet announced job cuts. Kmart opened one in 2018. The companies said roles needed to move to cope with rising costs and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). The Finance Sector Union has called the cuts "callous" and "ruthless" in the face of soaring corporate profits. From call centres to corporate hubs India is home to about 50 per cent of the world's GCCs, the latest evolution of offshoring, which began with contracting out call centre work decades ago. Global Capacity Centres take up a huge footprint in the city of Bengaluru in India's south. ( Reuters: Vivek Prakash ) In 2024, Australia's high commissioner to India, Philip Green, estimated Australian companies directly employed about 30,000 people in Indian GCCs. "In very simple terms, a GCC is setting up another office for a company. Instead of hiring contractors, you're hiring employees," said Lalit Ahuja, the chief executive of ANSR, which helps companies establish GCCs in India. Mr Ahuja said tighter immigration restrictions were accelerating the trend. Rather than waiting for skilled workers to migrate to Australia, he said, companies were moving operations to where the talent was. The shift could eventually extend to senior executives. "It's quite conceivable that one day for a large Australian company, they may have some key leaders sitting in Bangalore or Hyderabad," Mr Ahuja said. Arya Roy Bardhan, a junior fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in Kolkata, said that while India did offer skilled workers, it was the cost savings that attracted foreign companies. "If you're comparing India with Australia, the average wage is one third of what you have to pay in Australia," he said. "The only incentive for opening a GCC in India is cost savings. It's lower tax rates and major savings in wages." Dr Kanupriya, an assistant professor in the Department of Economics and Trade Policy at the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade, said it was a combination of both. "It's a cost-saving measure, and it taps into the diverse talent pool that India has to offer." A big part of that is the sheer number of potential employees available. India has marketed its large, mostly English-speaking workforce to foreign businesses since the 1990s, offering cheap wages and tax breaks to offshore companies. India has a huge number of tech graduates to offer Australian companies amid a domestic skills shortage. ( Reuters: Rishika Sadam ) By the early 2000s, more technical jobs shifted to the country as India prioritised tech and engineering graduates. With the world's largest youth population and about 830,000 engineering and technology graduates annually, according to India's Ministry of Education, creating jobs is a major priority. "Post-COVID, people realise this workforce has the skill and technical expertise needed to work with new products and even innovate," Mr Bardhan said. Time zones also did not matter when the work was not customer service. "Now you want us for tasks which can be done overnight, we don't have to operate at the same hours," he said. Before COVID, Mr Ahuja said his pitch to foreign companies was "anyone, any work, anytime, anywhere". With remote work normalised, companies became more comfortable running operations across borders. "You can run the company from India and have stores in Australia," Mr Ahuja said.

events.title: Hardware-Based Location Checks Target AI Chip Smuggling (Texas A&M)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at Texas A&M University published “5G CATS: 5G-Based Cryptographic Authorization Against Trafficking of Semiconductor Devices.” Abstract : “Enforcing export controls on AI accelerators requires verifying where a chip operates after deployment. Round-trip time measurements can bound a chip’s distance from a trusted landmark, but any jitter in honest replies forces the verifier to loosen its timeout, giving an attacker slack to relay traffic over fiber from a restricted region. Prior approaches either cross the untrusted host stack or rely on noisy power-line channels that inflate this slack. We present 5G CATS, a location certification system that pairs a co-packaged 5G radio, cryptographic engine, and hardware interlock on the GPU package with 5G Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) base stations. Terminating the radio link inside the package removes the host software, PCIe fabric, and baseboard management controller from the verification path. We map an authenticated challenge-response protocol onto 5G’s slot structure, replace permanent key erasure with short-lived execution leases, and specify a cross-check of the chip’s reported serving cell against the carrier’s own attachment records. In ns-3 and 5G-LENA simulations of an unloaded cell, our URLLC-based radio profile narrows the 99.9th percentile round-trip spread to 2.60 ms, more than ten times narrower than default 5G. A tracer rejects every round of a fiber relay from 300 km, against 2,000 km for default 5G. Against a 3,000 km attacker, a tracer stays safe at up to 1,410 km from the chip, against at most 619 km for PowerCATS’s published model, while default 5G is never safe.” Find the technical paper here . events.title: Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
events.summary: Poundland looks set to avoid immediate collapse after its US owners told MPs on Wednesday they were in favour of extending a deadline to find a rescue deal. The discount chain, which has 11,000 employees, has been edging towards administration after being blocked by Gordon Brothers from accessing cash in its bank accounts. A deadline to secure a buyer for the business is set to expire at midnight, but sources close to the situation told the BBC they expect more time will be given thanks to the release funding in recent days. A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers following accusations that the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 shops and stock piecemeal. Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock shops, and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period. The investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claims. But pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham. About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops. The BBC understands that Gordon Brothers agreed to release a further £9m from Poundland's accounts, on top of £10m announced earlier. This will grant the company an additional 10 days to find a new buyer. There are three bids currently on the table for Poundland, all of which have so far been rejected by the Gordon Brothers, who stand to profit from selling the company and its stock in parts. Following the meeting between MPs on the business and trade committee and representatives of Gordon Brothers, chairman Liam Byrne told the BBC that he was "deeply concerned" and described the firm's behaviour as "much like a wolf on Wall Street, on the British High Street". "They refused to prioritise protecting jobs and stores over and above their own financial returns," he said. "It's clear that they've taken millions out of Poundland at a time when they themselves said the business was on a knife edge." Byrne said the committee's message to Gordon Brothers was to ensure Poundland had "access to the funds that it needs to trade at what should be one of the busiest periods in the year". He urged Gordon Brothers to "do what is right to save jobs and stores and do that now". "It's a good business, it's a much-loved business and, particularly in the middle of the cost of living crisis, communities up and down the country rely on access to the kind of stores that it operates," Byrne added. Following the private meeting with MPs, Poundland's chief executive Barry Williams told the BBC that the chain's board would hold an urgent meeting on Wednesday night. Views on Poundland performance differ Views on the chain's performance differ between those running operations and the owners. Poundland boss Williams told staff last week that like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4%. The sales period included Halloween, but Williams said this was £1.5m ahead of budget. He added that the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year when there were losses of £68m. However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading". It has argued that the best way of securing jobs may be to split up the business and sell chunks of its 600 sites to other retailers. There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up Poundland shops, which could mean continuing employment for workers at those sites. The main issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland as a national chain. Are you affected by issues discussed in this story? events.summary: Meta's head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering Santosh Janardhan will leave in 2027. Janardhan's successor, former AWS senior vice president David Brown, will lead Meta's infrastructure efforts of the Meta Compute initiative, spearheaded by Dina Powell McCormick and Daniel Gross. The executive move underscores Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg's efforts to expand the company's data center operations under newer leaders at a time of increasing investor scrutiny on capital expenditure spending by the social media giant and its hyperscaler rivals. Meta's long-time infrastructure leader will leave the company in the new year, setting the stage for a recently hired former Amazon Web Services executive to oversee its massive data center technical operations. Santosh Janardhan, Meta's head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering, revealed his upcoming departure on Wednesday in an internal memo obtained by CNBC. Janardhan, who has worked at Meta since 2009, said "it's time to pass the baton" to former AWS senior vice president David Brown, who joined Meta in July from AWS. Brown will now formally lead Meta's infrastructure efforts as part of the Meta Compute initiative, which is spearheaded by the company's president and vice chairman Dina Powell McCormick and technical leader Daniel Gross. Zuckerberg is relying on these new executives to continue developing cutting-edge data centers and related infrastructure needed to support its AI ambitions. The company said during its recent third-quarter earnings report that it expects full-year capex to fall in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. Meta also logged negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, which S&P Global Ratings noted as part of its decision in late October to revise Meta's credit rating from AA- stable to AA- negative. Janardhan said in the memo that he will help support Brown through the first quarter of 2027 as part of "the transition." "As we make the next set of choices about our priorities, this is the right time for Dave to take the lead in shaping that work," Janardhan said in the memo. "Dave has spent his career building and operating dependable infrastructure for a wide range of demanding workloads. He has the instincts, depth and judgment this moment requires." Bloomberg News first reported on the executive transition. WATCH : AI challenge is lack of compute in the marketplace .

events.title: Personal data stolen after National Parks booking service hacked in three states
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Personal user data breached after Qld, Victoria and SA's National Park booking systems hacked Park users are being warned to keep an eye out for Queensland Parks and Wildlife staff impersonators. ( ABC News: Peter Quattrocelli ) The National Parks booking system for Queensland, Victoria and South Australia has been hacked. Queensland's environment department says it does not believe financial information has been compromised. Park users should be wary of phishing attempts. Hackers have stolen personal user information from Queensland, Victoria and South Australia's National Parks booking systems. The Queensland Department of Environment, Tourism, Science, and Innovation told 612 ABC Brisbane that the third-party provider Bookeasy had been hacked. Bookeasy processes camping and vehicle access permits for the National Parks Booking System, storing personal emails, addresses, and phone numbers. The spokesperson said "at this stage" they did not believe customers' financial information was accessed, as payments are processed through a separate system. The department spokesperson said park users should remain wary of phishing attempts by hackers impersonating national park staff. "If you receive an unexpected email, text message or phone call claiming to be from the department and asking you to confirm or provide personal information, do not respond, click on any links, or provide any personal information," the spokesperson said. "We take the privacy and security of your information extremely seriously and will provide further information to affected customers as soon as we know more." The spokesperson said any suspicious activity should be reported directly to the Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service at QPWS@detsi.qld.gov.au. A Parks Victoria spokesperson said they were aware of "suspicious Whatsapp messages" being sent to their customers. The spokesperson said they had temporarily suspended all new campsite bookings while investigations continued. "We are working urgently with Bookeasy to understand the issue and proactively communicating with our customers who may be impacted," the spokesperson said. "Existing bookings have not been cancelled and remain valid. "While we investigate, we are also temporarily unable to make changes or modifications to existing bookings." In an email, National Parks and Wildlife Service South Australia told users to remain vigilant. "Bookeasy recently detected unauthorised activity within its platform and has engaged cyber security experts to investigate," the email said. "As part of this investigation, it has been identified that some customer information, including names, contact details, and booking information, may have been accessed. "At this stage, there is no evidence that credit card details were accessed." events.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
events.summary: Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security. United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, the Times has reported. The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang , and Nvidia’s shares fell in after-hours trading. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. November 11, 2026: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per the Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. November 11, 2026: Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, NYT says The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. November 11, 2026: Congress plans to subpoena Huang to answer questions about affair Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressman to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China committee Chairman Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . November 9, 2026: Huang pulls out of various speaking engagements The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. November 9-10, 2026: Details emerge about the business relationships between Nvidia and the alleged spy Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported. November 8, 2026: Trump shows support for Nvidia CEO, calls him a “fine person” On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO. “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said.

events.title: Scott Colom ousts Cindy Hyde-Smith in historic Mississippi Senate flip
events.summary: Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a stunning Mississippi upset , becoming the first Democrat elected to the state's Senate delegation since 1982, AP projects. Why it matters: Colom's victory marks another extraordinary breakthrough for Democrats in the Deep South, extending the historic blue wave that handed the party control of both chambers of Congress. Colom also becomes Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction. Hiram Rhodes Revels became the nation's first Black senator in 1870. Mississippi's last Black senator, Blanche K. Bruce, served until 1881. Catch up quick: Colom's victory expands Democrats' 55–44 advantage over Republicans in the Senate. Worries of a recount — which requires a court order, as Mississippi has no recount law — seemed moot as Hyde-Smith posted a video message to X shortly after AP called the race, appearing to concede to Colom. "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Cologne and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state," she said. Hyde-Smith also addressed another worry from Mississippi voters following a significant purge of the state's voter rolls, saying that her campaign "has worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election." "I am proud of what we have accomplished together, but I want to make one thing very clear: an election may come to an end, but our commitment to Mississippi never will," she said. The big picture: Colom's victory followed a late surge of Democratic spending and organizing in a state Trump carried by 23 points in 2024. Hyde-Smith faced warning signs in the campaign's closing months, when Colom raised twice as much as the GOP senator despite her overall cash advantage. She was also outspent on TV advertising , with a flood of ads from left-leaning PACs and super PACs pushing support for Colom and attacking the senator for her vote not to release files related to the convicted human trafficker Jeffrey Epstein. Hyde-Smith's campaign also faced criticism over an interview she gave to WLOX-TV in Biloxi, Mississippi, where she fumbled an answer about the price of beef, saying that Mississippians had "so many other proteins to choose from." Colom's campaign capitalized on her blunder, creating a viral campaign ad urging voters to "choose another senator." The GOP made a late push to help Hyde-Smith, including President Trump speaking at a rally for her in Alcorn County, where he won by 68% in 2024. But it wasn't enough. Hyde-Smith's term will end after eight years. She was appointed to the Senate in 2018 by then-Mississippi Gov. Phil Bryant, and ran for a full term in 2020, where she bested her Democratic challenger Mike Espy by 10 points. Zoom in: Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney from Columbus, campaigned on lowering the cost of living, raising wages and protecting rural hospitals. His campaign also drew in heavy Democratic hitters to stump for him, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock. The bottom line: Colom's win adds Mississippi to a growing list of Republican strongholds where Democrats broke through in the midterms, including Texas and South Carolina. It also reinforces the role of Black voters in the Democratic comeback, after the party rebuilt support among a crucial voting bloc that showed signs of shifting toward Trump in 2024. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated. This story has been corrected to show that Hyde-Smith's interview was conducted in Biloxi (not Jackson, Mississippi).

events.title: Jim Cramer says investors need to pay attention to CoreWeave. Here's why
events.summary: Jim Cramer said he's becoming less skeptical of CoreWeave after strong earnings and reassuring comments from its CEO. CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said demand for computing capacity far exceeds supply, while also detailing improving financing options and the lasting value of Nvidia chips CNBC's Jim Cramer said Wednesday that he's becoming less skeptical of CoreWeave after the neocloud's strong earnings and the CEO's "refreshing and reassuring" comments. CoreWeave shares surged nearly 25% on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly revenue and raised its 2026 guidance. The results, which were out Tuesday evening, helped ease concerns about a slowdown in AI infrastructure spending. CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator's subsequent interview with Cramer on CNBC just after Wall Street's opening bell offered further reasons for optimism. One of the most encouraging takeaways from Intrator was disclosure that demand for CoreWeave's computing capacity is 10 times greater than what the company can supply. It was also discussed on the post-earnings conference call. That dynamic has allowed CoreWeave to consistently increase prices, supporting stronger gross margins even as it spends heavily to expand its infrastructure. Intrator also addressed concerns about CoreWeave's substantial debt load , which has weighed heavily on its stock . Despite Wednesday's surge, shares are still down 15% year to date and down 55% from its 52-week high of $138 on May 6. The past month has been particularly tumultuous for the neoclouds, which also include Iren and Nebius . Iren reported strong earnings last week. Nebius reports its quarter Thursday morning. Rather than relying solely on traditional bond markets, CoreWeave has increasingly turned to financing backed by its equipment and customer contracts. "When I pressed him, asking why he doesn't just go into the open market and buy these bonds that are trading so poorly, he admitted that he's been tempted to, but ultimately he still believes he can make an even better return building data centers," Cramer said. "Take that red flag off the table." Another surprising revelation involved the value of CoreWeave's Nvidia chips. Intrator said some H100 chips purchased four years ago are now being contracted at premiums of 20% to 50% above its original cost, suggesting the equipment is retaining its economic value longer than many investors anticipated. The Intrator interview also helped ease concerns about growing political opposition to data center construction. The CEO maintained that demand for computing power would continue to drive expansion, even if stricter regulations pushed some projects overseas. For Cramer, the comments offered a welcome counterpoint to the recent pessimism surrounding AI infrastructure stocks. While he has grown more cautious about the sector amid political and financing risks, the "Mad Money" host maintained that abandoning it altogether could mean missing substantial upside. "We've taken some data center and related stocks off the table, unfortunately not Nvidia, [for the CNBC Investing Club ] because our composure and our prudence dictates that to have too much data center is still too dicey. Still, we've left plenty of exposure to the group, which includes semis, software, networking, builders, turbines and cooling equipment, because we think the AI theme has much more room to run." The Club does not own any neoclouds. But it does have diversified, albeit recently reduced, exposure to the AI boom via chip stocks and names that help run and power data centers. events.title: MSCI says Indonesia’s Barito Pacific will be removed from its indexes
events.summary: The latest setback comes a month after MSCI warned Indonesian stocks could be removed from its indexes next year and the market relegated to “standalone” status. MSCI will remove Barito Pacific from its indexes and move Bumi Resources Minerals to small cap, forcing index funds to sell after Nov 30. The move adds pressure on Indonesia, whose market is down over 40% in 2026 and faces a possible downgrade to “standalone” status. Authorities have tightened rules and MSCI is seeking feedback until April 30, 2027, but investors have already pulled out US$5.4 billion this year. SINGAPORE/BENGALURU / JAKARTA – Global index provider MSCI will remove one Indonesian company from its indexes, it said on Nov 11 , dealing a blow to the country’s efforts to avoid a downgrade and retain its emerging-market status. The latest setback comes a month after MSCI warned Indonesian stocks could be removed from its indexes in 2027 and the market relegated to “standalone” status, a much harsher fate than the one the index provider first threatened in January. The deletions will force funds that track its indexes to sell the shares, and take effect after the close of trading on Nov 30. Barito Pacific will be removed from MSCI’s global standard index, while Bumi Resources Minerals will be moved from that index to the small-cap index. Neither firm immediately responded to requests for comment. Once the removal takes effect, MSCI’s Indonesia index will be left with seven companies after the index provider culled six firms in May and two more in August. At the start of 2026, the Indonesia index had 18 firms. Barito Pacific, a company with interests in petrochemicals, energy and infrastructure, is controlled by business magnate and billionaire Prajogo Pangestu. In May, MSCI removed from its Indonesia index three firms in which Prajogo has controlling stakes: Chandra Asri Pacific, Barito Renewables Energy and Petrindo Jaya Kreasi. Indonesia’s benchmark stock index was up 1.3% at 0340 GMT (11.40am Singapore time), while the rupiah slid 0.6% to hit a new all-time low of 18,248 a US dollar. The currency was affected by US monetary policy expectations, concerns about MSCI’s decision on Indonesian stocks, domestic economic issues and higher year-end demand for foreign exchange, Bank Indonesia said in a statement on Nov 12. The threat of a downgrade has cast a shadow over Indonesian markets, with the benchmark index down over 40% in 2026, making it the world’s worst-performing major stock market. In October, MSCI cited Indonesia’s failure to improve ownership transparency and curb coordinated trading, turning what had been a downgrade risk to “frontier” market status into a full-blown crisis of investor confidence. The Indonesian authorities have spent much of 2026 trying to address MSCI’s concerns, tightening disclosure requirements and laying out plans to raise minimum free floats. In October, the regulator announced sanctions linked to alleged manipulation. Earlier this week, the stock exchange removed the 5 trillion rupiah (S$352 million) market cap threshold for screening companies that breach high shareholding concentration rules. MSCI is seeking feedback on the reclassification proposal until April 30, 2027, and will announce its decision on or before June 30, 2027 , although analysts worry that many active investors may exit Indonesia before that . Foreign investors have already pulled out US$5.4 billion (S$6.9 billion) from Indonesian equities in 2026. Goldman Sachs has estimated MSCI’s removal of the country’s stocks from its indexes could spur US$5.6 billion of passive outflows. Indonesia has been an MSCI emerging market since 1989, and a downgrade would be a huge reversal for a market that until recently was a favourite of foreign investors. More than US$1.8 trillion in assets are benchmarked to MSCI’s emerging-market indexes , according to the index provider’s website . REUTERS

events.title: Feds arrest top official of healthcare company, alleging illegal drug importation
events.summary: U.S. authorities are accusing the two top officials of a Canadian company of operating a long-running scheme to illegally import prescription drugs into the U.S., according to court records. John Thomas Howard, treasurer and a director of the company, CANARX, was arrested Sunday on smuggling and conspiracy charges. His brother Bob Howard, CANARX president and director, is wanted in the investigation, according to records. CANARX was featured in a CNBC investigation "RiskyRX" last year that revealed how the company and others known as alternative funding programs, or AFPs, are becoming more pervasive around the U.S. as drug costs skyrocket. U.S. authorities are accusing the two top officials of a Canadian company of operating a long-running scheme to illegally import prescription drugs into the U.S., according to court records filed Tuesday. John Thomas Howard, treasurer and a director of the company, CANARX, was arrested Sunday on smuggling and conspiracy charges, according to the records. Bob Howard, his brother, who is president and a director of CANARX, is also wanted in the federal investigation, according to an affidavit from Dustin Dobbs, a special agent with the Food and Drug Administration's Office of Criminal Investigations. He has not yet been taken into custody. Besides conspiracy and smuggling, the arrest warrant said John Thomas Howard was charged with introducing misbranded drugs into interstate commerce and illegal drug importation. No plea has been filed. CANARX was featured in a CNBC investigation last year that revealed how the company and others known as alternative funding programs, or AFPs, are becoming more pervasive around the U.S. as drug costs skyrocket. The investigation found these companies have penetrated the country's healthcare system by offering high-cost specialty drugs at more affordable prices through private and public employers. In some cases, employers are requiring their staff to use an AFP. AFPs often obtain the medications overseas and ship them directly to patients, a practice that federal authorities have said is illegal and poses safety risks. CNBC traced the trail of drugs from abroad to the U.S. via a supply chain that the pharmaceutical companies producing the medications have not authorized. On its website, CANARX, founded in 2002 and based in Windsor, Ontario, Canada, described its business as the first international prescription provider for the U.S. and the safest such program in the industry. The company said it sources its medications from Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand. But the affidavit said that the FDA's investigation found "there is probable cause to believe that (CANARX) illegally imported or caused the illegal importation of prescription drugs into the United States …." The affidavit does not specify which medications the agency believes were illegally imported. The criminal complaint covers the period from Feb. 22, 2017, through April 15, 2026. The company's general counsel, Joseph Morris, told CNBC in a statement: "The Howards deny all the charges against them, will defend vigorously, and expect to be vindicated in court." The company has been under FDA scrutiny for several years. In 2023, the agency seized medication being shipped by CANARX that it says was potentially misbranded and counterfeit, according to an email sent to a patient that was obtained by CNBC. And in 2019, the FDA sent a warning letter to the company, saying it was operating "in a manner that substitutes the FDA-approved drugs prescribed by the U.S. healthcare provider with unapproved drugs." Morris, in response to that warning, argued CANARX was not misleading patients, but agreed for the company to stop importing drugs that need to be administered by a doctor. In an interview as part of the CNBC investigation, Morris said last year that the medicines shipped to U.S. patients come from highly regulated countries. He said CANARX was operating legally. The central question for AFPs is the legality of importing prescription drugs into the U.S. for personal use. The FDA allows Americans to import medications for individual use in some cases if the drug is not available domestically. That is the basis on which the AFPs built their models for shipping medicines directly to patients. But an FDA spokesperson told CNBC last year that "in most circumstances, a person cannot import prescription drugs from other countries into the U.S. ... as substitutes for FDA-approved drugs." In a separate civil lawsuit that is pending, Gilead Sciences accused CANARX and other companies of illegally importing Biktarvy, its medication to treat HIV. In a statement to CNBC on Wednesday, a Gilead spokesperson said the company "has taken strong legal action to protect patients and the integrity of the U.S. medicines supply chain. We welcome the government's efforts to hold accountable those whose conduct may put patients at risk." CANARX has not responded to the Gilead lawsuit.
