events.title: Oil rises on mixed signals over Iran war outlook
events.summary: The Iran war, which started on Feb 28, has caused gas prices to rise worldwide. Oil climbed on Nov 11, as traders weighed mixed signals on the prospects for a conclusion to the Iran war. While US President Donald Trump has said further strikes on Iran would not be necessary , regional flare-ups have persisted and peace talks have shown little progress. Iran will not remove “a single atom” of enriched nuclear material from the country, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaee said in an interview with Al Mayadeen. West Texas Intermediate futures rose above US$86 a barrel after sliding about 5% in the previous two days, while Brent closed near US$93. “We’ve shifted from a market that needed things to get worse to move higher, to one where things simply not getting better could be enough to push prices up,” said Rebecca Babin, senior energy trader at CIBC Private Wealth Group. The US benchmark is up roughly 50% this year, but the market has reversed sharply in November, with Brent tumbling from a six-month high on hopes the conflict will ease and as Persian Gulf energy exports rise. Saudi Arabia’s crude output climbed 26% in October to the highest since the war began despite attacks on ships, as a recovery in regional flows pushes prices lower. Saudi Arabia told OPEC that its output rose to 10.56 million barrels a day in October, according to a monthly report seen by Bloomberg from the organisation’s secretariat. The bigger flows from the Saudis and other exporters around the Persian Gulf are showing up in physical markets at a time when consumption remains constrained. “We have seen a sharp re-pricing of the oil market over the past two weeks” as election results in the US and Israel “reduced the likelihood of renewed escalation in the conflict,” said Jens Naervig Pedersen, a strategist at Danske Bank AS. Still, “Iran seems hesitant to meet US demands on its nuclear programme, which may test the durability of the recent decline in oil prices.” Meanwhile, the American Petroleum Institute reported US crude inventories rose by nine million barrels last week. Stockpiles of distillates such as diesel, which had fallen below 100 million barrels for the first time since 2003, climbed by 1.5 million barrels, API said. Official data is due on Nov 12. Separately, the Energy Information Administration raised its 2027 forecasts for retail gasoline prices to an average US$3.73 a gallon and diesel to US$5.03, citing tight global fuel supplies. The agency left its US crude production estimate unchanged at 14.3 million barrels a day in its Short-Term Energy Outlook. A tanker carrying Russian diesel that had briefly signalled a US destination made a U-turn off New York, adding uncertainty over deliveries to the North American market. Last month, Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to supply fuel to the US and global markets in a deal with Trump, though the arrangement drew criticism from Democrats. BLOOMBERG

( ABC News: Isabella Garrido ) Mr Gnocco's marine tourism business in north Queensland takes people on snorkelling tours on the Great Barrier Reef, jet ski tours and guided walks around Magnetic Island. He said hands-on, manual and interpersonal interactions were core aspects of the job. "With a reef tour guide, there's literally no part in the process that could be replaced by AI. Luke Gnocco says it is unlikely AI will affect hands-on jobs in the tourism industry. ( Supplied: Poseidon Adventure ) "Especially being Australia, a lot of our tourism and a lot of our products are the country, they are the reef, they are the water, and I don't think it's ever going to go backwards." While he is confident the tourism industry will weather any AI boom, recent research by public policy consultancy firm SGS Economics and Planning found about 30 per cent of work tasks across regional Queensland could be exposed to AI automation. Principal and partner Alison Holloway said regional locations were more resilient to change from AI. Data centre industry butts up against community challenges With Jensen Huang under pressure, Nvidia finds itself with no succession plan ANZ boss warns global markets in 'dangerous situation' as interest rates rise How India is marketing its skilled workforce to Australian businesses Alison Holloway says AI will affect some locations differently than others. ( Supplied: Alison Holloway ) "A lot of the knowledge jobs and professional services jobs are located in the city centres … and they're the jobs that are most exposed to AI automation," Ms Holloway said. The report found almost 40 per cent of work tasks in Brisbane were at risk of AI automation, followed by the Gold Coast on 37.1 per cent. The Sunshine Coast sits at 36.4 per cent, followed by Cairns at 36, followed by Townsville and Rockhampton at 35.6, and Mackay at 34.9. Despite the Gold Coast's status as a major tourism hub, Ms Holloway said there was a mix of occupations in the region, including many administrative tasks within tourism that were not in-person. The Gold Coast is just behind Brisbane in the number of jobs at risk of AI automation. ( ABC News: Emily Dobson ) SGS Economics and Planning drew upon research by Jobs and Skills Australia and data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics to determine the risk of exposure in different locations. Ms Holloway said roles susceptible to automation were concentrated in the professional hearts of cities, such as finance, professional services and office-based jobs. She said those less exposed to AI disruption required in-person engagement or a physical presence. SGS Economics and Planning says AI is set to disrupt how work gets done at a pace and scale few industries have faced before. ( AP: Michael Dwyer/File ) "If you think about the care economy, nursing and aged care, they're all things where a physical person is engaged in that job," she said. Christoph Breidbach, an associate professor of Business Information Systems at the University of Queensland, said many regional occupations were inherently different because they required local knowledge, human relationships or engaging with unpredictable natural environments. Dr Breidbach said farming, for example, required responding to changing weather or soil conditions and livestock behaviour. Christoph Breidbach says this time around, jobs in cities are more likely to be affected by AI than those in regional areas. ( Supplied ) "What AI does is that it could assist with planning or with scheduling or with decision support, but you simply can't replace the physical execution of these tasks, unless you have very advanced robotics," he said. While previous waves of technological change disproportionately affected regional economies, Dr Breidbach said the AI wave was different for industries like agriculture and manufacturing. "It's not so much the physical labour that is now being automated or even augmented, but you can see change to cognitive tasks. So, your writing, your analysing of information, preparing of reports, and those are tasks that you would associate with white-collar jobs.

events.title: Clashes erupt in Barcelona after thousands join Spain general strike
events.summary: Watch: Protesters and police clash in Barcelona Clashes have broken out between groups of masked men and police in Barcelona after tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike for 14 years, called by the country's main unions over housing and the high cost of living. Some 120,000 people joined a demonstration in the capital Madrid and more than 50,000 turned out in Barcelona, where footage showed masked men setting fire to rubbish bins and smashing shop windows as police fired tear gas. Transport and other public services across Spain faced serious disruption. Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November. The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant." There was a heavy police presence in the centre of Barcelona on Wednesday evening, with officers wearing helmets and riot shields. Some of the disturbances took place in the Passeig de Gràcia, close to the iconic Plaça de Catalunya in the centre of the city. Small fires burned in the middle of the streets as bins were set alight. Local media reported that a group of people fired fireworks towards police and looted shops including the Lego store. Protesters were also seen trying to enter the Apple Store. The BBC spoke to a woman who attended the protests in Barcelona who said it was mostly very peaceful and "joyful". She said she was there to protest about the housing costs and that "there were a lot of children and old people there." She was in the area of Las Ramblas in the evening and saw fires in the streets. "The fires were everywhere, it was very intense," she said. Earlier in the day there was major disruption around Madrid and Barcelona, with traffic halted on several main roads. The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices. Police said they had made dozens of arrests "We've completely brought the city to a standstill," a protester in Madrid told Reuters news agency, adding there was widespread support for the general strike. "Everyone's out there, despite the rainy weather; everyone's out on the streets." Another protester, 37-year-old teacher Olga Domingo, said she was protesting because "the housing situation is outrageous. The current cost of living compared to wages is completely unsustainable". The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later. Rental prices in the capital have risen in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50 sq m apartment in Madrid was an average of €1,170 ($1,300; £1,000) in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about €2,460. That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions. Watch: Protesters gather across Spain for first general strike in 14 years Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his plan for housing reform. Not since 2012, under the conservative government of Mariano Rajoy, has Spain held general strikes. And while previous strikes have been problematic for the government in power, this one is different. Sánchez and his ministers have even encouraged workers to down tools and demand affordable housing. "Your eight-hour day. Your pension. Your public healthcare… These were collective conquests," he wrote on social media, praising those who took part in previous strikes. Tyres were set on fire in the city of Gijon in northern Spain The conservative People's Party (PP), by contrast, has accused the government of attempting to weaponise the strike for electoral gain. PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo called the general strike "nonsense", calling the unions "mafia" and "trash". Feijoo's party is leading in the polls and party spokesman Miguel Tellado accused the government of exploiting the strike to warn voters against allowing a right-wing government to be formed, which looks the most likely outcome of the 29 November election. Sánchez told Spanish TV this week: "What is nonsense is to question the rights of workers to strike." Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Álvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid. Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights. The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC.

events.title: Developer says gigantic WA data centre will not use fracked gas
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Gingerah says it will not use fracked gas to power proposed WA data centre Gingerah Energy's proposed data centre project includes a local micro-grid powered by a 5,200-megawatt solar farm and 250 wind turbines. ( Supplied: Jop van Hattum ) The company behind a proposed data centre has sought to ease fears it will power the facility with fracked gas. Gingerah Energy says the centre will be mostly powered by renewables, with gas sourced from "the domestic gas market" as backup supply. The company intends to refer its project to the WA Environmental Protection Authority for review within weeks. The company proposing to build a massive data centre in northern Western Australia has sought to ease concerns the facility will be powered by gas sourced through fracking. Gingerah Energy referred its plan to build a 1,000-megawatt data centre and renewable energy hub to the Commonwealth's environmental agency last month. The site proposed is on Karajarri country, near Broome, about 2,000 kilometres north of Perth. Jop van Hattum says Project Meridien will be mostly renewables-powered. ( Supplied: Energy Club WA ) Chief executive Jop van Hattum said Project Meridien, which Gingerah hopes to be delivered by 2030, would initially be powered by solar, batteries, gas, and later also by wind. He said renewables would initially provide more than 85 per cent of the facility's total energy demand, with that figure rising as it expanded towards its full one-gigawatt capacity. The gas used would most likely come from Karratha, Mr van Hattum said. "We target for that renewable energy capacity to increase to 94 per cent," he said. Environmentalists have suggested Gingerah might source the gas it needs for the centre through fracking in the Kimberley. While there is no ban on fracking in the region's Canning basin, no projects have received the required approvals to proceed. Critics of fracking, or hydraulic fracturing, say it is harmful due to risks involving water contamination and long-term climate impacts. Mr van Hattum said the project's gas would be sourced from "the domestic gas market". "As energy storage systems and technology improve and costs reduce, our preference would obviously be to be free of the gas and use those technologies to make the project fully carbon-free if we can," he added. Environs Kimberley director Martin Pritchard called for greater clarity on where the gas would come from. "Could it come from another company that is planning to do fracking in the Kimberley? Could it come from a new conventional well that Buru Energy is working on at the moment? Could it come from Theia Energy, and are they going to want to start fracking to supply gas to this AI data centre?" Meridien is proposed to be developed on the KTLA-held Frazier Downs pastoral lease, about 100 kilometres south of Broome in WA's west Kimberley. ( Supplied: Jop van Hattum ) Gingerah is a joint venture between Karajarri Traditional Lands Association (KTLA), Dutch geodata company Fugro and Australian geoscience firm Longreach Capital Investment, which owns Theia Energy — a company that previously applied to drill and frack exploration wells in the Kimberley. Grattan Institute energy expert Alison Reeve estimated the Meridien data centre would need about eight terajoules of gas a day in its initial 240-megawatt phase and about 32 terajoules at full capacity. "All of WA consumes about 1,100 terajoules a day," she said. Ms Reeve said the project was not large enough to lead to more gas exploration or fracking in the Kimberley because the state already had enough gas to cover it. Traditional owner confident no fracked gas will be used KTLA director Justin King Senior said the gas needed for Meridien would "absolutely not" come from fracking. KTLA director Justin King signed the Gingerah Energy Indigenous Land Use Agreement in 2024. ( Supplied: Jop van Hattum ) "I say with conviction and reassure the people, our members, and the public [fracking] would never be part of the project make-up of energy," he said. Among KTLA members, Mr King said "a small minority" were opposed to the project for several reasons, including the increase in negative sentiment towards data centres online. "Social media plays a big part in giving out information," he said. The Raging Grannies protest data centres and power hikes in North Carolina, US. ( ABC News: Bec Symons ) This month's US midterm elections put data centres in the spotlight , with voters overwhelmingly rejecting their development. Ms Reeve said this resistance was also prevalent in Australia.

events.title: Commonwealth Bank allegedly overcharged business customers
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ASIC accuses Commonwealth Bank of overcharging tens of thousands of business customers The CBA faces allegations it failed to report cash transactions made through intelligent deposit machines. ( ABC News: Margaret Burin ) Commonwealth Bank allegedly overcharged millions of dollars in fees to tens of thousands of business customers, many of them small businesses, according to the corporate regulator. ASIC has started civil penalty proceedings against Australia's biggest bank, alleging customers have been overcharged fees they were never told about. ASIC alleged CBA's CommBiz terms and conditions were misleading because they failed to clearly and accurately disclose all the fees business customers would be charged for direct debit and direct credit payments. Business customers were told they would be charged a fee for a payment to or from a third-party account. If you have more information about this story, please contact Nassim Khadem at khadem.nassim@abc.net.au or nassimkhadem@protonmail.com However, ASIC alleges CBA also charged an additional, undisclosed fee for the corresponding movement of money into or out of the customer's CommBiz account. ASIC alleges that between November 2020 and May 31, 2025, about 42,000 CommBiz customers were overcharged about $8.5 million in fees. ASIC alleges that in one example a small business paying the fortnightly wages of 10 employees from two CommBiz accounts was charged 12 fees: 10 for the payments to its employees and another two undisclosed fees for the money being withdrawn from its own accounts. "We allege Commonwealth Bank broke a basic promise to its business customers," ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said. "Small businesses are busy enough. They should not have to scrutinise every transaction to make sure that their bank is charging them the right fees." ASIC says customers were overcharged for years ASIC alleges business customers were overcharged for about 19 years, with the allegedly misleading terms and conditions in place from the launch of CommBiz in 2006. ASIC further alleges CBA received customer complaints about the issue from at least 2015, while a 2016 internal audit identified overcharging of direct debit fees and required corrective action. ASIC also alleges governance failings at CBA meant the alleged misleading statements were not identified and corrected, and that CBA allegedly failed to act efficiently, honestly and fairly. "What makes this particularly concerning is how long the alleged conduct went on, despite customer complaints to Commonwealth Bank pointing to a problem years earlier," Mr Kirkland said. ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland says "Commonwealth Bank broke a basic promise to its business customers". ( ABC ) CBA temporarily ceased charging the relevant fees in June 2025 and amended the CommBiz terms in August 2025. Since February 2026, the bank has waived the "contra leg" fees for processing direct debits and direct credits. CBA has completed a remediation program covering December 1, 2006, to present for past and current CommBiz customers. This has resulted in more than $26.4 million in remediation payments to about 93,000 CommBiz customers, including about 40,000 small businesses. The case was filed in the Federal Court on late Wednesday afternoon. However, the court has not yet listed the matter for a case management hearing. It is the second legal action ASIC has taken against a big bank in as many days, with Macquarie Bank on Monday admitting to failures in the promotion of its "welcome" interest rate for new savings account customers, which could result in a $14 million penalty. CBA apologises but says it will defend aspects of litigation The Commonwealth Bank said in a statement to the ASX that it intended to defend aspects of the litigation. "While CBA charged the fee consistently over time, the issue arose from changes made to certain Terms and Conditions intended to simplify them, which did not accurately reflect the fee charging method," the CBA statement said. "The relevant fee was 25 cents (plus GST). "CBA self-identified this matter, reported it to ASIC, and has cooperated fully with ASIC throughout its investigation. "CBA has taken additional rectification steps to reduce the risk of similar incidents." It said up to October 20, the median payment made to affected CommBiz customers was about $85, and the mean payment was about $442, inclusive of interest.

events.title: Singapore’s first Moxy hotel to open at former Novotel building site in Clarke Quay in 2027
events.summary: Guests at Moxy Singapore Clarke Quay will be able to enjoy a view of the Singapore River once the hotel is complete. Singapore’s first Moxy hotel will open by end-March 2027 at the former Novotel site in Clarke Quay. The 21-storey, 475-room hotel is part of CanningHill Piers. CDL Hospitality Trusts will buy the hotel for $474.6 million. The deal should lift its Singapore room count by 19% and its global room count by 10%. CDLHT will fund the purchase with a $148.8 million preferential offering and debt. It will also raise payouts from 90% to 100% of distributable income. SINGAPORE – Marriott’s first Moxy hotel in Singapore is expected to open by the end of March 2027 on the site of the former Novotel Singapore Clarke Quay. The 21-storey, 475-room Moxy Singapore Clarke Quay is part of the CanningHill Piers development, a mixed-use project currently being developed on the former Liang Court site. CDL Hospitality Trusts (CDLHT) expects to complete its $474.6 million acquisition of the hotel when it opens, it said in a stock exchange filing on Nov 10. In a separate announcement on the same day, CDLHT also said it would raise its dividend payouts from 90% to 100% of distributable income, starting with the six months from July 1 to Dec 31. CanningHill Piers is being developed by CapitaLand Development and City Developments Limited (CDL), in partnership with CapitaLand Ascott Trust. CDLHT in 2019 sold the Novotel, which was part of Liang Court, while agreeing to buy the new hotel once it was built. The Moxy hotel is expected to have more than 93 years left on its 99-year lease when the deal is completed. Moxy is Marriott International’s lifestyle hotel brand, known for its compact rooms and lively communal spaces where guests can work, drink and socialise. The hotel will have a rooftop pool and restaurant overlooking Marina Bay, while guests can choose rooms from about 17 sq m to 27 sq m in size, with views of the Singapore River, Fort Canning Park or the city skyline. Guests will also have access to shops and dining outlets in the development, which will be linked to Fort Canning MRT station by an underground walkway. The deal will increase CDLHT’s Singapore room count by about 19% to 3,030 and lift its global hotel room count by about 10% to 5,399, it said. Singapore is expected to account for about 67% of the trust’s portfolio value after the deal, up from about 62% as at the end of 2025. CDLHT’s managers said the Clarke Quay location would help the hotel draw both leisure and business travellers, while Marriott’s global booking network and Bonvoy loyalty programme could help it build occupancy after opening. They also expect limited growth in local hotel supply, with Singapore’s room inventory projected to rise by just around 1.3% a year from end-2026 to end-2029. The acquisition is expected to increase the cash payout investors receive for each CDLHT security they hold once the hotel’s operations stabilise. The estimated purchase price for the hotel, excluding fees, is $468.8 million, or 5.7% below Knight Frank’s Oct 30 valuation of $497 million. At that price, CDLHT’s managers estimate that annual net property income could reach about 4.8% of the purchase price once operations stabilise. The hotel received its temporary occupation permit on Oct 30, and CDLHT made its first payment of $23.4 million on Nov 4. The remainder will be paid in two later instalments, with $421.9 million due when the deal is completed. The acquisition will be partially funded through a preferential offering to raise about $148.8 million from existing investors, CDLHT said. Under the preferential offering, eligible investors can subscribe for 18 new stapled securities for every 100 they hold. The issue price of 64.3 cents is 9.9% below CDLHT’s volume-weighted average traded price of 71.35 cents on Nov 10. The offer opens on Nov 23 at 9am and closes on Dec 1 at 5.30pm, with a later deadline of 9.30pm for applications via participating banks’ ATMs. The new securities are expected to begin trading on Dec 9. CDLHT plans to use about $145.6 million in net proceeds raised through the offering and about $324.7 million in debt to finance the acquisition. Gearing, a measure of debt relative to assets, is expected to rise from 35.6% as at Sept 30 to 39.5% after the deal. The managers expect the hotel’s income to cover its associated interest costs from 2028. They estimate it will take about two to 2½ years for occupancy at the hotel to stabilise, with 2030 expected to be its first full year of stabilised operations. In a separate announcement, CDLHT’s managers added that they will raise the trust’s payout ratio to 100% after reviewing its portfolio’s performance, financial position and cash needs. It has paid out 90% of its distributable income since July 2009.

events.title: US stocks end higher as CoreWeave results ease AI spending worries
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in New York City on Nov 10. NEW YORK – US stocks closed higher on Nov 11, with the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq each rallying more than 1% as earnings from neocloud firm CoreWeave cooled investor concerns about the durability of the artificial intelligence trade, while Nvidia stabilised after two straight sessions of sharp declines. Battered CoreWeave shares surged 24.7%, their biggest daily percentage jump in more than three months, to close at the highest level in two weeks. The company said it would become profitable in the first half of 2028 on an adjusted basis, seeking to reassure investors that strong demand and customer commitments could support its debt-fuelled expansion. Sentiment improved across AI infrastructure stocks as Nebius Group surged 15.4% and Applied Digital shot up 7.4%. Nvidia advanced after shedding about US$430 billion (S$552 billion) of market capitalisation in the previous two sessions as investors worried ​about chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s relationship with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Equities have been volatile in recent days. Investors have expressed concerns about more regulation in the AI space after sweeping Democratic victories in the US midterm elections last week. That, and worries about Nvidia’s leadership, pressured one of the biggest pillars of the current bull market. Contributing to choppy stock trading, investors have been encouraged by cooling oil prices, but concerned by hot inflation data that pushed Treasury yields sharply higher. “Everybody’s looking for a canary in a coal mine every single day, every minute of every day, and then they’re reacting every single day,” said Thomas Martin, senior portfolio manager at Globalt in Atlanta. “What we’ve seen is that you’ve gone back and forth, back and forth, back and forth between AI is good, AI is not so good. We’re worried about it, then oh, it’s great.” The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 254.6 points, or 0.49%, to 52,486.49, the S&P 500 gained 98.45 points, or 1.31%, to 7,619.38, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 400.31 points, or 1.60%, to 25,466.19. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index jumped 5.7% to close at its highest since Nov 3. Every component of the index advanced. Recent pronounced selling pressure prompted some investors to buy the dip, but early indicators show it is too soon to sound the all-clear. Investors bought equities even during last week’s sell-off , with all net inflows coming through exchange-traded funds and institutional clients leading the purchases, Bank of America Global Research analysts said in a note. The S&P 500 technology index, up 2.7%, was the best-performing of the 11 major S&P sectors and has risen in three of the past four sessions. The CBOE Volatility Index fell for the fourth straight session to close at a one-week low of 17.49. Last week, Wall Street’s fear gauge hit its highest in more than seven months. Investors also examined the terms set by Anthropic on Nov 10 for its blockbuster initial public offering. The Claude chatbot creator is aiming for a valuation of up to US$1.4 trillion in the share sale. Vanda Research said in a note that the IPO could attract record buying by retail investors, with the potential to surpass SpaceX as one of the biggest single-day retail purchases ever. Hotter-than-expected inflation data on Nov 10 cemented market expectations the US Federal Reserve would raise interest rates in December, with traders now fully pricing in a hike of at least 25 basis points and a 10.4% chance of an increase of 50 basis points, according to CME FedWatch. Comments from multiple Fed officials also suggested the US central bank was open to a more aggressive path of rate hikes as price pressures worsen. events.title: What it takes to bring an AI research assistant to thousands of medical experts
events.summary: From custom infrastructure to hosted agents What we learned rebuilding Novo’s clinical trials data agent on Microsoft Foundry: a simpler operating model, a stronger session isolation, and a direct path from tracing to evaluation and optimization. Clinical research rarely ends with the questions defined in a trial protocol. Medical experts also explore the data from new angles: testing a hypothesis, comparing patient populations, visualizing a trend, or identifying a promising direction for further research. As part of a forward-deployed engineering engagement, a joint Microsoft and Novo Nordisk development team built an agent that helps medical experts perform this kind of secondary analysis of clinical trial data. We described the original project in a Microsoft customer story . More recently, we reimplemented the solution as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry . The move gave us a simpler operating model, stronger session isolation, and a direct path into Foundry’s tracing, evaluation, experimentation, optimization, and governance capabilities. It also taught us practical lessons about infrastructure planning, observability, and preserving the learning loop that already made the agent better over time. Here’s what changed, what we measured, and what we would recommend to teams making a similar move. An agent for questions that don’t have a fixed workflow Secondary analysis of clinical data is a great task for an agent because the execution path depends heavily on the question. The agent interprets the request, inspects the available data, writes and executes analysis code, examines the result, and often revises its approach before returning a summary and visualization. This isn’t just attaching a chat interface to a single API. The agent needs a reasoning loop, access to domain-specific skills, and tools for working with data. In our implementation, code execution is the central tool. The agent can generate analysis code and visualizations inside a controlled environment while the surrounding application manages the conversation and presents the result to the user. Our first production architecture ran the agent in Azure Container Apps . We used PostgreSQL for conversation storage and Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions for sandboxed code execution. That architecture gave us explicit control over every component, and it proved the value of the use case. It also meant that our team owned much of the platform around the agent: container scaling, session lifecycle, conversation persistence, execution isolation, networking, telemetry, and the integration among them. Foundry hosted agents offered a simpler division of responsibility. Moving the runtime boundary into Foundry A hosted agent is our code, packaged as a container, running on infrastructure managed by Foundry Agent Service . We retain control of the orchestration logic, models, tools, and runtime behavior. Foundry manages the endpoint, agent identity, session compute, state persistence, scaling, and lifecycle around it. At runtime, each session gets its own VM-isolated sandbox. Foundry provisions compute on demand, keeps it active while the session is in use, and de-provisions it after the configured idle period. Session files can persist and be restored when the session resumes. Scaling follows active sessions rather than a replica count that we have to predict and configure. For Novo’s workload, that model aligned well with the unit of work we were building for: one expert conducting one analysis session. It also changed the architecture in four important ways: Scaling became session-native. We no longer needed to connect application-level session creation to a separately scaled pool of execution environments. The platform owns that lifecycle. Isolation became the default unit of execution. Each session runs in a VM-isolated sandbox rather than sharing a process or general-purpose application container with other sessions. That matters when the workload includes model-generated code operating on sensitive clinical data. Network isolation became part of the service architecture. Foundry Agent Service supports private networking, including virtual network integration and private access to dependent Azure resources. This lets us design controls for both ingress and egress around the agent environment. Those controls are especially important for data that must remain inside an approved network boundary. The agent joined a broader development lifecycle. Traces, evaluations, experiments, monitoring, and optimization can now be connected through the same platform. Microsoft Agent 365 integration also provides a path to enterprise inventory, identity, access control, and lifecycle governance. Using Foundry hosted agents didn’tt remove our responsibility for security or quality. We still had to define access controls, minimize and protect telemetry, test the agent for our use case, and review every system it can call. What changed is that several controls we previously assembled ourselves are now platform capabilities we can configure and operate consistently. Here are the top lessons we learned during this project—and some practical advice for your own hosted agents projects in Foundry: Lesson 1: Treat infrastructure choices as product decisions Private networking should be an early architecture decision, not a production hardening task left until the end. Hosted agents consume network capacity according to sessions. The Foundry account, its projects, hosted agents, concurrent sessions, and agent revisions all contribute to IP usage. Because the assigned subnet is an immutable reference at the account level, an undersized range can turn a capacity adjustment into a broader infrastructure migration. Our advice is to estimate peak concurrent sessions across the account, include headroom for deployments and growth, and involve the network team before creating the Foundry resource. The current networking guidance recommends a /24 subnet for production hosted agent deployments and documents /27 as the supported minimum for smaller deployments. We used Azure Verified Modules as the foundation for repeatable environments. That gave us a strong starting point, but infrastructure as code doesn’t remove the need to inspect generated dependencies. Throughput for resources like Azure Cosmos DB should reflect expected concurrency and data access patterns. Where a setting requires an operational adjustment, capture it in the deployment process or operator runbook rather than leaving it as unwritten production knowledge. Subnet sizing, database throughput, private endpoints, DNS, and concurrency aren’t separate infrastructure details. Together, they shape the scale ceiling and reliability of the product. Lesson 2: Make traces easy to navigate Foundry tracing uses OpenTelemetry and stores telemetry in Azure Monitor Application Insights.

events.title: Developer 'pauses' AI data centre proposal after it 'misread' community feeling
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Quantum DC halts approval process of Adelaide Hills AI data centre A community protest event held in Mannum against the Tungkillo data centre last month. ( ABC News: James Wakelin ) Quantum DC has delayed its planned hyper-scale AI data centre at Tungkillo following "deep frustration" in the Adelaide Hills community. The technology developer says it will not apply for development approval this year but has not ruled out progressing the data centre in the future. The company says it will now convene a panel of independent experts to review specialist studies and make their findings public. A developer says it has paused its plans to build a 1200-megawatt AI data centre in the Adelaide Hills, saying it "misread" community feeling about the proposal. Quantum DC chief executive Alby Tomassi said the company would not seek development approval this year and would instead undertake a "longer-term and more comprehensive engagement programme" to address community concerns. "We misread the strength of feeling about this proposal and acknowledge the first weeks of our early engagement created more questions than answers," he said in a statement. "We sincerely apologise for this, and we understand the disappointment and frustration it has caused. That is why we are pausing and intend to take a fresh approach to how we engage and how this proposal is tested." Quantum DC is proposing a hyper-scale data centre along with energy infrastructure on Collins Road in Tungkillo, about 41 kilometres directly east of the Adelaide CBD. Mr Tomassi said the company has been contacted by more than 350 people about the proposal and the community had submitted a consolidated list of 432 questions. He said the issues raised related to water, energy, noise, lighting and the night sky, traffic, bushfire, farming land, location and the local environment. "There is such deep frustration amongst the community, which was not our intent at all, and I admit we misread these responses and the only responsible thing to do now is to pause and reset," he told 891 ABC Adelaide. The company had scheduled two community consultation sessions last month but postponed them to later this month amid safety concerns. In their absence, locals instead convened their own protest meetings where a few hundred attended . Mr Tomassi said those November community sessions were now cancelled because "it wouldn't be effective to meet 500 people and answer 432 questions in an emotive open forum". Magdalene Lippett looking over the proposed site for the hyperscale data centre and energy hub. ( Supplied: Magdalene Lippett ) Tungkillo resident Magdalene Lippett opposed the data centre and welcomed the pause. "I think that Quantum DC need to get the hint that no means no," she told 891 ABC Adelaide. "Our community have done the research, we've spoken to the experts, we've had a look at the issues … and this just isn't the right place, the hills is not the right place for their data centre." Quantum DC said it would now convene a panel of independent experts to review specialist studies and make their findings public. Mr Tomassi emphasised the development application would not proceed until "we set up these groups to scrutinise this project appropriately", but has not ruled out progressing the Tungkillo data centre in the future. "It's a global issue in regards to social acceptance [of data centres] and I think South Australia is appropriately poised to take this opportunity if the framework is right," he said. The proposed site of the Tungkillo data centre. ( Supplied: Magdalene Lippett ) Mid Murray Council Mayor Simone Bailey said the council had received one briefing from Quantum DC and further information provided since would be discussed at an upcoming meeting. She said the council has "big concerns" about the location of the proposed data centre, its proximity to a dark sky reserve , distance from an SA Country Fire Service station, limited access on unsealed roads and how the centre might affect noise pollution and the water table. But about a two-hour drive north of Tungkillo, an elected member at a different regional council expressed his support for the project to relocate to his patch. Northern Areas councillor Hank Langes said he would put a question without notice to the chamber to see if the council will support the data centre in their area, which covers Jamestown and Spalding. "We are a pro-development council so we'd love to have the data centre up our way," Cr Langes said. "It gives us a bit more employment and so forth, and widens the employment structure.

events.title: Local media startup City Cast reshuffles leadership
events.summary: The locally-focused media startup City Cast has named Andi McDaniel, the company’s chief creative officer, its new CEO, replacing David Plotz. City Cast launched in 2021 as a local podcast and newsletter venture aimed at serving cities where local news was shifting from old newspapers and radio to screens. The company has since expanded to 13 cities, including Austin, Las Vegas, and Philadelphia, among others. “This next chapter for us is about expanding audiences. It’s about adapting to AI, and it’s about making the business successful,” McDaniel, a veteran public radio executive and co-founder of City Cast , told Semafor. City Cast has gained greater visibility in recent months, primarily for its expansion in its hometown. As Semafor first noted last year, in response to what the company saw as an opportunity created by the turbulence at The Washington Post, City Cast scaled up its newsroom and business in Washington. City Cast is backed by Graham Holdings, which owned the Post before selling to Jeff Bezos. City Cast DC now has 20 people on staff, and said it has found some success attracting a younger audience to its content, tripling the size of people it reaches regularly from roughly 100,000 at the beginning of the year to around 300,000. Not every bet has paid off. The company shuttered two arms, in Boise and Houston. In a telephone interview, Plotz said Houston was too large and sprawling an area to cover with the company’s resources — most cities operate with a staff of just 5 or 6 employees — while he said the company didn’t understand Boise enough when City Cast launched there. The company learned that their podcasts were not a replacement for radio, and that the City Cast model seemed to resonate best within mid-sized cities with concentrated downtowns that orient residents’ perspectives. Plotz said that revenue was up 40% this year, but the company was still not profitable. In the six years since the company’s launch, the company’s founder told Semafor he’d grown to better understand habits in the local media landscape. He noted that many people under the age of 60 largely got their information from social media, neighborhood listservs, local newsletters, and Reddit. “People do not want local news,” Plotz said. “They want to know about things to do in their city. They want to know what’s going on in their city. But if you ask them about local news, they do not express an interest. “Local news as a concept does not really have a lot of valence. It’s more like learning about my city.” He also noted that national media narratives and big political fights were not as animating to local audiences, who seek out information to be connected to their local communities. “The need that people are finding met in local media has almost nothing to do with the highly partisan, cortisol-driven conversations that drive national media and national news media,” he said.

events.title: Scoop: Lutnick stalled curbing Nvidia chip sales to China — again — after Oval Office showdown
events.summary: President Trump on Thursday authorized a crack down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year — even consulting Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead. One administration official has repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Why it matters: This standoff illustrates a breakdown in efforts to keep American technology out of China's hands as the world wonders why the Trump administration has not taken action against the company at the center of suspected chip smuggling — and an espionage scandal. This report was assembled from interviews with six high-level sources who were briefed on or, in some cases, heard the discussions. Inside the room: On Thursday, as the spy scandal rocked the administration, Lutnick met in the Situation Room with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. During the meeting, Bessent confronted Lutnick about why his department has resisted implementing the export controls, particularly on Megaspeed, the company at the center of the spy scandal. The group sided with Bessent. Lutnick appeared to agree, but then muttered under his breath, "I need to check with the president." Friction point: Lutnick's seemingly innocuous comment raised concerns, the sources said, because officials have repeatedly believed the Commerce Department would impose the export controls, only to have nothing happen. "He's stalling it out," said one official, describing how Lutnick had previously met privately with the president to change his mind about the export limit. "This is an ongoing concern with Howard and this issue," said another. This time, one person in the room called his bluff by saying: "Great. Why don't we do it today?" Around 5pm, the group headed to the Oval Office. Trump called tech advisor Elon Musk and agreed to move forward. Musk supported Rubio, Bessent, Greer and Hegseth's case to impose the controls while Lutnick warned it "will start a trade war with China." "Everyone argued back that China is already doing to us what Lutnick warned would happen," a source said. Behind the scenes: With Lutnick the lone holdout, Trump made his decision: "Let's get it done." But once everyone was outside of the Oval Office, Lutnick proposed a new delay tactic. "I'll develop some options and come back," he said. "Everyone was like: 'No, no, the decision's been made. Go fucking execute,'" one source said. "Well, it still hasn't happened." The other side: Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer denied that Bessent confronted Lutnick and would not immediately comment on the other allegations. Flashback: On at least three separate occasions — in May, August, and Nov. 5 — Trump approved taking action against suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China. But Lutnick and Commerce Undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler resisted pressure from Bessent and others to move forward. In May, a highly classified memo warning about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed employee suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese agent, was shared with the president and other officials. In a subsequent meeting, Bessent, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Hegseth and White House officials pressed Lutnick and Kessler to act, the source said, "and they were refusing." Catch up quick: The Trump administration last year announced it would loosen export controls on Nvidia H200 chip sales to China — something Nvidia has lobbied hard for. Trump has taken a more lax approach to export controls on China, agreeing to allow sales of Nvidia's H200 chips, which are older but still powerful, in exchange for a 25% tariff. Long before the affair with Alice Huang, Jensen Huang has pushed for tapping into the Chinese market. The CEO at the center of an AI boom Trump is dead set on winning has largely been successful at convincing Trump and Lutnick that selling less powerful chips to China is good for national security because it prevents China from developing its own alternatives and keeps the adversary dependent on the U.S. The bottom line: While Lutnick oversees the department squarely at the center of export control policy, Trump is the ultimate decider.

events.title: Why the data center you dread might never even be built
events.summary: The data center boom is running into serious real-world obstacles, from widespread local opposition and permitting delays to a scramble for electricity . Before those challenges even come into play, though, there’s a more basic problem: A lot of the projects being announced may never get built in the first place. With billions of dollars in AI infrastructure investment at stake, separating realistic projects from speculative ones is becoming increasingly important. On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, hosts Rebecca Bellan and Tim De Chant are joined by Brent Nelson , senior managing director of markets and strategy at Ascend Analytics , to separate the data center projects that are likely to get built from the ones that may never get off the ground. events.title: Meta is losing its longtime head of infrastructure
events.summary: A key figure in Meta’s growth into a social media and tech industry powerhouse is leaving the company. Santosh Janardhan, the company’s longtime head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering, will be stepping down, Meta told TechCrunch. He will be replaced by Dave Brown, who joined the company as vice president of infrastructure earlier this year, the company added. Previous to coming aboard at Meta, Brown spent 19 years at Amazon, where he focused on compute, cloud, and AI, his LinkedIn shows . It sounds like Janardhan will remain at Meta for a little bit, although he is expected to leave next year. “Santosh will stay on for transition and he is moving into an advisory role on Meta Compute,” said a Meta representative. Janardhan, who originally joined the company in 2009, helped the firm grow into the massive internet presence that it is today. Bloomberg originally reported Janardhan’s departure, citing an internal memo that had recently been circulated. It’s unclear why Janardhan is stepping down from the role. The memo did not specify the reasons for his departure and Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for clarity on the issue. However, Janardhan’s memo apparently cited the need to “pass the baton.” In recent years, the company’s investment in infrastructure has exploded , as it seeks to keep up with its competitors in the AI race. Earlier this year, Janardhan was tasked with leading Meta Compute , the company initiative to scale its data center investments and strategy. events.title: Olaf Sakkers is betting he can beat the emerging-manager squeeze
events.summary: Entering into the world of venture capital has never been easy, especially as a first-time fund manager. But it’s especially daunting right now. According to PitchBook data, firms raising their fourth fund “or later” captured a whopping 88.2% of U.S. VC fundraising dollars through the first three quarters of this year, while first-time funds captured a measly 4.5% . Just 81 first-time funds closed in the first nine months of 2026. That puts the year on track to be the worst for first-time managers in at least a decade, according to PitchBook’s estimate. Olaf Sakkers has spent the past five years proving that difficult doesn’t mean impossible. He founded his firm RedBlue Capital in 2021 and closed its first fund with roughly $5 million in capital commitments in 2023. He has now held a first close on a second fund that he says will total at least $50 million. Raised in South Africa, he studied anthropology at Princeton, focusing on global health and health policy, and wrote his thesis on HIV in his home country. He moved to Israel after graduating and was drafted into the Israel Defense Forces, where he says he had a desk job liaising with the U.S. military, and where he became interested in autonomous vehicles. An introduction led to Michael Granoff, founder of the venture firm Maniv Mobility and an early backer of electric-vehicle startup Better Place. Granoff, who had money to invest, hired him on the spot, Sakkers says. Neither had been a venture investor at that point, so they built a fund “almost by accident,” learning as they went. Sakkers says he ran the investment process day to day, backing Israeli founders who were bringing cybersecurity skills into the automotive world, and later expanding to the U.S. and other markets. By 2021, Sakkers says, he was an equal partner in Maniv’s economics, but he wanted something different — more formal and scalable — so struck out on his own. Today, RedBlue backs what he calls the “real economy,” including robotics, logistics, manufacturing and energy. Getting to this point has been a test of endurance as much as salesmanship, seemingly. Sakkers says that institutional limited partners, outfits like endowments and pension funds, have been the toughest to win over because his checks are small (and theirs are comparatively huge) but also because their risk model is built to “avoid getting a zero,” which is why they tend to gravitate toward established brands. Says Sakkers, it’s akin to founders who come to be seen as “inevitable,” after they’ve previously founded another company. Meanwhile first-time founders often battle against the “gravity of perception,” meaning a more dominant brand can bend how people perceive a newer one. His answer has been to let the results speak, but it takes time. “It’s a long-term game of building trust, demonstrating performance over time,” Sakkers says. The first fund was a proof of concept, backed by LPs he had known for a while, including family offices. The second draws on family offices and institutions. RedBlue writes small checks, $50,000 to $100,000, mostly joining deals led by other investors rather than leading them. That lets it do more deals and be “the last investor that they take” on by promising practical help, including introductions to lead investors like Andreessen Horowitz and Thrive Capital, and to customers. Founders expect little from VCs, in Sakker’s view, so RedBlue tries to overdeliver on the support part. By his account, the results are strong. Of 28 investments, he says that 15 have been marked up, and he cites a net internal rate of return of “significantly above 50%.” There has been just one exit — an acqui-hire — so most gains from the tiny fund remain on paper and unrealized. Public records support part of Sakker’s story. HappyRobot, which RedBlue backed early, raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.2 billion valuation in August. Westmag, which makes motors for drones and robots and which Sakkers backed at pre-seed alongside Nat Friedman, emerged in June with an $11 million seed led by Andreessen Horowitz. Flai, an AI startup for car dealerships, followed its 2025 seed with a $27 million Series A. And Humble Robotics, a driverless-truck startup in whose $24 million seed round RedBlue participated, announced a $51 million Series A led by Obvious Ventures earlier this month. Sakkers argues that discipline is his edge. RedBlue publishes thesis essays, such as one on robotics, and runs on a custom database that he built with Claude Code to log relationships, meeting notes and introductions. That lets him and his lone full-time principal, based in New York, work asynchronously. AI agents, he says, are “useless if they just have to guess,” so everything gets written down. He contrasts that with Benchmark’s more artisanal model, which he says suits a firm with a record he lacks.

events.title: Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe
events.summary: The U.S. has asked Russia to submit a new proposal for a future security agreement with Europe that includes Russian steps to ease tension with the continent, two sources with knowledge of the matter said. Why it matters: For years, Russia has sought a European security deal that limits NATO expansion and scales back its military presence in Eastern Europe. The U.S. has rejected those demands in the past, but now appears open to them in some form as part of a broader agreement to end the war in Ukraine. But many European governments are deeply suspicious of the administration's approach. State of play: President Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday to reiterate the request. They also want Putin to allow European representatives to join the next round of Russia-Ukraine peace talks, a U.S. official said. From Moscow, Kushner and Witkoff are expected to travel to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday night. Catch up quick: The talks on Tuesday and Wednesday were the first time Ukrainian and Russian officials met with U.S. mediators present since February, when they were suspended due to the war in Iran. In recent weeks, Witkoff and Kushner met with both Putin and Zelensky, creating a bit of momentum. Putin agreed to resume peace talks and release U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, who was detained by Russia in 2022 . Together with First Lady Melania Trump and her team, Witkoff and Kushner also brokered a humanitarian ceasefire in the city of Oleshky. Driving the news: The talks in Abu Dhabi started on Tuesday with Witkoff, Kushner and commander of the U.S. European Command Gen. Alexus Grynkewich mediating between the Russians and the Ukrainians. The parties agreed to a prisoner exchange deal that Kushner and Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said could be the biggest since the war began. U.S. and Ukrainian officials said the exact number of prisoners to be released will be decided during meetings with Putin and Zelensky on Thursday. Before and after the talks, the U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams briefed a delegation of senior diplomats from Germany, the UK, France, Italy, the EU and NATO. Behind the scenes: The meetings between the Russians and the Ukrainians on Tuesday were tense and at times emotional, with both sides airing grievances after nine months of not talking directly, according to a source in the room. Kushner and Witkoff tried to lower the temperature, telling Russian and Ukrainian negotiators that the goal is to end this round of talks with options for the leaders on both sides. Eventually, after each party made its case, the discussion became more constructive, the source said. "We had pretty tough discussions," Kushner said at a press conference after the talks concluded on Wednesday. "The Russians came with strict directives. It was very hard to soften it, but it ended productively," Arakhamia said. Zoom in: The U.S. proposal to secure a deal on a new Europe-Russia security architecture as part of an agreement to end the war in Ukraine was a key focus of the Abu Dhabi talks. Russian negotiators said Putin launched the invasion of Ukraine because then-President Biden did not reply to his 2021 letter laying out his security concerns, two sources with knowledge of the talks said. According to one of the sources, Kushner and Witkoff told the Russians that the world has changed a lot since 2021. They proposed that Russia draft a new proposal that includes its security concerns and demands, but also lays out what "symmetrical steps" it's willing to take to de-escalate and reassure Europe that it will not attack in the future. Kushner and Witkoff also told the Russians that in order to seriously discuss security issues in Europe, they need to agree to allow European representatives to participate in future peace talks. "We told the Russians, they have their desires and fears, but they have to provide different de-escalation and different proposals as well, if they want Europe to be able to receive those proposals in a good way," Kushner said at the press conference. The other side: So far, Russia has been unwilling to allow Europeans to be part of peace talks with Ukraine. "As for the leadership of a number of European countries, they are essentially engaged in a collective deception of the Ukrainian people and contributing to the mass deaths of civilians," Putin adviser Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation, said at a press conference after the talks. "Therefore, I don't understand what can be discussed with them." Still, Medinsky said that Russia wants to reach a broader security deal with Europe as part of an agreement to end the war. "In Ukraine, an abscess has simply burst. The entire body needs to be treated — a Band-Aid won't do the trick," he said. What to watch: The Trump administration wants to negotiate a new Europe-Russia security architecture and a Russia-Ukraine peace deal simultaneously. But the implementation of a security arrangement would only happen after a deal to end the war is reached, according to a source familiar with the White House's thinking. The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said before the talks in Abu Dhabi that Europe will discuss a new security architecture only after the war in Ukraine ends. But two sources with knowledge said European officials who were in Abu Dhabi this week agreed to engage on both tracks simultaneously, while stressing that final decisions on European security architecture would be made only after the war in Ukraine ends. The U.S. hopes giving European representatives a seat at the peace talks will make their governments more willing to discuss and agree on a broader security agreement before the war ends. "Zelensky won't agree to a deal until he knows what happens next regarding security guarantees and Putin wants to know this, too. This is why the security issue is so important," the source said. The source added that the U.S. made it clear to European countries that it would not agree to a security deal with Russia unless Europe and Ukraine are on board. The U.S. also wouldn't give Russia a veto over Europe's security considerations, the source said. The bottom line: Security will be a key issue at a summit of European leaders in Dublin later this week. European diplomats said the idea of a Russia-Europe security arrangement still faces a lot of resistance and unanswered questions.

events.title: Trump administration to pursue public land sales and a decrease in federal ownership
events.summary: President Donald Trump’s administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments as part of an effort to “decrease the size of the federal estate.” BILLINGS, Mont. -- President Donald Trump's administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments as part of an effort to “decrease the size of the federal estate," according to a new five-year plan presented by the Interior Department. Agency officials said the sale of federal property would allow the government to focus resources on “nationally significant" lands. They offered no details on what lands could be sold, nor the scope or location of potential sales. The proposal drew quick objections from some lawmakers, including Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke of Montana, who was Interior Secretary in Trump's first term. The plan also calls for strategic land transfers and exchanges to support greater energy production, a centerpiece of the administration's pro-fossil fuel policies. It reflects the Trump administration’s view of most public lands as assets to be used, rather than to be set aside for preservation . The Interior Department oversees more than 750,000 square miles (1.9 million square kilometers) of land — an area greater than Texas and California combined — along with vast underground mineral reserves. That puts the agency at the center of a contentious, decades-long debate over whether the government controls too much land. The Associated Press sent emails to Interior officials Wednesday requesting comment and further details. Most public lands are in Western states. In some, the government controls the vast majority of land, protecting it from potential exploitation but also hindering growth. Nevada, for example, is almost 80% under federal control. Interior officials said that under the plan a portion of any land sale proceeds would go back to the buyer for conservation purposes elsewhere. Yet it’s uncertain if Interior Secretary Doug Burgum can achieve the administration’s goals without cooperation from Congress. Zinke’s office said in a statement that he “remains firmly opposed to the sale or transfer of public lands." He will vote against any legislation on the issue if it happens before the lawmaker leaves Congress at the end of this term, the statement said. The ranking member of the Senate Natural Resources Committee also pledged to fight any federal land sales or privatization efforts. Public lands belong in public hands,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich, a New Mexico Democrat. Some Western lawmakers last year sought to sell vast tracts of land in Utah and Nevada, saying that could generate revenue and ease growth pressures in booming cities. Among the proposals, Utah Republican Sen. Mike Lee suggested selling more than 2 million acres (8,000 square kilometers) to states or other entities. Those efforts failed amid bipartisan opposition. The plan sets out a road map for the Interior Department's priorities and actions between 2026 and 2030. Future administrations would not be bound by it. The department regulates mining, drilling, grazing, recreation and other activities that many state and local officials want greater control over. Interior includes the Bureau of Land Management, National Park Service, Fish and Wildlife Service and Bureau of Indian Affairs. The agency's strategic plan was last updated four years ago under former Democratic President Joe Biden. events.title: I Saw the Future of Robotics in a Virtual Duck That Chases My Cat
events.summary: Allow me to introduce you to the robot cat butler I’m developing with help from AI. Using OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol , I taught a virtual version of Microduck —a cute robot from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face—to walk around a room and identify any bengal cats in its vicinity. (The clip above shows the robot waddling toward a target feline; its eye view is shown top right.) I’m still waiting patiently for a physical Microduck— please hurry up and ship it, guys —but simulated behavior is relatively simple, so it should transfer over to the real thing. I plan to have the robot automatically dispense a treat for my pet bengal, Leona, perhaps by bowing its head to release one from a 3D-printed, head-mounted storage chamber. I was able to code and train the virtual robot in just a few hours, which is, quite frankly, incredible. Previously, this kind of thing might have taken me weeks to figure out. It was possible because OpenAI’s latest models are remarkably good at understanding and manipulating 3D representations of the physical world and then translating that into useful code, agentic actions, and robot training. Real roboticists are using the latest models to do some amazing stuff. When OpenAI released Astra this past September, University of California, Berkeley professor Ken Goldberg and his students saw demos that showcased its ability to render 3D images. They wondered if it could help with the simulations required to train different kinds of robots. These simulations need to be incredibly detailed and extremely accurate to ensure that sophisticated behavior—a humanoid that can dance or a robot hand that can grasp—will transfer faithfully to the real world. One member of Goldberg’s lab gave Astra access to an Nvidia tool called Newton , showed it a video clip of a real robot in action, and asked if it could create a simulation of the scene. “What blew us all away was that within an hour it had produced a full 3D simulation with all the parameters set—the position of the camera, the lighting, the background, all the materials,” Goldberg tells me. Astra is also able to automate much of the drudgery involved with training a robot in simulation, Goldberg says, by running experiments and examining the results. This is precisely what I found while training the virtual Microduck. Along with GPT-6 Sol, I used an agentic harness from Nous Research called Hermes and a Nvidia DGX Spark, a personal computer that contains a powerful AI chip. I’ve previously written about using agents and coding models to configure, program, and debug physical robots. Normally, this kind of work requires significant expertise; modern coding models make it a cinch. But OpenAI’s newest model went far beyond just writing code. It used a piece of Nvidia software called Isaac Sim to feed instructions to a model that controlled the virtual robot, watch videos of it in action to assess how well things were working, and suggest tweaks to its training regime. This process allowed me to train the Microduck to walk around without toppling over. I initially tried getting GPT-6 Sol to teach the robot to moonwalk—I fed it a GIF of Michael Jackson sliding across the stage, which it tried to copy—but after hours of effort, it only resulted in a very jaunty backward jog. (The robots don’t have us totally beat quite yet.) Jim Fan, a researcher at Nvidia who has collaborated with Goldberg, says the way AI can now control robots mirrors how software agents function. LLMS can use models trained to control physical actions—visual language action (VLA) models—just as they access different software on a computer. This week, Fan, Goldberg, and others open sourced an agentic framework for robots called Aspire , which allows a robot to discover and use new skills. One example: GPT-6 Astra figured out how to use a pair of robot arms to solve a Rubik’s cube. “It picks it up, tries to twist it, but has the wrong angle,” Fan says. “Then it reasons for a very, very long time, but it eventually is able to solve it because it learns the skills over time.” At the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), held in Austin, Texas, this week, Fan gave a keynote speech in which he talked about the incredible realization that AI models can automate a lot of the work needed to have a robot do sophisticated things. Fan showed off a demo in which Astra was put in control of a robot arm and told to paint a picture of the Golden Gate Bridge. Using some paint and brushes nearby, it duly completed the task . Of course, getting robots to work reliably and efficiently is still extremely difficult, requiring significant engineering expertise. The vision system on my robot duck does not work well enough to be deployed in a real product. Still, the ease and speed of training robots with AI could soon have an enormous impact on manufacturing and e-commerce, and Goldberg says a number of industrial robotics and automation firms have shown an interest in the approach.

events.title: CoreWeave turns to customer prepayments, shorter contracts to fund AI growth
events.summary: CoreWeave is rewriting how it pays for the AI boom, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings , reported on Tuesday. CoreWeave, a neocloud that rents out the computing power behind AI, said it’s increasingly asking customers to pay up front, borrowing against specific contracts, and even pursuing short-term deals that could lead to higher prices. The new strategies could help CoreWeave finance its growth more efficiently while squeezing more cash from existing infrastructure. But these bets only hold if today’s demand and pricing power continue. CoreWeave reported $3.66 billion in revenue, up 168% from the year prior, but it also posted a $709 million net loss and $846 million in quarterly interest expense. “We will not use the unsecured debt market to fund our business at current yields, nor do we need to,” CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said during Tuesday’s earnings call. Instead, CoreWeave’s plan is to rely on loans backed by specific customer contracts, drawing on funds as needed to finance most of the infrastructure it still has to build to deliver on its significant backlog of $132.5 billion. CoreWeave also said it expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months, including more than $3 billion tied to signing new customer contracts for capacity it has already built, which requires no additional spending on hardware. Rivals Nebius and IREN have also relied on hefty Microsoft prepayments to pay for computing capacity, signaling that the industry is moving toward asking Big Tech to pay up for their buildouts. Upfront payments could alleviate CoreWeave’s immediate borrowing needs, but they also commit the company to providing services at a price that might be less attractive down the road if compute demand continues to surge. CoreWeave is also looking to capitalize on that growing demand by signing more shorter-term contracts that can command much higher prices. The company raised prices across its offerings by about 25% in July and by another 10% later in the quarter. Prices are still climbing this quarter, in a way that “more than offset[s] cost increases,” said Intrator. “We are also allocating more capacity to short-term opportunities, where the pricing justifies it, selling capacity at more than $40 million per megawatt annually, while pricing for new infrastructure on four- and five-year contracts is moving to $20 million to $25 million per megawatt,” the chief executive said. CoreWeave’s financing strategy now revolves around those opportunities. In August, the company closed a $2.6 billion loan, its first designed specifically for shorter-term customer contracts. Known as DDTL 5.5, it lets CoreWeave borrow in installments as it needs the money. While short-term deals let CoreWeave charge higher prices and change them more frequently, it’s a trade-off. Lenders give more weight to longer-term contracts, even if they’re priced lower, because they value predictable cash flow and consistency to repay the loan above all. Even though Wall Street reacted positively to CoreWeave’s earnings, bond investors are much less sanguine. Last month, yields on some of the company’s bonds hit above 15%, highlighting that investors are concerned about the debt needed to fund data center buildouts before those investments see a return. In short, CoreWeave is finding new ways to expand without relying on unsecured debt. The strategy it has chosen could boost profits, but it also carries greater risk around contract renewals and pricing — and it just goes to show how dependent the AI infrastructure boom is on sustained, and as yet unproven, demand. events.title: With $720M round, Britain’s Fractile gets a leg up in the race for AI chips
events.summary: Fractile , a British startup developing AI chips, has raised a $720 million Series C backed by Britain’s Sovereign AI Fund with hopes of “ensuring the U.K. has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy,” its government stated . Alongside the likes of Axelera , Etched , and OLIX , this makes Fractile one of the top-funded startup players in the race for purpose-built AI chips. Such chips are one of several avenues being explored to reduce the cost of inference — aka using increasingly demanding AI models in production. However, Fractile seeks to go beyond hardware with a full-stack approach that also includes a machine learning compiler to maximize the speed at which LLMs will get executed on its chips. As a result, the company frames itself as a frontier AI company, and its latest round led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Redpoint was priced accordingly. According to the British government, the valuation was “over £5 billion” — quite possibly $7 billion, a figure reported both by the Financial Times and a Reuters source . Still, Fractile’s main differentiator will arguably be its hardware design. After a pivot , its approach now revolves on DRAM, the most common type of RAM, but stacked on top of each chip in such a way that it is hoping will bypass the usual trade-off between memory and capacity. This trade-off has become more problematic with the rise of agentic AI, as companies seek to perform longer chains of tasks with large models without compromising on speed. As compute struggles to keep up, hopes are high for AI chips, despite their limited availability to date. In a LinkedIn post , Fractile CEO Walter Goodwin wrote that “there is still a lot of work ahead” for the company, and that the new funding will enable the startup to “ship [its] first chips and systems next year.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .
