events.title: Labor pledges to boost regional rail and attacks Liberal costings
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Labor announces $420m regional rail boost and attacks Liberal leader's surplus claim Topic: State and Territory Elections Labor is promising to increase the number of regional train services if elected. ( Supplied: Thomas Hobley ) Labor will commit $420 million to boost Victoria's regional rail services if it wins the election. The plan would mean an extra 550 extra weekly V/Line services to regional centres. Labor is also attacking the Liberal leader's pledge to reach a budget surplus by 2032. Regional and outer suburban commuters would get an extra 550 weekly V/Line train trips if Labor is re-elected, as the party costs Jess Wilson's commitment to reduce the public service to claim she cannot reach her promised cash surplus. Premier Ben Carroll will today commit $420 million to increase the regional train network by 24 per cent, targeting voters in regional and outer-fringe seats where Labor is under pressure from both the Coalition and One Nation. Victoria election 2026 live updates: For all the latest news from the campaign trail, read our blog. Transport in the outer-west and south-west has been especially painful for the government. Melton and Wyndham Vale still rely on V/Line, two elections after Daniel Andrews promised to electrify the tracks. Under Labor's announcement today, Melton would get an extra 162 weekly trips from 2027 so that services run every 20 minutes. Longer nine-car trains previously announced will also run from next year. The plan to increase regional rail services has been costed by Labor at $420 million. ( ABC News: Ethan Seiderman ) Wyndham Vale would get a dedicated new service with 249 weekly trips, to minimise crowding. Geelong would get more express services as a result, cutting 10 minutes from the journey with double the number of total services. An extra two services would also run on Sundays to Geelong and Waurn Ponds. Government attacks Liberal surplus claim Labor has separately turned to the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) in an attempt to undercut the opposition leader's commitment to reach a cash surplus by 2032, a key plank of Ms Wilson's election platform. Ms Wilson has largely relied on her announcement that she would reduce the Victorian Public Service through attrition to save $22 billion over a decade to reach the cash surplus. But analysis by the PBO, requested by Labor, found the majority of the savings would not be realised until after 2032. The budget office estimated the Coalition policy would save $8.5 billion by 2032, billions short of what would be necessary. Treasurer Colin Brooks used the findings to claim Ms Wilson would need to cut essential services, in particular health, to meet their commitment. Labor is challenging Liberal leader Jess Wilson's pledge to reach a budget surplus. ( ABC News Melbourne ) In a statement, Ms Wilson said she would not take lectures on costings from Labor. "Only our Liberal and Nationals team has a costed and credible plan to repair the budget, underpinned by more than $26 billion in responsible and disciplined savings," she said. Ms Wilson has not released the full copy of her version of the PBO's analysis, and has been under pressure to explain how she can scrap taxes, make a suite of spending commitments while also bringing down debt — on track to reach almost $200 billion by 2029-2030. PBO analysis can vary depending on the assumptions put to them. More express trains from regional centres Under Labor's transport announcement, the Seymour line to the outer-north through Wallan and Donnybrook would get an extra 29 services from 2028. Another 101 weekly services would also run through the Bendigo line from 2028; 21 to Bendigo and 80 to Kyneton, allowing most off-peak trains to run express from Bendigo. The Warrnambool line would also get an extra eight weekend services from next year, while the Traralgon line would wait until 2028 for an additional Sunday service. V/Line services have been plagued by overcrowding as demand increases. ( Supplied: Kate Young ) Most weekday off-peak trains from Ballarat would also run express to Melbourne from next year, shaving up to 10 minutes off the journey, Labor said. The Coalition has previously promised $1.7 billion to run hybrid trains to Melton and Wyndham Vale, though the government disputed this was feasible with the rest of the network. After delaying electrification, the government now says the new Sunshine station hub must be built first to separate the V/Line and Metro tracks.

events.title: Rising costs hurt South Australia's regional high streets
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Rising costs and online shopping hurt Mount Gambier's historic Commercial Street Kathy Gandolfi says there have been some tough periods for Mount Gambier businesses. ( ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook ) Businesses operating on Mount Gambier's main street say increasing costs and changing consumer habits are hurting retail. The city's chamber of commerce says large shop fronts are becoming increasingly unsustainable. The city is planning upgrades to the street, and some small retailers are setting up shop. Empty shops and "for lease" signs line Mount Gambier's main retail strip as high costs and online shopping drive customers away. The city, in South Australia's South East, is home to about 30,000 people. It also serves as the commercial hub for the wider Limestone Coast region. Mount Gambier's economic heart has always been based around Commercial Street, but that is rapidly changing. A historic photo of Commercial Street shows the heritage-listed town hall. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine ) A walk down the 1.2-kilometre retail strip between Wehl and Crouch streets reveals retailers are few and far between. Country Attitude co-director Kathy Gandolfi, who has been in business on the main street for 22 years, said having fewer shops hurt everyone. Kathy Gandolfi has been in business on Mount Gambier's main street for 22 years. ( ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook ) "It's good to have a vibrant main street," she said. As high interest rates and inflation hurt consumers' pockets, increased overheads are putting added pressure on businesses. Businesses are finding it hard to maintain large shop fronts. ( ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook ) Mount Gambier Chamber of Commerce chair Samuel Taylor said having a large shopfront on the main street was increasingly unviable. He said bigger shops required more stock to display, but those items just racked up costs for the business every day they were not sold. Mount Gambier's Commercial Street in 1964, from the Life in Australia film series. ( Supplied: National Film and Sound Archive ) "We're seeing a big shift away from large-scale businesses and you're moving into a more cost-effective model which is a smaller shopfront," he said. For larger retailers, a move away from the main street made more sense in terms of rental and operating costs, he said. Like bricks-and-mortar shops everywhere, Mount Gambier's retail sector has also been hit by the online shopping boom. Commercial Street during SA's COVID-19 lockdowns. ( ABC South East SA: Bec Whetham ) Ms Gandolfi said more food and service businesses, like health clinics and hairdressers, were now opening on the main street "because you can't buy a job by a physio or something online". Retailers like Keiran Hein, however, are hopeful for the future of Commercial Street. Ms Hein opened her ice cream and confectionary shop, Lollies & Scoops, just two weeks ago. She believed her business would succeed. Two previously empty buildings have also now been leased. Keiran Hein hopes her new shop can fill a gap in the market. ( ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook ) "I would have loved to have spent so much money in decorating this place and doing it up into a wonderland, but the reality is that I can't," she said. "So it's basic, it's bright, it's clean. We've got good food and produce and that's all that matters at the moment." As some businesses move out, others are taking a chance on Commercial Street. ( ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook ) Mount Gambier Mayor Lynette Martin described the movement of businesses along the street as "cyclical", and said the council was working on a master plan for the CBD which was set to include updates to the main street. Lynette Martin says Commercial Street is a "survivor". ( ABC News: Isadora Bogle ) "It's been there for over 100 years, shops have come and gone, businesses have come and gone, but it always seems to come back to be fully or almost fully occupied," she said.

events.title: Burnham raised safety concerns about Manchester ‘monster’ warehouse, inquiry hears
events.summary: PM wrote to transport commissioner to oppose ‘megashed’ in Astley shortly before he entered No 10 Andy Burnham raised safety concerns about dozens of lorries leaving a “monster” warehouse near a primary school because there was “no safe crossing” for children, a public inquiry has heard. Concerns about the 18-metre-high “megashed” in the village of Astley , Greater Manchester, are being examined by Britain’s office of the transport commissioner. A deputy transport commissioner, John Baker, launched an environmental public inquiry after significant local opposition to the round-the-clock operation by the logistics company Whistl. Whistl is asking for a licence to increase its number of HGVs at the site from 40 to 50 and the number of trailers from 60 to 70. But people living nearby told the inquiry on Wednesday that granting the licence would worsen the “catastrophic” impact on those living nearby, with some left suffering with anxiety, sleep deprivation and depression. The inquiry also heard that shortly before he became prime minister, Burnham wrote to the transport commissioner’s office to oppose Whistl’s plans. In the letter sent in February, which was not shown at the inquiry but has been seen by the Guardian, the then Greater Manchester mayor expressed concerns about the route taken by dozens of HGVs to access the 17-acre site near his Makerfield constituency. Burnham said schoolchildren would be forced to share the road with huge lorries “despite there being no pedestrian crossings, no lollipop service, no traffic calming and sections where the pavement is extremely narrow or ends entirely”. John Peters, who co-founded the Astley Warehouse Action Group, told the inquiry, at the Brick Community stadium in Wigan, that it was a recipe for disaster, adding: “I hope I never have to say I told you so.” The Whistl warehouse, which was named Britain’s joint-worst new building this year, was approved by Wigan council in 2024 after a planning application by PLP, a firm part-owned by Peel Group, one of Britain’s biggest landowners which is run by the billionaire John Whittaker. The outcome of the inquiry, expected in early December, is seen as a test case of how local groups could challenge similar large industrial developments across Britain. The Labour government has relaxed planning rules to allow big logistics projects on previously protected land as the UK strives to compete in the race for AI and the growing e-commerce market, which increasingly relies on next-day deliveries. Peters, who said he had lived in the village since 1979, was in tears as he likened Whistl’s “megashed” opening in the summer to “a plane crash-landing in that field”. He said one year ago the only medication he took was a single statin to lower blood cholesterol levels: “I now take high blood pressure [medication], statin, anti-depression and a sleeper. That’s the state I’m in. I know in our group we’re in a truly bad state so I dread to think what would happen [if Whistl’s licence was approved].” David Gerrard, a builder who lives opposite the site, appeared emotional as he described the effect on his wife and their three daughters. He said they were routinely woken throughout the night by the sound and light from lorries. Gerrard, whose house has declined in value by an estimated £170,000 as a result of the disruption, said he recently counted 113 wagons over a seven-hour period from 5.30am. “How are we supposed to live with this? It’s ruining our lives,” he said. James Healey, a leading acoustics expert commissioned by the residents, said he had never before seen planning approval given to such a noisy warehouse so close to people’s homes. He said: “In my 22 years in consultancy I’ve never seen a planning application be approved with a sound impact such as this, so it’s unprecedented in my experience.” A report by Healey, who chairs the UK Institute of Acoustics building acoustics group, concluded that those living closest to the site faced “severe health risks” from the excessive noise. Carole Retford, whose property is overshadowed by the warehouse, became close to tears as she described being “exhausted through lack of sleep” and mood swings from “anxious to quite depressed”. Another resident, Paul Bullow, said: “Physically, mentally, it’s draining, it’s constant. It never stops. It just brings levels of stress that weren’t there before but are now there all the time. It’s completely unacceptable.” In September, Whistl volunteered to pause overnight operations between midnight and 6am and introduced quieter electric vehicles. Giving evidence, Whistl executives conceded that they might not have chosen the site had they known the level of concern it would cause. Patrick Sadd, Whistl’s barrister, said the company accepted the “extremely moving” evidence and that the impact on some residents had been “far-reaching”.

events.title: Plug-in solar push sparks house fire warning from electricians
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Plug-in solar and batteries risk causing house fires, warn electrical trade groups Germany has plug-in solar and few safety issues, but "Australians aren't Germans" and may not follow the rules. ( Getty: Stefan Sauer/dpa ) Advocates are calling on the federal government to legalise plug-in solar and batteries by mid-2027. Industry groups say the devices could cause house fires and a "rushed process" could repeat the mistakes of the 2009 "pink batts" scheme. Australia's energy ministers have agreed to explore pathways for "safe deployment" of plug-in solar across the country and will report back in December. Solar panels and batteries that can be plugged into regular power outlets could cause house fires due to rushed implementation and lack of safety oversight, according to electrical trade groups. Advocates want the devices to be legalised in Australia by mid-2027, saying it would allow renters, apartment dwellers and low-income households to benefit from lower energy bills. The federal government is working with states and territories to develop a safety framework, with Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen telling a webinar last week he had asked Standards Australia to fast-track the project, which would be completed "very quickly". Australia readies to lift a ban on plug-in solar, unlocking access to the technology for millions of apartment dwellers and renters for the first time. Western Australia has struck out on its own, releasing a draft technical standard that would bypass this national process and aiming to be the first state or territory to legalise the technology. But industry groups and unions are warning of safety risks, saying a rushed process could result in deaths. The organisations include the peak body for electricians, Master Electricians Australia (MEA); the peak body for electrical contractors, National Electrical and Communications Association (NECA); and the Electrical Trades Union (ETU). The solar panels and batteries can be plugged into regular power outlets They feed power into the home's network to help offset electricity used by appliances Overseas, plug-in panels are commonly attached to apartment balconies or mounted in backyards MEA CEO Kate Raymond said the current proposed safety measures, including those in WA's draft standard, could cause house fires, the release of toxic battery gases, and other dangerous outcomes. "We understand the cost of living; we understand people want and need to reduce their energy bills," Ms Raymond told the ABC. "But what's the cost of a house fire? What's the cost of someone losing their life?" Could plug-in solar and batteries cause fires? Power pushed into a circuit by a plug-in solar panel or battery bypasses circuit breakers that protect wiring in walls and switchboards from overheating. Germany, which has added more than 1 million plug-in solar systems in two years without disaster, limits the output of such devices so extra current cannot overload wiring. Plug-in solar, or "balcony solar", has also been legalised in the UK and some US states. ( Supplied: Holger's Pictures ) The same approach is being proposed by plug-in advocates and the WA government, which permits one plug-in system per household in its draft standards. But "Australians aren't Germans", MEA national technical manager Matthew Duncan said. "Households either won't read the safety instructions or they'll ignore them. Multiple solar panels or batteries can overload a circuit, and the risk is higher in houses with faulty wiring. Plug-in batteries may also be riskier than panels because they can push power into a circuit for longer. NECA director of safety Neil Roberts said misuse was inevitable. "You're trusting the competency of the general public to install these," he said. This is a small plug-in battery, but stacked systems can exceed 15 kilowatt-hours, which is about the size of an average home battery. ( Supplied: Fuse ) Carl Copeland, the CEO of the Electrotechnology Training Institute (ETI), which represents hundreds of electrical contractors and trains thousands of apprentices in WA, warned of a repeat of mistakes from the 2009 home insulation program. The pink batts scheme's rushed rollout and a lack of safety oversight contributed to the deaths of four installers , according to a later royal commission. "We're going to end up with a situation like we did with the pink batts insulation where we'll have home owners plug in three or four of these things into the system, overloading their system, and causing house fires," Mr Copeland said.

events.title: ITV to cut show budgets as UK TV and film production spend drops by more than £2bn
events.summary: Broadcaster plans to make £30m in ‘temporary’ savings before inquiry into takeover by Sky ITV plans to slash its programming budget as new figures showed that spend on the production of films and prestige TV shows in the UK was down more than £2bn over the last year. The broadcaster plans to make £30m in “temporary” savings, including £25m in content and £5m elsewhere in the business. The announcement by ITV, which has agreed to sell its television and streaming business to Sky, came amid a backdrop of ditched commissions , falling advertising sales and job reductions in the TV and streaming industry . The Love Island and I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! broadcaster said it expected ad revenues to fall between 5% and 10% in the crucial final quarter of the year, despite the typically busy Christmas season. Ad sales are expected to drop between 2% and 3% over the course of the full year, ITV said. ITV’s programming cuts will mostly affect small external commissions, pushing them into 2027, it is understood. Separately, the latest update from the British Film Institute (BFI) showed that spending in the UK on making film and high-end TV shows – those that cost at least £1m an episode – had plunged by £2.08bn year on year. The figures showed that £5.2bn was spent by domestic and international broadcasters, Hollywood studios and streamers in the year to the end of September. This was a 28% decrease on the £7.26bn spent in the same period in 2025, a record year that included productions such as Avengers: Doomsday, Spider-Man: Brand New Day and the first instalment of the Harry Potter TV series. A spokesperson for the BFI said: “The figures are the result of a complex picture, ranging from significant shifts in the global industrial context through to increased competitiveness [for productions] from other international territories, and set against a backdrop of a strong [2025]. This is obviously something we and the British Film Commission are looking at very closely.” The latest figures are classified as “first reported”, with the BFI typically significantly revising up spending levels as it receives more information over the coming months. The BFI said the final figures for 2025 was revised up £900m from their “first reported” level. However, with the latest provisional figures showing a more than £2bn plunge in investment, 2026 is on track to be a dismal year for the UK production industry. Carolyn McCall, ITV’s chief executive, said demand for ads had weakened because of “continuing broader macroeconomic uncertainty” and “increased digital advertising on global streaming platforms”. She also cited new rules this year that imposed a 9pm watershed on TV advertising for less healthy food. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The business has struggled in recent years to keep up with deep-pocketed streaming companies such as Netflix and YouTube, which have muscled in on traditional media’s audiences and commercial revenue. Other mainstream broadcasters are also struggling, with the BBC intending to shed as many as 2,000 jobs and Channel 4 planning layoffs . ITV indicated the proposed cost savings would not involve staff cuts. McCall has argued that the £1.6bn sale of its TV and streaming business to Sky is ITV’s route to survival. However, last week, the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy , issued a public interest intervention notice, triggering an investigation by the media regulator Ofcom and the Competition and Markets Authority. Nandy raised concerns that the combined broadcasters would account for about 86% of linear news and current affairs viewing in Britain, as well as concerns over potential US political influence on editorial independence. Sky is owned by the US broadcaster Comcast. ITV said on Wednesday that the deal was “progressing as planned” and it was still expected to complete in the second half of 2027. The sale will leave ITV with its studios business, which makes shows for ITV and other broadcasters and streamers. The company told investors that studios revenue was down 1% in the first nine months of the year, but it had made five of the UK’s top 10 most-watched dramas in the third quarter of 2026, including The Gentlemen for Netflix and The Blame for ITV.

events.title: Lithium Americas raises Thacker Pass cost estimate by 31% to $3.83bn
events.summary: Lithium Americas on Wednesday increased its cost estimate for its flagship Thacker Pass lithium project to $3.83 billion, an increase of 31 per cent, the company said, giving higher labour, ⁠construction and logistics costs as reasons. The company said the revised budget adds $895 million in capital costs and raises the Nevada-based project's funding requirements by about $995 million. It said it expects the additional funds to be met through company contributions and available loan reserves from the US Energy Department. The company's shares plunged more 12 per cent during Wednesday trading. Lithium Americas chief executive Jonathan Evans said Phase 1 construction on the project is planned for late 2027, increasing throughout 2028. “Despite external and internal factors impacting the project’s capital cost estimate, the anticipated capital cost for Thacker Pass is expected to remain funded as we continue to deliver on our execution plan and bring the project safely into production,” Mr Evans said in a statement. The Canada-based company said labour installation rates for piping, steel and equipment accounted for $245 million of the increase, with tariffs and logistics adding a further $100 million. Logistics costs have been heavily affected by rising fuel prices, challenges to global and national shipping conditions and reduction in the availability of US fabrication. The Thacker Pass mine, a joint venture with General Motors, is one of the largest known lithium deposits in the US. Lithium Americas said it expects Thacker Pass to produce 40,000 tonnes a year of battery-quality lithium carbonate when at full capacity. Lithium carbonate is critical for electric vehicles. Total global demand for rechargeable chemical batteries is expected to more than quadruple from 2023 levels by 2030, according to an analysis from the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. The Silver Peak Lithium Mine is the only active, commercial-producing lithium mine in the US and generates about 1 per cent of global production. “Thacker Pass is essential to America's economic and national security, and we are committed to delivering it,” Mr Evans said. However, the project's rising estimated costs expose the challenges of establishing a US supply chain. Mining is mainly concentrated in Australia, Chile and China , which together account for 90 per cent of production, according to an analysis from Columbia's Centre on Global Energy Policy. And about 65 per cent of global lithium processing is done in China, making it the dominant player. In September 2025, the Energy Department took a 5 per cent equity stake in Lithium Americas and another 5 per cent ownership in the form of warrants in the Thacker Pass joint venture, restructuring a multibillion-dollar loan that the department said would help to solidify the launch of the only US-based source of lithium carbonate. Mr Evans said on a panel at Future Initiative Investment's Miami summit in March that Lithium Americas is "very fortunate to have the us government as a big backstop", adding the US has been losing the critical minerals race "for a long time". US President Donald Trump's administration has taken equity stakes in other mining companies including MP Materials , USA Rare Earth , Vulcan Elements and Trilogy Metals as part of its multibillion-dollar push for self-reliance on critical minerals. The administration is also backing a project from Korea Zinc in Tennessee. It has also been looking to diversify the critical minerals supply chain through diplomatic channels, including through the Quad and G7 memberships. The US and Saudi Arabia last year announced a framework for co-operation on securing uranium, metals, permanent magnets and the critical minerals supply chain during Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's visit to Washington. The mining agreement is intended to help support two-way investment in minerals. And the Defence Department, through its partnership with MP Materials, announced that it would finance a 49 per cent equity stake in a new rare earth refinery in the kingdom through a joint venture with Maaden.

events.title: KKR and RWE are rich firms. Why do they need a UK state loan for their windfarms? | Nils Pratley
events.summary: Deep-pocketed windfarm developers shouldn’t need a £1bn state loan National wealth fund is to lend £1bn towards the Vanguard projects – but whether the private equity giant needed help is debatable “This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain,” declared the prime minister. Andy Burnham is obviously correct that the two Vanguard windfarms off the coast of Norfolk are huge investments . Together, they require almost £13bn of debt financing. But he can’t claim they represent a fresh expression of confidence. The project has been on the runway since the German utility RWE, the developer, was awarded a contract to build the windfarms in January’s renewables auction. Instead, the new news on Wednesday was how the project will be financed, which is where the story becomes interesting. On the equity front, RWE said it had sold a 50% share in the Vanguard schemes to KKR, the giant US private equity and infrastructure investor. On the debt side, £12.8bn has come from “a consortium of 35 international banks”, including £1bn from the UK’s own national wealth fund (NWF). It is fair enough, one might say, for the NWF to get involved – directing capital to energy transition projects is, in part, what it was set up to do. But here’s another key aspect of its role: the state-backed body is not meant to be a substitute for private capital; instead, its funding is supposed to be “additional”, in the terminology, to ensure infrastructure is built that might not otherwise be. Here is how the NWF describes the process: “For each investment we are considering, we test and assess the extent to which impact would not have materialised without us, so we are confident we are delivering financial and non-financial value that would not otherwise be achieved.” So how does that work with the Vanguard windfarms? Would they have been scrapped if the NWF had not chipped in its £1bn? That seems highly unlikely. Consider that RWE is one of Europe’s biggest electricity generators and that KKR is a giant among private equity houses. These rich firms are experienced at raising capital. Consider, too, that the main way in which offshore wind projects are de-risked for developers is the auction process that sets a guaranteed inflation-linked price for their electricity for 20 years. In this case, the price is £91.20 a megawatt hour (in 2024 money), or high by historic standards. If the cost of borrowing has risen post-auction – and it has – that’s unfortunate for RWE and KKR. They might have to pay a bit more for their debt, or pony up more equity, both of which would depress their returns. But that is an everyday risk of commercial life. Why did the NWF, having stayed away from fixed offshore wind until now, think it had to join a lending syndicate on a project where it is a stretch to think its contribution was the make-or-break element? The NWF’s argument is that its involvement “widens the pool of capital available to offshore wind developers and helps to meet unprecedented liquidity requirements after the success of AR7 [the last auction round]”. In other words, the sector will need so much capital over coming years that the state-backed lender needs to be on standby. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning It’s a defence, but it will sound very appealing from the point of view of developers. They can bid for an index-linked contract that guarantees revenues for 20 years; then, if borrowing conditions are tight, they are invited to think that the state will lend a hand to try to ease funding pressures. No wonder KKR wanted in. The NWF, note, says it is lending at market rates. Even so, its definition of how it adds “additional” value seems to have become very stretched. Many of the NWF’s other big loans, such as billions for Sizewell C and £599m for Rolls-Royce’s development of small modular reactors , are far easier to understand. Those projects genuinely might not have happened without state backing. The same applies to the myriad of its smaller investments in battery technology and so forth. Offshore wind generation, by contrast, is an established market with an effective mechanism – the contract-for-difference – for incentivising developers. The NWF’s pot of capital is not bottomless. Better targets for loans right now might be anything to do with electrification, meaning the take-up of heat pumps and electric vehicles, or storage solutions. As half the energy world is pointing out, it is where the big decarbonisation gains are available. A bit of state activism to accelerate energy transition is a good thing, many of us would say. But, as argued here previously , more scrutiny of that “additionality” principle is overdue. There is little point replicating what the private sector would do anyway.

events.title: Airwallex’s CEO isn't worried about AI
events.summary: Jack Zhang isn’t worried about AI taking over global finance, but he is concerned about cybersecurity. Zhang co-founded Australian fintech unicorn Airwallex, which allows businesses to make cross-border payments and manage finances in dozens of countries, and is now morphing into an agentic finance company. Zhang joined Future Proof to discuss how his company is using AI to build systems to help companies handle their finances — essentially building an AI-managed CFO office. The company currently relies mainly on ChatGPT and Claude, but Zhang also said it’s looking at developing proprietary models using open-weight solutions. Zhang doesn’t think AI will get so good that it can entirely replace humans, at least not in his field. “The laws still require you to have somebody sign off as auditor, and how the auditor does that sign-off can be assisted by agents,” he said. “I don’t think we can completely get rid of the human in the loop.” What Zhang is “very, very, very, very worried” about is cybersecurity. With news about cyber breaches emerging almost daily, the company is tackling the issue by using behavioral monitoring and hiring experts from the Australian Department of Defence and Palantir, among other strategies. “We’re moving hundreds of billions of dollars today ... We’re constantly paranoid about how good our defense [is] against this type of threat,” he said. — Reed Albergotti

events.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
events.summary: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia. Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June). The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com. Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub . The head of Qilin goes by the handle “ Haise ,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise. The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP , a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44 . Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog]. The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com. Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations. The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk , which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals. IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure. Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket , Verified , and Zloy . Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru . The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru , the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation. Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia. Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521 , recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems. A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number + 79602347275 . Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru . IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites. That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014. More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane. Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful. Further reading: GangExposed , an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helpi

events.title: Scoop: Inside Bessent's Situation Room confrontation with Lutnick over China chip security
events.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over a failure to place Nvidia customer Megaspeed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, sources familiar told Axios. Why it matters: The Commerce Department oversees the export of sensitive U.S. technologies and Lutnick's actions — or lack thereof — are increasingly under scrutiny following revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huan g had an affair with Megaspeed employee and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. Driving the news: At a White House Situation Room meeting on Thursday after the midterm elections, Bessent pressed Lutnick on why Megaspeed had not been added to the Commerce Department's entity list, to which Lutnick responded he would "look into it." Commerce Undersecretary Jeff Kessler also was repeatedly warned about Megaspeed in deputy meetings. But Kessler deferred to Lutnick, saying "That's a decision for the secretary." Sources told Axios that Lutnick has spent the last year "undoing" efforts by other administration officials to hold Megaspeed — a company accused of illegally diverting U.S. chips to China — accountable because of concerns it would escalate the trade war with China. Spokespeople for Treasury couldn't be immediately reached for comment. The other side: The Commerce Department denied the Situation Room confrontation occurred. "This is false. Secretary Bessent and Secretary Lutnick had no such conversation," spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said. Catch up quick: The Commerce Department is increasingly at the center of scrutiny over the broader Trump administration's handling of an intelligence memo overseen by State Department head Marco Rubio. Lutnick was among the officials who received the report in May, ahead of a trip to China, Axios first reported. On Tuesday, the New York Times reported Commerce Undersecretary Kessler abruptly stopped an investigation into Megaspeed after Nvidia intervened. The Financial Times reported the department was delaying efforts to blacklist Megaspeed despite several U.S. government agencies pushing it to do so. Inside the room: White House and intelligence officials have pressed Lutnick and his top advisers to take action against Megaspeed since the fall of 2025, sources tell Axios. But they refused, so Bessent spoke up Thursday. "How come Megaspeed isn't on the entities list?" Bessent asked Lutnick, according to a source briefed on the meeting. Lutnick initially stammered, sources said, and then replied: ""I don't know. I'll look into it." One source, who has extensive experience concerning the chip controversy, said the reply was "bullshit" because Lutnick had resisted action ever since he was personally handed a memo, drafted by National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, that outlined the problems with Megaspeed. The big picture: Nvidia's AI chips provide the computing power needed to develop cutting-edge artificial intelligence, including systems that could transform warfare and cyberattacks. events.title: Nvidia is more than a chip company
events.summary: Reed’s view Nvidia has been battered over the past couple of days, but it could get worse. That is, if founder and CEO Jensen Huang is forced or chooses to step down, or if investigations pin him down for doing something illegal. In most sectors of the economy, CEOs are expected to run businesses well, but they are generally interchangeable parts — albeit expensive ones. Google and Apple show that founder CEOs, which are harder to replicate, can be replaced. But even among founder CEOs, Huang stands apart for bold bets that helped him endure short-term suffering in return for long-term gain. Most people know Nvidia for the climbing stock in their portfolios, or the GPUs on every tech company’s Christmas list. But his creation of the CUDA platform in 2006 is perhaps the best example of how he’s been able to step ahead of the industry for decades. Nvidia’s computing platform and programming model, the software that essentially underpins the modern AI industry, created one of the most valuable moats in business history. A half dozen years later, seeing the progress in neural networks, he pivoted to AI. Huang realized AI would require massive data centers with interconnected chips, and concluded that networking would become the bottleneck. He bet billions on the development of NVLink, a nervous system that allows discrete GPUs to act as one massive supercomputer, and the $6.9 billion acquisition of Mellanox Technologies, the Israeli networking company, in 2019. He funded neoclouds so he wouldn’t be reliant on a few customers and acquired Hugging Face to stay ahead of the game on open source. Huang is 63, and while he has said he could run the company for decades to come, the current investigations raise questions about the future of one of the world’s most consequential companies. Even if he does ride out the turmoil, will he still have the same bold personality that got him here? Nvidia may still mint money, as demand for the company’s products shows no signs of slowing down. But it’s difficult to imagine anyone stepping into the role with the strategic vision and gravitas to match Huang’s. The next handful of years are going to be even trickier. China is ascendant. Once it gains independence on semiconductors, it will be able to scale faster than the US. There won’t be any data-center red tape and China will have abundant energy compared to the US. Because Moore’s law is dead, AI chipmakers are no longer making exponentially better chips every year. Now, they must design entire systems with compute and cooling crammed into server racks like the world’s highest-stakes game of . They involve immensely complex supply chains colored by geopolitics, big personalities, and vast sums of money. Nvidia will be a crucial player in the effort to stay ahead of China. Without Huang, it will be fundamentally weakened. It may be already. Notable Semafor analyzed how Huang’s rhetoric on China has evolved in the past few years.

events.title: Kurdish minister rebuts 'nonsense' claims over Khor Mor gasfield attack
events.summary: A Kurdish minister has dismissed claims that a Kurdish group could have attacked the gasfield at Khor Mor, and warned against speculation while an investigation is under way. Ahmed Mufti, Deputy Minister for Natural Resources of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq , said he had confidence in the investigation launched by Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi in the aftermath of Sunday's attack. “We are open to giving all the related data to the related party for the investigation,” he said, speaking at the foreign affairs think tank Chatham House. Earlier on Wednesday, Basim Al Badri, the head of Iraq’s National Security Department, said the Iraqi government had not ruled out the possibility of an internal attack by feuding Kurdish groups on the facility. “Perhaps a Kurdish party made use of these attacks. We cannot definitely attribute it to a specific faction - it could even be a foreign entity. Therefore the Iraqi government must exercise great precision in handling this important matter,” Mr Al Badri said. Mr Mufti told The National the claims were “nonsense”. “I’m surprised that within 24 hours [of the investigation’s launch] a bold statement like this can be made. I believe this is emotional. Let’s wait for a conclusion,” he told a Chatham House panel. “My advice to all and everyone is to refrain from making any statements right now until the final investigation is out,” he said. Around 10 million people in Iraq were left without electricity and cooking fuel as a result of the attack, according to estimates by Crescent Petroleum, which had operations at the gasfield. The price of electricity more than doubled. Mr Al Badri’s comments come as Iraq's government is struggling to disarm Iran-backed Shiite militias in the country, which have attacked energy facilities in the Gulf in response to the US war in Iran. Oil and gas insiders in Iraqi Kurdistan told The National that Khor Mor oil and gas operators would be able to know which direction the drone came from, with one describing Mr Al Badri’s comments as “really insulting, it’s like saying the sky is green”. Majid Jafar, Crescent Petroleum’s chief executive, said that although it was the 12th attack on the facility, it had been among the worst. “This last one really was a shock, especially at a time when the wider war seems to be de-escalating. We saw significant damage to the production facilities. We’re still assessing the scale. There will be lots of repairs,” Mr Jafar said. But he praised the Iraqi government’s response. “The attack was an attack on the people of Iraq and on Iraq’s sovereignty. We welcome Prime Minister Al Zaidi taking quick action, sending an investigation committee,” he said. Mr Al Zaidi had met oil and gas companies in June, promising to protect the companies and ensure their compensation in case of attack, he said. This was followed up with an official letter from the Iraqi government reiterating those assurances. “This time we hope to see, unlike previous attacks, concrete steps for protection and for identifying and holding accountable the perpetrators,” Mr Jafar said.

Surging demand for AI infrastructure is driving a wave of new server farms across America, but it is exposing long-term underinvestment in the grid networks required to deliver power where it's needed. Insurance broker Howden calculates that datacenters would need to source up to 58 percent of their power off the grid by 2030 just to keep their share of grid capacity from growing. Gartner warned in June that the energy consumed by AI datacenters is on track to grow 26 percent this year, and grid supply may be unable to keep pace with demand by the end of this decade. Howden's analysis of data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and S&P Global found that since the year 2000, power being fed to data campuses has risen 19 percent a year on average, while the electricity grid expanded capacity by just 2 percent per annum over the same period. Datacenters' share of US grid capacity was circa five percent in 2025, up from 0.1 percent in 2000 – a 50-fold increase. Management consultancy Bain & Company issued a report two years ago warning that energy companies must switch gear and invest in building out grid capacity faster , as energy draw by server farms is expected to more than double by 2030. This doesn't mean that datacenters are in danger of eating all of America's electricity, at least not in the immediate future. The graph makes it appear that the two lines are about to cross, but the chart uses different scales: 1,400 gigawatts on the left axis for grid capacity, versus just 80 on the right for datacenters. Keeping datacenters at five percent of grid capacity requires 110 gigawatts of behind-the-meter capacity by 2030, Howden estimates – an expansion it considers unlikely. Instead, it expects a combination of greater reliance on the grid, slower development at power-constrained sites, and alternative supplies. For the largest, most power-constrained projects, Howden warns that grid delays of two to six years could mean $800 million to $2.4 billion in forgone revenue. "Power availability is becoming one of the defining challenges of the datacenter boom," says Howden head of Natural Resources Stuart Adam. "As demand for AI infrastructure accelerates, developers are increasingly looking beyond traditional grid connections to secure the electricity they need." events.title: Progressives try to have it both ways on Medicare for All
events.summary: The News Progressive Democrats are trying a tricky feat as their party takes power : endorsing Medicare for All while quietly pushing for smaller steps toward it. Their dilemma began with the party’s remarkable midterm success. Democrats are united in attributing their electoral triumph in part to voter backlash against GOP healthcare moves — and this year, even purple-district candidates won while backing Medicare for All. But now, the left is split on how to make it happen. Without a filibuster or veto-proof majority in Congress next year, Democrats are calibrating their expectations for change based on what can potentially pass through the maneuver known as reconciliation, which requires only a simple majority. Some progressives are calling for a unified drive to lower the Medicare eligibility age, add guaranteed coverage up to age 19, and add dental and vision coverage. That could offer a middle ground for party leaders who are looking to stave off fights over bills likely to be vetoed by President Donald Trump. Embracing a big step toward pure Medicare for All could also hand a victory to progressives who have long pushed for legislative action — if they can settle for something less than the litmus test they set up. “It’s the perfect way for us to get ready for the next trifecta if we pass those three bills, and then if we mark up the entire Medicare for All bill,” said Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., the lead sponsor of the House’s Medicare for All bill. Others on the left may not be content with pushing off action on the marquee policy until later. An incoming cohort of progressives want to push their party to vote on the full government-run healthcare package now. Rep.-elect Melat Kiros, D-Colo., said the program was “one of our number one priorities.” “I’ll never let perfect be the enemy of the good,” she added. “But if we’re not fighting like hell to actually get healthcare to every single American, then I don’t know what we’re doing here.” Centrists wanted the party to work towards consensus — a tall order for Democrats. Quite a few in the caucus want the party to focus on the underlying drivers of healthcare costs before considering a system where taxpayers pay for all healthcare. “I think we should talk more about cost and less about coverage,” said Rep. Jake Auchincloss, D-Mass. Democratic leaders have said they would need to have a “family conversation” on their path forward; a working group led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., laid out a menu of options that included Medicare for All alongside many other proposals. “Are we messaging or are we getting something done?” said Rep. Adam Gray, D-Calif., a member of the moderate Blue Dogs. “We know that we have broad agreement that we want healthcare to be affordable, that we want it to be accessible … and that every American should have it, and so what are the solutions we can get agreement on to do that?” The Plan Democrats across the ideological spectrum have coalesced around their healthcare agenda in the near term. After relentlessly campaigning on reversing GOP-enacted Medicaid cuts and restoring lapsed health care subsidies, Democrats plan to put those up for a vote. They may even use the issues as leverage in the looming December government funding fight. “I think everything should be on the table,” said Rep. Glenn Ivey, D-Md. “It’s important for us to make sure we listen to and respond to the message of the voters, and I think they want to really get relief.” Rep. Kim Schrier, D-Wash., said that she wants both of those priorities to advance, but cautioned that “we still have the same president in the White House.” The View From The Senate Across the Capitol, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., is pushing to use reconciliation to immediately advance his bill to lower the Medicare eligibility age to 55, add dental, vision and hearing coverage to the federal health insurance program for seniors, and ensure universal coverage for children through age 19. Sanders already has one powerful ally: Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., the expected chair of the Senate Finance Committee, said he wants “to push for the boldest, best bill possible.” “I’m not taking anything off the table,” Wyden said, when asked about whether he supported using reconciliation to advance the legislation. Other senators are already calling for a more moderate approach. On Tuesday, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., introduced a bill that would lower the Medicare eligibility age to 50 and allow adults to buy into traditional Medicare or Medicare Advantage plans. The legislation would allow adults eligible for Affordable Care Act cost-sharing subsidies and premium tax credits to continue to use such assistance to help make Medicare plans more affordable. But it would not give adults taxpayer-funded Medicare before they turn 65. Nicholas and David’s View Democrats are going to eventually grapple with what exactly “Medicare for All” means to the disparate factions in their caucus. While Republicans will be quick to paint any effort as a first step toward implementing a single-payer healthcare system that replaces private insurance, the truth is more complicated. The reality is that very few Democrats on the campaign trail explicitly called for the enactment of a single government-run insurance plan. But with dozens of Democrats expected to launch presidential campaigns over the coming year, supporting universal healthcare coverage may quickly become, yet again, an up-or-down question for primary voters.

events.title: Revenge of the China hawks: Jensen Huang’s enemies take a victory lap
events.summary: The News In the fall of 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was riding high on the wave of the AI boom. He also landed at the center of an ideological war over chip exports that the $4 trillion company and its allies now think played a pivotal role in his undoing. On one side were the China hawks inside the Trump administration — and circling outsiders — who worried Huang’s chips were helping fuel China’s AI ambitions. On the other side were Huang, David Sacks, and other technologists that argued for spreading US tech around the globe to ensure American-backed AI became the world standard. Huang’s long-held, pro-trade views were already unpopular with many of the think tankers, academics, national security staffers, and US government officials that make up a loosely held group of anti-China ideologues. But in a podcast interview with influential venture capitalists Bill Gurley and Brad Gerstner, Huang took things further, arguing the term “China hawk” is a badge of “shame” and that those who wear it are not “patriotic.” The slight did not go unnoticed, drawing the ire of anti-technology voices like far-right podcast host Steve Bannon and other critics who had railed against Huang’s lobbying against strict China export controls. “Let’s just say this — China hawks are patient and have long memories,” wrote Eric Sayers, a former Congressional defense staffer and current managing director of lobbyist Beacon Global Strategies, a firm that has done work on China policy, according to people familiar with the matter. Sayers re-upped his year-old X post again on Nov. 2, days before Huang admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, on the back of weeks of media coverage digging into Megaspeed, an AI data center company based in Singapore that US government officials allege might be smuggling Nvidia chips into China. The implication was clear: Huang’s fate was not simply a result of the Nvidia CEO’s own personal failings or bad judgment. He had also made powerful enemies at the highest echelons of government that Nvidia now believes has all but stopped the company’s ability to lobby for the export of chips to China, according to a person briefed on the matter. Although there’s no evidence to suggest they are connected to any leaks, among the most prominent of the China hawks that have been mentioned, these people say, are Sayers’ former colleague, Ivan Kanapathy, who serves as senior director for Asia at the National Security Council, and Tarun Chhabra, who served as deputy assistant to the president and coordinator for technology and national security on the National Security Council, and Landon Heid, an NSC staffer who nearly became assistant secretary of commerce for export administration at the Bureau of Industry and Security. Chhabra now works for Anthropic, another vocal critic of chip sales to China, with CEO Dario Amodei comparing the practice to selling nuclear weapons to North Korea. Anthropic has also accused Chinese AI companies of stealing its intellectual property in order to train open weight AI models. Spokespeople for Nvidia, the White House, Commerce Department, State Department, NSC, Marco Rubio, and Beacon Global didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. It’s unclear who was responsible for leaking national security documents that were used to discredit Huang. And whether the Nvidia CEO was the target of an espionage plot, or if there was any wrongdoing on his or Nvidia’s part, will be determined by investigators in the months ahead. But the damage has already shaved about $280 billion off the market value of the $4.2 trillion company. Huang’s now facing a board probe, shareholder lawsuits, Congressional questioning, and the near-certain prospect of details leaking out in drips and drabs. Several people familiar with their China policy agenda say the group of hawks wield considerable power and influence in DC, and the elimination of Huang from the other side of the debate will make the upcoming fight over export controls being added to the National Defense Authorization Act significantly easier. Reed’s view Huang obviously walked into a scandal, but the US government bears some responsibility for clearing up whether or not it’s investigating the founder of the country’s most successful company, potentially harming a company with massive strategic value and shaving off billions of dollars of a stock that’s in most people’s investment accounts. Nvidia’s success and failure has direct and indirect impacts on almost everybody in the US, and many around the world. We should get a full accounting of the impacts of an extrajudicial action against a US citizen by the government with enormous economic implications, positive and negative. Either something is classified or it’s not. Now that it’s been leaked, the rest of the information should be made public. Room for Disagreement From James Czerniawski, head of emerging technology policy at the Consumer Choice Center. “The government shouldn’t be able to weaponize a surveillance file against an American and their business. It should concern every American whenever intelligence is selectively surfaced and leveraged to advance certain policies, whether that means tighter chip export controls or building support for reauthorizing a deeply flawed surveillance program. When the government wields this kind of power, it isn’t just disrupting an individual’s life; it can put a target on an American company and create economic uncertainty in the marketplace. That kind of power demands real limitations and accountability. Protecting our national security is important, but giving the government carte blanche to use its surveillance capabilities is a recipe for disaster that will ultimately leave everyone worse off.”

events.title: A Tool Built by Election Deniers Said These Voters Were Dead. We Found Them Alive.
events.summary: A voter departs after casting a ballot at a polling location in Atlanta on Nov. 3. Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Image Ahead of the midterms, conservative election activists discussed plans to wield a powerful new weapon in the war against fraud: a data tool built by one of their own that could identify suspicious voters and help with contesting their ballots. The system was put to the test this week in Forsyth County, Georgia, where a member of the county’s election board provided other officials with what he suggested was evidence of wrongdoing: four allegedly dead voters. But it turns out all four are alive and well, ProPublica determined. The board rejected the attempt to challenge their ballots. The effort, though, shows that even after last week’s blue wave, those who believe the 2020 election was stolen have continued to relentlessly search for ways to contest Republican losses. In Georgia, Democrats swept statewide offices . The board member who initiated the Forsyth County challenge, Max Clavijo, is a member of the Election Integrity Network, a group led by conservative lawyer Cleta Mitchell that works to restrict voting and tighten election laws and rules. Mitchell worked closely with Donald Trump in his attempt to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election and, since he retook the presidency, has been central to his push to assert greater federal control over voting . In the run-up to the midterms, on right-wing media and on private organizing calls, EIN participants outlined plans to search voter rolls with a software tool known as ELLY’s Election Monitor and contest ballots the tool deemed suspicious. ELLY was developed by EIN member Rick Richards. It aggregates public data from state voter files, federal change-of-address records, tax documents, obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other sources. In Georgia, State Election Board members and top staffers have urged counties to use the tool to search their voter rolls for signs of fraud. Richards talked about ELLY’s national potential on a podcast in late September, on which right-wing media personalities and activists touted its capacity to help GOP candidates contest their defeats. “We can prove the fraud that’s gone on in every state,” one commentator said. “This data will be able to set up challenges to those who lose.” The following month, on a private call with EIN members and other conservative activists, Richards promised to provide data from more than 3,000 counties to “citizen monitors” and GOP candidates to try to prove fraud, according to a recording reviewed by ProPublica. Read More How Cleta Mitchell Turned Trump’s “Big Lie” Into a Movement In an interview, Richards told ProPublica that he gave Clavijo data on Forsyth County at Clavijo’s request. He said in a subsequent email that their actions were meant to inform the board and remain confidential. Clavijo didn’t respond to questions from ProPublica. Richards refused to answer questions about whether Clavijo’s effort was part of a wider EIN campaign to contest votes cast in the midterms. “That’s irrelevant,” he said. “The data is the data. People can use it for what they want to.” Mitchell, EIN’s leader, didn’t respond to questions about the group’s plans related to ELLY, either in Georgia or nationally. In the months since some on Georgia’s State Election Board started promoting ELLY’s use, its accuracy has been much debated. The tool doesn’t have access to personal identifiers such as voters’ Social Security or driver’s license numbers or full dates of birth, which increases the potential for mismatches involving people with the same names. Voting rights groups have called ELLY error-prone . The Cherokee County election director complained to the state board after the tool falsely flagged a county board member’s spouse as dead . State Election Board members and Richards have defended ELLY. Accusations that the data is unreliable were “horse hockey,” Richards told ProPublica, explaining this was “a Southern colloquialism for B.S.” Late last week, according to several people familiar with the matter, Clavijo circulated documents to board members and Forsyth County’s election director. Based on data from ELLY, Clavijo questioned whether the names of more than 22,000 people on the county’s voter roll were correct and disputed the eligibility of 69 voters. In addition to four he claimed were deceased, he alleged others had moved out of the county or state, had voter ID irregularities or had registered under fictitious names, giving an initial as their first name. During the meeting, Clavijo claimed that he was not trying to disrupt the election’s certification or formally challenge the voters, a process outlined in statutes that can lead to ballots being tossed or voters removed from the rolls. (Richards also said they had not formally challenged ballots.) Clavijo said he was merely seeking “to clean the voter rolls” and inform the board so officials could investigate further. But other board members accused him of doing an end run around the formal challenge process. Barbara Luth, the board chair, said she felt “sorry for” Clavijo because activists were bypassing the challenge procedure “by coming to you and having you submit it.” Under fire from fellow board members, Clavijo admitted he could not vouch for the data’s accuracy. “I did not make any explicit accusation that the information was 100% correct,” he said. The cover letter Clavijo submitted with the challenges said that they had not been verified with any “human review,” according to sources familiar with the matter. Richards and Clavijo submitted obituaries for the voters they claimed were dead, but there were discrepancies between the information in them and the voters’ records. All of the obituaries said or suggested the deceased lived outside of Forsyth County, which would have made it impossible to vote there. One said the person lived in Arizona . ProPublica confirmed that all four are actually alive. Alexis Ramirez, a night-shift nurse, told ProPublica that she cast her ballot during early voting. She was surprised to hear her vote had been contested — and why. “It’s kind of crazy that they attempted to do that without trying to prove it first,” she said. Saramma George, another voter Richards and Clavijo claimed was dead, said she was “really angry” to have the validity of her ballot questioned. In the third case, ProPublica spoke with a voter’s son, who said she was alive but didn’t want to talk to ProPublica. Her “ballot is valid,” he said. The fourth voter, Chris Strickland, said, “I don’t know where they’re getting their information from, but it’s false. I’m alive. I’m here.” The majority of the challenges — 38 of them, according to people familiar with the matter — involved voters who’d registered using an initial. events.title: Dubai's Parkin posts record profit as fines outpace fees for first time
events.summary: Dubai's public parking operator Parkin reported a 27 per cent annual jump in third-quarter profit, with income from fines and seasonal permits outpacing parking fees for the first time. Net profit after tax was at Dh199.2 million ($54.2 million), as revenue grew 21 per cent year-on-year to a record Dh415.2 million, the company said in a filing to the Dubai Financial Market. Its enforcement category – which groups fines and seasonal parking passes – contributed Dh136.4 million, surpassing parking fees that added Dh127.8 million, which was a 5 per cent annual drop. Earlier this year, Parkin introduced micro cameras on kerbsides to catch motorists who avoid tickets. Cars with automatic cameras to scan entire streets have been operating for several years. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation – a key metric for profitability – for the three-month period jumped 28 per cent to a record Dh255 million. For the third quarter, Parkin sold a record 110,600 seasonal passes, which was a 37 per cent annual jump, while total fines issued jumped 34 per cent to about 916,100. For the first nine months of 2026, Parkin's profit grew by a quarter to Dh550.6 million, as revenue through September climbed 24 per cent to more than Dh1.16 billion. Ebitda for the period also grew by 24 per cent to Dh703.4 million. During the period, seasonal permits grew 58 per cent to about 308,600, while fines rose 24 per cent to more than 2.36 million. The company added about 53,500 parking spaces over the past 12 months to lift its total to a record 272,500, it said. Parkin's results demonstrate “the strength of our diversified business, with growth across developer parking, seasonal cards and our other revenue streams more than offsetting softer public parking revenues during the quarter”, chief executive Mohamed Al Ali said in a statement. “We continued to execute our growth strategy with discipline,” he added. Parkin has been playing a major role in Dubai 's strategy of expanding its paid public parking network to curb illegal parking and better manage available spaces. Last week, paid parking was extended to certain areas of the emirate's Jebel Ali Industrial area and Al Furjan. Last month, Parkin partnered with Q Mobility to manage smart parking facilities across Etihad Rail’s passenger station network .

There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong. This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data. The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica. Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape. Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. The new approach used closed triplets (using three telescopes for error correction) rather than station pairs in an effort to reduce error. To the relief of the EHT team, the new image recreated the iconic ring-like image seen in the original, according to a paper published in Nature today . In a prepared statement, Lai said taking pictures of black holes was not easy. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the Moon," he said. He explained that when his team applied new advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to the original Event Horizon Telescope dataset, they found a black hole almost identical in size and shape to the historic EHT image. "Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data. This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process," he said. Event Horizon Telescope director Laurent Loinard welcomed the new study.
