events.title: A 13-Year-Old Asked AI About Suicide on Her School Laptop. It Didn’t Get Flagged for Weeks
events.summary: A 13-year-old girl spent three months using her school-issued laptop to discuss depression, research suicide, and plan her funeral before self-harm-monitoring software finally prompted school officials to alert her parents, who intervened and stopped her, according to a lawsuit filed this month by her parents. The lawsuit alleges that Google and parent company Alphabet were negligent in their rollout of a Gemini model, claiming that the AI chatbot “coached” the North Carolina teenager to consider taking her own life. The case, which was previously reported by The New York Times, is one of several that allege harm from AI chatbot use, including claims of delusions and suicide . But it also illustrates the limitations of surveillance tools that thousands of schools have adopted in recent years, which are ostensibly designed to protect students from themselves when browsing and chatting online. Andrew Liddell, a lawyer for the family, tells WIRED that, according to information the school provided to the family, the alert went to the personal phone of a former counselor who had left the school nine months before. The ex-employee was diligent in passing the alert along to current staff, who then notified the girl’s mother, he says. As classrooms continue to rely on Google’s low-cost offerings, including Gemini, their ability to keep up with the potential risks is front and center. Just last week, parent and teacher groups across the country decried Google’s new requirement that schools must turn on generative AI features if they want to use Search. US senator Ed Markey cited Emma’s lawsuit in a letter to Google demanding the company let schools disable AI Mode and AI Overviews, writing that “Google is recklessly forcing AI on schools and treating kids like collateral damage.” According to the lawsuit, the North Carolina girl, identified as Emma Doe, descended into “a severe psychological crisis” after Google Search routed her to Gemini on her school-issued Google Chromebook. Though Emma’s school had blocked the stand-alone Gemini website, the lawsuit alleges that she was steered into interacting with the chatbot through AI Mode, which lets people ask follow-up questions about a query or begin an unrelated conversation. Emma queried AI Mode about mental health issues starting last December. She asked about “severe depression” and “reasons to live,” and by late January she was asking about suicide, per the lawsuit. Over the course of two days around Valentine’s Day, she began writing a 1,500-word eulogy for herself with help from AI Mode in a Google Doc titled “Funeral.” The lawsuit says she worked on the document for more than four weeks while continuing to interact with the Gemini tool thousands of times. After school on St. Patrick's Day, she deleted most of the file and restarted. But Liddell says the themes and thoughts the girl expressed didn't materially change. Around 7:30 pm, her mother allegedly received a message from the school indicating that her daughter was in “imminent danger,” the lawsuit states. Her mother used her phone to log in to Emma’s school account and “watched her daughter compose a suicide note in real time,” according to the lawsuit. Google spokesperson José Castañeda says that the company is seriously “reviewing the claims in the lawsuit” and that its systems, including AI Mode, “aim to prevent users from engaging in harmful conversation.” "We’ve worked extensively with medical professionals and academic experts to build features that help young people find critical support and trusted resources when they need it,” Castañeda says. Lawyers for the family have sought to withhold the school's name to protect Emma's privacy. WIRED was able to identify the school, which did not return requests for comment. In recent months, the school added links to suicide prevention resources to the bottom of its website, according to WIRED’s review of the Internet Archive. Liddell tells WIRED that Emma’s school only learned about her mental health crisis because it used at least one third-party student-activity-monitoring system. Citing information that was allegedly previously provided to the school’s parents, he says these may have included products from the companies GoGuardian and Gaggle. Liddell says that the family lacks a definitive answer because the school’s “window of cooperation” with them was brief. GoGuardian spokesperson Natalia Switala tells WIRED that the company cannot “discuss any individual student or district” due to “student privacy obligations.” Gaggle did not immediately return WIRED’s request for comment. The screening tools generally work by capturing keystrokes or scanning files and using algorithms and human review to identify potentially concerning content . It’s unclear whether the school’s third-party screening tools monitor AI Mode interactions or, if they do, how well they actually work.

events.title: Linux joins Heathrow's grounded fleet of information screens
events.summary: UK travelers had more than fog to contend with this week, as Linux proved that if Windows could bork anything, it could bork it better. Spotted by Andy Hinks at Heathrow Airport's Terminal 2, this information display has seen better days. While its neighbors offer walking times and terminal maps, it presents a sideways Linux boot log – useful only if your next connection involves mounting a filesystem. There aren't many clues to what has befallen the machine behind the screen. The boot messages mention systemd , an Intel PRO/1000 network adapter, and an EXT4 filesystem on what appears to be a logical volume named LV_ROOT . Whether mounting that filesystem is the problem, or simply the last thing displayed before something else went wrong, isn't clear. Heathrow's information displays clearly accommodate a mixture of technologies. Recent examples ran Microsoft Windows, which had - naturally - suffered a moment of its own. Linux can evidently be just as unreliable in the right hands. The question is which Linux distribution is having its moment in the sun. Heathrow has been rolling out Raspberry Pi-based signage, although the Intel PRO/1000 adapter leaves the hardware behind this particular display something of a mystery. Pi hardware makes sense for signage: it's relatively cheap – at least until AI ate all the RAM – and low-powered compared with a full-fat Windows PC. Heathrow's senior product owner for displays described the approach as a "reliable, secure solution that has a significantly lower hardware cost and are 30-40% more energy efficient than our previous hardware." Readers might be interested to know that Heathrow has spent years working on its new screens. The product owner again: "We've completely re-engineered our content distribution system to be flexible and device-agnostic." So Windows in one place, and Linux somewhere else. All rubbing along famously. Assuming, of course, the displays can show more than a virtual cough and splutter during boot. ®

events.title: Dems put Noem on notice
events.summary: President Trump fired Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in March, but Democrats aren't finished with her. Why it matters: Armed with commanding House and Senate majorities, they're preparing to haul the architects of Trump's mass deportation agenda before Congress to answer for their actions. "Noem, Markwayne, Miller, Homan, Bovino, what's up? Clear your schedule," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), a member of the House Homeland Security Committee, warned on X. She was referencing current DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin (who replaced Noem), White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, Border Czar Tom Homan and former Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino. Dems on the House Oversight Committee included former DHS Special Government Employee Corey Lewandowski in a list of people who should "lawyer up." Zoom in: Rep. Bennie Thompson, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee, said in a letter to colleagues he'd prioritize investigating every death in DHS custody and during arrests. Thompson, who is running for committee chair and the subpoena power that comes with it, also plans to investigate alleged financial corruption at the agency and oversight of spending, particularly the gargantuan budget supplied by the One Big Beautiful Bill. "I called for Kristi Noem's impeachment in January, and she was gone by March. But the questions she refused to answer are still open," Thompson wrote. "Tom Homan and Stephen Miller would not appear [for a hearing] when we invited them this spring. In the majority, they will not have that choice," he wrote. Zoom out: Democratic leaders in both the House and Senate have a lengthy list of areas for oversight, according to sources familiar with their plans. That includes: The billions spent to expand ICE detention , including Alligator Alcatraz and a warehouse buying spree. Oversight agencies have been reviewing these purchases. Noem's purchase of luxury private jets that she claimed could be used for deportation flights. A senior administration official called these purchases "abuse" at the time. Alleged conflicts of interest involving Lewandowski, Noem's top advisor, who was accused of seeking payments from DHS contractors. Lewandowski has long denied wrongdoing. Dems have welcomed reports that the Justice Department was investigating Lewandowski. Use of force incidents involving ICE agents , including fatal shootings. They also want to investigate a whistleblower complaint about how ICE's hiring spree reduced the amount of training new agents received before being put on the streets. Between the lines: Noem was dismissed from her role in part because of a $200 million DHS ad campaign, starring her. Noem claimed in a congressional hearing that President Trump was aware of the cost of the ad campaign, which encouraged self-deportations. Noem also oversaw a policy of personally signing off on all agency spending over $100,000, creating a bottleneck that slowed down everything from border wall construction to FEMA grants. The agency said at the time the policy fought waste, fraud and abuse. The other side: DHS declined to share comment from Mullin, who formerly served in both the House and Senate. DHS general counsel James Percival said in response to Ramirez on X, "It is unfortunate that Democrats are more interested in political shenanigans than in governing. Rest assured, however, that we are well prepared to deal with this nonsense so Secretary Mullin can continue focusing on protecting the homeland." DHS declined to say which oversight priorities Percival considers nonsense. The White House referred comment on Noem and Lewandowski to DHS, but spokesperson Lauren Bis said of Homan or Miller's potentially being called to testify: "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people." DHS did not respond to a follow-up request on Noem or Lewandowski. Bovino, who is now retired, replied to Ramirez on X, "Honey, slow your totalitarian roll. Citizens don't answer to communists in this country as much as you seem to believe that." Lewandowski did not respond to an Axios request for comment.

events.title: The AI industry's week from hell
events.summary: A week of political upheaval , financial turmoil and salacious scandal delivered one final indignity to the AI industry Tuesday, as Anthropic's staggering IPO target fell short of expectations. Why it matters: The bubble is wobbling. Investors, businesses and governments need a spectacular success from Anthropic to stave off a crisis of confidence that could tear through the broader economy. Facing new political headwinds, the industry can scarcely afford another setback — much less the spectacle of AI's crown jewel losing its luster on Wall Street. Zoom in: Anthropic announced plans Tuesday to raise as much as $64.4 billion in one of the largest IPOs in history, targeting a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion. That's roughly $600 billion below what investors envisioned just months ago, as slowing revenue growth, soaring infrastructure costs and a punishing market selloff tempered expectations. Anthropic's annualized revenue reached $81 billion in October, but its long-term commitments to chips, data centers and computing infrastructure have also climbed to nearly $901 billion. Zoom out: Anthropic's valuation reset caps a punishing stretch of new challenges that began with last week's stunning midterm results: 🌊 A blue wave of AI-skeptical Democrats will arrive in Congress armed with subpoena power and an appetite for investigating the industry's safety failures and vast political influence. Voters delivered another blow at the local level, favoring restrictions on data-center development in 40 of 41 ballot measures nationwide. 🤖 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the central cog in AI's global gears, was swept up in an espionage scandal after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. His board, the FBI and Congress are investigating. Nvidia has shed more than $1 trillion in market value since the first New York Times revelations on Oct. 29, with shares plunging further Tuesday as the company faces a new shareholder lawsuit. 📉 Wall Street went into a tailspin as investors reckoned with the implications of the Democratic sweep — including in data-center havens like Texas — for AI's sprawling infrastructure ambitions. The Nasdaq lost $2.5 trillion in market value Thursday, its worst session since April 2025, before staging a sharp rebound. ⚠️ Financial warning signs are mounting: OpenAI scaled back its fundraising ambitions, while SoftBank reported a $3.7 billion write-down on U.S. data-center equipment, contributing to a $7 billion quarterly loss. Amid renewed fears of rate hikes , anxiety is also spreading to credit markets , where lenders have grown wary of financing the industry's astronomical infrastructure spending. Reality check: Anthropic is still poised for one of the largest IPOs ever, with Google, Nvidia and other technology giants committing another $26 billion in private investment alongside the public offering. The company could emerge with roughly $85 billion in net new capital — a historic financial windfall for a company founded less than six years ago. Yes, but: Bubbles don't run on "good enough." They demand more, better and faster — indefinitely. Even a $1 trillion or $1.5 trillion valuation of Anthropic may not be enough to reassure investors, who thought just a few weeks ago it'd be worth as much as $2 trillion . What to watch: Whether Anthropic can deliver a spectacular debut and sustain it after trading begins. SpaceX's stock surged after its record June IPO, only to surrender those gains and fall below its offering price within weeks.

events.title: House GOP bets on MAGA "fighter" Jim Jordan
events.summary: House Republicans are turning to one of their fiercest fighters to lead their diminished conference after one of their biggest drubbings in decades. Why it matters : Jim Jordan , 62, a founding member of the hardline House Freedom Caucus, has completed a stunning insurgent-to-establishment turn after spending much of his nearly 20 years in Congress battling Republican leaders from the right. The Ohio Republican's victory over House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) represents a bet by Republicans that they shouldn't move away from President Trump to claw their way back to power. But Republicans are divided over what went wrong in the midterms, and whether a more confrontational approach is the right answer. Driving the news: Republicans emerged from last week's defeat hungry for change , handing Jordan a 106–73 victory over long-time GOP leader Scalise. GOP Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) and Conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) survived their elections. Jordan pitched himself as a battle-tested fighter capable of defending Trump against Democratic investigations and winning back the majority. What they're saying: "I think when you take a beating like we took, you need to make some changes, and I also think we're gearing up for war," Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.), who backed Jordan, told Axios. "We need someone who can punch hard, and I think that he'll do that," Fine said. "We just got beat bad. We can't just go in with the same step forward," Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pa.) told Axios. McClain told Axios: "Don't count Jim Jordan out. He's a fighter. He's been able to get stuff done." Yes, but: Not all Republicans are convinced they have the right response to their losses. Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R-Fla.), who backed Scalise, argued that Republicans lost too many independent and Hispanic voters, pointing specifically to the Trump administration's immigration enforcement policies. Asked whether Republicans should have examined their losses before electing new leaders, Gimenez said: "Yeah, we probably should have," adding he was "not sure" whether Jordan is the right person to lead Republicans back to the majority, though he pledged to support him. "We've got to do a lot of introspection," Rep. Mark Alford (R-Mo.) told Axios. "It's going to take some really deep thought and really looking at what we did wrong and what we can do to gain back the trust of the American people." Zoom in: Jordan's victory marks a major shift in the relationship between GOP leadership and the hardline House Freedom Caucus, whose members have spent years clashing with party leaders. Rep. Eric Burlison (R-Mo.), who is running to chair the Freedom Caucus, told Axios he hopes the group won't have to push leadership as hard under Jordan, though it will still try to serve as the party's "moral compass." But Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.), a Freedom Caucus member who voted for Jordan, warned that changing the man at the top won't change the conference's ideological divisions. "I still don't expect a ton to change," Crane told Axios. The intrigue: Jordan's elevation could also sharpen tensions with Senate Republicans, whose leader, John Thune (R-S.D.), has frustrated House Republicans over his handling of Trump's legislative priorities . Asked whether Jordan would push back harder on the Senate than Scalise, Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pa.) told Axios: "That's to be seen, but I think he was voted in with that in mind." The bottom line: Jordan inherits a conference eager for a new direction but still deeply divided over what that should look like.

events.title: Scoop — Stephen Miller's post-midterm focus: MAGA and men
events.summary: Stephen Miller wants to use his new role as White House chief of staff to win back young and minority men who helped elect President Trump in 2024 but swung toward Democrats in the midterms, two people familiar with the administration's plans tell Axios. Why it matters: Miller, named last week to replace Susie Wiles, plans to focus on reviving the populist agenda that helped the president build his 2024 coalition, with an emphasis on working-class voters. Young, working-class and minority men fled the GOP in droves in last week's elections , amid high prices fueled by Trump's tariffs, the war in Iran, and concerns about AI's impact on the job market. Another key factor in last week's voting: Latino men also swung sharply toward Democrats, as the administration's hard-line immigration crackdown became an increasingly contentious political issue. Driving the news: Miller wants to spend more time highlighting administration policies he believes haven't gotten enough attention, and that will appeal to working-class voters concerned about the economy, insiders tell Axios. His priorities will sound familiar to Trump watchers: eliminating what the administration considers "woke" policies from colleges and workplaces, lowering prescription drug prices, and rooting out government and health-care fraud. He also wants to emphasize reducing the federal bureaucracy and push for permitting reform , while highlighting how those efforts could help address affordability. Sources in the business community say Miller's ideological drive makes him mostly impervious to typical Washington lobbying. Yes, but: With Democrats taking control of Congress in January, Miller will have to advance that agenda without the help of Republican majorities in either the House or Senate. Some of his plans could be pursued through executive orders by Trump. Others, including permitting reform, would require bipartisan cooperation. That could be a challenge: Miller, a political fighter who's been called Trump's " wartime consigliere ," isn't popular among Democrats. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who's in line to become House speaker in January, has said he has "zero interest" in working with Miller, whose immigration policies have made him a frequent target of Democratic attacks. Flashback: Trump won men under 30 by 14 points in the 2024 election, according to a Tufts University study of election data. Last week, Democrats won that demographic by 22 points in House races — a 36-point shift. The shift was even more pronounced among young Latino men, who went from backing Trump by 2 points in 2024 to favoring Democrats by 37 points in 2026. Young voters with a high school education or less swung 37 points toward Democrats — from backing Trump by 12 points in 2024 to favoring Democrats by 25 points in the midterms. More than half of voters under 30 cited the economy and jobs as one of the country's three biggest issues, according to the Tufts study. Among young voters who said they were falling behind financially, 73% backed Democratic House candidates. Miller's focus on young men isn't new. He made direct appeals to them during Trump's 2024 campaign. During a Fox News appearance just before the 2024 election, he urged young men to embrace their support for Trump, telling them to "show that you are a real man" and "not a beta." On Election Day 2024, Miller posted on X : "Get every man you know to the polls."

events.title: LinkedIn Is Testing a Feature That Lets You See Your Profile Stalkers
events.summary: Big news for LinkedIn stalkers: If you keep visiting the page of a potential hire—or ex-romantic partner—you might not be lurking as stealthily as you once were. LinkedIn is testing a "frequent viewer” feature that allows certain users with LinkedIn Premium to know if someone has looked at their profile multiple times. Krista Mollion, the founder of creative agency Unignorable Brands, first noticed the added detail last month. “I called it the ‘stalker alert,’” Mollion tells WIRED. Every few days, Mollion, who has nearly 79,000 followers on LinkedIn, gets a notification to “check out who has viewed your profile.” LinkedIn has long allowed users to see who has looked at their profile. If you pay for LinkedIn Premium, like Mollion, you can access even more details on who has visited your page, including a full list of every viewer over the previous year. But now when Mollion visits the Who Has Viewed Your Profile section, she sees certain people tagged as Frequent Viewers. LinkedIn confirmed the test but declined to share further information about the feature. For Mollion, the new insight has been a boon. She runs the names of frequent viewers through Claude, asking the AI to identify any she should be paying attention to. Claude groups the viewers into three groups: friends, people who probably want to sell her something, and business development or sales leads. Mollion reaches out to those who aren’t trying to pitch her and, she says, nine times out of 10 it leads to a good conversation. One frequent viewer was an organizer looking for speakers for an online summit; another was a host seeing if Mollion was a good fit for their podcast. “This stalker button—the Frequent Viewer—is a way to capture those invisible lurkers who are considering you for an opportunity,” Mollion says. For the average LinkedIn user, the best-case scenario might be the chance to reach out to a recruiter looking to hire for a new role. It also lets you know if an unwanted individual—like a former boss or an ex—is keeping tabs on you. Since the frequent viewer feature is triggered by someone looking at your profile, not just seeing your posts or comments in their feed or as the result of a search, it’s a good signal that this person is specifically seeking you out. While LinkedIn tends to be “safe-for-work” compared to other social media platforms, Mollion says that there are “definitely weirdos.” She herself has blocked one frequent viewer. If you don’t want to show up as a Hinge match’s frequent viewer before a first date, it might be time to change your privacy settings. As a reminder: LinkedIn allows users to peruse profiles in public, semi-private (showing your job title, industry, and school but not your name), or fully private mode. To change your settings, go to Visibility in the Settings and Privacy section, then click Profile viewing options. If you want to stalk in peace and relative secrecy, we recommend Private mode. events.title: “We Have No One”: How Trump’s Dismantling of the VA Left a Veterans Hospital in Crisis
events.summary: Hokyoung Kim for ProPublica John Falchetto was a survivor. In Vietnam, his river gunboat came under devastating rocket fire. He was the only one to make it out alive. But this February, Falchetto, who had just turned 80, began to have piercing stomach pains. He was in distress for days. Finally, Falchetto went to the VA hospital in East Orange, New Jersey. A CT scan of Falchetto’s abdomen suggested his appendix had not only burst, but that it was gangrenous. His gut was so filled with bacteria and pus that tissue was dying. Doctors wrote that he needed surgery immediately. But that night, the hospital’s operating room was closed. Months earlier, the ventilation system had malfunctioned, and the repair team was short-staffed. So Falchetto lay there, his life in the balance, for seven hours. This was not normal. But nothing had been normal at East Orange since President Donald Trump returned to office last year and set his sights on the VA.  The behemoth agency, which traces its roots to the Civil War, is both the country’s largest healthcare system and one of its most effective. It provides 9 million veterans what is essentially socialized medicine, often for free, under the cover of the American flag. The doctors, nurses and other staff are employed by the government.  Despite the occasional scandal and persistent short-staffing , studies have shown that the VA — where the doctors coordinate with one another and have deep expertise on veterans’ needs — has better outcomes than private care. But in his second term, Trump has moved aggressively to upend this system, embracing a decades-long conservative campaig n to effectively kneecap the VA’s government-run healthcare and shift veterans toward private doctors and hospitals.  Under Trump, the VA has increasingly acted like an insurer, paying doctors in the community for vets’ care. This, the reasoning went, would allow the government to cut thousands of needless bureaucrats while giving veterans more choices if the VA can’t provide the care.  Do You Know About Staffing Shortages at a VA Hospital? Tell Me About Them. Have you seen setbacks in care amid the changes at the Department of Veterans Affairs? ProPublica wants to hear from you. Share Your Experience “We love our veterans,” Trump said during an Oval Office photo op shortly after his inauguration. “We are going to take good care of them.” Days after that pronouncement, a memo leaked showing the administration was considering sweeping job cuts at the agency. “Things need to change,” warned Doug Collins, Trump’s new VA secretary, in a video message to staff.  After pushback from vets groups and others, the administration retreated from its threat of mass layoffs. But it found another, less attention-getting way to shrink the VA.  If Trump’s appointees couldn’t lay off employees, they would make work conditions so untenable that staffers would leave on their own. The administration canceled the contracts of the agency’s unions — citing national security concerns . They ordered remote staffers back to the office. Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency demanded employees report what they had accomplished each week. And the administration offered staffers early retirement packages and other incentives to quit . Throughout it all, the VA’s leadership said front-line medical workers would be immune from any cuts. But amid the upheaval, many left anyway. Six months after Trump entered the White House, the VA had 3,800 fewer doctors, nurses and other “mission critical” staff than it did at the start of his term, according to the department’s own data . While the losses made up a small percentage of overall employees, the drop compounded longstanding shortages — and contrasted sharply with a hiring spree under President Joe Biden that had begun to address them. Many of the front-line workers who quit in Trump’s early days have never been replaced. Instead, the VA has eliminated thousands of open positions, including doctors, nurses and other providers.  The administration has denied that it is hurting veterans’ care. “There’s actually an excitement about what’s going on,” said Collins, a former personal lawyer for Trump, in congressional testimony this spring. A spokesperson said the eliminated jobs for healthcare providers were simply “not needed.” That is not what we have found. Over months of reporting, ProPublica has watched the East Orange VA Medical Center — a typical agency facility — spiral downward. The hospital and its affiliated facilities in New Jersey lost nearly a tenth of the staff they had when Trump took office. Over the past two years, a VA watchdog report shows, the number of roles with “ severe shortages ” in East Orange has tripled, from around 30 to roughly 90. Among them: oncologists, radiologists, surgeons, cardiologists, anesthesiologists, critical care doctors, nurses, mechanics, cleaners — nearly every job that makes a hospital run.  “It’s scary,” one East Orange administrator said in a meeting this year. “We have no one.”  It’s not just there. According to the VA’s watchdog, nearly all VA hospitals — 97% — reported having severe shortages of doctors. (The agency argues that the report — titled in part, “Staffing Shortages” — is simply about shortages of candidates and not actual staffing.)  The exodus of healthcare providers has increasingly forced veterans into the private care program — called Community Care — that the Trump administration has pushed. Amid soaring caseloads there and what a government report describes as “insufficient staffing,” many vets have been facing interminable waits. ProPublica and other outlets have previously detailed problems with particular areas of VA care under Trump, such as mental health . But our reporting suggests far more care for veterans is being put at risk.   At East Orange, the damage wrought by the administration’s approach has cut like a scythe across nearly every area of the hospital. Wound care is harder to get, since the nurses who specialize in it have mostly gone. The standard tests for blood clots weren’t available for most of the year, because there were no technicians. Even radiation treatment was stopped for months, after one of the key specialists left.  “Care has gotten worse for the patients,” said one doctor. “The services available. The wait times. We’re not providing the care that we wish we could.” Another doctor, who recently quit, recalled how vets coming in with chest pains couldn’t get cardiac tests for months. “It felt dangerous practicing in a place like that,” said the physician, who, like others, declined to be named for fear of retribution. “That’s something you don’t want on your conscience.”  VA employees across the country told ProPublica they are seeing remarkably similar issues at their hospitals.  In Albuquerque, New Mexico, short-staffing forced the hospital to take many of its beds offli

events.title: AMD: Where we're going we don't need (as much) DRAM
events.summary: AMD's latest sales pitch: Up to 99 percent of the performance with half the DRAM, provided you're willing to buy a Mext license alongside your shiny new Epyc server. This is made possible by using AI models to load memory pages in and out of cheaper NVMe storage before your operating system or apps ever know they need it — kind of like SWAP or a Windows page file, but smarter. AMD acquired the tech from Mext back in June, and according to former CEO Gary Smerdon — now CVP of business development at AMD — the tech could cut enterprise server costs by as much as 83 percent by replacing costly RDIMMs with flash storage. Of the initial 145 systems the software has been deployed on so far, he estimates customers have already saved $5 million in avoided DRAM costs. "Conservatively, 60, 70, even 80 or 90 percent for very large memory systems, of the cost of a server can be in memory," he explained. Everyone's favorite buzzword to the rescue Even in systems with high memory utilization, where (say) 95 percent of the memory is "in use," a lot of it isn't actively being used, he explained. He cited a Meta research paper that showed that between 50 and 80 percent of memory pages hadn't been touched in five minutes, ten minutes, or even longer. "Five minutes to Epyc is an eternity." Mext technology aims to offload those infrequently accessed pages to flash. The challenge, Smerdon explains, is that while flash may be 50x cheaper per bit, 30x lower power per bit, it's also 500x slower. This is why most folks, when provisioning VPCs or servers, generally avoid swapping out to disk wherever possible: it kills application performance and sends service level agreements out the window. So for Mext's tech to work, it needed to ensure that any pages offloaded to storage were back in DRAM before they're needed. Kind of like running an errand in the middle of the workday – so long as you're back before your boss needs you again, they'll never know you left your desk. The problem was that the "R" in DRAM stands for random. Predicting which pages the system was going to need at which time isn't exactly trivial. The solution? (Brace for it.) "We realized we could use AI to monitor the system and proactively push those pages back into DRAM, so that as far as the application or the operating system knew, they were there the whole time," Smerdon said. In other words: "We transparently make flash appear as DRAM." So, "instead of buying two terabytes of DRAM for your Epyc-based server, you could buy one terabyte of DRAM, and then the next terabyte comes with Mext." To do this, AMD’s Mext employs a number of machine learning algorithms. "The workhorse model is a transformer derivative model, just like ChatGPT or Claude or the other famous models, but instead of predicting, for example, in the case of text, what word is next, what we're doing is predicting what page of memory is going to be required next," Smerdon explained. So long as the pages are in DRAM before they're needed, the pages don't even need to be in the right order, he added. Training the models to predict memory access patterns accurately presents its own challenges, which, Smerdon says, makes pre-training the models impractical. Instead, they take a single Epyc core and train the model "in under one second," he explained. From there, the model is further refined and retrained over time until it is able to predict accurately where the pages need to be and when they need to be there. All of this training, he emphasizes, takes place on the CPU core — no GPU required, which means essentially any Epyc customer can take advantage of the software platform. While no GPU may be required, it's worth noting that in virtualized environments, the software requires one core per VM or VPC, so the overhead scales with virtualization. Container runtimes presumably don't suffer from this same limitation. We've reached out to AMD for clarification. 99 percent of the perf, half the DRAM According to AMD, the technology actually works. Initially, Smerdon says, the company targeted memory-hungry applications like electronic design automation (EDA) and content creation, but later expanded to support latency-sensitive applications like databases and agentic AI pipelines. "When pages of memory are cold, we can push them off to flash, and there's literally no impact on performance," he said. Smerdon is overstating things just a little here. Depending on the application and how much memory is offloaded to flash, there is a performance penalty. According to tests against Synopsys' PrimeTime EDA suite, he claims, half the memory can be offloaded to flash using Mext and the system still achieves 95 percent of the performance of DRAM. With 25 percent DRAM and 75 percent flash, performance fell to 80 percent of the DRAM-only baseline in AMD's tests. EDA tools are extremely memory-hungry, but the amount of data the cores are working on at any given moment is often measured in megabytes. This is why AMD's Epyc X-chips remain so popular with EDA customers and why Mext targeted it initially. In other scenarios, like Apache Spark, AMD's Mext team says it is seeing 99 percent of the performance even after replacing half the DRAM in the system with flash. While implementing the tech may cost some performance, AMD is betting that customers will be willing to make that compromise in exchange for substantial DRAM savings, as memory remains constrained thanks to the AI datacenter buildout. Right now, AMD is working to integrate Mext into its broader enterprise portfolio. The software, we're told, will be exclusive to AMD hardware and will be offered as a license sold through OEM partners. Systems running Linux require only a kernel driver to take advantage of the software, while a separate RAM View application is being offered to help enterprises understand which systems and workloads it should be enabled on. The chip designer says it's currently in the first phase of its Mext rollout, which means working with OEMs like HPE to ensure systems are so-called "Mext ready." In the second phase, the company aims to begin selling licenses for the software and shipping Epyc platforms with RAM View preinstalled.®

events.title: House Democrats lobby against China committee
events.summary: Some Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee are encouraging leaders to scrap the chamber’s Select Committee on China once their party takes over next year. “For a lot of what the China committee was doing — we’ve already got a Foreign Affairs Committee, we’ve already got the Subcommittee on Asia and the Pacific,” California’s Rep. Ami Bera, the top Democrat on that subcommittee, told Semafor. “We could do a lot of the work; I think Ways and Means [Committee] could do a lot of the trade policy stuff.” A spokesperson for New York’s Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs committee, told Semafor that “we will follow the lead of the incoming speaker on how he wants to handle the China select committee, but the Foreign Affairs Committee is well poised to conduct oversight of this administration’s China policy.” The committee’s current chair, Michigan Republican Rep. John Moolenaar, released a statement last week urging Democrats not to dismantle it. Other Democrats are pushing for the committee to broaden its focus beyond China if they opt to keep it next Congress. Still others in the party are worried about the politics of axing the committee for parochial committee leadership reasons, given recent China-related controversies . “Politically, they’re not smart, because they could use this against Trump, who’s being basically pro-China,” a person familiar with the jockeying told Semafor. “Maybe modify it [or] alter it in terms of scope — but to shut it down or make it part of the Foreign Affairs Committee is honestly dumb.” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who as speaker would have the final say over the future makeup of select panels, said earlier this week he would discuss the issue with incoming committee leaders this morning. Some of them have also pushed back against the idea of forming a select panel on AI next year as Democratic committee leaders look to reserve their own turf on AI and other high-profile issues. Other observers have noted that the China panel’s jurisdiction extends across that of others, and it has collaborated with the House Oversight, Financial Services, Energy and Commerce, Homeland Security, Appropriations, and Natural Resources committees. At least five groups have sent letters, shared with Semafor, urging leaders to reauthorize the committee come January: the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, With Honor Action, the Alliance for Trade Enforcement NOW, the American Mold Builders Association, and the Forging Industry Association.

events.title: Miller’s promotion extinguishes hope for immigration deal
events.summary: The News President Donald Trump’s flirtation with a bipartisan immigration deal is running into a wall of skepticism in Washington. For one, Democrats scoffed at Trump’s decision to promote Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration policies, to chief of staff following the departure of Susie Wiles. There’s little indication that Miller has softened on immigration whatsoever. And while Trump acknowledged in a CBS interview that his deportation policy might “be too tough” and said a bipartisan deal could be “doable,” many in the White House agree there’s simply far too much daylight between Trump and newly-empowered Democrats. There’s “too big a margin” between the two sides “for it not to be a crazy bill,” one administration official told Semafor.“The Dems are going to overreach almost immediately, there will be no amnesty,” the official added. Still, Trump on Monday suggested that Miller would look to work with Democrats, while quickly drawing a clear line on what an immigration deal could include: “We’re not going to have amnesty or anything,” Trump said. White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement that Trump’s “strong immigration policy remains unchanged.” “The administration will continue removing the worst of the worst from our country,” Rogers said, blaming former President Joe Biden’s administration for creating an immigration crisis. “What the Democrats did to our country will not be forgotten, and the president is willing to work with anyone to ensure it never happens again.” The View From democrats Democrats have no interest in working with Miller given his record. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries dismissed the White House aide on Monday as “a stone-cold racist,” adding that he has “zero interest in working with that kind of individual.” Jeffries has talked up the “Dream and Promise Act” as a comprehensive immigration bill that Democrats want to move through both chambers, though it’s unlikely to break a filibuster in the Senate next year. Some lawmakers are also looking to the “Dignity Act” as one potential bipartisan compromise on border security and immigration reform, but that bill already fractured Republicans this Congress who balked at its pathways to legal residency for “Dreamers.” “The three things that Latinos expected Democrats to do is ICE accountability, pathway to citizenship, and to lower costs,” María Teresa Kumar, president and CEO of Voto Latino, said at a National Partnership for Women and Families Event Tuesday. Rep. Veronica Escobar, D-Texas, said the “Dignity Act” would be reintroduced next Congress and could be rewritten to include more Democratic priorities now that they’d be in control of the House and Senate. She too, conceded that Miller would be “a problem” but added “the ultimate decision is Donald Trump’s, and he said he was open to making a deal. Let’s see if he’s a man of his word or not.” Room for Disagreement A Trump adviser echoed the president’s dismissal of any sort of deal on broad immigration amnesty, but suggested a longshot plan: “If [Trump] can get the Democrats on board with increased funding for ICE and law enforcement to specifically target murderers, rapists, drug dealers, and the most hardened criminals, I think that’d be a great deal for the country.” That adviser emphasized that Trump and Miller will be focused on doing “what’s best for the MAGA base.”

events.title: Republicans reckon with Iran war funding quagmire
events.summary: The News Senate Republicans spent this week wrestling through divisions, reelecting John Thune as their leader, and pledging to confirm conservative judges while avoiding a government shutdown during their last two months in the majority. They still haven’t figured out how to use their greatest power in the lame duck: another big party-line bill that would send billions to the Pentagon. Such a proposal could contain other GOP priorities; Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, dubbed it the “last supper” for the party’s reign. Republicans have just a few more weeks to use the blunt power of budget reconciliation, which allows them to evade a filibuster to send President Donald Trump funding viewed as crucial by many in the Republican Party for depleted military reserves and ammunition after nine months of war. Using the tool, which Republicans wielded last year to pass a party line tax bill and this year for immigration enforcement funding, represents a crucial calculation for Thune to make as Democrats weigh blocking a government funding bill if it includes money for the Iran conflict. But passing a party-line bill is not going to be easy: It requires 50 Senate votes, a majority in the House, and two unlimited Senate vote-a-ramas that defeated or retiring members may have little interest in enduring. And Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who would set the stage for another big party-line bill, said he’s worried the party isn’t moving quickly enough. “Right now, I’m not getting engagement from the White House, from either Senate or House leadership. So if that’s going to happen, it’s going to come from the pressure from members here,” Johnson told Semafor on Tuesday. Republicans are divided over whether they should shovel more money towards the Pentagon with the Iran war is ongoing, particularly since many in the GOP cite the conflict as one of the main reasons for the party’s brutal losses in this month’s midterm elections. Republicans are also growing more frustrated over the leadership of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who avoided a House impeachment on Tuesday but is facing sustained questions from congressional Republicans over Iran and his blocking of military promotions. And Republicans say there still isn’t a blueprint on how to move forward. “I think we’re going to have a plan,” said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., after a day of literally hours of internal GOP meetings. “If you’re asking me if we have a plan right now, I wouldn’t recognize it if it jumped up and yodeled and bit me in the butt.” When it comes to more Pentagon funding in a party-line bill, there are real divisions emerging behind the scenes already. On one side is Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., who said “we need to get reconciliation done.” Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Semafor the party needs to pass a “strong” reconciliation bill and that it’s not going to be aimed at Iran: “That has a lot more to do with funding our military and giving them what they need than it does the war.” But Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., argued it would be “tone-deaf” to pass such a bill and vowed to oppose it. He said passing anything “to further or enhance the Iran war, I think that’s not listening to the electorate.” Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said, “I can’t imagine why we would do that.” Both Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, are wary of using reconciliation. Republicans would not brand the effort as an Iran war funding bill, but they would have a difficult argument to make if the conflict continues. Many Republicans have wanted the war to end as soon as it started. unanswered questions Thune said repeatedly this week that he’s not sure he or House Speaker Mike Johnson can round up the votes to get another reconciliation bill done. He said Pentagon funding is a “major issue that has to be addressed” but that he doesn’t know if he has 50 Republicans ready to pass a budget resolution and endure those prolonged amendment votes. With a government funding deadline bearing down on Congress next month, putting a party-line funding bill on the table is “the only way we create some leverage with the Democrats,” argued Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., a close Thune ally. “If we just sit and wait for them to come to the table, they’ll figure they have leverage because they’ll have the majority in the new Congress. So the thing they have to recognize is we can put a reconciliation bill together,” Hoeven said. There are competing priorities among Republicans of what that reconciliation bill would do. While Pentagon funding is the most obvious must for some Republicans, others would push to include measures to address the cost of living, elections, farm aid, and more. “What we’re trying to do is jam 18 things into a four-thing box,” said Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va. “I may be a proponent of it. Because it’s very possible to try to get as much done as you can possibly get done before the other folks take over.” Room for Disagreement Justice said even Republican critics of the Iran war would have to come around eventually. “We’re there, like it or not like it. And if we’ve got folks there, and they need bullets and we can’t give them the bullets, shame on us,” he said. “However you feel about [the war], really, if we don’t fund the military, we’re sending the wrong signal for even the ones who want to settle out sooner,” Hoeven said. Burgess’s view Welcome to the first legislative battle after the midterms. Democrats are starting to line up against anything funding the Iran war, which could leave reconciliation as Republicans’ only play. But it’s still a risky one. There are logistical challenges: The Senate is only scheduled to be in session for four weeks the rest of the year, although Thune said he’s willing to add days and weeks to complete their agenda. If Republicans are going to move a big party-line bill, the earlier the better. If they wait until late in December to do it, lame-duck fatigue will have set in and outgoing Republicans will be itching to leave Washington. In other words, it’s already late.

events.title: UK's 'buy British' tech ambitions hit reality as less than £1 in £6 stays at home
events.summary: The UK government talks a good game about buying British, but less than £1 in every £6 spent with its biggest technology suppliers goes to British firms, according to research exposing how much Whitehall relies on foreign tech. A report from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) found that while 42.5 percent of spending with the public sector's 150 largest technology suppliers appears to go to UK companies, that figure collapses to just 15.4 percent once you look beyond where those businesses happen to be headquartered. A UK headquarters doesn't necessarily make a company British. Some are owned from overseas, others have most of their staff abroad, and many simply resell technology from US giants such as Microsoft. In fact, 43 percent of the spending attributed to UK-headquartered suppliers goes to resellers. Bytes and Softcat alone account for around £2 billion, making them two of the three biggest recipients of public sector technology spending. Once researchers traced reseller contracts back to the companies behind the products, the US emerged as the biggest beneficiary, accounting for £9.2 billion of the £19.2 billion spent with the largest suppliers. And the money isn't exactly being spread around. Just 150 companies receive 83 percent of public sector technology spending, with the largest 15 accounting for almost half. Smaller suppliers aren't getting much of a look-in either, receiving just 12 percent of government technology spending compared with 27 percent of spending across government as a whole. Competition is another concern. According to IPPR, 89.9 percent of government IT contracts over the past 12 months had no published record of how many suppliers bid for the work, making it difficult to assess how competitive those procurements were. Things get murkier when AI enters the picture, naturally. Government spending records show relatively little money going directly to the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, but that doesn't mean Whitehall isn't buying their technology. Much of it is bundled into existing cloud agreements, enterprise software licenses, and partnerships. One example is NHS England's rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot to 505,000 staff , which IPPR says was carried out under a national licensing agreement signed in June 2023, before Copilot was even generally available. That means AI tools can reach hundreds of thousands of public sector workers through deals negotiated before those products were on the market, potentially leaving rival suppliers without an opportunity to compete. The report, Locked In: A Realist's Agenda for Digital Sovereignty, warns that Britain's dependence on American technology could become particularly troublesome if Washington restricts access to advanced AI systems. It points to recent US restrictions on Anthropic models and limits on early access for Britain's AI Security Institute as evidence that such concerns are no longer entirely hypothetical. The government has already committed £500 million to a Sovereign AI Fund, but researchers reckon throwing money at homegrown technology companies won't be enough to loosen Silicon Valley's grip. Instead, they want Whitehall to negotiate technology contracts as a single customer, make it easier to switch suppliers, and work with countries including France, Germany, Japan, and South Korea to secure access to advanced AI. Roa Powell, senior research fellow at IPPR, said: "But we cannot do it alone, and building domestic capability can't be our only bet. The UK should be working with other middle powers, pooling our buying power to shape markets and using shared leverage to secure access to frontier AI." Darren Jones MP, who wrote the report's foreword, made a similar argument, saying Britain should work with international allies rather than attempting to build everything itself. "We can change how the state buys technology, back industries where the UK has a genuine opportunity to lead the world, and shape markets – but we can't go it alone. We need to join with natural allies like France, Germany, Japan and Korea and make ourselves indispensable together," he said. Whitehall might have grand plans for digital sovereignty, but it's going to be a tough sell when so much of its technology comes from across the Atlantic. And with AI already bundled into software contracts worth billions, US tech giants aren't making it easy for the government to shop elsewhere. ®

events.title: Japanese automaker Nissan reduces red ink and vows to return to profit for the full year
events.summary: Japanese automaker Nissan has trimmed its losses over the first fiscal half, compared to the previous year, and reaffirmed its promise to turn profitable for the full year TOKYO -- Japanese automaker Nissan trimmed its losses over the first half of the fiscal year, compared to the previous year, and on Wednesday reaffirmed its promise to turn profitable for the full year. Losses at Nissan Motor Co. , based in the port city of Yokohama, for the April-September period totaled 39.7 billion yen ($250 million), smaller than the 221.9 billion yen red ink for the same period last year. Nissan’s six-month sales rose 8.8% to 6.07 trillion yen, helped by a favorable exchange rate and pricing. U.S. and Japanese markets did well as far as vehicle sales, while the situation remained challenging in China, where competition remains fierce . The unrest in the Middle East , which has raised the price of some raw materials, while blocking shipments, continues to hurt Nissan, as with other Japanese companies. Nissan stuck to its earlier projection to return to profit for the fiscal year through March 2027, at a net profit of 20 billion yen. That marks a recovery from the last two fiscal years, when Nissan has been in the red. “The second half offers real opportunities to make progress,” said Chief Executive Ivan Espinosa, stressing that model launches will build on the recovery “momentum, market by market.” “The next step is to build on that foundation,” he told reporters. Nissan’s new business plan is set to be announced in February next year. China and ASEAN make progress on South China Sea pact but can't finish talks this year Alice Huang, who reportedly had an affair with Nvidia CEO, is a Chinese banker turned tech exec Dad arrested after allegedly leaving 6-year-old daughter in line for Pokémon cards Nissan, which makes the Rogue sport utility vehicle, Z sports car and Infiniti luxury models, is allied with Renault SA of France and Mitsubishi Motors Corp. of Japan. It also has a partnership with Japanese rival Honda Motor Co., sharing technology and some parts. Nissan’s results were hurt by an earthquake that struck Kumamoto, southwestern Japan, earlier this year. Nissan’s plant there lost days of production, but no employee was injured. Nissan’s stocks, which have declined over the past year, slipped 1.5% in Wednesday trading, ahead of the earnings announcement. events.title: Alice Huang, who reportedly had an affair with Nvidia CEO, is a Chinese banker turned tech exec
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is reportedly involved in a scandal with Alice Huang, a former tech executive accused of being a Chinese spy She was building a career in Chinese finance before turning to tech with a leadership role at a data center company in Singapore. He is the high-profile CEO of Nvidia , the California-based company that makes computer chips relied upon by advanced artificial intelligence systems. An affair between Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who reportedly was suspected of working as a spy for Beijing, has rocked the tech and political worlds . The Chinese businesswoman also known as Huang Le had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, according to reports over the past month by the New York Times. The newspaper also reported that top policymakers were informed in a memo that intelligence indicated she was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security, recruited to influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available in China. In one widely shared photograph of the pair, Jensen Huang and people surrounding him are holding drinks in Taipei, while Alice Huang sits behind him, apparently watching him in conversation. The picture was posted in 2024 by software company NetThunder to its LinkedIn page. It remains unclear how long the affair lasted, and when exactly the relationship might have ended. The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang for comment. Publicly available information about Alice Huang is scant. She was a Chinese finance executive before becoming involved in artificial intelligence, data centers and computer chips. In 2023, she became a director at Singapore-based Megaspeed, which describes itself as an “NVIDIA cloud partner.” Last year, Megaspeed faced scrutiny from the U.S. over its alleged skirting of U.S. export restrictions and routing of a large amount of advanced Nvidia chips for Chinese users. Megaspeed was incorporated in 2015 in Singapore with the name 7Road International, after being spun off as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer, according to corporate registration records. Filings show that in March 2023, it renamed itself Megaspeed International, with all of the shares transferred to Huang Le Limited, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands. That same month, Alice Huang became Megaspeed’s controlling shareholder, according to research by the C4ADS, a Washington-based nonprofit focused on global security. But by November 2023, she was no longer listed as a director at Megaspeed, and all her shares were transferred to a Singaporean businessman, Tan Yong Pong, who also is known as James Tan. While public records suggest Alice Huang left Megaspeed, short seller Culper Research issued a report in May this year that cited a Megaspeed employee saying Huang was “actually still our boss” and was still involved in the company’s daily operations. Here's what Nvidia's stock struggles could mean for 401(k) accounts Japanese automaker Nissan reduces red ink and vows to return to profit for the full year China and ASEAN make progress on South China Sea pact but can't finish talks this year Before Megaspeed, Alice Huang previously held senior positions at the Chinese firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Co. from around 2015 to 2017, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database. Her roles at Hexi included deputy general manager, executive director and member of the investment committee, according to Hexi's social media posts, among possible other roles. Hexi's founder Kang Wei, who appeared on some records alongside Alice Huang, was fined in 2018 by China's securities regulator 400,000 yuan ($60,000) over financial misconduct behaviors while Hexi was fined 17.7 million yuan ($2.7 million). Before that, Alice Huang worked at HSBC’s Hong Kong private banking arm and at CITIC Securities, a Chinese investment bank. HSBC and CITIC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on her employment history. Beijing has refuted claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Its Foreign Ministry said this week that the “Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.” With the emergence of the latest scandal, Singapore-based AI computing company Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was a senior executive, is once again under the spotlight. Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, was originally incorporated in 2015 before changing its name to Megaspeed International in 2023. Nvidia lists Megaspeed as a partner on its website, while Megaspeed says on its website it's “a core business partner of NVIDIA’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region.” It was the overseas gaming arm of Shenzhen-based developer 7Road Holdings Ltd.

events.title: DIP Holding shares surge on debut in first UAE IPO this year
events.summary: Shares in DIP Holding, the first company to list in the UAE this year, rose more than 6 per cent during early trade on its debut in Dubai amid strong investor demand. The company’s stock was trading 5.8 per cent higher at at Dh1.185 at 11.18am. It was the second-biggest gainer on the Dubai Financial Market after Al Ramz Capital, which rose more than 8 per cent. With more than 65.6 million shares worth Dh77.4 million changing hands, DIP Holding was the most traded stock on the bourse in a declining market. The emirate’s benchmark Dubai Financial Market General Index was down 0.2 per cent, led lower by Shuaa Capital, Mashreq and Dubai Islamic Bank. The surge in DIP Holding underpins strong investor demand for new listings in Arab world’s second-largest economy. Last week, Dubai Investments raised Dh1.9 billion ($529 million) from the sale of a 20 per cent stake in its subsidiary DIP Holding. Dubai Investments offered 1.74 billion shares in its unit at Dh1.12 a piece, to investors, which implied a market capitalisation of Dh9.7 billion at listing. The share sale received strong investor interest and the initial public offering was several times oversubscribed. The deal broke the lull in the UAE IPO market, which had been a hotbed for public floats before disruption caused by the regional conflict, with the DFM and the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange both attracting a steady stream of listings over the past few years. The IPO market in the broader Middle East slowed last year, amid the volatility in oil prices and geopolitical unrest. The Iran war , which has severely disrupted economic momentum in region, has further dented investor sentiment. DIP Holding, which operates the mixed-used master development Dubai Investments Park, last week said the success of its share offering signals “confidence in the country’s capital markets”. Dubai Investments Park is home to 1,000 primary tenants, 5,700 subtenants and more than 150,000 residents. The district was established in 1997 and hosts warehouses, hotels, retail outlets, schools and medical centres, making it one of the largest mixed-use developments in the emirate.

events.title: AD Ports third-quarter net profit jumps 73% on Hormuz impact mitigation efforts
events.summary: AD Ports Group posted a 73 per cent surge in its third-quarter net income as revenue climbed on its push to mitigate the effect of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Net profit attributable to the owners of the company for three-month period to the end of September rose to Dh767 million ($209 million), the Abu Dhabi-based global ports and free zones operator said on Wednesday in a statement to the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, where its shares trade. The sharp increase in the quarterly earnings was primarily driven by the company’s push to further consolidated “ alternative multimodal trade routes and operations” across the UAE to strengthen supply chain resilience. The move, AD Ports said, helped to minimise the effect of Strait of Hormuz traffic disruptions on its customers in the UAE and the broader Gulf region. “Continuity measures implemented since March include the rerouting of cargo operations and feeder shipping services to Fujairah Terminals and Khor Fakkan Port,” the company said. They also include the “deployment of new land and air bridges, and the establishment of additional warehousing and storage facilities”. Operational flexibility and agility helped AD Ports to “mitigate the negative effects of regional disruptions on UAE operations, especially in the shipping business”, it added. Revenue surge Revenue for the reporting period surged to almost Dh8 billion, a 48 per cent year-on-year increase, driven by “double-digit top-line growth across the four core business clusters”, the company said. A sharp quarter-on-quarter rise in the company’s ports cluster, as well as strong gains in maritime, shipping and logistics, as well as its economic cities and free zones businesses also drove revenue growth. “In one of the most challenging periods in its 20-year history, AD Ports Group achieved record results during Q3, a testimony to the group’s operational resilience … which overcame macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty to reach new levels of income and revenue growth,” said group chief executive Afif Al Yafei, who took charge of the company last week. Cluster performance The Strait of Hormuz, a key energy shipping route and a vital artery for global commerce, has been effectively shut since the start of the US-Iran war on February 28. Despite a lull in the all-out war, efforts to reopen the strait for commercial vessel traffic have failed. A deal between the US and Iran remains elusive, which has forced ports, shipping and logistics operators such AD Ports to explore alternative export routes. Despite regional challenges, the company's ports business rebounded, with the quarterly UAE container throughput jumping 30 per cent from the second quarter. On an annual basis, it still remained 57 per cent lower. Ports cluster third-quarter revenue, which accounted for 10 per cent of the total, rose 12 per cent year-on-year to Dh798 million. Revenue for its economic cities and free zones cluster rose 15 per cent annually to Dh690 million, accounting for 8 per cent of group's revenue. Maritime and shipping cluster revenue soared 56 per cent to Dh4.74 billion, about 58 per cent of the total. The company’s logistics revenue rose 76 per cent to Dh1.96 billion, 24 per cent of the group’s total quarterly revenue, it said. AD Ports Group, which operates 40 terminals in the UAE, has a presence in 50 markets globally. The company is transiting from a publicly-traded firm to a private enterprise and in the process of delisting from the ADX. Abu Dhabi sovereign investment vehicle L’imad in September met all necessary requirements to proceed with its voluntary cash offer to acquire up to 100 per cent of the ports company.

events.title: Christmas toy rush being driven by squishies and building sets
events.summary: Traditional games, squishies and building sets are helping to drive a bumper year for toy sales, figures show. The data comes ahead of the crucial Christmas run-in for retailers, which peaks at 23 toys sold every second in the UK. The number of toys sold up to October was 17% higher than the same period last year and growth is at a 10-year high, according to research company Circana. The increase comes despite consumers' cost-of-living pressures, and there are signs that some of the biggest growth in sales is for toys priced between £5 and £10. Despite relatively low sales in recent years, the toy sector has been buoyed by sales to "kidults". The kidult market - which is toys and games for those aged over 12 - has been growing, particularly as adults buy toys for themselves. This growth has continued with a 22% increase in the value of sales in the first half of the year. But Melissa Symonds, UK toys director at Circana, said that toys for children - which still represents the majority of sales - had recorded a good year so far. Growing public debate around children's screen time and the role of technology meant squishy toys, stickers and building sets such as Lego were popular. "Connected toys account for less than 1% of market sales, showing that traditional, hands-on play remains overwhelmingly popular," she said. Concerns have been raised about the suitability of some connected devices. A BBC investigation found an AI teddy marketed as being "perfect" for children as young as three said "I can't help with killing you" after seemingly mishearing a question. Meanwhile, debate has intensified about keeping youngsters free from smartphones during the school day . One in five parents of children aged three to nine say the chance to play together as a family influences what they buy, according to market intelligence company The Insights Family. Paul Reader, who chairs the Dream Toys selection panel of retailers and experts across the sector, said that parents wanted to engage with their children's play. "Nothing beats a board game with that. Nothing beats a bit of interaction," he said. The panel he chairs has selected a list of toys that retailers believe will be some of the most popular this year. It includes variations on popular toys of recent years, including slime, a soft tiger that roars and grows, and a shark that breaks out of an egg. Symonds said that, despite rising sales in the year so far, nearly half of toy sales came in the build-up to Christmas, and families were still looking closely at costs. There was significant growth in toys priced between £5 and £10, she said. Reader also urged anyone looking for a bargain to shop around, but to ensure that toys were bought from reputable traders so they were genuine and safe. events.title: Dubai's airport showcases transport ties to UK businesses seeking expansion
events.summary: Dubai’s transport infrastructure has allowed the emirate to build on its status as a financial centre, a former leader of the City of London has said. Prof Michael Mainelli, who served as the City of London’s lord mayor in 2023 and 2024, said Dubai’s financial districts have maintained expansion mode as sustained growth at its international airport demonstrates. “As long as those air routes can be kept open, I don’t see that Dubai is going to have much of a problem,” he told The National. “It's not a commercial calculation, it's just a human necessity.” Dubai remains in the top 10 cities on the Global Financial Centres Index, coming ninth in the biannual report’s latest findings in September. The index, which Prof Mainelli helps co-writes, had shown no “great loss of faith in Dubai”. The Iran war has led to airspace restrictions, while some flights to the UAE remain suspended . The UK's national carrier British Airways resumed flights to Dubai last week, after an eight-month suspension. In a speech at the Arab Chamber of Commerce on Tuesday, Prof Mainelli said the Gulf should not be defined by crisis moments. “We should acknowledge that tragedy without allowing us to define the region's future. The hope must be for restraint, diplomacy and durable peace, in which people can rebuild their lives and businesses can once again plan their confidence,” he said, speaking at an event about the Dubai Airport Free Zone. Uncertainty London faces its own questions about building a third runway that would expand capacity at Heathrow Airport. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has refused to say whether he backs plans to build the third runway, which were first proposed in 2006. His predecessor Keir Starmer approved construction on the project last year but it has since been mired in uncertainty. Government ministers claim no one has yet applied to build the runway and that Londoners must to be consulted on any proposal once a submission is lodged. The government is also coming to terms with a new spate of complex security risks affecting the country, in the absence of all-out war. Major cyber attacks, state-backed sub-threshold attacks from Russia, and alleged Iranian use of organised crime groups and petty criminals to conduct arson and other attacks led the UK government to publish its Resilience Action Plan last month. The war, climate crises and the increasing range of technology available to track their implications have changed how finance professionals in the City of London and elsewhere make their calculations, Prof Mainelli told The National. “We’re very dependent on space observation, we’ve got much more integration on biology and crops, and how those interact with the market,” he said. “The models that we used to have, which were purely financial, are now having to integrate with real-world models of what’s going on out there.” Risks everywhere British company founders are still hoping to expand to Dubai, while also becoming increasingly aware of the risks of conflict at home. “I also think even in the UK, it’s something we’ve got to give thought to because we never know what’s coming tomorrow,” said Lisa Hicks, chief executive of Snoap, which produces hard soaps to reduce global plastic waste. Ms Hicks is planning to open an office at Dubai Airport Free Zone as part of ambitions to expand her company. She hopes that establishing herself in a free zone will provide “some protection” against regional conflict. Her main concern is how to choose distributors in an unfamiliar and possibly fractured region. “We will be looking at partnering with distributors, that’s where we will certainly do our due diligence,” she said. “I try to stay away from politics even within the UK, but it’s important to understand what they [our potential partners] believe in, [what] sides they’re on. Ninfeng Fiona Lee, an oncologist and co-founder of VasoDynamics, a pharmaceuticals start-up, is also planning to open an office in Dubai to collaborate on clinical trials and sell her products. The company is developing drugs that could support patients against side effects of cancer therapy, such as hair loss and dermatitis. Its global trial included patients in the Middle East, she said. “We are looking into how to collaborate locally to develop the trial at a high-quality level,” she said.

events.title: Democrats urge Rubio to act on Ethiopia
events.summary: Democratic senators are urging Secretary of State Marco Rubio to intervene diplomatically to address the crisis in Ethiopia, warning that renewed fighting in Tigray and escalating tensions with Eritrea could spiral into a multi-front war destabilizing the region. In a letter shared first with Semafor , lawmakers led by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., the Senate Foreign Relations Committee’s top Democrat, asked the State Department to back an immediate ceasefire and new mediation including groups left out of the 2022 Pretoria Agreement. They also called for halting new arms sales to Ethiopia, reinstating Temporary Protected Status for Ethiopians in the US, and surging food aid as the fighting worsens the impact of drought on a deeply food insecure population. Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del. — expected to succeed the retiring Shaheen and chair the committee when Democrats take the Senate in January — also signed the letter, alongside the other three Democratic members of the committee’s Africa panel. “US diplomatic engagement has lacked the urgency, visibility, and coordination commensurate with the threat of another devastating civil war in Ethiopia and regional conflict,” the senators wrote. They warned against putting Eritrea’s Port of Assab — which Ethiopia wants to control — on the negotiating table. “Since the September 23 outbreak of fighting within Ethiopia, the United States has repeatedly called for Ethiopia and Eritrea to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors,” a State Department spokesperson said. “This message has been delivered by the highest levels of the US government to both sides privately and in our public statements over the last six months,” they said. Clashes in Tigray resumed in August, and in late September the Tigray People’s Liberation Front-led regional government launched an offensive after weeks of drone and artillery attacks from Ethiopia’s government. The TPLF was fighting alongside other armed opposition groups, but the campaign stalled within days and federal forces retook most of Tigray. Eritrean forces reportedly crossed the border to support the TPLF, though the country denies it. The Trump administration imposed visa restrictions on TPLF “hardliners” in June, but lifted its arms-export ban on Ethiopia in May and let the sanctions program targeting the conflict lapse in September. Rubio called for de-escalation during an October call with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed; a State Department statement described “peace through dialogue” as “the only path toward sustainable security, economic growth, and prosperity.”
