events.title: Nvidia’s crisis has corporate governance experts reaching for the popcorn
events.summary: Nvidia’s stock sank 5.47% on Tuesday, following a 4% drop on Monday, a loss of about 9.5% in two days, even though there wasn’t much news out of the company. CEO Jensen Huang has reportedly been trying to conduct business as usual after admitting to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The biggest development: the board hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an internal investigation. What comes next is mostly a guessing game, even for the people who study how boards are supposed to handle crises. Two corporate governance professors, Ann Lipton of the University of Colorado and Todd Henderson of the University of Chicago, say there is no real precedent for a CEO caught up in a suspected honeypot. And while they have views on what the investigation should ask, like everyone else, they’re watching to see how it plays out. “There have actually been affair cases and sexual harassment cases,” Lipton said, but she was quick to add that she doesn’t know of previous cases that also involve potential national security compromises. Henderson, whose research interests include corporations, securities regulation, and law and economics, said much depends on facts few people have yet, including, most importantly, what, if anything, Alice Huang got out of Jensen Huang. (Secrets about Nvidia’s fabs or chip designs would matter to the Justice Department. Ordinary corporate information probably would not.) Lipton described the investigation led by Nvidia’s independent board members, with their own outside counsel, as perhaps the most “standard” aspect of the whole affair so far. She also observed that an investigation will be “exactly as thorough” as the directors running it want it to be, which is also standard. Henderson made a related point about incentives, saying that Washington law firms that conduct internal investigations “know who pays their bills.” He didn’t suggest that’s happening here. Lipton said she sees three lines of inquiry, including whether the law was broken, whether Huang violated Nvidia’s internal policies, and whether the board was misled, including how forthcoming he was and when he was on notice. It’s notable, as Wired reported Monday , that Huang hired a PR crisis firm known for handling sex scandals a full year ago. Of course, the driver could have been about the affair alone. It’s unclear when Huang learned Alice Huang was a suspected spy. The board said in a Sunday statement about the matter that Nvidia “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” Henderson similarly stressed the importance of what Huang knew and when. He described two scenarios. In one, Huang hires a PR firm because an extramarital affair is embarrassing, without knowing who the woman is. In the other, he knows she is a suspected Chinese spy. “I think that’s very different,” he said. “If I were a board member and the CEO of a company with very sensitive technology was in that situation, I would be furious if they didn’t tell me.” Not telling the board that you have cancer “or that you’ve been sleeping with a Chinese spy,” said Henderson, “seems to me to be a fireable offense.” Either way, Lipton expects shareholder suits, and she said two kinds are possible. Securities fraud, which she said is “only about lying,” is the most obvious, and as we reported yesterday, Nvidia is already facing a proposed class action lawsuit that alleges Nvidia and Huang misled investors by concealing Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang while describing dealings with her former employer as routine. “You can have as many affairs with Chinese spies as you like,” Lipton said. “You just can’t lie about it under the federal securities laws.” A mismanagement claim under Delaware law, where Nvidia is incorporated, is much harder. Employees do “stupid or reckless or damaging things all the time,” she said, and courts don’t let shareholders sue each time. Shareholders bringing such a claim on the company’s behalf, known as a derivative suit, must first show the board is incapable of handling the problem, usually by proving directors are implicated or so beholden to the CEO that they can’t act independently. Nvidia’s 10-member board has a track record of loyalty and deference to Huang, as outlined by a New York Times piece Tuesday morning. Still, the investigation those “independent” directors have announced with outside counsel makes that very hard. Lipton cited, for example, a shareholder suit over alleged mismanagement at McDonald’s several years ago, after its chief people officer was accused of harassment and its CEO had a relationship with a subordinate. Ultimately, the court found no reason the board couldn’t deal with the misconduct on its own. Even if none of this ends up threatening Huang’s job, the episode raises other governance questions that don’t look great in retrospect.

events.title: How Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affair could cause collateral damage in Washington
events.summary: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, is under scrutiny after revelations of an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying WASHINGTON -- Extramarital affairs are usually private matters. Jensen Huang’s has global implications. The 63-year-old is the leading face of the artificial intelligence revolution with his black leather jackets and fluff of grey hair. He runs the company Nvidia, which produces highly coveted computer chips. That's landed him on a late-night-phone-call basis with President Donald Trump, a promoter of the industry. But Huang was also liaising with a Chinese businesswoman who has allegedly fed intelligence — as well as advanced chips — to China. The woman, Alice Huang, is a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed. It's a saga of personal betrayal, corporate espionage and high-tech development, and the fallout is spreading across Washington. There are bipartisan calls for investigations on Capitol Hill. The U.S. Department of Justice has opened its own probe. Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, is conducting an internal review. Some expect the technology to reshape human civilization by imbuing computers with the vast powers of creation and analysis, and Trump has repeated that “whoever wins AI, wins." Nvidia is the backbone of America's plans for dominating the field. When asked about Huang's affair, Trump said this week that he had spoken to the tech executive as the scandal grew. “I think he’ll be in good shape," Trump said, adding that "he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.” As for when the president first learned about the concerns involving Alice Huang, Trump brushed off the question. “They could have been mentioned," he said. "Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” With the AI race between the U.S. and China often framed as a fierce and consequential rivalry, the Justice Department has persistently warned of the espionage threat posed by Beijing. That includes efforts to cultivate well-placed relationships in government and private industry, as well as to acquire sensitive technology such as AI chips developed in the U.S. Last year, Megaspeed faced scrutiny from the U.S. Commerce Department over its alleged skirting of U.S. export laws and routing of a large amount of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese users. The company denied those allegations. U.S. intelligence officials eventually concluded that Alice Huang had spied for China, according to The New York Times. The Commerce Department's probe was handed off to the Justice Department, and its National Security Division is investigating whether Megaspeed violated export control laws in an inquiry that will also include scrutiny of Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing law enforcement probe. Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday, and The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang. Jensen Huang has apologized to his company about the affair, saying he hurt his wife and their children, but he didn’t address reports that Alice Huang was a suspected spy. Nvidia’s board said that it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, and that Huang would remain in charge while cooperating with the investigation. Beijing has said the “Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated" and called it “nothing but smears.” Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged House tables Hegseth impeachment, effectively killing it in current Congress Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE After their first dinner together at Mar-a-Lago in early 2025, Trump latched onto Huang as a tech titan positioned to deliver on the president’s own promises of an economic renaissance. The computer chips produced by Nvidia would essentially turn data centers into factories that made raw intelligence, which could then be applied across the economy to produce cars, new pharmaceutical drugs, advanced weapons and seemingly unparalleled wealth. Trump would regularly phone Huang to discuss this future. “From the moment that I met him, the only thing that he’s ever talked to me about is creating more jobs, re-industrializing the United States, of protection, of national security,” Huang told AP in an interview this summer. "He knows that if America is wealthy, we have a lot of tax revenues. We can fund the military, we can fund our economy, we fund our communities, create more jobs.” Trump saw his political fortunes — and that of the country — in Huang's Nvidia. Huang joined Trump on Air Force One for a state visit to Beijing earlier this year. Just last month, Trump awarded Huang with a National Medal of Science.

events.title: Prada’s new Milan exhibition turns a century of fashion into fresh discoveries
events.summary: Prada has launched a new permanent exhibition in Milan called “Pradasphere,” showcasing over a century of fashion history MILAN -- MILAN (AP) — Iconic A-line skirts twirl overhead, silver-covered handbags gleam in a secret underground passage and a spacesuit prototype brings more than a century of fashion history into the future at Prada’s new permanent exhibition in Milan, called “Pradasphere.” The highly visual journey through the Italian luxury brand’s evolution is connecting Prada aficionados with the fashion house’s heritage in ways that go beyond nostalgia, and already is promising a commercial payoff. “The exhibition is a multiplier,” said Lorenzo Bertelli , Prada Group's chief group marketing officer. Prada projects that the Pradasphere exhibition anchoring the brand's expansion in the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele shopping arcade will add 100 million euros ($111 million) in annual revenues, and Bertelli said that target could be surpassed. Pradasphere is fully booked into the new year and Bertelli said visitors have shown a tendency to spend more after immersing themselves in the brand’s history, sometimes going back to make an additional purchase after walking through the eight Pradasphere spaces. “We see that the customers who go through the museum have a completely different perspective of the brand and also they browse the store with completely different minds,” said Bertelli, who has been identified as the future leader of the Prada Group. The 38-year-old, whose roles include executive chairman of Versace, is the son of creative director Miuccia Prada and Prada Group chairman Patrizio Bertelli. Longtime Prada lovers will know that Mario and Martino Prada founded Fratelli Prada in 1913 in the historic Galleria. But they may never have seen in person the luxury bags and accessories, including a pleated evening bag with a devilish head-shaped clasp, its tongue sticking out, a detail that appeared on the Spring-Summer 2024 runway. And it may be news that the brothers designed the brand’s signature inverted triangle logo. Miuccia Prada’s third-generation entrance into the family business is announced with trademark nylon bags that she began designing in the 1970s, embodying the Prada high-low, industrial-luxury paradox, and a chocolate brown opera coat from her first runway collection presented in 1988. The exhibition contains many runway hits, including the 2012 Flame heels and the Formica tile prints that gave birth to Prada’s “ugly chic” reputation, while also highlighting Miuccia Prada’s and the senior Bertelli’s reach into art, architecture, film and sport. “Curiosity and having fun is what drives my parents,” the younger Bertelli said, adding that experimentation doesn't always bring immediate financial success, “but for sure it drives the enrichment of our story, and our culture and our knowledge.” Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged House tables Hegseth impeachment, effectively killing it in current Congress Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE He cited as an example investments in sports and engineering made with the formation of the Luna Rossa America’s Cup sailing team in the 1990s, which helped develop the kind of materials expertise that led Prada to collaborate with Axiom Space on a space suit, a prototype of which is displayed at the end of the exhibition. Prada helped design the suit’s outer layer, which is engineered to withstand extreme thermal conditions, as well as the high-performance inner layer, with a focus on thermal regulation and comfort. It is intended for astronauts walking on the moon on NASA’s Artemis IV mission , targeted for 2028. Just 20 visitors are admitted to Pradasphere by appointment each hour to explore the compact eight rooms of the exhibition, which Bertelli promises will be in constant evolution. Prada’s presence in the Galleria now spans eight floors, encompassing the existing Marchesi 1824 pastry shop and Osservatorio Fondazione Prada contemporary art space, alongside the new exhibition, private salon and apartment. Most visitors end their journey in a secret underground passage connecting the menswear and womenswear boutiques, the latter occupying the original Fratelli Prada premises. The passage contains “lesser-known” chapters from the brand’s history, including a chandelier dress created for Baz Luhrmann’s “The Great Gatsby.” “It was a great experience,” said Luca Missio, an architect from the northeastern Italian city of Udine. “I recognized the stores I’ve visited around the world, in Tokyo and New York, in the models and displays. events.summary: November 10, 2026 Category: Company News Annual currency adjustments to Microsoft Commercial Cloud pricing 1 minute Effective January 1, 2027, Microsoft will update its commercial cloud pricing in select currencies as part of its annual review of local currency pricing. events.title: OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models
events.summary: In 2019, OpenAI decided not to publicly release a new model because its research uncovered “concerns about malicious applications of the technology.” And on Tuesday, the company announced it has built a kill switch for the models deployed in its research labs, months after some of them displayed disturbing behavior. “As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed,” OpenAI explains in a Tuesday post . The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.” The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster. “The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises. A rookie mistake in critical infrastructure design is to build both production and resilience tools on shared resources that could be taken offline by a single incident. OpenAI seems conscious of that risk, because it says the tool “has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.” OpenAI hasn’t explained why it took so long to build a kill switch or why it decided now is the moment when it needs one. The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face , causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation , or going a little too deep when researching Australian healthcare data – may have influenced the timing of this development. “Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest,” the company’s announcement states. “Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.” OpenAI says it plans to “strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches.” That’s a variant of Big Tech’s usual “We’re sorry and we promise to do better in future” proclamation that follows the latest SNAFU. Yet back in 2019, OpenAI pulled the pin before matters ever reached that state. ®

events.title: Poland’s Orlen becomes first buyer to cancel QatarEnergy LNG contract
events.summary: Poland’s Orlen has terminated a long-term liquefied natural gas supply contract with QatarEnergy, blaming the Qatari company’s inability to deliver cargoes as the Iran war continues to disrupt shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Orlen exercised its right to end the agreement because of an “ongoing force majeure” that had left QatarEnergy unable to meet its delivery obligations, it said in a regulatory filing late on Tuesday. The contract, for 1 million tonnes of LNG a year priced against crude oil, had an estimated value of €570 million ($637 million) this year. It was signed in 2009, with deliveries starting in 2016, and was due to run until 2034. The agreement will remain in force for 60 days following the notice of termination. Orlen will keep a second contract with QatarEnergy, linked to gas prices, for up to 1 million tonnes a year until 2034. The company said the decision “does not affect the security of gas supplies” to Poland, which has its own gasfields and other long-term supply agreements. It is the first cancellation by a customer of QatarEnergy, which supplied about a fifth of the world’s LNG before the war, Bloomberg reported. Missile strikes in March badly damaged two of the 14 production units at Qatar’s main LNG export plant, forcing QatarEnergy to declare force majeure on shipments for the first time . Force majeure is a legal clause that allows suppliers to miss deliveries because of events beyond their control. Prolonged use of the clause typically gives buyers the right to walk away from a contract. QatarEnergy has extended the measure every month , with its latest notice covering shipments until the end of the year, forcing buyers in Europe and Asia to turn to spot cargoes at prices that are at their highest in years. Orlen has since signed deals to buy LNG from projects in Texas and Louisiana, including Port Arthur and Plaquemines.

events.title: How AI Helps Recyclers Turn Mixed Waste Into Reusable Material
events.summary: As world leaders gather for COP31 in Türkiye, the event’s emphasis on zero waste puts a practical challenge in focus: how to keep products and materials in use for longer. Globally, less than 7% of the materials entering the economy come from recycled or reused sources. Municipal solid waste generation accounts for over 2 billion tons of trash per year — a figure that could nearly double by 2050 . AI and robotics are helping change this trajectory, as innovators around the globe improve sorting to recover resources that would otherwise end up in landfills. “A more circular economy relies on making better use of what we already have,” said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at NVIDIA. “AI can help us understand what’s in a waste stream, identify what can be recovered and automate the work of sorting it. We’re giving innovators the computing tools to make those processes more effective and bring them to more places.” See how four members of the NVIDIA Inception program for startups are applying AI to keep valuable materials in circulation. AIRECO Gives Plastic Waste New Life Recycled plastic is only used if its cost and quality can compete with new material. Too often it can’t: Incoming waste is of inconsistent quality, sorting depends on hard-to-find manual labor and mixed scrap ends up downcycled into low-grade products. The founders of AIRECO, a Taiwan-based startup, believe that AI sorting can cut down the cost and improve the quality of recycling to make these materials more commercially useful. The company uses vision AI to sort plastics more finely, enabling materials to be plucked out of mixed scrap piles for closed-loop recycling, where used items are reprocessed into new versions of the same product. “The finer you sort, the more you can recycle,” said Chun-Feng Liu, founder and CEO of AIRECO. “With finely sorted material, it’s more likely that an item can stay in the loop — a plastic bottle recycled back into a bottle again and again, rather than ending up in other products that are hard to recycle further.” The company uses NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX modules to run inference across its pilot line at a recycling plant in Tainan, including to drive robotic arms that pick targets off a conveyor belt. Recognition accuracy on the test line tops 95%. In a full production line planned for next year, the team aims to nearly triple annual waste processing capacity from 18,000 to 48,000 tons while cutting operating costs by 85%. EverestLabs AI Puts Robotics on the Recycling Line At material recovery facilities, the plants that separate household recyclables, sorting must be done in real time at fast-moving conveyor belts — requiring rapid analysis to identify and sort items. EverestLabs AI, a U.S. startup, deploys computer vision-guided robots on those sorting lines. About 150 robots are currently deployed in facilities across North America and Australia. “Other robots have infinite time to finish their tasks,” said R. Paul Singh, CEO of EverestLabs AI. “We don’t have that luxury because our conveyor belts are going to come in at a certain speed, and we have to act at a fast clip before the material moves. It’s a real-time game.” EverestLabs runs AI inference on NVIDIA RTX GPUs at the edge and trains its models on NVIDIA data center GPUs , optimized using NVIDIA CUDA. The company estimates its deployed systems have so far identified about 40 billion objects, recycled roughly 25,000 tons of material and avoided about 30,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions. Their team is constantly working to improve its models to correctly classify and pick every kind of object while capturing metadata about the material type, brand and packaging of each. They’re also shipping agentic AI tools to provide actionable data to recycling facility staff, from floor managers to executives responsible for multiple facilities — and are looking to extend that capability to adjacent industries. Greyparrot Gives Recyclers a Clear View of the Waste Stream Recycling plants can process tens of thousands of tons of waste a day, yet operators have long judged what’s on the belt by manually sampling less than 1% of it. U.K. startup Greyparrot built its Analyzer platform to change that. Mounted above conveyor belts, it uses computer vision to identify each passing object by material and brand, even in dusty environments or poor lighting on belts moving up to 4 meters a second. “Waste changes all the time. It shifts by hour, by season, by supplier,” said Ambarish Mitra, cofounder of Greyparrot. “Before, operators guessed based on a tiny sample, and now they can see exactly what’s on the belt.” Greyparrot uses NVIDIA GPUs to train AI models on billions of objects, while NVIDIA Jetson modules run rapid detection at the edge. More than 300 Analyzer systems, operating in over 20 countries, have made over a trillion bounding box detections to date — reducing the time needed to check 15 tons of waste from 375 hours to just six. Facilities using the real-time data from Analyzer report efficiency gains of 10% to 30%. At global packaging company Amcor, the solution helped increase the yield of food-grade plastics by 12% . Brands including Coca-Cola, Colgate-Palmolive and Kenvue also use Greyparrot technology to measure how their packaging is recycled in real sorting plants. reverse.fashion Gives Discarded Garments a Second Look Europe generates nearly 7 million tons of used textiles a year. About a quarter of these textiles are collected separately and sorted by hand into hundreds of categories, destined for uses ranging from vintage resale to downcycling as furniture filling or cleaning cloths. The work is slow, costly and hard to staff, which keeps the value of reusable garments buried. reverse.fashion, a Berlin-based startup, is helping automate the job with high-resolution computer vision. Its system identifies product type, defects, color, size, brand, fabric construction, season and style and assigns each garment to its most valuable category. “Compared to classical waste sorting, our AI models have to run at very high resolution because humans are picky with textiles,” said Karsten Pufahl, cofounder and chief technology officer of reverse.fashion. “The computer vision pipeline needs to spot small defects to determine the quality and potential value of each garment.” As it moves across a conveyor belt at 3 meters a second, each textile analyzed by Reverse Fashion passes through over a dozen vision AI models optimized with NVIDIA TensorRT software and running on NVIDIA Jetson modules at the edge. The models are trained on NVIDIA GPUs in workstations and the cloud. The system sorts in an hour what would’ve previously taken a week to sort, Pufahl estimates, and is currently rolling out to facilities in Europe. events.title: The Democratic leadership revolt has a glaring problem
events.summary: The Republican leadership fights are over. For Democrats, the pain has only just begun. Why it matters: All the talk about changing party leadership is empty if no one steps up to run. Senate Republicans demanded more time and deeper conversations about their leadership, but no one stepped forward to challenge John Thune, who won by acclamation. Democrats are demanding their own conversations about the party's future and the leadership of Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries. Neither has a challenger. ‼️ The intrigue: Where there was a contested leadership fight, the challenger won. Rep. Jim Jordan, the Freedom Caucus founding member who spent years tormenting Republican leaders, will now lead the battered House GOP after defeating 12-year leadership veteran Rep. Steve Scalise by 33 votes. Jordan is the kind of fighter House Republicans want to take on Democrats as they enter the minority, lawmakers told Axios. "We're gearing up for war. And you're talking to a guy who's known as a hammer. You know we need someone who can punch hard, and I think that he'll do that," Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) told Axios. 🤺 Zoom in: No such fighter has emerged to challenge Democratic leaders from within their ranks, and Schumer said he is "confident I will be elected majority leader." The closest thing to a challenge is Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who's listening to calls to run for Democratic leader while also considering a presidential campaign. It's hard to do both. Meanwhile, opposition to Schumer is building: " [T]he time is now for change," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said Tuesday. He appeared with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who said she's not "actively seeking the job" but demanded a plan for change. 🏛️ Over in the House, Jeffries is dismissive of the idea that anyone would challenge him after the midterms gave him a massive majority. "You think I don't have the vote nailed down? I guess we'll find out next Wednesday," he told reporters on Monday. Some of his new members are signaling that they're not afraid to defy their new leaders. Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) said it "aches" his heart to potentially oppose the first Black speaker, "but Rome is burning." But other new members are on Jeffries' side, like Reps.-elect Marni von Wilpert (D-Calif.), Denise Powell (D-Neb.) and Cait Conley (D-N.Y.). 🤝 Jeffries also has high-profile progressive incumbents on board, such as Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.). "There is one candidate in this race , Hakeem Jeffries, and I think that everyone is far more concerned about what that leadership means, what is it promising?" Ocasio-Cortez told reporters on Tuesday. Between the lines: Thune and Jordan don't have much of a relationship; Thune had left the House for the Senate two years before Jordan arrived. What's next: Senators say they plan to be in the Capitol working on Veterans Day. Thune committed to working more days during the lame-duck session to ensure they leave no judge appointments behind, senators said.

events.title: Australia may make knowingly selling unsafe AI a crime
events.summary: Australia’s government will consider creating a new criminal offense to punish AI companies which knowingly release harmful models. Canberra dangled that possibility yesterday when releasing the results of an investigation into OpenAI’s admission that its agents accessed non-public medical records – and that it didn’t disclose the incident for weeks. Security at the agency which held those records fell short of contemporary best practice but Canberra nonetheless ordered a rapid review into Australia’s ability to handle infosec incidents involving AI. That review landed yesterday, complete with 18 recommendations including one that would make it mandatory for AI companies to report misaligned behavior or security incidents involving their models, and perhaps impose criminal penalties for “egregious regulatory non-compliance.” Another recommendation calls for consideration of “A standalone ‘failure to prevent’ offence which would criminalize instances where the company is responsible for developing an AI model that engages in harmful conduct, and the company fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm.” The review suggests two ministries and Australia’s Federal Police consider those reforms, meaning this is not something that will happen in a hurry, if at all, for a couple of reasons. One is that Australia yesterday proposed a new regulator which will require AI players to do six things: Maintain security controls across all stages of development and deployment Identify and manage serious risks associated with their models Allow independent evaluation of their models Provide mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian Government rapidly Maintain and publish safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency Respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change. If AI companies straighten up and fly right, Canberra might not need to do more. The other reason Australia might not criminalize AI is economic pragmatism. Canberra wants to ensure leading AI companies invest in local datacenters, especially facilities where they train and run frontier models. Such investments would mean Australia scores some of the AI boom cash sloshing around the world, while also giving the government the ability to at least point to leading-edge AI running on local shores and therefore theoretically remaining accessible even if war or a diplomatic rupture makes it hard to access advanced AI hosted offshore. Other nations in Asia, such as South Korea and India, are addressing those risks by building substantial sovereign infrastructure and working to develop sovereign frontier-class models trained on local data and especially data in their local languages. Canberra can’t match that investment without pouring petrol on its raging inflation problem. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is therefore instead trying to regulate AI without scaring away investment. Threatening to lock up AI executives is not likely to make them enthusiastic when asked to approve building datacenters down under. Some sections of Australia’s population won’t mind it if big tech doesn’t show up: Protests against datacenters are already widespread. Your correspondent recently spoke to the organizer of a protest group opposed to development of a new datacenter which is just three kilometers from four existing bit barns, one of which abuts a sizable apartment complex and has operated without incident or opposition for years. The organizer was blissfully ignorant of those facilities and eventually said their group is opposed to AI in all forms. ®

events.title: "Rome is burning": Incoming House Democrats prove unusually willing to defy leaders
events.summary: House Democrats' incoming freshman class is barely a week old and already threatening to defy party leaders in ways most of their incumbent colleagues wouldn't dare. Why it matters: It's a dynamic House leaders may have to learn to live with as they integrate a massive group of new members who were swept into office on a wave of populist, anti-establishment anger. "My class is huge not because of ... the Democratic Party and its brand but despite it," said Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio). "Many of us are outsiders who didn't come up through the machine, don't buy into the conventions." Congressional Progressive Caucus chair Greg Casar (D-Texas) told Axios: "Any members that are new and have just run their elections are going to be very close to where the voters are, and we know the voters are very upset." State of play: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is on track to become speaker, in part thanks to his rock-solid support among sitting House Democrats. His supporters include high-profile progressives such as Casar and Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.). "There is one candidate in this race, Hakeem Jeffries, and I think that everyone is far more concerned about what that leadership means, what is it promising," Ocasio-Cortez told reporters on Tuesday. Things get more spotty when gauging Jeffries' support among incoming freshmen, some of whom have openly declined to commit to supporting his leadership. That includes members of the informal progressive "Bloc," including Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.), Melat Kiros (D-Colo.), Claire Valdez (D-N.Y.), Adam Hamawy (D-N.J.) and Chris Rabb (D-Pa.). "As far as I've heard, Jeffries is the only one running," said progressive Rep.-elect Randy Villegas (D-Calif.). "But ... I think we need to see some prioritization of some legislation, particularly around health care, foreign policy and immigration." Some incoming and sitting House Democrats have been flooded with calls and emails urging them not to elect Jeffries speaker, Axios previously reported . The intrigue: It's not just progressives hesitating to throw their full-throated support behind Jeffries. The list also includes some moderates in districts President Trump carried by double digits in 2024. Said Rep.-elect Teresa Benitez-Thompson (D-Nev.), a member of the center-left New Democrat Coalition: "I just won a district that went for Trump two years ago by 14%. … I've got to turn around and show that we're making change." "For anyone running for speaker, that's my message back to them," she added. "It's much more about, like, what can you do for Nevada?" "I'd like to see who's on the ballot," said Rep.-elect Jake Johnson (D-Minn.), a member of both the New Dems and the centrist Blue Dogs. "Until I've had an opportunity to chat, until I've had an opportunity to see who's out there, I'm not making any decisions." Yes, but: Plenty of freshmen are supporting Jeffries as well. Well-represented in that contingent are incoming members who ran in marquee races with substantial backing from House Democrats' campaign apparatus, including Reps.-elect Marni von Wilpert (D-Calif.), Manny Rutinel (D-Colo.), Denise Powell (D-Neb.), Cait Conley (D-N.Y.) and Rebecca Bennett (D-N.J.). Rep.-elect Zack Mullock (D-N.J.), who didn't have support from the national party, told Axios he is "not making many big splashes" as a new member: "You're going to have pretty strong support for Hakeem, and I'll be part of that support." Zoom in: Several members, such as Leonard and Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.), have said they want to see Jeffries commit to a ban on corporate PACs as a prerequisite for voting for him. "We need a 28th Amendment in the year 2028 or before to shut down Elon Musk and corporate money and Israeli lobby money, for that matter," Leonard said. Said Ojeda: "I have hard lines: I want to make sure that we are making sure we are getting big money out of politics. It's time for us to stop allowing the billionaire class to buy our elections." The bottom line: Leonard said it "aches" his heart to potentially oppose the first Black speaker of the House, but that "Rome is burning." The Ohio Democrat said he needs to be able to tell his districts "the leader shares our sense of urgency for transformational change and is willing to take the size of his caucus and take it for a spin."

events.title: X launches its own clipping feature to spur influencer engagement
events.summary: Over the past few years, X has released a number of features to make itself a friendlier hub for influencers. The latest effort to attract social media talent? Its own clipping tool. Clipping is the pivotal social media technique by which longer videos are spliced into TikTok-attention-span length “clips” and then strategically posted to engage as many eyeballs (and thus derive as much ad revenue) as possible. On Monday, X announced the tool, which, from what we can tell, appears to be little more than a straightforward video-trimming feature that lets users edit videos and post them to X. The site says that every clip includes a “Clip from” label that links back to the original video from which it was derived, allowing X users to see more about the creator and the creator’s content. “Grab your favorite moment from any video, add your take, and post it without leaving X,” the company posted . The platform added that both creators and clippers can “earn from views on the clip through Original Content Rewards,” X’s rewards program . The program is only available for eligible creators and pays out based on specific levels of audience engagement. In many cases, influencers pay special firms to handle clipping for them. More and more large companies are also turning to such services to run marketing campaigns, and the technique has been used in political campaigns as well . Over the last several years, X has tried to compete with other social sites by expanding the kind of content it supports. To take on sites like YouTube, X introduced long-form videos in 2022 (when the site was still known as Twitter), and they have since taken off on the platform. To be more like Substack, it long ago dispensed with the site’s traditional character limits and introduced long-form blog posts , which are available to premium subscribers. X has kept at it this year. In March, it added a feature called “ exclusive threads ” that lets creators put parts of a thread behind a paywall so only subscribers can read them, and in July it launched a livestreaming studio and set aside $1 million for creators who go live. events.title: Robot vessels take on the dangerous work of mine hunting
events.summary: This South Korean vessel is among the ships damaged in the Strait of Hormuz Traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most dangerous trips a vessel can take. Despite assistance from the US Navy, ships are still being attacked . "To transit the Strait of Hormuz you need agreement between the captain and the crew to take the risk. You need war risk insurance. And the captain has to make the final decision," says Steve Cameron, a former merchant navy officer and maritime consultant. Missiles and drones are a threat from the air, but under the surface mines may also be lurking. "If you're a captain, you'd like to see evidence mines aren't present," Cameron adds. Modern mines rest on the seabed and detonate when they detect an acoustic or magnetic signal, triggering a pressure wave that will break the keel of a passing vessel. Others can rise through shallow waters or float, or be powered towards a target. The technology itself is not difficult or costly, but the mere threat can stop a tanker fleet from sailing. Ian McFarlane of French defence group Thales is a naval architect who knows mine warfare well. "Mines are a very cheap way of waging a naval war, as the Royal Navy is acutely aware," he says. Finding sea mines has traditionally been the job of specialist mine-hunting vessels, with crews of around 80 sailors. To keep humans out of harm's way, an increasing amount of the work is done by systems that are autonomous and monitored from the shore. They might only need 20 personnel, working in shifts on land. With the recruitment and retention challenges facing Nato navies these highly-portable robot systems are very attractive. Such tech has been under development for 20 years. During the 2003 Iraq war the US Navy poked around the seabed looking for mines with a torpedo-shaped robot called the Remus 100. Pinging around with sonar these little machines operated down to around 100ft depth and spared divers a difficult and dangerous task. Iran's military published this picture of a US submersible captured in the Gulf The latest conflict in the Gulf is testing much more capable systems. The US military is sparing with details about their mine-hunting craft, but we have seen glimpses of them. Iranian forces hauled an uncrewed US autonomous sub , external out of the waters of the Strait of Hormuz in early September. The Pentagon claimed this robot, an Extra Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV) from US autonomous defence tech venture Anduril, was a malfunctioning older device with no classified equipment on-board. Whatever its mission, no sailors were imperilled. That, says William Lupton, a naval analyst with Shephard Group, "was a drop in the ocean compared to having prisoners taken", and part of the point of uncrewed vessels. What if an uncrewed vessel is captured? Nato navies are reluctant to go into details, but computer drives can be wiped or destroyed remotely by various means. This may have taken place inside the humming circuit boards of the XLUUV seized by Iran. The Thales Uncrewed Surface Vehicle is packed with sensors Such autonomous tech is being embraced by forces around the world. Cooperation between Thales, the Royal Navy, and France's Marine Nationale has produced a robot motor launch. The Thales Uncrewed Surface Vehicle (USV) is packed with sensors programmed to detect mines via sonar that was developed for the oil and gas industries. It tows a 5m long rectangular box, similar to a large torpedo, that takes a hi-resolution look at the seabed and creates a 3D picture refined by AI. The latest mines are designed to blend into their surroundings and the software spots anything that looks like a mine. Autonomous systems are cheaper than conventional minehunters, plus they can be deployed, along with containerised control centres, by air. Steve Prest, associate fellow at the RUSI defence think tank, introduced uncrewed mine hunting into the Royal Navy and was its first fleet robotics officer, a title he acquired in 2014. "There is a bunch of ways to look for a mine using robot boats or robot subs, and while you can't prove the negative, that no mines are there, you can reduce the risk." He says US robot minehunters can either blow up a mine or just mark the spot as somewhere to avoid. "We'll see more use of autonomy but also the missions and capability will expand. And AI will be analysing data from those vessels on the spot as opposed to data being analysed when a drone returns." The Royal Navy recently announced its concept of a hybrid navy - mixing drones with conventional warships. But Prest thinks for this vision to succeed the fleet must operate as one distributed force, sharing data in what he terms a cognitive architecture. The robot only makes a real difference as part of this scheme and it's a mistake to focus on individual uncrewed assets. "Uncrewed or autonomous vessels are not the operating system. They are applications running on it.

events.title: Scoop: Commerce Department received national security warning on Nvidia CEO affair
events.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was sent a highly classified memo warning about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, multiple sources familiar told Axios. Why it matters: Lutnick oversees the agency charged with keeping sensitive U.S. technology out of the hands of American adversaries. The warning raises questions about how the department weighed potential security risks as it cleared advanced Nvidia chip sales to China-affiliated entities. Driving the news : Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of the memo detailing Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese intelligence agent, according to The New York Times. The memo, which drew on surveillance of Alice Huang and a chip-smuggling investigation into her company, Megaspeed, circulated before President Trump's May 13–15 trip to China. Rubio also warned Trump directly aboard Air Force One before a refueling stop in Anchorage where Jensen Huang joined the delegation. He hadn't initially been invited to participate, the Times reported Tuesday . On May 14, Reuters reported that the Commerce Department had cleared around 10 Chinese companies to purchase Nvidia's H200 chips. Some export approvals predated the warning. Nvidia disclosed in February it had received an H200 export license, and Huang told Axios' Ina Fried in March the company had licenses covering Chinese customers. Yes, but : It's unclear how those approvals ultimately translated into sales, as China's government has halted some chip-buying activity in spite of U.S. approvals. Megaspeed purchased billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips, according to multiple media outlets. What they're saying : Trump said on Monday that it was possible intelligence officials had shown it to him, but he didn't recall: "Certainly, it didn't make much of an impact on me." The Commerce Department did not comment. Catch up quick : Nvidia has been rocked by the scandal , losing about $1 trillion in market value since the Times' first reported the relationship, although some of that decline also came after an overwhelming number of Democrats promising to slow an AI data-center buildout were elected in the midterms. Huang acknowledged an affair Sunday , and Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation. The board expressed confidence in his leadership and said it had no reason to believe national security secrets were compromised. What to watch : New revelations continue to drop almost daily about the administration's handling of the Nvidia CEO's relationship. Lawmakers in both parties have promised investigations and demanded more information, including closed-door testimony from Jensen Huang next week. Top Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs committee have also demanded answers from Lutnick about the administration's chip approvals, "including to companies with concerning links to China and amid alarming reports of potential Chinese intelligence ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang."

events.title: Anthropic tiptoes into MS Office territory
events.summary: Anthropic has introduced three new types of artifacts that show the company tiptoeing into the office productivity market long dominated by Microsoft and Google. On Tuesday, the Claudefather announced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, and promised the imminent arrival of Claude Meetings. These artifact types join existing ones – Docs, Slides, Design, and Motion – to form a nascent Claude-dependent productivity suite. Anthropic initially used the term artifacts to refer to shareable AI-based interactive tools, like dynamic charts. But the scope of the term has been stretched to cover specific artifact types, which refer to what traditionalists might take to mean files associated with specific hosted applications. "An artifact is anything Claude makes for you that you'd put in front of someone: a design, a deck, a document, a dashboard, or a small interactive tool," the company explains. The key thing that distinguishes an artifact from a file is that users are meant to interact with artifacts through Claude, rather than storing and transferring them independently. Think of it more as a container or managed object that opens in Claude (via a sharing URL), because artifacts in fact consist of various content types – .txt, .md, .html, .jsx, .svg, .pptx, .docx, .zip, .pdf, and .mp4, among others. Anthropic's vision of Claude as a container for other applications goes beyond artifacts. The AI biz has also expanded its interactive connectors , which turn Claude into a landlord for other software applications. Its own promotional video for the feature hammers that point home in its title: " Your apps have moved into Claude ." "Starting today, partners can embed their apps directly in Claude, so you can work in Adobe, Atlassian, and others without switching tabs," Anthropic said. "Plugins from Salesforce (beta), NetSuite, and Workday (beta) come with built-in skills, so sellers can prep for a call, accountants can analyze financial data, and HR teams can handle time off and expenses." In a prior era, those would be fighting words. Tech companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft have worked for years to maintain their positions as platform landlords. Anthropic's invitation to become a Claude tenant ought to set off competition alarm bells. But perhaps with LLMs being able to re-create other people's apps on demand, there's less interest in defending app boundaries as if they were moats to keep out rivals. With AI, the call is coming from inside the house. Alongside the rollout of Claude Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data, Anthropic is pushing the notion that Claude is useful for people working outside of computation and mathematics, the occupational category that, according to the company's own data , accounts for a larger share of Claude usage than any other. "Inside Anthropic, non-technical teams are starting to get as much out of Claude as our engineers," the biz insists, hauling out canned testimonials from the likes of Accenture and Datadog. If Anthropic can demonstrate that there's an untapped market of non-coders who would welcome a Claude subscription, investors in the company's pending IPO will be glad to see it. ®

events.title: Trump swung between war and diplomacy — then chose a third way
events.summary: When Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with his G7 counterparts in Paris on Tuesday, he told them that President Trump had considered resuming the war with Iran or cutting a deal — but chose a third option: strangling the Iranian regime, three people who attended the meeting told Axios. Why it matters: The Iran war has become a political albatross in Trump's second term, costing Republicans dearly in the midterms. For months, the president has alternated between threatening to obliterate Iran and predicting it will capitulate and give him the deal he wants. "He's been searching for the solution, but he wasn't sure what's the best way to go," a U.S. official close to Trump said. This debate over which course to follow has led to strife between several factions within the top echelon of the administration. Each faction had the support of U.S. allies in the Middle East — namely Israel favoring renewed strikes and most Gulf countries opposing them. Driving the news: After meeting with the Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani on Monday, Trump said that a new round of strikes against Iran is "quite unlikely" and "doesn't seem to be necessary." Trump said he instead favors continuing the economic crackdown and naval blockade against Iran, in addition to a new operation dubbed "Iron Gate" to cut off land routes that Iran uses to move advanced weaponry and other technology. Behind the scenes: Rubio explained the U.S. Iran policy in a closed meeting on Tuesday with the foreign ministers of the G7 countries in Paris. "The President doesn't just have two options. It's not just return to war or sign a ridiculous peace deal. We won't do a stupid deal. The third option we have is to continue to do what we do now," Rubio said, according to three people in the room. Rubio went on to say that the U.S. is imposing devastating costs on Iran's economy, making it harder for it to fund terrorist organizations or rebuild its military. And there's no end date. "The President is not under false time pressure, the Iranians are inflicting major damage on their own economy," Rubio said. The intrigue: U.S. officials say that Rubio was among the members of Trump's national security team who pushed for the strangulation strategy, along with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Jared Kushner, Trump's adviser and son-in-law. That group opposed the resumption of war, didn't believe Iran's current positions could lead to a deal that serves U.S. interests and lobbied for the third option. State of play: Rubio is deeply skeptical of a diplomatic breakthrough. " Iran would love a deal. The problem is the conditions they continue to place are absurd. Like, they're not even serious right now," he told reporters after the G7 meeting. That could change if the Iranians feel more economic pain, he said. "Eventually you have to eat," he said. "Eventually the economic realities penetrate the skull of even the most radical lunatic. So I think as time goes on that will have an impact." Yes, but: Several U.S. allies — such as Turkey, Iraq and Pakistan — are concerned about Trump's intention to prolong the economic squeeze, a U.S. official said. The person said those allies worry that U.S. pressure on them to stop doing business with Iran — including by stopping flights and closing their borders — will create instability in their own countries. The other side: The course Trump has chosen is completely at odds with the directive Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei gave his government and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Khamenei ordered an end to the "no war, no deal" status quo, demanding a clear conclusion to the war. Iran's civilian leadership interpreted this as a green light to negotiate a deal. But if the current stalemate continues and pressure on Iran intensifies, the IRGC could see it as a green light for more aggressive attacks in the region in an attempt to break the status quo. "Iran has no intention of simply accepting this situation indefinitely," said Danny Citrinowicz, an expert on Iran at the Atlantic Council. "Tehran may conclude that increasing the economic and security costs for Washington and its regional partners is the only way to force a change in American policy." He added: "The danger is obvious: Iran escalates, Washington responds, and both sides find themselves in another military confrontation that neither necessarily wanted." What to watch: Qatar's prime minister briefed the G7 meeting on mediation efforts and his conversation with Trump the previous day. Al Thani said he came away from his meeting with Trump believing there's more breathing room for diplomatic efforts. The sticking points remain which side will take the first step toward de-escalating and which confidence-building measures the parties will agree to take. The Qatari prime minister said he wants to bring in China and European countries as guarantors, to help ease deep Iranian suspicions that Trump will break the agreement and resume the war in a few months.

events.title: Ye olde server consolidation has made Cisco push top-of-rack switching to 100G
events.summary: Server consolidation has led Cisco to boost the speed of top-of-rack switches to 100G. The networking giant last week announced the catchily named N9348C8D-H2, a 1U device packing 48 100G SFP-DD ports and eight 400G QSFP-DD uplinks. At the Cisco Live event in Melbourne, Australia, this week, Cisco’s senior veep for datacenter and internet infrastructure, Kevin Wollenweber, said one reason the company created the device is that modern servers often feature a pair of fast network interface cards. The twin cards are needed because sixth-gen server processors from Intel and AMD offer dozens, or even hundreds, of physical processor cores and therefore generate a lot of traffic. The density of computing power those processors provide has led chipmakers and server manufacturers to suggest replacing handfuls of machines running older, power-guzzling Xeons and Epycs with boxes running more efficient sixth-gen chips. The Register hears it’s not uncommon to achieve 6:1 server consolidation ratios when moving from third- or fourth-generation Xeons or Epycs to current models. Users who make that move can pack many more server cores into the same rack. Power bills go down, but the quantity of data leaving a rack goes up. Wollenweber said Cisco realized it had “tons” of switches that offer 25G ports but felt it had a gap in its range for non-AI scenarios like server consolidation that produced increased data flows. The exec admitted that the 100G ports may be overkill for a modest collection of new servers, but argued users recognize it won’t be long before they grow into the excess capacity – perhaps as they use more agentic AI applications. Cisco sees traffic from AI agents stressing the north-south connections that link organizations to the cloud and also driving much more east-west traffic across internal networks. At Cisco Live, the company’s execs suggested that network upgrades are therefore an inevitable necessity. That’s not entirely self-serving, because agents will vastly outnumber humans and constantly create traffic, compared to the flurries of network activity that happen when humans use generative AI or chatbots. Cisco argues that deploying agents at scale will therefore only be possible on highly automated networks. “Humans can no longer comprehend the amount of data that we actually have in a network,” Wollenweber told The Register . Cisco’s Canvas agentic operations platform aims to at least make humans aware when their attention is needed, by detecting problems and offering to make repairs. Joe Vaccaro, Cisco’s senior vice president and general manager for Network Platform and Assurance, told The Register he believes network administrators don’t feel threatened by suggestions from AI agents when they concern familiar, routine, low-risk tasks that IT pros are confident the agents can handle. Over time, he said, networking pros will learn to trust agents with more complex work. ®

events.title: GOP House rejects Hegseth impeachment effort
events.summary: House Republicans voted Tuesday evening to block an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , shielding a top Trump administration official from a politically embarrassing rebuke. Why it matters: The vote marks a victory for Hegseth, the Trump administration and Republican leaders, who were bracing for the prospect of a rebellion within their own ranks. But the reprieve is probably short-lived: Democrats are all but guaranteed to force the issue again when they retake majorities in the House and Senate in January. The vote to refer the impeachment measure back to committee passed 211-204, with Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), the measure's sponsor, the lone GOP "no" vote. Driving the news: Massie forced a procedural vote on his resolution to impeach Hegseth, alleging he has defied Congress and illegally continued the U.S. war in Iran. The Trump administration has been vehemently defending Hegseth , including through a statement opposing the impeachment effort issued shortly before the vote. "Has Pete Hegseth committed impeachable crimes? The question is absurd and the answer is: obviously not," Vance said Tuesday on X . "Like so much of Congress , impeachment has become a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking. Congress has so many tools for registering its policy disagreements," Vance added. Axios' Marc Caputo and Alex Isenstadt previously reported that Hegseth is on " thin ice " with Trump officials. Between the lines : Republican leaders protected their members from having to go on record on the politically difficult issue before Election Day after Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) sent lawmakers home early to campaign. What's next: Tuesday's vote effectively kills any effort to impeach Hegseth this Congress.

events.title: VMware floats new standard to make sure apps don’t break in hybrid K8s environments
events.summary: Advocates for cloud-native software have long argued that their approach to development makes applications portable across different Kubernetes environments. But VMware argues that’s not happening across hybrid clouds, and has taken the lead in an effort to improve matters. That effort, the new Workload Conformance Working Group in the Kubernetes community, aims to establish a shared standard for how workloads run on Kubernetes. The group’s web page points out, “Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. Every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support,” the group asserts. The proposed solution? “A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from.” Prashanth Shenoy, VP of product marketing in Broadcom's VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) division, told The Register that standard is needed in part because applications packaged to run in public clouds don’t always run well in hybrid clouds. That’s challenging for VMware, and other vendors of hybrid clouds like Nutanix and Red Hat, because they all sell tools to create and run a stack that users can deploy to both on-prem infrastructure and public clouds. VMware therefore thinks it will find support for an effort to ensure that cloud-native apps run predictably and efficiently in any Kubernetes environment. The effort to create this standard is in its very early days. “The first step is deciding which workloads and behaviors the specification covers,” states the announcement of the working group’s formation. “The scope includes security, resilience during disruptions, resource use, networking, storage, API usage, and observability, but the group hasn’t yet agreed on specific requirements or on how to test them. “However, one rule is already set: every requirement needs an objective test that a test binary can run, so nothing subjective goes into the specification.” Shenoy thinks application vendors will likely support this effort because they want to package their wares once and have them run anywhere. VM API to CNCF Sandbox VMware this week announced another contribution to Kubernetes by moving its VM API to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox. The CNCF, which maintains Kubernetes, is already home to KubeVirt, a tool that allows users to create and manage VMs inside a Kubernetes cluster. The VM API lets Kubernetes users create VMs that run under other hypervisors – including VMware’s own ESXi. VMware previously integrated Kubernetes into vSphere with Kubernetes, introduced as part of vSphere 7 in 2020. Chronicling Virtzilla’s long and convoluted attempts to package and sell the container tech it acquired along with Pivotal Software would be a tedious exercise. Suffice to say past efforts didn’t catch on, and VMware is now trying a different approach to making VMs a first class citizen of Kubernetes. The CNCF’s interest shows this is not a vanity project for VMware, because while developers generally prefer to write for containers, operations folk often decide to run those abstractions within lightweight VMs. The two abstractions are therefore going to coexist for years to come, both for new apps and as organizations run new containerized apps alongside legacy VMs, and do so in an infrastructure-as-code world in which automated deployments are assumed. VM API will therefore likely be a welcome addition to Kubernetes, representing another option to make life a little easier for ops and dev teams. ®

events.title: Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has become the face of the US AI boom Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy. Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing. Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe . The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday. Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools. It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race. Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia. Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked. Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern. What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy Published 9 hours ago Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Published 2 days ago According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington earlier this year warning that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. Beijing has rejected claims that the Nvidia chief has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China". US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang, who had said he had "no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed him. However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing. The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC. The committee has the authority to subpoena Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before it, if deemed necessary. When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe. Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce. Joon Kim is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focusing on fraud and other criminal acts. The Nvidia investigation will likely be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the matter, as Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with the company. He has become a key public figure in the development on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity. It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang. A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI. events.title: He took down Andrew Cuomo. Now Jensen Huang is in his crosshairs
events.summary: The Scene Joon Kim has taken down mobsters, pursued a congressman, and investigated sexual harassment claims that toppled a New York governor. His latest assignment will decide the fate of a $4 trillion dollar company the global economy depends on. The former acting US Attorney for the Southern District of New York was tapped to investigate whether Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese espionage campaign, following Huang’s bombshell admission Sunday that the chief executive had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Kim, a 55-year-old prosecutor who joined Wachtell Lipton last month, will lead an internal probe overseen by a committee of independent directors, into whether Nvidia’s Huang compromised trade secrets — or, more pressingly, the US’ national security interests. The company has said it has confidence in its CEO and has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” A spokesperson for Wachtell declined to comment on the firm’s and Kim’s behalf. Shares in Nvidia have dropped 10% since Huang’s admission, knocking $500 billion off the company’s market value and stoking worries about the future of a company that underpins an AI financing buildout that has ensnared most of the global financial system. It comes against a fraught national security backdrop in which US officials have been warning for months of foreign influence campaigns and corporate espionage. A tangled web Huang, a close confidant of US President Donald Trump, has pushed Nvidia to take stakes in hundreds of companies across the AI boom it supplies. The company has also entered into billions of dollars worth of financing deals up and down Wall Street. Even Kim’s own employer, Wachtell Lipton, is not immune: OpenAI is one of Wachtell’s highest-profile clients, and the law firm’s M&A advisors are working on the company’s pending IPO, according to people familiar with the matter. Nvidia is a major OpenAI investor and the primary supplier of the chips that underpin the data centers (which Nvidia also finances) that power OpenAI’s models. Corporate probes can range from window dressing to essentially prosecutorial in nature, and Nvidia has 4 trillion reasons to limit its damage. It’s unclear how far Nvidia’s board will let Kim roam, but the board has already drummed up corporate governance concerns: The unusually long-tenured board lacks the experience and stature typically found at companies as large as Nvidia’s and has let Huang run the company with no clear successor and more than 50 direct reports. Mob bosses Kim began his career at New York’s Southern District more than two decades ago, working in the organized crime unit before leaving for Cleary Gottlieb in 2006. The son of a South Korean diplomat, Kim traveled around the world, including in Jordan and the UK. In his first stint as a federal prosecutor, Kim took on mob boss John “Junior” Gotti in a federal racketeering trial, trying him for the kidnapping of future New York mayoral candidate Curtis Sliwa. “His entire adult life, John Jr. has thought himself special, entitled to everything, accountable for nothing,” Kim said at the time. His former colleagues describe Kim as dogged, citing his time at the Southern District in 2013, under Attorney Preet Bharara, where Kim pursued a successful case against disgraced former Congressman Anthony Weiner and briefly ran the Southern District after Trump fired Bharara. Kim returned to Cleary in 2018, where he led a number of internal investigations into allegations of executive wrongdoing at large corporations, including Nissan Motors’ probe into former CEO Carlos Ghosn. But among his most defining cases was New York Attorney General Letitia James’ investigation into sexual harassment allegations against then-Governor Andrew Cuomo, which led to his 2021 resignation. Cuomo’s office was “rife with bullying, fear and intimidation,” Kim said when announcing his findings. A sensitive assignment Before Sunday, Huang and spokespeople for the company had publicly denied that the Nvidia CEO had an affair with Alice Huang. The company abruptly changed tack on Sunday, when Huang wrote a letter to employees admitting to the affair and announcing a plan to initiate an independent probe. The company had assembled an independent committee to oversee the investigation and was on Sunday leaning toward tapping former Cooley CEO Stephen Neal, the Financial Times reported and Semafor can confirm. Some Nvidia directors also suggested tapping Cooley to run the independent probe, other people familiar with the matter said. Cooley is Nvidia’s longtime outside counsel and would have exposed the company to criticism that the probe wasn’t independent, especially since Cooley is best known for its tech and IP practices, and isn’t considered by white-shoe lawyers to have a top-tier white-collar investigations practice. Nvidia declined to comment on either the nature of the independent committee or on whether directors considered tapping Cooley. Notable Neal has been involved in other high-profile misconduct cases , including representing disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes.

events.title: November Patch Tuesday boasts over 1,000 bugs, one already under attack
events.summary: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at exposure management firm watchTowr, succinctly said in an email to The Register : “Maybe we should just go home.” “Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and ‘2shell’-branded everything, and we’re yet again at another Patch Tuesday,” Knott told us. Starting with the zero-day: It’s an Outlook spoofing vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194 , and it only garnered a 6.5 out of 10 CVSS rating. But as Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative, warns, don’t let the score or the name lull you into thinking it’s OK to put off patching this one. “It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests,” Childs said in his monthly Patch Tuesday review . “An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it,” he wrote. “Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user.” Microsoft marked CVE-2026-124194 as exploited, but per usual didn’t say when the attacks started, who is battering this bug, and what they are doing with the access post exploitation. These details will likely start trickling out soon. Plus, now that there’s a public fix, other miscreants are undoubtedly already scanning for vulnerable versions and reverse engineering the patch for their own attack purposes. So prioritize this fix, and keep an eye on your inbox for any suspicious files. Back-to-back months of 1K+ CVEs Despite the second month of more than 1,000 CVEs (October had 1,474 ), CVE-2026-124194 is the only one under active exploitation, and none of the 1,094 are listed as publicly known. Childs says this shouldn’t give organizations “false comfort.” “Logging back-to-back months above 1,000 CVEs proves automated bug-hunting has permanently reset patch volume,” he told The Register . “With AI making patch-diffing and exploit generation near-instant, the threat window opens the minute these updates drop.” For defenders, this means two things, Childs added. “What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action: patch Exchange and Domain Controllers (LDAP/Kerberos) first to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on your cloud services,” he said. Zero-click threats There are two zero-click threats in this month’s batch of fixes: CVE-2026-116928 and CVE-2026-119958 . Both are critical, carrying 9.8 CVSS ratings, in part because they don’t require any user interaction to exploit. CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component that could lead to remote code execution. An unauthenticated attacker could abuse this search feature in Exchange “by sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment,” Redmond warned. “Exchange automatically processes the attachment for indexing, so the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to execute code with the permissions of the affected processing service.” CVE-2026-119958 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Windows' implementation of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely without user interaction. This one can be exploited by sending specially crafted LDAP requests to vulnerable systems, potentially compromising domain controllers. Childs also counts 30 CVEs that pose a “wormable risk,” requiring zero authentication and zero user interaction over a network. All of those are listed in his blog, so prioritize fixing those as well. And…Xbox remote code execution And finally, for funsies, a critical flaw in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service, CVE-2026-112967 , that could allow remote code execution also made this month's roundup. It's a heap-overflow vulnerability with a 9.8 CVSS rating that doesn't require authentication or user interaction to exploit. So don't take a gaming break between testing November's updates. Or, if you do, at least make sure vulnerable Windows systems running the Xbox Live Networking Service are on your patching list, too. ®
